News.title: Brit tourist, 33, ‘groped by cyclist’ while on a run on Bondi Beach – as ‘attacker’ charged
News.content:
Next

A BRITISH tourist was allegedly ambushed in the dark and groped by a cyclist on Bondi Beach.

Jenna Dollard, 33, was allegedly grabbed from behind by the man on a red bike during her morning run along the famous beach in Sydney, Australia.

4 Credit: 9NEWS



The suspected attacker was arrested the following day and charged with sexually touching another person without consent.

Jenna was wearing headphones in the early morning darkness on Thursday, leaving her unable to hear the suspect approach prior to the alleged assault.



She said: “Suddenly, I felt him grab me from behind. He grabbed my bum.”

Although stunned, Jenna managed to film the cyclist as he sped down Bondi Road to hand over to the police.



She said: “I need to have evidence of this guy for the police.”

In the clip, the alleged offender can be seen turning and lashing out at Jenna, fiercely denying the claims.



He shouted: “I did f***ing nothing to you, you dog.”

The Brit said the alleged incident left her frightened and concerned about women’s safety.

She said: “It just really scared me.

“It’s a violation, and you feel so scared at that moment because not only is it your personal space, but it’s a violation.”

Now instead of running outdoors, she said she will continue her morning workouts inside at a Bondi gym.



After Jenna shared the footage to social media, cops arrested the suspected attacker on Friday.

The 51-year-old man was taken to Newtown Police Station where he was charged with sexually touching another person without consent.

He was refused bail and is set to appear in court on Saturday.

It comes after another alleged attack on a tourist after a woman was allegedly raped in the toilets of a Majorcan nightclub.

The man allegedly filmed the attack and posted the footage online.



She was left bleeding from her knees as she desperately tried to escape her attacker at the nightspot in Playa de Palma, earlier this month.

A German man, whose age has not been revealed, was arrested on suspicion of rape following the horrifying ordeal.

In another horrific instance, a Brit tourist said she was sexually assaulted in the air by a parasail operator.

Michelle Wilson, 52, says the man pressed himself against her and groped her during the thrill ride last summer.

She said: “I felt violated and dirty and was scared.”

News.title: Cash-strapped Putin forced to scrap his largest nuke-powered warship ‘Peter the Great’ over £1.5 billion repair bill
News.content:
GREAT COST Cash-strapped Putin forced to scrap his largest nuke-powered warship ‘Peter the Great’ over £1.5 billion repair bill







Next

CASH-strapped Vlad has been forced to scrap his largest nuke-powered warship after he could not foot the £1.5billion bill.

Putin has previously boasted that his guided missile cruiser Peter the Great has “virtually no equal in the world”.



The £750 million battleship – which has bolstered Russia’s fleet for 28 years – is now destined for the scrapheap.

Vladimir Maltsev, head of the a Russian naval advocacy group, said bluntly: “The cruiser is beyond repair. The ship has a certain degree of wear.”



Peter the Great’s sister ship Admiral Nakhimov, from the same Kirov class, has cost an astonishing £1.5billion to repair and is now eight years late.

It finally took to the sea last year for the first time after a 28-year absence.



The Admiral Nakhimov is still undergoing its sea test runs and is not yet on patrol with the Russian Navy.

Peter the Great is currently the largest “operational” attack warship in the world that is not an aircraft carrier, yet the vessel has not been on active duty for some time.

The ship’s main power plant is equipped with two fast-neutron nuclear reactors and two main turbo units with 70,000-horsepower each.

Its maximum speed is 31 knots, or around 35mph.



Putin declared in 2013 that his prized naval asset had “”no equal”.

“The cruiser has repeatedly distinguished itself in long sea voyages,” he told its crew.

“It was on active duty, displaying the Russian flag in key strategic areas of the world’s oceans.



“The crew performed the assigned tasks perfectly, showing impeccable professionalism, skill and courage.”

It comes during a humiliating week for the dictator, who was recently mocked for his stature at a Moscow summit hosting African leaders.

A viral snap showed Putin being dwarfed by Mozambique’s towering 6ft 8in president Daniel Chapo.

Putin is known to be sensitive about his diminutive stature of just under 5ft 7in and he routinely wears high platform shoes to boost his height.

The picture, which was notably absent from any Kremlin press releases, spawned several memes.



One depicted Chapo as Lord of the Rings wizard Gandalf while the diminutive Kremlin leader was a barefoot hobbit.

Hours later, Putin declared that he is “ready for war” with Europe.

Speaking at the Russia-Africa summit, the tyrant said: “We are ready for war with Europe, but we don’t want it.

“As for them – if anyone desires such a thing, let them prepare.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Putin went on to claim that the West had “failed to achieve their goal of inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia.”



“It is highly unlikely that this will be possible by 2030,” he boasted, before warning: “If things go too far, there will be no winners at all.”

News.title: Man, 26, arrested after 38-year-old ‘murdered in armed gang attack’ outside house as tributes paid to ‘adored’ son
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BRUTAL ATTACK Man, 26, arrested after 38-year-old ‘murdered in armed gang attack’ outside house as tributes paid to ‘adored’ son







Next

A 26-YEAR-OLD man has been arrested after a 38-year-old man was killed in an alleged armed gang attack as his family pay tribute.

Police were alerted to reports of a man being assaulted with weapons outside a home in Leeds, West Yorkshire, on October 24.



Paramedics arrived at the scene but despite treatment Rahiem Jackson was sadly pronounced dead a short time later.

In a tribute, Mr Jackson’s family said: “Rahiem was loved and adored by his sisters and family.



“He had a beautiful heart and beautiful soul; his smile was so infectious, and he lit up the room with his presence.”

The family said Mr Jackson was killed in “a very cowardly, cruel and senseless act of vicious violence”, adding they were “heartbroken” and “left inconsolable.”

Police say Rahiem was attacked by four people during the horror incident.

The Met Police has since arrested a 26-year-old in London on suspicion of murder in connection with the incident.

He remained in police custody on Friday following his arrest.

A probe into the fatal attack remains ongoing with homicide detectives leading the investigation.



Detective Chief Inspector Dan Bates, of the unit, said: “This arrest is a significant development in the murder investigation of Rahiem Jackson.

“Officers are continuing to support the family.

“Extensive inquiries remain ongoing and we continue to appeal for information around the attack.

“We continue to ask anyone who may have seen people arrive or leave the scene on Hedley Chase on Saturday night to come forward.”

News.title: One dead and 6 injured in horror shooting inside Halloween store at shopping centre – as manhunt launched for gunman
News.content:
Next

AT least one person has been killed after a gunman opened fire at a store packed with Halloween shoppers – sparking a SWAT team manhunt.

Shots rang out inside the Spirit Halloween store as people bought last-minute costumes at the Solano Town Center mall in Fairfield, California.



One person was pronounced dead at the scene, while six more were rushed to hospital, where three are fighting for their lives.

A fleet of squad cars was seen outside the store, which was cordoned off for investigation.



Police did not share a description of the suspected shooter, nor did they confirm if there was more than one suspect.

A motive behind the shooting was not revealed.



“This is still a very active crime scene,” police said in a statement.

“Detectives are speaking with witnesses and diligently working to identify the suspect responsible for this horrific shooting.”

The ages and identities of the victims were not immediately released.

The pop-up store was filled with customers when the shooting began, prompting terrified shoppers to flee for their lives.



One witness said his wife described a scene of horror.

He told KCRA: “She just told me she heard some shots and the people running, yelling and crying already.”

The man said his wife heard seven shots ring out before people fled to the car park for safety.

The temporary shop had taken over a space once occupied by Best Buy at the mall, which holds around 130 stores.

One person told the Vacaville Reporter: “I was in Chipotle [when] a girl working in Spirit ran in and said they came in and just started shooting.”



SWAT teams swept through the mall to see if any shooters were hiding inside.

One was conducted in a cinema where about a dozen people had been watching the horror film Halloween.

One witness, Caitlin Fry, told CBS Sacramento: “Towards the end of the film a police officer in full SWAT gear came storming in with a very large Maglite and asked us if anyone came in that had a gun.”

Moviegoers said the scary scene inside the theatre evoked images from the Aurora cinema shooting that left 12 dead.

Caitlin’s partner Marty McCoy said: “I was afraid after (the SWAT officer) came in, I thought about Dark Knight in Colorado – the shooting that happened there years ago.



“I told her I don’t know what’s going to happen when we walk out of here, just remember ‘run, hide, fight’ and I love you just in case.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The FBI was among multiple agencies sent to the mall to help in the investigation.

“FBI Sacramento is aware of the shooting incident in Fairfield, California, and we are deploying our Evidence Response Team to assist the Fairfield Police Department,” the office said.

News.title: Riot cops deployed as protests erupt outside Poland’s court amid ‘coup’ over sacked judge & President returns mid-flight
News.content:
Next

RIOT police were deployed to stave off baying crowds after one of Poland’s top judges was sacked in what the court called a “coup”.

The chaos prompted Poland‘s President Karol Nawrocki to turn his plane around while en route to Senegal.



“At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland,” Nawrocki said on X hours before he was snapped arriving at Warsaw Constitutional Court.

Three protesters were arrested after breaching the tribunal’s fence, while others threw objects at officers.



Shocking pictures showed sparks fly as people tried to break through a fortified line of cops with their shields forming a wall.

Furious protesters waving Polish flags could be heard chanting slogan’s against Prime Minister Donald Tusk‘s pro-European government.

The riots erupted after the court’s longest-serving judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska suspended Bogdan ​Swieczkowski, an appointee of Tusk’s far-right predecessor.

Poland’s top judicial bodies, including the Constitutional Tribunal, have been a major bone of contention between the current government and the main opposition party, national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS).



Critics accuse PiS, which led the country between 2015 and 2023, of imposing political control over key courts.

The PiS reforms even led the EU to impose fines on Poland.

Tusk came to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the independence of the judiciary.



Since then, the governments efforts have been blocked by veto by two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including President Nawrocki.

Tusk said on X: “Restoring the rule of law is our obligation.

“After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”

Right-wing politicians addressed the protesters under heavy police presence, accusing Tusk’s government of staging a coup against the court.

“This is a blatant, criminal attack on the constitutional order,” former Justice Minister Zbigniew Ziobro wrote on X.



“That is why I call for resistance that will be loud, firm, solidary and fearless.”

Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court’s worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis “for a million reasons”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He wrote: “Today’s action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades.

“Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come.”

News.title: ‘I got BOOB JOB with my benefits but it’s still not enough!’ Brits living on taxpayers’ cash share their Budget verdict
News.content:
Next

BRITAIN’S notorious Welfare Queen has admitted it’s FINALLY time she gets a job after spending most of the last 25 years living on taxpayer-funded handouts.

Mum-of-eight Marie Buchan, 44, who previously made headlines for buying a horse and splashing out on a boob job and a designer vagina while claiming benefits, says she can no longer rely on welfare payments to raise her family.



Speaking after this week’s Budget, which did nothing to tackle Britain’s ballooning £400billion welfare bill, the controversial benefits celebrity admitted: “Not everyone can claim Universal Credit for the rest of their lives.”

“It’s got out of control now. The country can’t cope.”



The single mum, from Selly Oak, West Midlands, says she receives £1,200 a month in Universal Credit and Child Benefit, but says the money is no longer enough.

And despite years of defending her lavish lifestyle, which saw her buy a horse and undergo breast enhancement surgery using her benefits, she now admits that returning to work may be her only option.

Asked whether she would consider getting a full-time job, she told The Sun: “It is going to have to come to that now.”

“I’m 44 now, my life has been raising the children and living on benefits.”

Marie, who has been on and off benefits for 25 years, claims she has qualifications as a car mechanic and has previously worked as a carer during Covid.

But despite spending five years at college gaining qualifications, she admits she hasn’t put her training to lasting use.



She said: “If a job landed on my lap tomorrow I’d take it, but it would have to work around my family.”



The Welfare Queen insisted she would be prepared to return to work for the new minimum wage of £13.20, provided she could find a job that fitted around her family.

But she admitted that previous attempts to return to employment had ended badly, including suffering a nervous breakdown while working as a carer during the pandemic in 2021.

She said: “I was trying to prove a point to people. No one could see I was having a mental crisis.”

Her change of heart comes after the Chancellor’s Budget this week, which saw millions of families promised an additional £100 to help afford their energy bills this winter.

But Marie, who still has seven children living at her four-bedroom property, says the latest Government handouts will barely scratch the surface.



She said: “£100 sounds like a lot, but it won’t go far, not if you’re raising a big family.”

Despite receiving £1,200 a month in benefits, she claims she is struggling to pay her bills and has been forced to rely on food banks.

She said: “It’s not a lot, not with the rise in food prices and energy bills. I’ve had bailiffs at my door because I didn’t pay a £2,000 water bill.”



She joked, “The most lavish thing I bought this year was a new tyre for my car… And I fitted it myself!”

But while Britain’s Welfare Queen admits she may finally have to swap welfare payments for wages, other claimants across the country insist the Government still isn’t doing enough to help them.

Locals living on taxpayer handouts on Britain’s notorious Benefits Street told The Sun: ‘We’ve got cheaper baked beans, but we still need more cash’.

This week the Government also revealed a cut in tariffs on 100 supermarket products such as baked beans and gherkins, which it says could save Brits £21 over the year.

But its taxpayers who will be forced to cough up the billions needed to bankroll the Government’s pledges, with income tax thresholds frozen again, meaning millions will pay more tax as their wages rise.



Lesley Mead, 45, says she also relies on a food bank each week to feed her family.

The mum-of-four moved to Jaywick, near Clacton-on-sea, to live with her auntie, over the summer holidays but claims she is unable to work due to arthritis in her spine.

The former Brentwood resident says she receives Universal Credit and is waiting for a decision on her Personal Independence Payment (PIP) claim.



Lesley welcomed the Government’s announcements but questioned whether they would make any meaningful difference to families already struggling with soaring household bills.

“We do like our baked beans, so we welcome the £21 off our food shop!” she joked.

But she added: “The cost of living is going up with the energy prices. We’ve got cheaper baked beans but how are we going to afford the fresh fruit and vegetables, especially when our electric is going to go up that high?”

When she was told the energy price cap is forecast to go up £469 in January, she responded: “What’s the £100 for, to keep us quiet? That’s disgusting, really!”

​Jaywick Sands has been named the most deprived area in England four times since 2010, with 75% of residents living in “income deprivation”, which means they are either out of work or require benefits to top up their income to get by.



As a result, the town has featured in a number of TV documentaries which have painted the 1930s holiday resort in a grim light, with boarded-up properties, rundown streets and fly-tipped driveways and gardens.

But behind the media reports is a tight-knit community where residents say the Chancellor’s Budget still doesn’t go far enough to help fund their lives or make working worth it.

As part of a raft of measures announced this week, the Government said it would scrap the standing charges on gas bills, which it estimates will save 60% of households an average of £45.



But Jaywick resident, Carol, who asked not to give her surname, dismissed the announcement as “not enough because the amount it will go up in January will far outweigh that amount. We’ll still be worse off.”

The grandmother-of-one claims PIP but says it is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis, and has cut down on her food shops and “stopped buying any luxuries”.

She added that the cost of heating their 3-bedroom house is their biggest problem, as her housebound 78-year-old husband needs the heating on all day.

Her concerns were echoed by Dawn Butler, 49, who was visiting Jaywick with her children for the half term holiday.

The community support worker from Southend, who claims Universal Credit to top up her minimum wage job, said the cut on VAT would do little to ease her financial struggles.



She told The Sun: “Once you put your gas on over the winter, you could easily do £20 to £50 a week”.

“I’m a single mum with three kids, it doesn’t really help.”

Down in South London, Angela Lewis, 40, who claims to suffer from anxiety and depression, welcomed this week’s Budget as “truly amazing”.



She last worked in 2002 and receives £1,460 a month in benefits, which will increase by 3.5 per cent.

The South Londoner will also get an extra £150 from the Warm Home Discount Scheme, plus the Government’s £100 cash payout to help with energy bills.

She told The Sun the additional support will help her “put extra food on the table that I can’t afford at the moment”.

She added that with the Labour Government’s latest handouts she “might be able to get away on a holiday”.

But 180 miles away in Ebbw Vale, south Wales, the reaction from some benefit claimants was very different.



The area is home to the highest number of people who claim the state’s disability benefit, PIP (Personal Independence Payment), due to mental health issues.

One in 30 people claim PIP for anxiety or depression and receive a standard rate of £76.70 per week or the enhanced rate at £114.60.

Jessica George, 28, told The Sun: “I used to be a carer but now I’m on PIP for anxiety and it’s barely enough to pay my rent and food.”

She added: “It’s very difficult, the Budget should have given us more.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Meanwhile, Dylan, who asked not to give his surname, said: “I’ve lived off benefits the last five years and it’s a struggle, especially with no jobs around.”



The 31-year-old added: “The Government hasn’t a clue on the things we miss out on, like taking the kids out, not being able to afford a decent Christmas. The Budget just ignored people like me.”

News.title: CCTV released as cops launch manhunt after year-long ‘frightening’ sexual assault spree in city centre
News.content:
Next

A MANHUNT has been launched following a year-long spree of alleged sexual assaults in a busy city centre as cops release CCTV.

Police say the attacks occurred in the Arboretum area of Nottingham between 2025 and 2026.



Two victims have reported being attacked by the man while two members of the public have also made reports.

Detectives say investigations have revealed a further five potential assaults.



Nottinghamshire Police has since released video of a man investigators want to speak to in connection with the alleged incidents.

The force is asking anyone who may recognise the man pictured to get in touch.

Detective Chief Inspector Ruby Burrow, who is leading the investigation, said:”These were frightening attacks on women and whilst we are keeping an open mind, we currently believe the same man is responsible.

“We have carried out extensive lines of inquiry including comprehensive CCTV trawls to locate the individual and house-to-house inquiries.

“We have also had plain-clothed patrols in the area at key times so that we can catch him when he least expects it.

“Thankfully no other incidents have been reported to us since September. However, our determination remains the same as the first day we received these reports and we won’t stop until the person responsible is in our custody.



“We are now appealing for the public’s help. We have released CCTV video of a man that could help us with our investigation. The footage is very clear.

“We would urge the public to please view this footage. Do you know the man in the footage? Are you the man in the footage? Please get in touch with us as soon as possible.

“We know incidents like this can be alarming to the public, but rest assured we are doing everything we can to ensure the person responsible is caught.”

News.title: Fireworks ahead as Andy Burnham’s smooth start threatens to go off with a bang
News.content:
POLITICS UNWRAPPED Fireworks ahead as Andy Burnham’s smooth start threatens to go off with a bang







Next



REMEMBER, remember the fifth of November.

For Andy Burnham, however, it could be a whole month he’d rather forget.



The Prime Minister has enjoyed a relatively smooth first 100 days in No10, with Labour bouncing back in the polls and his promise of a fresh start striking a chord with voters.

And his first Budget this week did little to upset the apple cart.



Chancellor John Healey handed 20 million households £100 towards their energy bills, extended the cut to electricity VAT and froze fuel duty to give struggling Brits some much-needed “breathing space”.

A YouGov poll found 45 per cent thought the Budget was fair, compared with just 20 per cent who disagreed.



But a thumbs-up for fairness is hardly a ringing endorsement of its impact.

More than half reckon it will make no real difference to their family’s finances, while nearly three-quarters still believe the economy is in a bad state.

And despite offering some welcome relief, the Chancellor left many of the toughest decisions for another day.

Even Burnham admitted the Budget was not quite the radical offering he had hoped for, conceding there was less “room for manoeuvre” than expected.



Instead, he is pinning his hopes on an ambitious 10-year plan to transform Britain, promising it will be the real “radical moment” of his premiership.

But November will provide a rather more immediate test of his leadership.

For as Bonfire Night approaches, a growing pile of political fireworks is waiting to go off.

Immigration, welfare, Brexit and policing are all heading towards crunch moments in the coming weeks.

And if that wasn’t enough, Burnham has a diplomatic marathon ahead, with four international summits taking him from the Caribbean to Turkey, Dublin and Brussels.



It is a daunting diary for a Prime Minister still settling into the job.

First comes immigration.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to unveil the Government’s long-awaited response to plans to make some migrants wait 15 years for permanent residency, potentially as early as next week.

The proposals have triggered a furious backlash among Labour MPs, particularly over plans to apply the changes retrospectively to people already living in Britain.

And behind the scenes, the whips have been working overtime to establish just how much trouble the Government could be in.



In Commons tea rooms, corridors and during votes, MPs have been quietly sounded out about the proposals.

One Labour MP says: “They’ve been doing the proper job of whips in estimating what size rebellion there would be if measures weren’t changed.”

Opposition is believed to stretch well beyond the 100 MPs who signed a protest letter, with others unable or unwilling to put their names to public complaints.

And there are growing expectations the final package will look rather different from what Ms Mahmood originally proposed.

One Government source said: “The PM is tougher on migration that many people think, but on ILR there is a clear direction of travel.



“There has been so much pitch-rolling for a softening that it will now be more surprising if we actually stick with the current proposals.”

Tensions have even reached the Cabinet, with one recent meeting described as “really testy”.

It leaves Burnham with an awkward choice between backing his Home Secretary and risking a rebellion, or softening her plans and facing accusations of going weak on immigration.

And it is not the only battle Ms Mahmood could find herself fighting.

Her ambitious plans to merge Britain’s 43 police forces into larger regional organisations have also hit a stumbling block.



The overhaul has run into difficulties over how it fits with Burnham’s determination to hand more power to local leaders.

Former Met Police chief Lord Hogan-Howe submitted his review of police force structures in September but ministers have yet to reveal their response.

Insiders insist Ms Mahmood has not been undermined and that the PM simply wanted to take a closer look at the proposals.

Nevertheless, the issue is expected to return to the agenda towards the end of November.

And with two of her biggest reforms facing potential changes, it could prove a testing month for the Home Secretary too.



And all this while Burnham juggles a whirlwind of international engagements.

First stop is Antigua for the Commonwealth summit, where he is expected to join King Charles and leaders from 56 nations.

Then it’s off to Turkey for the COP31 climate conference, followed by a gathering of around 50 European leaders in Dublin.

But while the PM racks up the air miles, the political headaches back home will not be going anywhere.

And November has plenty more in store, with two potentially explosive reviews into Britain’s ballooning benefits bill finally due to land.



Former Cabinet minister Alan Milburn is preparing to deliver his recommendations on tackling the crisis of almost one million young people not in education, employment or training.

Meanwhile, Sir Stephen Timms is due to publish his review into Personal Independence Payment, the disability benefit at the centre of Labour’s damaging rebellion last year.

And some Labour MPs fear another showdown could be brewing.

One backbencher warned: “I think it’s going to be a lot meatier than people realise.”

The review is examining how payments could better reflect the additional costs people face because of their disabilities, rather than relying solely on the current assessment system.



While no final recommendations have been made, the MP fears some claimants could lose out.

“For many people, there’s no ongoing weekly cost, so you can imagine what that means for potential benefit losses,” they warned.

After previous welfare reforms ended in humiliating retreat, it is another potential headache for Burnham.

Then comes Brussels and the bigger question of where he wants to take Britain.

On November 20, Burnham will meet EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa for a crunch summit.



He hopes to secure deals on food exports, energy and youth mobility that could boost the economy by more than £10billion a year by 2040.

But having reopened the possibility of Britain eventually rejoining the EU, he has also revived one of the most divisive arguments in British politics.

And not everyone in his Cabinet appears to share his enthusiasm.

Asked this week whether he wanted Britain back in the EU in his lifetime, Mr Healey quipped: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”

Was that a prediction or a polite way of saying “over my dead body”?



The summit will also help shape Burnham’s longer-term vision for Britain.

His much-anticipated 10-year plan, due around the summit, is expected to set out how he intends to revive manufacturing, strengthen public control of essential services and transform the economy.

The PM believes the country needs a fundamental change of direction, rather than another collection of short-term fixes.

And his allies argue that giving difficult questions room for proper debate is better than rushing into decisions that unravel before an election.

But not everyone in Government is enjoying all the talking.



There are growing grumblings about the PM’s seemingly endless “open conversations” – with some insiders complaining it puts them in a difficult position.

And sooner or later, those conversations will have to end with decisions that won’t please everyone.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

More than 400 years after Guy Fawkes tried to blow up Parliament, Burnham will be hoping November doesn’t blow up in his face.

News.title: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but not reparations
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is "open" to the possibility of the UK issuing a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out considering financial reparations.

Burham said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected by the slave trade" and was open to "calls for an apology".

He dismissed the idea of paying financial reparations, saying they were "not the right answer".

The comments come ahead of a Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean next week, which Burnham will attend. Caribbean nations have renewed calls for the UK to apologise for its role in the slave trade, and for reparations, as King Charles III tours the region.

Burham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".

The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.

"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in his piece for the Guardian, external.

He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation". Burnham said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue" adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."

A government source told the BBC this was "morally the right thing to do".

Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.

Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.

News.title: Mahmood expected to announce changes to rules around indefinite leave to remain
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce her final decision on immigration rules for legal migrants next week.

She had proposed to extend the wait for permanent settlement from the current five years to 10 with some lower-paid migrants facing a 15-year wait. The BBC understands the proposals are likely to be revised for most of those currently working in social care.

The home secretary was concerned about the number of people who would be eligible for permanent residency after a period of very high net migration under the previous government.

Mahmood has faced opposition from within the government for proposing to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.

Before she rejoined the cabinet, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner described the proposals as "un-British" because they sought to change the rules for people who had come to the UK in good faith.

In particular, many lower-paid social care workers were facing a wait of up to 15 years rather than five.

But the BBC understands that social care workers already in the UK are now likely to be exempt from the longer wait.

But as originally proposed, it is likely most other workers will have to live and work in the UK for 10 years before being eligible for permanent settlement. That can be reduced if they contribute to their local communities or have higher incomes.

The government's consultation on the proposed reforms has drawn 200,000 responses.

The Home Office will not comment on Mahmood's final decisions until they are presented to Parliament in the coming week.

In September, a Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain."

"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

News.title: He left 28 years ago, now after 36,000 miles Karl Bushby is almost home
News.content:
With his journey almost complete, Karl Bushby reflects on adventures that have taken him across four continents, as well as strained relationships and how life as he knows it is about to change dramatically.

Back in 1998, the former paratrooper, then aged 29, set off from Punta Arenas, Chile, to walk an unbroken path to his home city of Hull, without breaking two self-imposed rules: not to return to the UK until he had completed his journey, and not to use transport to advance.

Now 57, he is embarking on his final few miles having hacked his way through the jungles of the DariÃ©n Gap, crossed the frozen Bering Strait and, just a few weeks ago, swum the English Channel.

At the end, he will be met by his 36-year-old son Adam, a 12-year-old granddaughter whom he has never met, his father and brothers. His mother will be waiting at his childhood home that he left 28 years ago.

News.title: Responsible or panicked? Meet the people around the world already preparing for crisis
News.content:
Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (Â£4,470), storing it on shelves in his basement.

"It's part of my responsibility as a parent," says Dan, 38, who has two children under 10.

A few years ago his house was cut off during a "very cold" February and the family was without power for two days. Though he'd already started keeping supplies, "there were numerous gaps in what I had prepared for," he says.

Dan's stash now includes 150 gallons of water and several large water storage containers made of soft plastic, which can be filled and kept in the bath. He also keeps things like chlorine dioxide tablets, which are often used to make water from streams or rivers safe to drink.

His "rotating pantry" - consisting of long-life food supplies like oats, quinoa and peanut butter - is regularly used for cooking then replaced so "it's not just sitting there expiring". For his family-of-four, he has about three months of food supplies.

Dan also has solar panels, a camping stove, a tent, wood supplies and a propane fireplace insert that can run off grid - without electricity or wood. He also keeps extensive medical supplies - including bleeding control kits.

In the US, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, external advises people to assemble an emergency kit, make a family emergency plan, and be informed about how to respond to different incidents.

Dan says when it comes to emergency planning, "there can be a tendency to catastrophise," but for him, it's about being a "responsible homeowner".

News.title: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
News.content:
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.

The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.

One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.

This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.

On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lÃ¨se majestÃ© law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.

This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.

"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."

News.title: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes
News.content:
As Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are not just competing on policy.

In our social media age, they're using their personal style to attract attention and project their message. Their clothing has become a measure of their authenticity and appeal.

"Politicians are dressing for two jobs at once: to look capable of holding office but to also look connected to the people they want to represent," said Joe Zee, a celebrity fashion stylist.

From Alaska to Texas, here is a look at how some candidates have been standing out on the campaign trail.

News.title: UK could see 10 days without rain after 'wettest week in two years'
News.content:
The UK could see as many as 10 consecutive days without rain after an unsettled end to October that featured back-to-back storms.

It comes after the Environment Agency said England experienced its wettest week in two years thanks to Storms Austen and Boelo.

Following this recent unsettled weather, the return of high pressure will bring a prolonged spell of largely dry and calm conditions, with very little rain in sight.

Mist and fog will remain a persistent feature, with some slow-clearing dense patches expected during the mornings.

News.title: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
News.content:
Police Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle.

The Daily Express reported, external that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.

Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking, are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.

Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.

News.title: Driver guilty of dragging head teacher to his death
News.content:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A man has been found guilty of murdering a head teacher who was dragged to his death for more than a mile while trapped under the wheels of a car.

Simon Richardson crashed into 56-year-old Michael Mullins, who was cycling home from his job at Stretford Grammar School on the evening of 20 April in the village of Warburton in Trafford, Greater Manchester.

Prosecutors claimed Richardson, 35, fled the scene of the crash before stopping to try to dislodge the injured but still-living cyclist and then driving on with Mr Mullins still lodged underneath the vehicle.

Richardson was also convicted of dangerous driving and will return to Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court to be sentenced on Monday.

There were shouts of "Yes!" from the court's public gallery as the guilty murder verdict was announced.

Others could also be heard crying.

The judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, told Richardson that there was only one sentence for murder, namely life imprisonment.

News.title: Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86
News.content:
Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".

Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."

Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft".

"Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.

Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.

The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."

The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.

Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".

Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".

"He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

News.title: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
News.content:
Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.

In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".

Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings".

Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.

Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.

She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".

None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."

Referring to Brand's accusers' evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality changeâ¦

"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.

She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushingâ¦ thrusting".

"In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."

The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened.

"There is no magic force in this documentary", she added.

"What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."

She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."

She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit.

"The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."

News.title: Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father
News.content:
The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had decided an investigation was required into the force's "failure to pass on allegations of serious offending... to relevant overseas authorities at the time".

The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.

He has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".

On Thursday the Met said it had voluntarily referred itself to the IOPC.

The letter at the heart of the IOPC investigation was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.

The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".

Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".

The IOPC will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas.

The policing watchdog also said it had decided a further matter, relating to an alleged data breach in which information was passed on to a third party, "should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with". No details were provided about the circumstances of the alleged breach.

The Met said on Thursday that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".

The letter was forwarded by officers to the Sussexes' royal office rather than to Meghan personally, while there have been reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to ask for one from the Sussexes.

The watchdog will have to consider how the contents of the letter were treated by the force at the time.

Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, previously told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".

"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken [and] why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies."

Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.

Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Police there have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.

However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they can examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

News.title: Stabbed boy felt Huntingdon train attacker 'was not sane', court hears
News.content:
A 14-year-old boy stabbed by a man who went on to attack people on a train said he did not feel the knifeman was "mentally sane", a court heard.

The teenager was attacked in Peterborough the day before Anthony Williams is accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train that had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon in November 2025.

In a video recorded interview played to jurors at Cambridge Crown Court, the boy said: "This random guyâ¦ he just pulled out a knife and stabbed me."

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder - four of which concern attacks prior to the mass train stabbing.

At the time of the attack, the boy, who cannot be named because of his age, was waiting with a friend on a footbridge over the River Nene, before going trick or treating.

Williams drew a knife from his waistband, he said, and "because I was closest to him, he's just stabbed me".

"I didn't feel like he was mentally sane. His eyes were wide open, like he was on something," he said.

"My friend said he was shouting something like 'are you involved?'."

"When he stabbed me, it's like he was there for a knife fight. Like he was waiting for me to pull out something."

The teenager said he had "so much adrenaline" that it felt "like a poke in the chest".

The jury heard the pair ran away and hid in some bushes, where they called the police.

News.title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
News.content:
Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.

"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.

He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".

In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.

Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.

The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".

Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.

He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.

The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.

News.title: Calls to end Antarctica krill fishing as governments from across the world debate upping quota
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Leading oceanographer Sylvia Earle is calling for an end to Antarctic krill fishing, as officials from the US, China, Russia and 24 other nations negotiate a deal this week to expand catches of the crustacean, a vital food source for whales surrounding the ice-covered continent.

"There is no sustainable extraction of krill in Antarctica possible, period," Earle, who in 1990 became the first woman to serve as chief scientist of the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, said in Rome while promoting her conservation work. "Krill are critical to the integrity of the entire system — whales, fish, birds, seals, sea lions, you name it."

Her comments come as delegates finish the annual summit in Australia of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, or CCAMLR, which manages the southernmost fishery. The body remains deadlocked over an industry plan to expand fishing. Environmentalists and CCAMLR's scientific committee insist any expansion require a long-delayed, California-sized marine protected area near the fragile Antarctic peninsula to restrict fishing, a measure first submitted a decade ago by Argentina and Chile.

Antarctic krill fishing was halted early in August for a second consecutive year after trawlers, mostly from Norway and China, reached a 620,000 metric tonne limit before the season ended.

open image in gallery View of Gentoo penguins (Pygoscelis Papua) and seals at the Yankee Harbour in the South Shetland Islands, Antarctica, on March 06, 2016 ( AFP/Getty )

The tiny crustaceans are primarily harvested for feed used to raise farmed fish and for the oil in red omega-3 capsules taken to improve heart, brain and joint health. But other sources of omega-3 exist — in fish oil, algae, even some vegetables — and nutritionists say it's not necessary to take dietary supplements if you eat a balanced diet rich in the fatty acids.

Researchers increasingly are also studying the role krill plays in removing huge amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Krill aren’t just a bulwark against climate change — they’re victims, too. As oceans warm, the krill populations, which need water colder than 4 degrees Celsius (39 Fahrenheit) to survive, have started to migrate toward cooler waters closer to the South Pole, research has shown.

open image in gallery American marine biologist, oceanographer and Mission Blue founder Sylvia Earle speaks to The Associated Press ahead of a conference in Rome, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

Earle, 91, was among those who pioneered the use of Scuba diving to conduct marine research after launching her career in the 1950s studying algae. In recent years, “Her Deepness,” as she is sometimes known, has focused on conservation through Mission Blue, an organization that champions so-called “Hope Spots” in the oceans critical to marine health. Its work supports a United Nations target of protecting at least 30% of the world's oceans by 2030.

Although krill are one of the planet's largest biomasses, Earle, a vegetarian, said there was no “safe number” that can be extracted without harming the surrounding Antarctic ecosystem. She singled out for criticism Norway's Aker BioMarine, the pioneer in harvesting and marketing products made from krill. The company was founded by billionaire Kjell Inge Rokke, who amassed a fortune in Norway's oil and gas industry.

“There’s one country, Norway, with one company really pushed essentially by one individual, that is responsible for taking about two-thirds of the krill to marketplace,” said Earle. “Some of it goes to make krill oil that has been marketed as good for our health. Maybe it is, but at what cost to the environment?"

“It’s all for choices. These are not necessities,” she added.

open image in gallery American marine biologist, oceanographer and Mission Blue founder Sylvia Earle speaks to The Associated Press ahead of a conference in Rome, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia) ( AP )

Rokke remains the largest shareholder in the company, which recently delisted from the Oslo stock exchange, through his Aker ASA industrial conglomerate. In 2024, Aker BioMarine spun off its fishing and krill meal operation, selling a majority stake to American Industrial Partners, a New York-based private equity firm.

Rokke did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Aker QRILL's Chairman, Matts Johansen, is attending the CCAMLR talks in Australia. Johansen over the past few years has tried to bridge differences among negotiators, pushing a proposed plan that would both increase the overall fishing quota but spread out the catch to avoid excessive pressure on any single hot spot. The company also supports the creation of a marine protected area near the Antarctic peninsula.

“Decades of independent science from multiple countries, including the latest assessment of the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, support the sustainability of the Antarctic krill fishery,” Johansen, who is also CEO of Aker BioMarine, said in a statement. "We recognize the concerns around concentrated fishing activity, which is why we support stronger science-based spatial management. With El Niño putting pressure on global marine resources and omega-3 supplies, responsible fisheries like this matter more than ever."
