News.title: Protests in Poland as president returns to country after Tusk accused of coup against court
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Polish President Karol Nawrocki turned back from a flight to Senegal on Friday following the suspension of a far-right ally leading the country's highest court, escalating a feud with Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government over control of the judiciary.

Earlier on Friday, the Constitutional Tribunal announced that its longest-serving judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, had suspended tribunal president Bogdan Swieczkowski—an appointee of Tusk's far-right predecessor—and had taken charge of the court.

Hundreds of protesters assembled outside the tribunal late on Friday amid a heavy police presence, as right-wing politicians addressed the crowd and accused Tusk's government of launching a coup against the judiciary.

Writing on X, Nawrocki stated: "At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning."

open image in gallery Poland's former Prime Minister and leader of the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, Jaroslaw Kaczynski (C) speaks as protesters gather outside the headquarters of Poland's Constitutional Court in Warsaw after police blocked access to the building on October 30, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist ‌president refusing to recognise appointees put forward by the other ‌side.

Tusk, writing on X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors — the Law and Justice Party — of subverting.

"This process is difficult, at times ⁠even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way," he said.

The dispute dates back to 2015, when the nationalist Law and Justice sought to appoint judges to seats already filled by the previous government.

Its nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, while critics at home and abroad said the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.

After Tusk's coalition took office in 2023 ‌it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court, but ​Law and Justice ally Nawrocki has acted to thwart those efforts since his ‌election as president in 2025.

Earlier this year, ⁠Nawrocki refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, ⁠while Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, declined to seat judges elected by the ‌current parliamentary majority.

Last month, the ​parliament appointed Tusk ally Maciej Berek to ‌the tribunal, which critics said undermined the ​government's stated goal of restoring checks and balances.

News.title: Beijing queer film festival cancelled amid ‘intensifying scrutiny and harassment’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An annual queer film festival in Beijing has been cancelled following alleged harassment from state authorities amid shrinking space for LGBT+ community in China.

The Beijing Queer film festival in the Chinese capital was cancelled a day before it was scheduled to begin on Friday.

Police had mounted pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in the run-up to the opening of the festival, The Guardian reported.

The organisers of the festival on Thursday wrote on Instagram: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled."

"We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”

The festival founded in 2001 by students of Peking University students is one of the only film festival in mainland China catering to LGBT+ issues.

The incident comes at a time when the Chinese Communist Party under Xi Jinping's rule have been intensifying its crackdown on activists and depictions of LGBT+ people in the media in China and abroad.

File. Two people take a selfie as they attend the 10th anniversary of the Pink Dot LGBTIQA+ community event at West Kowloon Art Park in Hong Kong on 22 September 2024 ( AFP/Getty )

China decriminalised homosexuality in 1997, but does not recognise same-sex marriage.

Chinese authorities have actively taken measures to reduce queer visibility in media by censoring content featuring same-sex themes, sidelining advocacy groups, and removing dating apps.

At least dozens of writers of gay erotic fiction danmei or “boy love” have been interrogated, arrested and charged with producing and selling obscene materials in China.

"Beijing under Xi has been tightening social and ideological control, so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and official harassment," Human Rights Watch deputy Asia editor Maya Wang said.

In June, the French embassy in Beijing cancelled the screening of films celebrating Pride Month due to police harassment.

Advocacy group Beijing LGBT, which served as a safe space for the queer community in Beijing, shuttered its doors as the government intensified its clampdown in 2023.

News.title: Country superstar Miranda Lambert: ‘I had a great childhood, but I saw how ugly the world can be’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Miranda Lambert knows the value of good advice. She received some gems from the late, great Dolly Parton, to whom she was compared early on as “another blonde beauty who was once underestimated”. In fact, they met while recording a duet version of Parton’s “Dumb Blonde” for the soundtrack to the 2018 comedy-drama film Dumplin’, when the queen of country offered some wise words Lambert would never forget. “I walk in the studio and there are cameras and lights and everything, and Dolly grabs my shoulders, says ‘nice to meet you’ and gives me a hug,” she recalls. “Then she turns me around and says, ‘Always find your good light first.’” Lambert uses that advice literally, whenever she finds herself under a spotlight, but more importantly in the everyday: “If I’m in a mood or someone pisses me off.”

Lambert has been kicking down the doors of country music for a long time, with great success. The Texas-born superstar spent most of the 2010s as one of the few women flying the flag in a scene dominated by male acts like Tim McGraw, Kenny Chesney, Toby Keith and Brad Paisley. Now, she’s proven instrumental in the rise of country newcomers like singer Ella Langley– with whom she wrote the year’s biggest hit, “Choosin’ Texas”. Thanks to that song, particularly, more two decades into her career Lambert’s own music is being discovered by a whole new generation of fans. Next month, these achievements will be acknowledged at the Country Music Association Awards in Nashville, where she and Langley are the most-nominated artists of the year. Suffice to say, things are going pretty well.

“I think [the CMAs] are a very good indication of where we’re at right now,” Lambert says. “Country always ebbs and flows, we go through different phases, but I don’t feel like women have had a moment like this in a really long time – not since the Nineties.” Then, acts like Shania Twain, The Chicks, Reba McEntire and Faith Hill were among the biggest artists of the decade, but by the 2010s, it was a different story. “Bro country”, the much-criticised blend of country with hip-hop, hard rock and electronic beats, along with a borderline obsessive focus on booze, partying and “pretty young things”, was everywhere. Women had an uphill battle just to achieve recognition and, even then, were consistently pitted against one another. In 2015, Lambert was among the stars who pushed back strongly against the legendary "tomatogate" row, where a radio consultant compared male acts to the "lettuce" forming the bulk of a salad – arguing they should be prioritised on the radio – and female artists as the "tomato" garnish.

Lambert rose to fame in spite of those hurdles, a scrappy young singer with a spitfire attitude. In her video for breakout 2005 single “Kerosene”, she sports a tank top bearing the words, “Mama Tried”, asserting her rebellious, take-no-prisoners nature from the start. She continued in this vein with her second album, Crazy Ex-Girlfriend, and its lead single “Gunpowder and Lead”, a revenge fantasy told through the eyes of a domestic abuse survivor: “He slapped my face, and he shook me like a rag doll/ Don’t that sound like a real man?” she snarls. “I’m going to show him what little girls are made of/ Gunpowder and lead.”

open image in gallery Firestarter: Lambert performing at the 39th Annual Country Music Association Awards at Madison Square Garden in 2005 ( Getty )

When Lambert was growing up, her parents, now-retired private detectives Beverly and Richard, offered their farmhouse as a shelter to survivors and their children, meaning she saw the impact of domestic abuse up close. “It taught me a lot,” she says. “Me and my brother had a really good childhood, but we saw a lot of terrible things – how ugly the world can be.” She’s grateful her family could help support those women, and that she was able to share their stories in her songs: “I absorbed all of it,” she says. “I hadn’t lived enough to speak about myself yet, and I knew these stories needed to be told… those women deserved that.”

We’re speaking over video call, but Lambert’s screen is black. Although I can’t see her, I’m transported to her Tennessee home by the sound of crunching gravel as she walks around the sprawling 400-acre farm she shares with her husband, retired NYPD officer Brendan McLoughlin. She’s a keen horse-rider – they also keep chickens and a few rescue cats – and their home is a welcome refuge away from her whirlwind of a career. McLoughlin now works on Lambert’s security team and co-wrote songs for her new album Crisco, a brilliant melding of country and disco that is by far Lambert’s most playful record to date.

“Oh heck yeah!” she exclaims, when I bring up its joyful tone. “I didn’t know what I was doing, but I was excited.” Today’s music landscape is markedly different from the one she started out in, which was ruled by the charts and radio play. Now, she agrees, it’s more democratic and fans can seek out what they like, rather than wait for it to be fed to them. “That kind of made me less afraid,” she says. “Like, what do I have to lose? The worst thing that could happen was nobody cared, but I had a great time, so we already won. I’d rather stay true to myself at the risk of failure.” She often tells younger artists coming to her for advice the same thing, to only put out music they really believe in: “If your songs work, you have to sing them forever. And if you hate them now, you’re damn sure gonna hate them in 20 years!”

open image in gallery Cover art for Lambert’s new album ‘Crisco’ ( MCA )

Lambert seems particularly protective of her legacy. She follows Parton’s example in remaining steadfastly tight-lipped about politics, while being a vocal supporter of the LGBT+ community (she threw a drag brunch earlier this year in Nashville to champion queer artists and performers). “I feel if we could be a little more like Dolly, and be good, be kind, be thoughtful,” she says, with a bit of a sigh. “You can have a stance on things without preaching it to people, and I also believe that my job as a musician, as a songwriter, is to be an escape. Songs are an escape, that’s a moment for us all to come together… and I just don’t ever think it's my place to get up there and push my agendas of any other kinds.” Listen to her songs, she believes, and people will know where she stands. “And I feel like Dolly did that well too.”

I just don't ever think it's my place to get up there and push my agendas

Parton’s influence is all over Crisco, not least in Lambert’s duet with fellow country star Chris Stapleton, on “A Song to Sing”, which is almost a sequel to Parton’s 1983 duet with Kenny Rogers, “Islands in the Stream”, with its mid-tempo rock and country grooves. It’s nominated for Musical Event of the Year at the CMAs, along with Lambert’s peacemaking collaboration “Horses and Divorces” with her one-time rival, Kacey Musgraves (“There were chips on our shoulders, but now that we’re older/ It’s all whiskey under the bridge.”).

open image in gallery Stapleton and Lambert performing at the CMAs last year ( Getty )

Lambert is on a winning streak when it comes to songwriting, a talent it took Nashville a while to acknowledge – to see past that fiery exterior. “When I had Kerosene and Crazy Ex-Girlfriend out, people thought that’s all I was,” she says. “But also I have grown as a person – I used to live in that character a little bit.” She laughs. “We’re so fiery when we’re in our early twenties.” Once she’d begun building her body of work, she saw a turning point: “And the fact that I could be recognised as a songwriter, not just this fiery blonde gal, helped me calm down a bit – I was being seen as an artist, you know?”

Even so, she wasn’t expecting the unprecedented reaction to “Choosin’ Texas”. Last month it unseated Mariah Carey to take the longest-running No 1 song on the Billboard Hot 100, and just this week returned to the top spot and extended its run to 25 weeks total. Meanwhile, Langley, who performs the song, was quickly established as country’s brightest new star. “I think you can tell when an artist is genuine and does the work and they’re authentic, that’s universal,” Lambert suggests. “These artists don’t come along very often – Ella burst onto the scene and is already an icon.”

She has her theories for why “Choosin’ Texas” has made such an impact: “It has a nostalgic feel. It’s brand new, but you feel like you’ve heard it before, and it’s telling a pretty simple story.” She loves the song’s theme, a classic love triangle that riffs cleverly on two sides of country music (with references to Hank Williams versus George Strait). “I also love the idea of, you know, ‘You can’t win them all,’” she says. “Even Ella, this beautiful strong woman, she couldn’t keep the guy, you know what I mean? It’s a relatable song.”

open image in gallery Lambert (left) and Ella Langley pose in the winner's walk during the 61st Academy of Country Music Awards at the MGM Grand Garden Arena on 17 May 2026 ( Getty )

Lambert has been admirably open amid intense public scrutiny over her personal life, previously describing love as “a hard road sometimes and it’s been a roller-coaster ride for me”. Before she met McLoughlin, Lambert formed half of one of country’s biggest power couples with Blake Shelton, who she was with from 2006 until divorcing in 2015 (they were married for four years). She dated musician Anderson East for two years, and had a brief relationship with Turnpike Troubadours frontman Evan Felker, who ended up reuniting with his estranged wife after splitting with Lambert in 2018. She’s been happily married to McLoughlin since 2019, although jokes that it was an adjustment for him, moving out of the big city and to the countryside.

“Oh yeah, my in-laws are actually in town right now, and they’re like, ‘Oh, it’s so peaceful out here. It’s so calm,’” she says, laughing. “It took my husband a while to get out of that mentality too.” One night in spring, they were sitting on the porch – the same one where Lambert writes her songs – and the crickets and frogs were making their evening racket. “He said, ‘You always said the city was so loud. But out here it’s loud.’”

My own favourite of her collaborations with Langley is “Butterfly Season”, which appears on the latter’s second album Dandelion and was inspired by the butterfly garden Lambert’s manager, Marianne, has at her office. “It’s one of my favourites,” she says, “It reminds me of Ella, but it also reminds me of me – of anyone growing or evolving into something new. There can be pain with that, but it’s beautiful on the other side, so it’s kind of a universal tune.” I tell her it feels particularly pertinent for a time when more women are choosing to be single instead of prioritising romantic relationships, instead finding other things in life that give them meaning. It’s a lesson that, perhaps, society isn’t so keen on us learning.

“It really is, but to me it’s the most important one,” Lambert says. “You really learn how to love yourself in a quiet moment and get to know who you are. And I think that’s something we’re going to keep doing forever… I don’t think there’s a finish line to that, but I think that’s the beauty of it. We can keep growing and keep evolving and listening to ourselves, our hearts, our minds, our bodies, and learning what we need to be to be the best version of ourselves.”

‘Crisco’, the latest album from Miranda Lambert, is out now. The CMA Awards take place on 19 November.

News.title: Thailand extends jail term of human rights lawyer Arnon Nampa to 34 years for offending monarchy
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A Thai court sentenced pro-democracy activist Arnon Nampa to a further two years and eight months in prison for insulting the monarchy, taking his total sentence to more than 34 years.

The criminal court in the capital Bangkok found Nampa and four other defendants guilty on Friday of insulting the monarchy at a protest on 25 November 2020 outside the headquarters of Siam Commercial Bank in Bangkok, Thai Lawyers for Human Rights said.

The court sentenced each of the five to four years in prison and then cut each term to two years and eight months, because their testimony was partly useful to the proceedings.

Friday's verdict was one of 14 cases brought against Nampa under the law, and verdicts in two are still to come.

The sentences from each case count towards a cumulative total, which stood at 31 years and nine months before Friday, Thai Lawyers for Human Rights said in February, so the extra two years and eight months takes it to more than 34 years.

Nampa's lawyer, Krisadang Nutcharut, told AFP that three of the five defendants sentenced on Friday were already serving sentences from earlier convictions.

Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer, has been in prison since 2023 on convictions linked to the protests and his social media posts.

open image in gallery A protester dressed in a Harry Potter themed outfit campaigns for the freedom of Arnon Nampa during a Harry Potter themed protest at Democracy Monument on in Bangkok, Thailand ( Getty )

At the 2020 protest he was calling for greater transparency over the transfer of shares in Siam Commercial Bank from the Crown Property Bureau, which manages the royal family's assets, Mr Krisadang said.

Thai king Maha Vajiralongkorn is the largest shareholder in the bank's parent company, SCBx, with 23.6 per cent, according to SCBx's website.

"It is now clear that the law has become a political tool used against opponents," Mr Krisadang told AFP.

Nampa told reporters after the verdict that it did not surprise him.

"If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely," he said.

The law, article 112 of the Thai criminal code, punishes anyone who defames, insults or threatens the king, queen, heir-apparent or regent with three to 15 years in prison.

Thai officials defend it as reflecting the country's culture and history, in which the monarchy is highly revered by most Thais, and critics say it is used to silence dissent.

More than 290 people have been prosecuted under it since 2020, including 20 under the age of 18, with sentences of up to 50 years.

Nampa rose to prominence in the youth-led protests of 2020, when tens of thousands of people took to the streets to call for reform of the military-drafted constitution and the monarchy.

At one rally in Bangkok in August that year he gave a speech dressed as Harry Potter, calling for the monarchy to be scrutinised.

News.title: Lando Norris offers advice to drivers unhappy with cars: ‘Do a better job’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Norris's message to drivers unhappy with their cars: adapt. His call comes amid claims Mercedes machine does not suit George Russell.

Kimi Antonelli can clinch the drivers' championship on Sunday after a stunning season in which he turned the tables on pre-season favourite and team-mate Russell.

His ninth win of the season came last weekend in Austin, moving the Italian to within two points of becoming the youngest F1 champion in history.

Russell trudged home eighth in that Texas race.

open image in gallery Mercedes have suggested that their car does not suit George Russell (Bradley Collyer/PA)

After the round, Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said the car “does not suit” Russell but that he would be back on song if the team could give him a machine more geared to his strengths.

Russell has admitted freely he has been outperformed by his young team-mate but, ahead of this weekend's round in Mexico, explained why elements of the sport's new regulations for 2026 have not suited him.

The 28-year-old said his driving style is heavier on the rear tyres on the 2026 cars, also adding: “There's just a few factors with the cars this year that potentially favour or hinder a certain driving style.

“I’m on the throttle earlier than most. With these new power units, that means I’m spending more energy, and it’s sometimes not the most efficient way to drive for the power unit.”

Antonelli has six more wins than Russell this season.

At McLaren, a similar picture has emerged, with Norris faring far better than team-mate Oscar Piastri.

open image in gallery Norris clinched his maiden title last season (David Davies/PA)

But reigning champion Norris is not a believer in cars suiting certain drivers, placing the responsibility on those behind the wheel to adjust their approach.

Put to him that a driver such as Russell may be behind his team-mate until the next regulation change in the 2030s, Norris said: “You can still try and do a better job. Every driver can always try and do a better job.

“If I get told, ‘Lando you can have a car that can win the World Championship, but you have to figure out your driving a little bit more. Or you’re not going to win a World Championship, but you’re happy in the car’.

“Which one are you going to choose? They (Mercedes) have a driver that can win a World Championship. They’re not going to start making it differently, are they?”

Norris is set to become a former world champion on Sunday as the 20-year-old Antonelli steps into his shoes.

open image in gallery

The 26-year-old overcame a deficit to Piastri to claim his maiden championship last season and says he had to change the way he drives to get on top of his McLaren.

“For me, to keep it as simple as I can, I always think if my team-mate has beaten me in a car, I haven’t done a good enough job,” Norris said.

“I've never blamed my equipment. I always look at myself first.

“I just had to change what I was comfortable doing. I had to change my expectation.

“I had to change what felt good versus what didn’t feel good. For me, that’s always been the expectation every year. It’s not, my way should be the way.”

Russell concedes he has endured the most difficult season of his career in the year he needed to deliver, having been given a championship-winning car for the first time.

open image in gallery Russell admits to being bruised by his difficult season (Bradley Collyer/PA)

The British driver admits feeling “bruised” by the experience.

“Naturally yes, but bruises recover. That is the thing with bruises,” he said.

“This year there have been a lot more bad days than good days. My first bad year, my first proper bad year, has come this year. I don't have an answer for it. It's not pressure.

“If you are a baseball player you are either hitting a home run or you are missing the ball, and that is how it feels right now.”

Russell's season has been defined by the contrast with Antonelli, who stands two points from history.

News.title: Man United latest: Michael Carrick fights for future as Bruno Fernandes decision made for Chelsea trip
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Michael Carrick surprisingly survived the sack this week but remains under huge pressure ( Reuters )

Michael Carrick is once again fighting for his Manchester United future as his side travel to Chelsea in the Premier League.

Carrick appeared on the brink following the 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth last week but survived crisis talks with the United hierarchy and remains in charge for the trip to Stamford Bridge, despite the club sounding out Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann as his potential replacement.

An eight-game winless run in all competitions has heightened the pressure on Carrick, who is set to recall Bruno Fernandes after holding clear-the-air talks with his captain. Fernandes was left on the bench last weekend after criticism of Carrick’s tactics.

There is some pressure on Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso, too, following the home defeat to rivals Tottenham last weekend and their exit from the Carabao Cup against Liverpool in midweek. Joao Pedro remains sidelined due to injury, although Cole Palmer returns from suspension.

News.title: Red Roses cruise to dominant victory over United States in final WXV game
News.content:
English rugby chiefs have been on a charm offensive in the United States this week, but the players on the pitch opted for more of a brute-force approach.

The Red Roses were in the unfamiliar position of coming off the back of successive defeats and Meg Jones had called on her team to respond. They certainly did that, looking far more like world champions than they have over the past fortnight with a convincing nine-try win – four of them scored by Claudia Moloney-MacDonald – albeit there is still room for them to “grow”, as Jones put it after the game.

That is what the Rugby Football Union (RFU) have been trying to do off the field. Bill Sweeney, the RFU chief executive, and his colleagues used this fixture in New Jersey as an opportunity to tap into the US market by “creating connections” with business leaders and potential investors.

It is little wonder English rugby is trying to get a piece of the American pie. There are an ever-growing number of US owners in British football and with the US hosting the men’s and women’s Rugby World Cups in 2031 and 2033 interest in the oval-ball game is sure to grow too, although the sparse crowd in New Jersey would suggest there is work to do on that front.

News.title: Embarrassing England on brink of historic World Cup exit
News.content:
It is, because they showed their quality and offered themselves a sniff with their Gallic heroics. They had to maintain that pace on Friday to put the pressure on Samoa, but after the ideal beginning they contracted a nasty case of white-line fever from which they could not recover. “It looks like we’re going out of the tournament,” McDermott said. “That second half got scrappy and we should have handled that a lot better.”

McDermott is not blameless. The directives were clearly to offload when they could, and perhaps when they should not have, and the call to start Jez Litten over Brad O’Neill at hooker was, on reflection, a mistake. Litten has so much more impact off the bench and the Hull KR livewire could have been the spark England required when it proceeded to fall flat. It was also strange to see Lewis coming on in the No 9 role.

Yet it must be noted that this was just McDermott’s third match in charge and that Tonga was his first. With no warm-up game and with his English-based players at a disadvantage because of travel and the jet lag, that all-important opener was appallingly timed. Yet having been a member of the exclusive top three for so long, England must now concede they are merely in the top five. This tournament proved as much.

News.title: Everton give Burnham something to shout about by booking quarter-final spot
News.content:
David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

News.title: Trump administration loses grip on bird flu, experts warn
News.content:
The Trump administration has been criticised for losing control of a bird flu outbreak that has spread among mink and cattle farms across the United States.

The H5N1 virus has infected around 1,000 people since it was first detected in the late 1990s, killing roughly half of them. While it currently does not spread among humans, scientists have long worried that it could trigger a pandemic, and that each human infection raises the risk of the virus mutating.

A new variant emerged in 2020 and has since spread to millions of birds and hundreds of animal species across the globe, leading to devastating losses in both wildlife and farmed livestock and poultry.

While some countries have introduced tough measures to curb its spread, including mandatory culls of infected animals, “flockdowns” (where birds are kept indoors) and vaccination of farm workers who handle at-risk livestock, experts say the US is allowing the virus to run rampant.

For more than two months, an outbreak has raged unchecked on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur, news outlet ProPublica reported last week.

Mink in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of the farms give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate.

Mink have very similar respiratory systems to humans, increasing the risk that a virus can spread between the animals and people, and undergo a process known as “reassortment”, when two or more viruses mix together to make a new, more dangerous strain.

News.title: Britain faces unprecedented squeeze on incomes, IFS says
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. John Healey has ruled out making “crude cuts” to welfare after he failed to tackle the rising benefits bill in Wednesday’s Budget.

The Chancellor acknowledged last night that the current benefits system is “unsustainable” but said he will only look to make cuts “in a Labour way”.

Speaking to the BBC in the wake of Wednesday’s Budget, Mr Healey promised that “there will be a reduction in the benefits bill” before the next election.

However, he said this will not include “crude cuts” to payments.

He said: “We will do that in a Labour way, and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain, or progressive, to have a bigger and bigger benefits bills.

“This system is unsustainable. I’ve been clear about that. The Prime Minister’s been clear about that. It’s what you do about it.”

He added: “We have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures.”

His comments on welfare come after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch accused Labour of presiding over a Government that had left Britain “overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system”.

She said: “Next year, under Labour, the tax burden will be the highest in our country’s history and our benefits bill is going up by tens of billions of pounds because this Government has put welfare first.”

The latest figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility released on Wednesday revealed that benefits spending is expected to jump by almost 30pc to £431bn by 2032.

Almost half the total is pensions and disability benefits for pensioners, despite the planned abolition of the triple lock. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Healey launches tax raid on savers as welfare bill spirals | Chancellor to pull in £4.3bn from landlords and savers as Badenoch calls for ‘tough love’ on benefits

2) Gulf states face tax raid on UK property investments | John Healey’s changes risk driving investment away from Britain, industry experts warn

3) UK hands Rolls-Royce £1.25bn to fund new jet engines | British engineering giant confirms plans for £2.5bn to be invested during next decade

4) Petrol drivers face threat of stealth tax raid to boost EVs | Official review recommends forcing fuel suppliers to fund new renewable energy subsidies

5) JP Morgan lashes out at ‘unprincipled’ bank tax | Wall Street giant criticises John Healey’s Budget announcement on surcharge increase

What happened overnight

The Chancellor will have woken up to jittery markets after Google-owner Alphabet revealed higher spending on AI.

Alphabet dropped 10pc in after-hours trading, wiping nearly $400 billion off its market value. Microsoft, by contrast, beat forecasts with better-than-expected cash flows that lifted its shares by 3pc.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dropped 0.7pc, while Japan’s Nikkei fluctuated between gains and losses and was last ⁠up 1pc.

Oil prices retreated as investors latched onto hopes that peace talks to resolve the Middle East conflict could be back on the table.

European stocks were on track to edge higher at the open after the US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady as widely expected on Wednesday. The European Central Bank announces its next interest rate decision on Thursday.

News.title: Risk of Ebola spread in UK is low, experts stress
News.content:
Infectious disease experts have stressed the likelihood of Ebola spreading to the UK is low after the head of Africa’s health agency warned that the haemorrhagic fever could reach Britain.

The Democratic Republic of Congo is struggling to contain an outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the deadly virus that began in the volatile eastern region of the country. There have been 10,000 cases, including nearly 5,000 deaths, since the outbreak was first reported in May and it has now become the second largest Ebola epidemic in history.

In recent weeks the virus has spread to Kenya, where there have been nine cases including two deaths, and Nigeria. The case in Nigeria is concerning because the patient, the wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, the country’s capital, had no history of travel to the affected region of DRC. She has now been evacuated to Switzerland.

In comments reported by the Guardian Jean Kaseya, head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, described the outbreak as “unprecedented” as it was the first time that the disease had spread to three geographic regions of the continent. He warned that there was scope for further spread.

“We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

On Wednesday the United States announced that travellers arriving by air would have to sign a statement affirming that they had not been in the DRC within the previous 21 days. Anyone found to provide false or misleading information would face imprisonment or a fine.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) stressed that the risk to the UK is low. Dr Sam Collins, head of guidance, clinical and public health response at the agency, said the Ebola outbreak in DRC is serious but “the UK is well prepared to respond safely and effectively to the risk of imported cases arising here”.

UKHSA is monitoring travel routes from the affected countries and is providing information on symptoms.

The UKHSA said it is rare for Ebola to occur in returning travellers and the NHS has “well established procedures in place” for such a situation.

News.title: Wesley Fofana’s Chelsea nightmare continues as Liverpool win shoot-out
News.content:
It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

Sports.title: Novak pulls three shots clear in Mexico as Hawaiian sensation Akina shines
Sports.content:
Andrew Novak caught up to the lead with an eagle and pulled away with three birdies on his last four holes Friday to match his low score on the PGA Tour, a 10-under 61 that gave him a three-shot lead in the Mexico Open.

Novak drove the reachable par-four 13th and holed a 12-foot eagle putt as he jostled with Ben Griffin to carry the lead heading into the weekend at Vidanta Vallarta.

But on 15, Griffin drove into the water and had to scramble for a bogey, while Novak holed a birdie putt from just outside 15 feet for a two-shot swing.

Novak closed with a 20-foot birdie putt to finish at 14-under through the opening two rounds, three shots clear of a group of five players that included Griffin (67) and Kihei Akina, the 20-year-old Hawaiian sensation who shot a 64 to post his ninth round of 67 or lower in his last four PGA Tour starts.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Two-time winner of the Ballon d’Or and double World Cup champion Ronaldo turns his hand to golf as he tees off at the DP World India Championship in Delhi. Credit: DP World Tour

Also in the mix were France's Matthieu Pavon (66), Belgium's Adrien Dumont du Chassart (67) and Kensei Hirata of Japan (68).

"There's a pretty bunched leaderboard, said Novak. "I separated a little bit, but we're halfway there, there's so much golf to play.

"I'm going to have to go out and keep hitting a bunch of fairways. If I'm hitting my irons like this, I'm going to be able to give myself a lot of opportunities.

"I don't know if I'll make as many putts as I did today, but as long as I'm maximising my opportunities and make a few of those with the putter, I should be in a good spot."

Akina chipped in for birdie on the last hole Friday to continue an excellent run of form which has him eight points away from the 20 required for a US college golfer to secure a PGA Tour card.

Image: Kihei Akina hits his tee shot on hole 10 on Friday (AP Photo/Denis Poroy, File)

"I'm feeling more comfortable with each round played," said Akina, who made three birdies on the par fives and picked up an eagle on the reachable par-four 13th when he drove the green from 296 yards.

"We had about 287 to the front of the green and that's what I was trying to hit," he said. "So just a nice, roasted draw mini-driver for me, landed in a perfect spot and rolled down to tap-in. So that was a bonus for me."

His life dream is to play on the PGA Tour and he's making remarkable progress, having already secured a top-10 finish in the Bank of Utah Championship. Dating back to August and the Wyndham Championship, Akina has picked up seven points in the PGA Tour University program for underclassmen and gets one point for every PGA Tour cut and one point for a top 10.

"I've just got to keep playing well and keeping my foot on the gas," he said. "Feel like I'm doing that pretty well this week."

Sports.title: Verstappen, Lawson receive grid penalties after 'unacceptable' practice collision
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson have both received one-grid place penalties for an "unacceptable" collision in second practice at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Verstappen tried to overtake Lawson up the inside at Turn 12 going into the old baseball stadium but the Racing Bulls driver held his ground, so the pair went side by side through Turn 13 and made contact at Turn 14 with a piece of debris falling off the Dutchman's car and causing a red flag.

Collisions of this nature between drivers in practice are extremely rare, and the stewards stated both drivers "behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable" and that a warning had been given at the team managers' meeting earlier on Friday about overtaking in the final sector.

The stewards also said that Verstappen and Lawson both admitted the moves were "unnecessary and clumsy".

They added: "Noting that there had been similar incidents this year of actions between drivers in Free Practice, the stewards have decided to escalate the penalty from that of a formal warning to a grid position penalty particularly in view of the warning that had been provided at the Team Managers meeting and consistent with other incidents involving contact between the cars in Free Practice in previous years."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from Friday's practice sessions at the Mexico City Grand Prix

'Not smart when you're fighting for your seat' - Verstappen hits out at Lawson

The incident was made even more surprising by the fact the two teams have the same owners, with Racing Bulls considered Red Bull's junior squad.

Racing Bulls have yet to confirm their 2027 driver line-up and Lawson's future is up in the air despite the New Zealander sitting ninth in the standings, 39 points ahead of his team-mate Arvid Lindblad and occupying the 'best of the rest' position behind the top four teams.

Asked about the incident before the stewards' verdict, Verstappen said: "I don't think it's called unlucky. Maybe not very smart behaviour what he was trying to do there.

"At the end of the day, it's not going to change my weekend.

"If I would be him, I would act a little bit smarter. Also, when you are fighting for your seat, it's not very smart behaviour."

Image: Red Bull driver Max Verstappen and Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson collided in second practice in Mexico (AP Photo/Moises Castillo)

Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov, who made his F1 practice debut on Friday in Mexico, is second in the Formula 2 championship and remains in contention for a Racing Bulls seat next year.

Verstappen, who wields major power at Red Bull and over the summer signed a new long-term deal with the team, appeared to be referencing that situation with his comments.

In a separate interview, the four-time world champion added: "When he saw me coming, he suddenly started to accelerate. I don't know what was going through his head, that he wanted to drive me off the track in the hairpin.

"That's not very sensible behaviour from someone in his position, to pick a fight with me."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Chadwick and Bernie Collins weigh into the collision between Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson during FP2 at the Mexico City GP

Lawson, who was Verstappen's team-mate for the first two rounds of the 2025 season before being brutally dropped by Red Bull, was not obliged to speak to the media after Friday's track action.

However, in the immediate aftermath of the incident, Lawson said on the radio that Verstappen "literally drove into me" and added "if I back out every single time, what the **** do I do? He actually came off the track into the side of me".

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane said both drivers were at fault for the "completely unnecessary" collision.

"I don't know what Max has said, I haven't heard or seen anything," Permane said.

"I'm sure he's got his opinion and Liam's got his opinion but mine is, it's just not needed and they can both do better."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Verstappen has criticised Liam Lawson after a collision between the two during the second practice session at the Mexico City GP

Which driver was more in the wrong?

Three-time W Series champion and Sky Sports F1's Jamie Chadwick agreed with Verstappen's comments on the incident, given the situation he is in.

"If it's any other driver on the grid, you can stand your ground a little bit but when it's the senior team, the team that also have an influence on the decision that goes into your race seat, does he need to do that? Probably not," she said.

"But he was the same even when he raced Max as team-mates - he raced him very hard and they know exactly what that team is about, so I don't think that was the wisest thing from potentially either of them, but particularly Liam's side."

Former McLaren and Aston Martin strategist Bernie Collins says both drivers will "regret their decisions".

"Both drivers had an opportunity to do something different there and both drivers will think 'was that corner, really worth that?'," she said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Liam Lawson teams up with Sky Sports F1's Simon Lazenby and Naomi Schiff to prank Racing Bulls team-mate Arvid Lindblad with a fake interview

Is Lawson's seat under threat for 2027?

Lawson is the highest-placed midfield driver in the F1 Drivers' Championship, with only the Mercedes, McLaren, Ferrari and Red Bull drivers ahead of him in the standings.

He has bounced back from a disappointing two races with Red Bull at the start of 2025 and did enough to be handed a full season at Racing Bulls this year, where he has outperformed rookie Arvid Lindblad.

Lawson has scored twice as many points as Lindblad and Sky Sports F1's Karun Chandhok thinks it would be "unjust" if Lawson lost his seat.

"He's done a fantastic job this season. He's come back carrying the mental baggage of being sacked from the Red Bull top team, went back to the Red Bull earlier this year for three races [when Isack Hadjar was injured] and did a good job there. And he's delivered really, really well," said Chandhok.

"I get the junior team is a university to prepare drivers for the top team. Today, they are a strong midfield team, have their own identity, own sponsors, own reasons to be competitive and not just be there to train drivers up."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player After Liam Lawson pranked Arvid Lindblad with a fake interview, Lindblad gets his revenge on his Racing Bulls teammate with some challenges in the F1 Paddock

Collins added: "There are two aspects to a feeder team. One is getting very young talent in, getting them ready for the big team but what Liam showed is he can step up into that big team seat and that's important to have someone current that can just step up at any moment.

"I don't really know what he can do and I'm a bit surprised we are talking about it because looking from the outside what's happened at Racing Bulls this year, the points he's scored and the races he's done, he should have done enough, more than enough.

"If anything, we should be discussing Arvid Lindblad's seat because he's the one who hasn't scored as many points. He's had a good year by rookie standards but if you're just looking at the scoresheet, which is what's important to the teams, that's the one you should be discussing - has he done enough against Liam Lawson?"

Sports.title: Moloney-MacDonald stars as Red Roses return to winning ways with USA thrashing
Sports.content:
USA 12-55 England: Red Roses return to winning ways as Claudia Moloney-MacDonald scores four tries in WXV Global Series

Wing Claudia Moloney-MacDonald scored four tries as England's Red Roses thrashed the USA in New Jersey

England's Red Roses responded to shock back-to-back defeats in Canada with a crushing 55-12 WXV Global Series victory over the USA in New Jersey, returning to winning ways.

John Mitchell's side entered the contest off the back of losing two Tests in a row for the first time in a decade, and having lost their 41-Test, four-year unbeaten run in Toronto.

A competitive first half against the USA saw 10 points in it at half-time, but the second half proved largely one-way traffic as England's superiority showed.

In all, the Red Roses scored nine tries through wing Claudia Moloney-MacDonald (four), centre Meg Jones, wing Mia Venner, replacement hooker Bryony Field and back-rows Maddie Feaunati and Sadia Kabeya.

The USA scored two tries through loosehead prop Hope Rogers and replacement back Kate Zackary, but shipped three second-half tries in nine minutes with prop Mona Tupou in the sin-bin due to repeat scrum penalties.

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Jones: We'll review this tour - we're hungry to get better

Red Roses captain Meg Jones said post-match:

"First of all, credit to the USA, I think they've come off the back of some amazing wins and gained so much momentum. They are doing such a good effort there, building and growing the game.

"For us, we just wanted to control the game and impose ourselves on them.

"When we got into it, we kept the ball and everyone was a threat at the line. That's when we were unstoppable.

"Off the back of two losses, we just wanted to learn, and we'll continue to learn. We've got so much feedback from this tour.

"We'll go and review it, reflect, and see where we can keep growing. Because I know there is so much growth in this team.

"We're hungry to be better."

Red Roses skipper Meg Jones said the squad will review their North American tour following the match

Moloney-MacDonald: Tonight was about proving it to ourselves

Player-of-the-match Moloney-MacDonald said:

"This week was all about proving it to ourselves.

"We've obviously had three really tough games against Canada, and the last two weeks did not go the way we wanted it to go.

"For us, it was about learning as much as we possibly could from those two performances. A challenge we've never really been faced with previously.

"We spoke a lot about going out there and being fearless tonight. That's exactly what we did. We attacked it from minute zero to minute 80.

"I'm just so proud of the girls, the way we turned up today.

"That's what the Red Roses is all about."

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Perris-Redding: We were in the game in first half - result does not take away our growth

USA co-captain Georgie Perris-Redding said:

"We were in it in the first half, and that was really tough because I was so proud of the girls.

"We came into this game confident, you've seen the streak we've had and we've been building.

"We lost it a bit in the second half, so it's frustrating.

"But I am so proud of the growth this team has made. Today's result does not take that away."

Sports.title: Arbeloa: We've made mistakes but Fulham on right path
Sports.content:
Having gone winless in your first six games and conceded goals at a rate of almost two a game, there are worse ways to recover than a pair of gritty 1-0 victories.

It is still early days in the Alvaro Arbeloa project at Fulham but the optimism that a narrow but entertaining opening-weekend 3-2 defeat to Chelsea had brought from his debut in the dugout had waned with that run, which had left them stranded bottom of the Premier League.

That openness which had initially seemed a welcome tonic from the sometimes pragmatic Marco Silva era had quickly become a problem, with the Cottagers losing 3-2 again - this time to previously winless Crystal Palace - and shipping two late goals to Ipswich earlier this month to lose at Portman Road too.

Something had to change, and after six league games with his players Arbeloa felt he had seen enough to know where that lay.

"We have been learning from our mistakes, and obviously we are a team in a process," he tells Sky Sports. "We are improving, we're working hard and for us to be a very solid team is so important.

Aston Villa

Fulham Saturday 31st October 7:45pm Kick off 8:00pm

"Of course, I have to adapt to my players - they are the most important thing. It's not just about my ideas, it's about them and their qualities, their talent.

"We're not the best team in open games, we're much better controlling the ball, the transitions. We're a much better team in this way.

"You can only control what you can control. That's what you want to do. We cannot control what our opponents want to do but we have been learning and improving, working on our mistakes.

"We can be aggressive when we press, but sometimes you need to drop into a low block or a medium block. There are moments for everything in a game. At the end of the day, we have to be a complete team.

"In every process there are some ups and downs. That's normal, but we're on the right track."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Coventry City and Fulham

Conceding an average of 1.69xG per game was never going to be sustainable. And it has left Arbeloa adopting, quite suddenly, a significantly more conservative approach.

Building from the back has seen Fulham let just 0.67xG go across their last two games, a reduction of almost 80 per cent. Those 1-0 wins against Coventry and Hull have not been as entertaining as the early matches - but entertainment doesn't go far when you keep losing.

Striking the balance remains a work in progress. Now record summer signing Gonzalo Garcia, who Arbeloa labelled one of the best strikers in world football upon his arrival, has found life increasingly tough going with Fulham's less front-foot approach.

The 22-year-old has made the second-most off-the-ball runs, and attacking runs, of anyone in the Premier League this season. But despite showing flashes, he has not scored a league goal since a promising opening-weekend debut against Chelsea.

"As a team we can do better in the final third. It's something we're working hard on.

"But at the end of the day he has to do many things well, and I think goals will come. For me, it's important as a manager that the strikers do their work for the team, and the goals are their reward."

Despite his Premier League experience as a player, it's something Arbeloa is still coming to terms with in management compared to his brief experience in LaLiga last season.

He said: "It's more physical here, more direct, especially in the last 15-20 minutes of games when it's less controlled.

"They're more open games, and you have to be ready for those moments where the game is more open."

Sports.title: Leicester top table after victory over Bristol
Sports.content:
Leicester Tigers' Freddie Steward scores a try against Bristol

Leicester moved to the top of the PREM table with a bonus-point 22-16 victory over Bristol at Ashton Gate in an error-ridden game.

Tigers took advantage of Bristol having two men in the sin-bin to score 10 points in their absence, which ultimately proved the difference.

Leicester's tries came from Freddie Steward, Adam Radwin, Ollie Hassell-Collins and Jamie Blamire, with Billy Searle adding one conversion.

Louis Rees-Zammit scored the Bears' only try, with James Williams adding three penalties and a conversion to secure a losing bonus point.

Bristol took a sixth-minute lead thanks to a solo effort from the Welsh flyer Rees-Zammit. The wing received possession 35 metres out from the try-line, but from an unpromising position, he skipped past two defenders to race in under the posts.

Leicester's response was swift with bursts from Finn Carduff and Cameron Henderson putting the defence on the back foot before a well-judged cross-field kick from Searle saw Steward collect to crash over.

Bristol Bears' Louis Rees-Zammit is tackled by Leicester Tigers' Adam Radwan

Minutes later, the visitors looked to have taken the lead when their skipper Ollie Chessum forced his way over, but TMO replays showed the ball had gone forward when Aaron Wainwright's penetrative run was brought to an end.

Bristol also came close when Rees-Zammit was presented with another opportunity but under pressure from the challenge of Tom Whiteley, he just failed to collect his own kick ahead as the line beckoned.

The hosts then suffered two blows in quick succession when centre Mathias Moroni and full-back Tom Jordan were both yellow carded for dangerous challenges.

Leicester capitalised when an alert Searle sent a long kick deep into the opposition 22 with Radwan showing exceptional speed to be first to the ball and touch down.

Radwan almost had another when he chased another kick ahead, but this time he failed to gather so the Tigers had to be content with a 12-7 interval lead.

Ninety seconds after the restart, Leicester extended their advantage when another cross-field kick found Hassell-Collins in acres of space to score his side's third.

Bristol were brought back to full strength before Williams reduced the arrears with a straightforward penalty.

Basic handling errors from Radwan and replacement Will Wand gave the Bears the chance to build an attacking platform, but they were too frenetic to benefit until Williams knocked over a second penalty.

The game hung in the balance but the away pack produced an unstoppable line-out drive for Blamire to secure the bonus point, with Searle missing his third conversion to keep the home side in the hunt.

A third penalty from Williams, seven minutes from time, set up a tense finish, but the Tigers held on for a deserved victory despite Searle hitting a post with a last-minute penalty.

Sports.title: Leclerc seals Mexico City practice double as Hamilton suffers technical issue
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc completed a Friday practice double at the Mexico City Grand Prix but Ferrari's strong showing was dampened by Lewis Hamilton suffering a technical issue.

Leclerc produced a time of 1:17.827s to finish just over a tenth clear of McLaren's Lando Norris and Mercedes' George Russell, with the British pair among 10 drivers who had earlier sat out the opening session to make way for rookie drivers.

Kimi Antonelli, who only needs to finish ninth in Sunday's race to become Formula 1's youngest-ever world champion, was a tenth down on his team-mate Russell in fourth.

Hamilton had been on course to go fastest as the session approached its midway point before suffering what appeared to be an engine issue in the final sector of his push lap, leaving him 11th.

He completed the lap but was then swiftly told by his engineer to pull over on track, ending his session early and denying him valuable information that his rivals were able to gather with their race simulations.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton complained about a power issue before retiring from FP2 at the Mexico City GP

Max Verstappen, another to have sat out first practice, was three tenths off the pace in fifth, with his team-mate Isack Hadjar slotting in behind him.

Verstappen was involved in a bizarre collision with his former team-mate Liam Lawson in the early stages of the session as the four-time world champion attempted to overtake the Racing Bulls driver, and both drivers received a one-grid place penalty for the incident.

Lawson defended and retained track position, only for the battle to continue on for several more corners before the pair made contact, leaving debris on the track that caused a red flag to be thrown so it could be cleared.

The stewards said both drivers "behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable" and that a warning had been given at the team managers meeting earlier on Friday about overtaking in the final sector, which led to their decision to give Verstappen and Lawson a grid penalty for Sunday's race.

Lawson was ninth in second practice, two places behind his team-mate Arvid Linbdlad with Alpine's Pierre Gasly splitting the Racing Bulls.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Red Bull's Max Verstappen make contact during FP2 at the Mexico City GP

Oscar Piastri endured another disappointing day as he could only manage 10th, finishing more than half a second down on his McLaren team-mate Norris.

Fernando Alonso produced an encouraging result for Aston Martin as he finished within eight tenths of Leclerc in 12th.

"Overall, our performance looks quite alright but we still need to work on some of our limiting factors. It was quite tricky on track today, as the surface was slippery, so we will work on that to find some improvements for tomorrow," said Leclerc.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ted Kravitz and Bernie Collins explain why Ferrari's upgrade meant they were the only team not using their reserve driver during P1 in Mexico City

Antonelli had a low-key day considering he's expected to become world champion on Sunday as he never threatened to challenge Leclerc's pace.

"There are definitely more things we can improve going into tomorrow and we have some work to do overnight," said Antonelli, who won last time out in Austin.

"Ferrari looked very quick, but we will focus on ourselves, see where we can find more performance and hopefully put ourselves in a good position for tomorrow."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton remains uncertain over the severity of the problem with his Ferrari after he was forced to retire from the second practice session at the Mexico City GP

Should Antonelli fail to score points on Sunday, he can still become world champion if Hamilton or Russell fail to win the race.

Hamilton was off the pace throughout Friday compared to team-mate Leclerc but said he was "feeling really good in the car" before his technical issue.

"I think we did a really good job in getting the setup in a better place and just really unfortunate. I think we are really competitive this weekend as a team.

"I don't think I need to make many changes to the setup. I will probably leave it pretty much the same because we were very quick.

"I already had a loss of power earlier in the lap and we were still quick. I will give it everything tomorrow and try to do the best with whatever I have."

Sports.title: Canelo and Mbilli make weight for world title fight in Riyadh
Sports.content:
Canelo Alvarez and Christian Mbilli both made the weight for their WBC super-middleweight world title fight on Saturday in Riyadh.

Canelo was 167.6lb with Mbilli a fraction heavier at 167.8lb.

Alvarez is looking to win back one of the world titles he used to hold in his first fight since his stunning loss to Terence Crawford last year.

When Crawford retired it left the four major world championships vacant and Mbilli became the WBC titlist.

"I'm the challenger now, but in my mind I've always been the champion, ever since I was a little kid," Canelo said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch highlights as Crawford stunned Alvarez to become undisputed super-middleweight champion. Canelo vs. Crawford is available to watch globally only on Netflix

He elected to go straight in with Mbilli, a high-calibre, tough, aggressive fighter, right off the back of that defeat.

"I don't believe in shortcuts. I want to become a world champion again, and that's why I want to face the best. Mbilli is the world champion," Canelo said.

Mbilli, unbeaten with only one draw in his 30-fight professional career, declared: "I have a lot of respect for Canelo and his career, and I congratulate him on everything he has achieved. But inside the ring, it will be a different story, and I'm coming to win.

"I'm ready to shock the world."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A look at occasions when boxers seemed to slow down time in a fight and make their opponent miss with everything

The event in Riyadh is going ahead amid escalating conflict in the region.

Houthi attacks have targeted Saudi airports, including Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, while security concerns have led to the postponement or cancellation of other sporting events in the kingdom.

"You know, fighting in Saudi for me is special and whatever it takes I'm going to be a world champion again," Canelo has said.

"Because I'm a fighter and I want to achieve a lot of things in boxing yet and that motivates myself. I love boxing."

Could Mbilli tarnish Canelo's legacy?

Matthew Hatton boxed Canelo back in 2011, in the first world title fight of the Mexican superstar's career. He thinks this fight could affect Canelo's legacy.

Sports.title: Arteta can take inspiration from George Graham to expunge painful Anfield memories
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta used a Spanish word to describe what it felt like to be helpless at Anfield while playing for Everton in 2011: bajar. “It’s when a cyclist is going up and looks amazing, then in one kilometre he goes ‘boom’ and he’s struggling again,” he said in Amazon’s All or Nothing documentary. “The game was going well and then suddenly I could only see red shirts flying around. The game is passing all over me and I cannot react. I only had that feeling in my career once, and it was at Anfield.”

Given Arteta’s record at Liverpool, Sunday’s showdown with his childhood friend Andoni Iraola – five days after Arsenal were dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Fleetwood – could be expected to fill him with dread. Arteta finally tasted victory there as a player with Arsenal in September 2012, after five failed attempts in the Merseyside derby, but ended up spending the night in hospital with concussion after colliding with Jordan Henderson in an incident he has described as “the biggest fear of my life”.

Arteta was part of the Arsenal side that won at Anfield again six months later thanks to goals from the new signings Lukas Podolski and Santi Cazorla. That was the last time the club triumphed there in the Premier League. They have not won at Anfield for 13 league matches, equalling the club’s worst run at Liverpool. Arsenal’s one victory at Liverpool in the interim came in the League Cup on penalties in 2020 on Arteta’s second visit as a manager.

The Spaniard tried to prepare his players for a trip to Anfield in November 2021 by playing You’ll Never Walk Alone over the training ground speakers but that ended in a 4-0 defeat. He was criticised after last season’s loss in late August, when Dominik Szoboszlai’s late free-kick ended a sequence of three Arsenal draws at Liverpool, for a perceived failure to take off the handbrake, having started Mikel Merino as his No 10. Gary Neville went as far as to say Arsenal lacked “the mentality to go and win big matches at big away grounds”, an assertion that will have hurt Arteta but does have credence: they have not beaten Manchester City in the Premier League at the Etihad since 2015 under Arsène Wenger.

Arteta will be keen to disprove such perceptions, especially after Arsenal struggled so badly against a team 84 places below them in the pyramid in a stadium that holds fewer than 6,000 people. The strikers Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyökeres surprisingly started in tandem at Fleetwood, presumably in an attempt to lighten the load on Martin Ødegaard, although both look badly out of form. Bukayo Saka is out with a thigh injury, there are concerns over Noni Madueke’s ankle and Arsenal’s failed appeal over Max Dowman’s red card rules out the teenager for three matches.

View image in fullscreen 26 May 1989: the Arsenal manager George Graham hugs Alan Smith after they won 2-0 at Anfield, clinching the league title in the most dramatic circumstances. Photograph: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty Images

With that in mind, Arteta’s best chance of beating Liverpool is probably by taking the cautious approach that has served him so well and was the cornerstone of last season’s Premier League title triumph. He can take inspiration from one of the most famous nights in Arsenal’s history 37 years ago when George Graham’s side arrived at Anfield needing a 2-0 victory to be champions.

“I told my players to keep things tight in the first half – it was imperative we did not concede,” said Graham in an interview to mark the 20th anniversary of that dramatic finale to the 1988-89 season, when Michael Thomas scored in stoppage time to end Arsenal’s 18-year wait for the title. “The papers were saying we’d have to attack from the off, but I was adamant that was wrong. If Liverpool had scored an early goal it would have been over. But they did very little attacking and played into our hands.”

Before the 1989 game, Arsenal’s players ran to all four corners of the ground to hand flowers to Liverpool fans as a show of sympathy after the Hillsborough disaster the previous month – an idea proposed by their longstanding director Ken Friar, who died this month.

Graham and Arteta were 44 when they won their first league titles and the similarities do not end there. The former Scotland midfielder, who scored almost 80 goals for Arsenal and helped them win the Double in 1971, was known for his emphasis on defending as a manager and “1-0 to the Arsenal” became synonymous with Graham, especially towards the end of his reign. Arteta has revived that tradition since he took over in December 2019, recording 1-0 victories 32 times in the Premier League, more than any club apart from Everton.

Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal of the season in a routine 2-0 win at home to Everton last Saturday and targeting Liverpool’s weakness from set plays while keeping things tight at the other end could be the most effective tactic against a team who have been finding their feet under Iraola in recent weeks.

“Collectively, we acknowledge the importance of defending,” said Arteta last year when asked about comparisons between his team and Graham’s. “We know that if we excel in that part of the game, the chances and the probabilities to win more matches is going to be very, very high.”

Arsenal flew back to London after losing to Fleetwood on penalties in a shootout that will have revived bad memories of May’s Champions League final defeat by Paris Saint-Germain.

The Carabao Cup has stretched Arteta’s squad in the past two seasons, when they reached first the semi-finals then the final, so that is one potential positive from their elimination – not that the ultra-competitive Spaniard would agree. For him, the only way to respond to the most embarrassing night of his managerial career will be to follow in Graham’s footsteps on Sunday.

Sports.title: Carrick tells players ‘hard truth’ in attempt to turn Manchester United’s season around
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick said he has had difficult conversations with the Manchester United hierarchy and his players during their turbulent start to the season.

United have not won in their past eight games and start the weekend in 16th place of 20 in the league, one point above the relegation zone.

Carrick’s position was under threat after losing last Sunday to Bournemouth but he has held on to his job for the time being and been given the chance to turn things around, starting at Chelsea on Saturday.

The head coach suggested he had spoken with the club’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, and the chief executive, Omar Berrada, this week.

“It’s pretty clear, it’s not always rosy and nice conversations between anyone, whether that’s between me and the players, whether that’s between me, Jason, Omar or the owners,” Carrick said. “It’s the truth, it’s the hard truth at times and it’s what we need to move forward. Whatever we need to move forward, we will do.”

The supporters cheered Carrick off after he did a lap of the pitch in the aftermath of Sunday’s 3-0 defeat, but once he entered the tunnel they booed the players after a poor performance and perceived lack of effort. Carrick said the players are “hurting” but are “hungry” to turn things around.

“I’ll be totally honest, it was mixed feelings for me,” Carrick said. “To have the appreciation from the supporters and that connection and that respect is something I feel strongly about.

“It wasn’t a nice situation but to feel that was important, of course, but it didn’t make me feel better in the fact that I’m with the players 100% and we’re all in it together. I’ve told the players that, I’m happy to say that.
