With fighting for control of Yemen between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government continuing, how significant is Russia’s support to the Houthis? Why can’t Saudi Arabia, the most powerful of the Gulf states that is backed by the US, hold back a group of rebel fighters?

Here’s what we know:

What did the investigation into the use of Russian satellites show?

As revealed by The Associated Press news agency this week, between July 1 and October 19, AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence examined 40 missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthis and, in every case, found a pattern of Russian government and military satellites observing the targeted areas both before and after the attacks.



Nawaf Obaid, founder of the geosignal intelligence firm, told Al Jazeera that by reconstructing Russia’s military reconnaissance architecture, the group had identified individual satellites, calculated their orbital trajectories and then established observation opportunities and correlated their activity with military developments across Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE and Yemen.

He said the satellites they identified include Russia’s Bars-M military mapping satellites, Persona optical reconnaissance satellites, Lotos-S1 electronic intelligence satellites, Pion-NKS maritime reconnaissance systems and Kondor-FKA radar-imaging satellites. They also examined the EKS/Tundra infrared early-warning constellation.

“The critical finding was not the presence of individual Russian satellites, but the sequencing and integration of their complementary intelligence capabilities,” he said.

Obaid also confirmed to Al Jazeera that based on the findings, “Russian military geospatial and signals intelligence has supported the Iranian-led intelligence architecture assisting Houthi operations in Yemen.”

He said the strongest operational example of this has been the Houthi offensive along Yemen’s western coast towards Bab al-Mandeb, where Russian-derived intelligence, Iranian command integration and local human intelligence all contributed to “the rapid deterioration of opposing Yemeni forces’ battlefield coordination”.

“We assess that this intelligence relationship is also relevant to Houthi missile and drone targeting against Saudi Arabia. Russian military reconnaissance provides capabilities far beyond ordinary commercial satellite imagery, particularly when optical, radar and electronic intelligence are integrated,” he said.

“The September attacks against Saudi Arabia’s East-West Petroline illustrate the sophistication of the targeting problem,” he said. That was when three pumping stations – PS8 at Afif, PS9 at Al-Dhekra and PS11 at Al-Mesba’ah – were struck within the pipeline’s “critical high-elevation western section”.

“Their selection reflected an understanding of the infrastructure’s engineering vulnerabilities and strategic importance,” he explained.

How significant are these findings?

Brussels-based military analyst Elijah Magnier said AURORA’s findings don’t necessarily show the whole picture.



“Inability to intercept an intelligence transmission doesn’t establish who had access to the Russian satellite information, whether Russia deliberately shared it, or whether Iran obtained it independently,” he said, adding that for this, there are four possible scenarios.

“First, Russia could have deliberately shared information with Iran,” he said.

“The second is Iran obtained Russian satellite imagery through commercial channels… However, the Russian military’s reconnaissance imagery is generally not publicly accessible, so the commercial Russian imagery would not necessarily establish Russian government involvement,” he noted.

“The third is Iran obtained information through another intermediary, so a third party could theoretically have supplied the intelligence originated from the Russian system, and there is no currently publicly verified evidence establishing such an arrangement,” he added.

But Obaid highlighted that distinguishing a Russian-supported intelligence architecture from proof that a particular Russian satellite supplied the targeting data for an individual Houthi strike is essential.

“Our assessment establishes the wider intelligence relationship; attribution of specific satellite-derived intelligence to individual missile launches requires additional corroboration,” he said.

Three officials, including one from Saudi Arabia and another in the top ranks of the Houthis, as well as a private intelligence analyst, confirmed to The Associated Press that the Houthis and other Iranian allies have benefitted from Russian intelligence, as well as Chinese capabilities.

Last week, the Saudi Foreign Ministry’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, Rayed Krimly, told reporters that the Houthis receive intelligence from Russia and China.

“We do discuss these matters regularly with China and Russia, and we will continue to do so,” he had said.

How important is access to Russian satellites for Iran and the Houthis?

Russian officials have not yet commented on AURORAH’s findings, but in recent years, technological and military ties between Russia and Iran have deepened significantly, anchored by joint strategic agreements, space cooperation, and the exchange of defence technology.

Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst on Yemen at the International Crisis Group, said Moscow reportedly supporting Tehran’s allies like the Houthis is particularly significant because it would mean a shift in the trajectory of the Yemeni conflict.

“It is increasingly moving beyond its domestic dimensions and becoming intertwined with wider regional dynamics. Supporting the Houthis is no longer a matter of interest to Iran alone. We are now seeing other actors, particularly Russia, providing Iran with intelligence support and sophisticated weaponry, from which the Houthis are also benefitting,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The question is whether this support is being channelled directly to the Houthis or indirectly through Iran. I don’t think that distinction is important. The bottom line is that the Houthis are benefitting from increasingly diversified external support involving several countries,” he added.



But Nagi warned that Russian support to the Houthis has implications for both the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia.

“Russia’s role also extends into the diplomatic arena, where Moscow has taken positions at the United Nations Security Council opposing stronger international action against the Houthis. Taken together, these developments point to a broader expansion of Russian engagement with the group,” he added.

Where have the Houthis struck in Saudi Arabia?

Yemen’s Houthis have attacked multiple locations across Saudi Arabia, spanning from the eastern and western coasts to the capital and southern regions, since fighting escalated over the summer.

In a statement on X on Friday, Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed attacks have hit vital commercial and military infrastructure, which spanned Saudi Arabia from its east and west coasts to Riyadh and the southern region of Najran.

Saree said the Houthis targeted the Ras Tanura oil refinery with a ballistic missile, an Aramco facility in Abqaiq with a missile, King Khalid International airport in Riyadh with multiple missiles, King Fahd International airport in Dammam with a drone, the Rabigh oil refinery with a ballistic missile and a Saudi military headquarters in the Najran region.

There has, however, been no independent corroboration of these specific claims.

However, Houthi attacks generally have resulted in multiple deaths and injuries in Saudi Arabia. A severe strike on King Khalid International airport in Riyadh earlier this month killed at least 12 people and injured 300, according to Saudi officials. The attacks led to the airport’s temporary closure, forcing the postponement of Saudi Arabia’s flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.

The airport has since reopened, and flights resumed on Sunday with the Houthis warning travellers to avoid the facility, calling it a “military target”.

An October 21 attack on King Fahd International airport in Dammam also killed two people and wounded eight.

Why are the Houthis so well-armed?

Since seizing Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, and swaths of northwest Yemen in 2014, the Houthis have demanded to be recognised as the legitimate governing authority in Yemen.

After taking the capital and state institutions, the Houthis gained access to large arsenals belonging to the Yemeni military and formed an alliance with forces loyal to former President Ali Abdullah Saleh.

The internationally recognised government decamped to Aden.

Once regarded as an armed group without many resources, analysts say this has changed since the Houthis seized Yemen state arsenals, received external backing from Iran, and evolved their military capabilities.

Saj Ahmad, chief analyst at StrategicAero Research, told Al Jazeera that besides learning the art of weapons assembly, the Houthis have scoured international black markets for components and carried out many military engagements to unearth a clandestine, but robust, market for sales, too.

“So while the Houthis have been expending their cache of weapons, they have been developing and expanding too – and we have seen that with their long-range missile attacks as far away as Israel – so targeting high-value targets in Saudi Arabia in contrast is very easy pickings for them,” he said.

When a truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition took effect in 2022 and continued until earlier this year, many within the Yemeni government expected it to pave the way for a political settlement, Nagi said.



“The Houthis, meanwhile, were preparing for the possibility that the conflict would resume. They used the relative lull to strengthen their military position. The extent of that preparation has become evident over the past few weeks. Their forces have demonstrated considerable military readiness, enabling them to advance across several areas and inflict significant setbacks on Yemeni government forces,” he said.

According to Magnier, the Houthis’ sophisticated missile propulsion and guidance technology remains heavily dependent on foreign expertise, however.

The Houthis receive substantial backing, training and weaponry from Iran. This includes Iranian-origin and-derived ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and one-way attack drones – such as the Palestine-2 and Toufan systems – although Iran officially denies supplying them.

Besides Iran, Magnier said Iran’s ally in Lebanon, Hezbollah, has also contributed with military training and organisational experience. “All the experience gathered from fighting Israel was transformed and offered to Ansar Allah [the name the Houthis are also known by] in Yemen,” he said.

“The cooperation has also extended to Iraqi armed groups, with the exchange involving military personnel and again operational experience in a vast area,” he added.

“This combination [of domestic expansion and foreign dependence] helps explain why years of Saudi-led military operation, followed by American and Israeli strikes, have failed to eliminate its military capability,” he added.

How has Saudi Arabia struck back at the Houthis?

The Saudi-led coalition has retaliated against Houthi targets in Yemen through air attacks and military operations.

On Friday, the coalition in Yemen reported that it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s Mecca region.

The drone was “intercepted and destroyed” on Friday morning, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post. It was also reported that a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was earlier brought down, as hostilities between the Riyadh-backed Yemen government and Iran-backed Houthis continue to escalate.

On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region. It later said two ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, were also intercepted and destroyed.

Al-Malki reported early on Friday that the coalition’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile which had targeted western Saudi Arabia.

Al-Maliki said on Monday its forces also destroyed four ballistic missile launchers and five tunnels used by the Houthis to store missiles.

In a post on X, he had said coalition forces attacked a missile depot, adding that the operation “focused on cutting off Houthi militia supply lines between areas under their control”.

The operation also targeted Houthi “fortifications, gatherings of their members, and their military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen”.

Al-Maliki said on Monday that Saudi air defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh”.

This month, Yemen’s government forces launched the “Operation Yemen Dawn” counteroffensive, aimed at recapturing territory held by the Houthis.

On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition said air defences intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles.

The kingdom’s civil defence agency said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, and reported damage to several buildings and vehicles.

Why are the Saudis struggling to contain the Houthis?

While high-level diplomatic talks such as recent meetings in Tehran involving Saudi and Iranian officials have aimed to de-escalate tensions, analysts say the Houthis are actively testing the limits of Saudi military restraint and air defence capabilities, transforming the Yemeni conflict into a wider national security test for Riyadh.

According to Magnier, the Saudis have been struggling because “nobody wins a war by air bombing.”

“The air bombing helps for the ground forces to capitalise on what the air force is doing and opens the road for the ground forces. If the ground forces are not sufficiently motivated to advance and offer sacrifices and accept large losses, then there is no point in wondering why the Saudis are struggling,” he said.

Crisis group’s Nagi shared a similar view. He added that the Saudi-backed Yemeni government camp has also remained fragmented, poorly organised and militarily unprepared.

“There was an expectation that quick fixes, particularly intensified air strikes, could produce rapid gains. But the government and its allies had not developed the military capabilities or organisation necessary to sustain a confrontation with the Houthis,” he said.

According to analyst Saj Ahmad, despite the billions spent on US and European weapons, the Saudis have failed to make effective use of their military capabilities.

“The Houthis have learned a great deal from Iran’s military strategists as well as those militias in and across Iraq that battled US troops for years after the fall of Saddam Hussein. And in that intervening period, the Saudi regime has made big weapon buys but has little skill in how to use or deploy them and has even less capability to effectively combat a guerrilla group like the Houthis,” he said.

“With Riyadh under siege, I would not be surprised if the Saudis eventually leave this combat zone, like the UAE did,” he added.

World.title: Hakimi’s hat-trick guides PSG to stunning 5-1 win at Le Havre in Ligue 1
World.content:
European champions PSG registered their sixth league victory, and sit two points clear at top of the Ligue 1 standings.

Share Hakimi’s hat-trick guides PSG to stunning 5-1 win at Le Havre in Ligue 1 on social media

Flying ‌fullback Achraf Hakimi grabbed a hat-trick as Paris Saint-Germain went on a rampage to thrash ⁠bottom-placed Le Havre 5-1 and extend their Ligue 1 lead on Friday.

The European champions, who have several regulars out injured, could afford to leave ⁠more of their key players on the bench and still come away with an impressive victory as they moved to 20 points from their opening nine league fixtures.

They ⁠are two points ahead of Lille and four above third-placed Rennes, who have 16 points.

Lille moved above Rennes into second, thanks to a late goal from veteran Olivier Giroud, who came off the bench to score an 86th-minute winner for a 1-0 derby ‌victory at home over RC Lens.

Rennes were handed a 5-2 drubbing at Nice, who continued their improving form with a fourth win in five outings.

Elye Wahi netted a hat-trick for Nice, who moved up to seventh after narrowly avoiding relegation last season.

An all-round display from Hakimi

On top of his three goals at Stade Oceane, Hakimi had two assists for the goals scored by Mika Godts and Senny Mayulu after Josh Maja had given the ⁠hosts the lead.

It was PSG’s ninth consecutive victory in all ⁠competitions.

Le Havre suffered a fifth consecutive defeat and sit bottom with two points, but they briefly dared to believe as Maja handed them an early lead.

Hakimi set up Godts for the equaliser before putting his side ⁠ahead in the 28th minute with a shot in at the near post.

The Morocco international then netted from a free kick ⁠into the bottom corner in the 55th minute before ⁠being at the centre of a counterattack that saw Mayulu make it 4-1 in the 62nd minute.



Hakimi completed his hat-trick with a deflected effort in the 69th minute.

“I am happy because some players had very ‌little playing time. If we want to win trophies, we need everyone,” said PSG coach Luis Enrique.

World.title: US, South Korea, Japan call for ‘complete denuclearisation’ of North Korea
World.content:
The joint statement comes as US President Donald Trump seeks a new meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

The United States, South Korea and Japan have reiterated their longstanding call for North Korea to give up its nuclear weapons, a move Pyongyang has repeatedly ruled out.

The three countries addressed the issue on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) meeting in the US city of Atlanta on Thursday, with their top diplomats reaffirming their “resolute commitment to the complete denuclearisation” of North Korea, according to a readout by the US Department of State.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also pledged the “full implementation” of United Nations Security Council resolutions, including a ban on supporting revenue for North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.

The statement comes despite repeated overtures to North Korea by US President Donald Trump, who held a series of historic summits with its leader, Kim Jong Un, during his first term in office and has continued to call Kim a “friend”.

Last year, Trump bucked a long-held US policy by conceding that North Korea was already “sort of a nuclear power”.

More recently, he has played down concerns about North Korea’s nuclear programme and expressed a desire to meet Kim again. Speculation is mounting that the two leaders could reconnect at next month’s APEC summit in China, which Trump is due to attend.



Analysts and South Korea’s spy agency say Kim may have conveyed Pyongyang’s position on potential talks with Trump to Beijing during a recent visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong.

South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung – who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions – suggested in September that Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North’s nuclear programme in return for sanctions relief.

Critics have said such an approach risks tacitly accepting North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to win sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal.

Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea, which is backed by Russia and China, has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law. Pyongyang’s government has declared its atomic arsenal to be permanent and irreversible.

Pyongyang denounced a joint statement on Saturday by a group of nations monitoring sanctions implementation against it, pledging that “the stereotyped sanctions racket of the US and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK (North Korea) as a nuclear weapons state.”

World.title: US midterms: 3 days to go – What latest polls say as early voting surges
World.content:
More than 43 million Americans have voted early as Democrats lead national opinion polls and Trump prepares for final rallies.

Share What latest polls reveal as early voting surges ahead of US midterms on social media

With three days to go before the US midterm elections, Democrats are leading national polls as millions of Americans cast their ballots early.

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has announced he will carry on with his campaigns in Kansas and Iowa as both parties make their final push ahead of Election Day on Tuesday.

Here is what you need to know:

What do the US midterm polls say?

According to RealClearPolling’s latest national congressional ballot average, Democrats still lead Republicans by 8.2 percentage points. Democrats lead by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent.

A separate Economist/YouGov survey released on Thursday found that 44 percent of registered voters expect Democrats to control the House of Representatives after the election, compared with 31 percent who expect Republicans to retain control.

Expectations were much closer for the Senate, with 39 percent expecting a Democratic majority and 36 percent a Republican one.

Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, told Al Jazeera that the Democratic lead in national polling suggests a different picture for the two chambers.

“A big Democratic lead in House generic ballot polling suggests that the House is almost certain to flip to Democrats,” Kondik said.

“However, that does not mean the Senate is going to flip – it certainly could, but it is much more up in the air.”

How many Americans have already voted?

According to an Associated Press analysis released on Friday, more than 43 million Americans had voted early in person or returned mail ballots five days before Election Day.



That’s nearly 10 million more than at the same point before the 2022 midterms, with some of the biggest increases recorded in states having competitive Senate races.

In Texas, more than 6.3 million people had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point in 2022, an increase of 50 percent.

Al Jazeera’s Phil Lavelle reported from Houston on Friday that voters were continuing to arrive at polling stations as the state’s early voting period was drawing to a close.

In Georgia, more than 2.5 million ballots had been cast by Friday morning, surpassing the 2.3 million recorded during the early voting period in 2022, according to Al Jazeera’s Matthew Torres.

Torres reported long queues at an Atlanta polling station and more participation among young voters.

“We all just really want a better future for everyone, especially like the next generation,” one young voter told Al Jazeera.

Another young voter pointed to social media as a reason for the increased interest in the election. “Definitely social media. Social media and the media has put voting in the limelight,” the voter said.

Democratic political strategist Celinda Lake said many voters were looking for change.

“You got a lot of voters who say, ‘I’m going to do a Hail Mary for change, but I hope you do something,'” she said.

Early voting also increased by more than 30 percent compared with the same period in 2022 in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, according to the AP analysis.

However, early turnout figures don’t show which candidates voters have chosen or what the final results will be.

What’s happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?

Trump reversed his decision to cancel two weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa, with the White House confirming that both events would go ahead on Sunday.

The rallies had been cancelled on Thursday, with the White House saying Trump would instead take part in nearly 20 telephone campaign events.

But less than a day later, the president put the rallies back in his schedule.

Al Jazeera’s Tanya Nouri reported that Trump’s campaign team sees his personal appearances as a way to mobilise Republican voters.

“He is energised to go back and rally in person on Sunday,” Nouri said, quoting her campaign sources.

She also said that Trump’s team believes his appearances have a stimulating effect on Republican supporters, especially in states where the Republicans are running for Senate seats against strong opposition.

Trump also campaigned in Florida on Friday, where Republicans are defending Senate and gubernatorial seats.



“You got to vote. Bad things happen when you get too confident, right? So let’s pretend they’re one point down,” Trump told the rally crowd.

Meanwhile, in Texas, Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico were focusing their final campaign efforts on Houston, according to Al Jazeera’s Lavelle.

Paxton cancelled an event in El Paso to concentrate on Harris County, Texas’s most populous county, as early voting drew to a close.

On Friday, former President Bill Clinton campaigned for the Democratic Party in Mississippi.

He also urged people to vote.

“I can’t tell you how many people I care for that have lost in Mississippi because of those who did not vote at all,” Clinton said.

Where will Trump and the Democrats campaign this weekend?

Trump is scheduled to hold back-to-back rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday. In Iowa, he is expected to support Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, and later travel to Kansas, where he will campaign with Senator Roger Marshall.

Recent polls have shown competitive Senate races in traditionally Republican states. In Kansas, Marshall faces a tough race against his Democratic challenger, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton.

An Emerson College poll suggests that Hamilton is leading with 49 percent support, while Marshall has 45 percent. Democrats are also making their final appeals to voters. Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear will join Ohio governor candidate Amy Acton at a campaign event.

Democrat Senate nominee for Alaska Mary Peltola is also expected to attend a rally in Bethel, Alaska.

Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-ups that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in Congress’s upper chamber.

The race has been complicated by a dispute involving two candidates named Dan Sullivan. Trump has accused Democrats of recruiting an independent candidate with the same name as the Republican senator to confuse voters and draw support away from him.

The Department of Justice has taken legal action over the dispute, while Peltola has denied involvement in the alleged recruitment effort.

Separately, Republican candidate Mike Rogers is also expected to campaign with House Speaker Mike Johnson over the weekend.

World.title: Canada’s in-form Leylah Fernandez reaches Pan Pacific Open final in Tokyo
World.content:
Fernandez fought back from a break down in both sets to reach the Tokyo title clash, her third final of 2026.

Canada’s Leylah Fernandez reached the Tokyo final with a 7-5, 6-3 win over Uzbekistan’s Kamilla Rakhimova on Saturday, continuing her hot streak on the Asian swing.

The World No 23 won her first title of the season in Singapore last month and followed that up by reaching the final of last week’s Ningbo Open in China, where she lost to World No 1 Elena Rybakina.

Fernandez will face either Russia’s Diana Shnaider or Slovakia’s Mia Pohankova in the final of the WTA 500 Pan Pacific Open on Sunday, as she aims for her seventh WTA Tour title.

Fernandez reached the semifinals when Rybakina withdrew from their match with a neck injury, a day after securing the year-end world No1 ranking.

Rakhimova, ranked 66th, was eliminated in qualifying in Tokyo but entered the main draw as a lucky loser and made it all the way to the semifinals.

She was attempting to reach her first final on the WTA Tour, but ran into a player in form in Fernandez, who hit nine aces.

The Canadian went a break down early in the first set but soon recovered with a break of her own, before tipping the balance her way.

Rakhimova also went a break up early in the second set, but Fernandez clawed her way back and took the match in just less than two hours.

World.title: LeBron James, Tyrese Maxey shine as 76ers beat Knicks in NBA Cup thriller
World.content:
LeBron scored 20 points and hit the go-ahead fadeaway late, and Maxey had 27 points to lead the 76ers to a victory.

LeBron James scored 20 points, including a late tip-in, to help seal the Philadelphia 76ers’ 98-93 victory over the NBA champions New York Knicks on Friday.

The 76ers notched their second win of the young season over the Knicks after spoiling their championship banner-raising with a victory at Madison Square Garden on opening night.

The win had a double edge as Friday’s games marked the start of the fourth edition of the NBA Cup, the NBA in-season tournament won by the Knicks before they went on to beat the San Antonio Spurs in the NBA Finals for their first championship since 1973.

Group-stage Cup games will be played throughout November, all counting in the regular-season standings. Quarterfinals will be played December 4-5 and semifinals December 8-9 before the final on December 11 at Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Indiana.

Tyrese Maxey scored 27 points to lead the Sixers, who took control early against the sloppy Knicks.

They led by 14 in the third quarter and weathered a late Knicks surge.

Jalen Brunson’s step-back three-pointer put New York up 90-89 with 1:32 remaining.

James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, answered with a basket that put Philadelphia back in front and pushed the lead to 96-91 with a tip-in off a Maxey miss with 11.9 seconds left.

LeBron’s ‘best game’

James, 41, added nine rebounds, eight assists, one steal and a vintage chase-down block in what 76ers coach Nick Nurse called his best game since joining as a free agent in July.

“I thought he was really good all the way through,” Nurse said. “When we got some downhill stuff, he used his size and knocked them around a little bit for some layups … kind of pushed and organised it.



“He’s been good, but that was his best game, for sure.”

Brunson led New York with 24 points, and Karl-Anthony Towns added 22 points and 12 rebounds for the Knicks, who fell to 2-4.

The Dallas Mavericks, fuelled by 35 points from Kyrie Irving and 33 from Cooper Flagg, rallied to hand the Houston Rockets their first defeat of the season, 116-111.

The Rockets had emerged from a back-and-forth first half with a 51-44 lead, pushing the advantage to as many as 11 before taking an eight-point lead into the final frame.

Irving’s three-pointer with 7:01 remaining put Dallas back in front, and they wouldn’t trail again, the Mavs finding an answer when Houston twice pulled level in the final stretch.

“It felt good,” Irving said. “We came in at halftime, we weren’t proud of our effort. We looked each other in the eye, and we were just like, we’ve got to do better.

“We didn’t bring it in the first half, but the second half we definitely brought it.”

Curry climbs scoring list

Golden State star Stephen Curry scored 31 points to lead the Warriors to a 112-95 victory over the Los Angeles Lakers in a rollercoaster contest in San Francisco.

The Lakers outscored the Warriors 38-15 in the first quarter, the Warriors erasing the 23-point deficit by outscoring Los Angeles 38-15 in the second to knot it 53-53 at halftime.

Luka Doncic scored 37 points for the Lakers. The night’s abiding image was of him crashing to the floor as he was wrong-footed by Curry – who fired over him for a three-pointer.

Curry took his career points tally to 26,674, surpassing Dominique Wilkins (26,668) for 18th on the all-time scoring list.

In Miami, Giannis Antetokounmpo delivered a triple-double of 31 points, 18 rebounds and 10 assists to propel the Heat to a 145-125 victory over the Indiana Pacers.

In Boston, the Celtics romped to a 125-111 victory over the Chicago Bulls. Payton Pritchard scored 30 points off the bench, and Jayson Tatum scored 26 for the Celtics, who led by as many as 32 points.

Orlando’s Desmond Bane scored 28 points, Franz Wagner added 26 and Wendell Carter chipped in 20 as the Magic fended off a late challenge to beat the Raptors 121-114 in Toronto.

The Magic drained 18 three-pointers and withstood a career-high 41-point performance from Toronto’s Scottie Barnes.

Detroit shook off a slow start to hand the winless Nets a fifth straight defeat in Brooklyn, where Cade Cunningham scored 20 points, and Ron Holland added 18 off the bench in a 110-94 Pistons victory.

World.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
World.content:
The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.

The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.

Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.

In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".

It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".

The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".

Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.

The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.

World.title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
World.content:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.

The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.

Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (Â£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.

The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.

America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.

While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.

The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle â cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.

Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".

It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".

World.title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
World.content:
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.

This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.

Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.

Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.

The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.

World.title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
World.content:
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has now entered the constitutional court, according to his chief of staff.

Nawrocki cancelled a trip to Senegal mid-air in order to attend to the confrontation in Warsaw. He had been on his way to the Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar.

Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.

In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.

"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.

In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."

The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.

Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.

The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.

Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.

Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.

One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.

World.title: Spain train disaster clouds Sánchez chances of re-election
World.content:
Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.

The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid.

"They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop.

"I'm no judge... But these are the facts."

So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister.

"I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."

But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading.

"This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.

An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz, near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails - very different to the latest collision.

But there is a similar impact.

"It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."

For Team SÃ¡nchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.

Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.

Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.

Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.

That's when SÃ¡nchez called an early election.

His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.

World.title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
World.content:
Ukraine is not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.

One British official told the BBC: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".

Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".

"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.

In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.

The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of midterm elections on Tuesday, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".

Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.

Still, the US State Department this week said it had approved the sale of more than $2bn worth of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for the country's air defences to protect itself from Russian attacks.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.

Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

World.title: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
World.content:
In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries.

The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.

Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan.

"And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan.

Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature.

That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.

They agreed that action was urgent.

The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.

But according to the UN this week,, external the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets.

As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind.

"While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora.

"We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added.

This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."

But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".

Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection, external - an area bigger than Greenland.

Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.

Countries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money.

In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (Â£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.

But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN. , external

At this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation.

World.title: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire
World.content:
Ukrainian MP David Arakhamia said on Saturday morning that four planes carrying residents evacuated from Oleshky had landed in the city of Gomel, Belarus.

The evacuees are then expected to board buses to drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.

Speaking to journalists on Friday evening, Lantratova put out a joint request with her Ukrainian counterpart "to the US First Lady... that humanitarian missions such as this one, delivering aid to residents in need, be conducted on a regular basis under the coordination of Mrs Melania Trump".

A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.

Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.

"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning.

"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."

Ukrainian military positions lie 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but evacuees first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa, before flying to Belarus and then driving into Ukraine.

Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE: Report details NSCDC officers’ contributions to detention tragedy in Niger, recommends dismissal, prosecution
World.content:
A federal panel of investigation into the deaths of 33 detainees at a Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) facility in Minna, Niger State, has detailed how senior officers authorised operations without clearance, ignored warnings of possible suffocation and failed to intervene despite repeated cries for help.

The Independent Investigation Committee’s final report described how an investigation officer inspected the overcrowded detention cell but left without ordering an intervention, while a guard refused to open the door even as detainees screamed and banged the door and walls for hours.

It also documented the detention of children alongside adults, alleged interference with evidence after the deaths and the unlawful detention of a man arrested over a private debt.

The report attributed the cruel and degrading detention conditions leading to the deats of 33 detainees, including 14 children, to the actions and negligence of the officers.

These findings formed the basis of the 10-member committee’s recommendations for the dismissal of six NSCDC officers, including the suspended Niger State commandant, Suberu Siyaka. The panel also recommeded criminal prosecution of Mr Siyaka alongside four others.

The report was submitted by the Jonathan Kure-led panel to Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo on 27 October, following an investigation into the deaths on 16 and 17 September. The committee’s conclusions are investigative findings, not criminal convictions.

Commandant Suberu Siyaka authorised operation without clearance

The committee found that Mr Siyaka authorised operations against suspected illegal miners in and around Minna on 15 and 16 September without an approved operational order, adequate planning or clearance from NSCDC National Headquarters. He also bypassed the corps’ zonal supervisory authority and did not involve the specialised Mining Marshal Unit stationed in Minna.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The operations resulted in the arrest of 75 people, who were subsequently detained. Mr Siyaka told investigators that the detention facilities were designed to accommodate 40 people in two cells. The committee found, however, that approximately 50 male detainees, including 17 children, were held in one overcrowded cell.

The report faulted the commandant for failing to ensure proper supervision and lawful detention procedures.

Mr Siyaka told the committee that he left the command at about 6 p.m. on 16 September and was informed of the deaths by telephone at approximately 7 a.m. the following day. He said he was shocked and subsequently notified the NSCDC Commandant-General, the Niger State governor and other security agencies.

The committee also faulted him for issuing a public statement attributing the deaths to a disease outbreak, which it characterised as an attempt to conceal the circumstances of the deaths.

It recommended his dismissal. It also recommended that the Attorney General of the Federation prosecute him and four others for murder, torture, inhumane and degrading treatment and criminal negligence.

Investigation chief inspected cell but took no action

Sunday Oluwadare, a chief suprintendent of corps who headed the command’s Investigation Unit, was accused of facilitating unlawful detention and disregarding legal and medical warnings.

The report found that he authorised the detention of suspects, including children, without complying with applicable procedures. It also identified two detainees held without remand warrants: Emmanuel Emeka, 25, arrested over a private debt, and Adamu Abdulkadir, 25, a suspected illegal miner who had reportedly been detained for 18 days.

On the evening of 16 September, guards alerted Mr Oluwadare to extreme heat inside the detention cell. According to the committee, he approached the cell and shone the torchlight of his telephone through its perforated door to observe the conditions. He then left without directing officers to decongest the cell or take other effective measures.

A legal officer had earlier warned that the suspected mining offence was bailable and raised concerns about the detention of minors. A medical worker also warned that overcrowding could cause suffocation. The committee found that these warnings were ignored.

It recommended Mr Oluwadare’s dismissal and criminal prosecution.

Guard refused to open cell despite screams

The report attributed separate failures to Usman Ndamaka, a suprintendent of corps in charge of cell guards, and Hassan Mohammed, an assistant suprintendent of corps I who served as the night guard.

Mr Ndamaka admitted that approximately 50 male detainees, including children, were confined in a cell he said should accommodate about 20 people. He instructed Mr Mohammed not to open the door without armed backup, warning that the detainees might be attempting to escape.

Mr Mohammed, who assumed duty at 8 p.m. on 16 September, admitted hearing desperate cries and persistent banging from the cell. Two armoury guards also heard the disturbance and urged him to intervene. According to their testimony, Mr Mohammed refused to open the door, citing his superior’s instruction.

One of the armoury guards told the committee that the screaming eventually ceased at about 2.30 a.m. The committee found that Mr Mohammed neither opened the cell nor organised reinforcement to inspect it.

It recommended Mr Mohammed dismissal and prosecution.

Supervisor missed emergency call

The committee separately examined Mr Ndamaka’s failure to respond to an emergency telephone call from the night guard.

The report records that Mr Mohammed called him at approximately 10.37 p.m. on 16 September. Mr Ndamaka said he did not answer because he was asleep. He returned the call at about 6 a.m. the following day and reported for duty at approximately 7 a.m.

When officers opened the cell, they discovered that 33 detainees, including 14 children, had died.

The committee faulted Mr Ndamaka for issuing the instruction that prevented intervention, failing to respond to the emergency and neglecting his supervisory responsibilities. It also found that he participated in cleaning and altering the detention area after the deaths.

An arms commander, Annas Shittu, a chief suprintendent of corps, told investigators that he saw Mr Ndamaka and four others washing the area before independent forensic examiners arrived.

The committee recommended Mr Ndamaka’s dismissal. It further recommended his prosecution under Section 167 of the Penal Code over alleged interference with the crime scene.

Profiling officer detained children alongside adults, probe finds

The committee implicated Abubakar Dabban, a deputy suprintendent of corps and profiling officer, in processing children into adult detention cells.

According to the report, Mr Dabban recorded four children under the age of 14 during profiling but nevertheless processed them into detention alongside adults. He also admitted that he had never read the NSCDC Standard Operating Procedure.

Survivors alleged that cash and gold dust belonging to detainees were not properly accounted for. During an identification exercise, some survivors identified Mr Dabban as an officer who allegedly intimidated a detainee after the detainee complained that N1.35 million was missing from his bag. Other allegations concerned approximately N130,000 to N170,000 in cash and gold dust that were not recorded in the exhibit register.

Mr Dabban denied intimidating detainees or collecting money or gold dust from the detainees.

The committee nevertheless faulted his handling of detainees and exhibits and recommended his dismissal. It also called for an investigation by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission and the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission into allegations of extortion and exhibit mismanagement.

Mr Dabban was not among the five officers recommended for criminal prosecution over the custodial deaths.

Officer implicated in unlawful private-debt detention

The committee also investigated the circumstances surrounding the arrest and detention of Emmanuel Emeka, 25, who died alongside the suspected miners.

Mr Emeka was arrested on 12 September over a private debt complaint associated with Wilfred Ugwu of Okoma Pharmacy Ltd, Minna. According to the report, NSCDC officer Musa Marafa, an assistant suprintendent of corps I, arrested him without a warrant, after which he remained in NSCDC custody until his death on 17 September.

The committee recorded that Mr Marafa admitted charging a N25,000 tracking fee, explaining that the command lacked the equipment needed for tracking operations.

The report found that Mr Emeka’s arrest and continued detention were unlawful. It recommended Mr Marafa’s dismissal and prosecution, alongside further investigation into the roles of the complainant and the NSCDC area commander involved in the matter.

Discrepancy in administrative sanctions

Beyond the six officers recommended for dismissal, the committee proposed administrative sanctions against four others for management failures.

Its formal recommendations named Philips Ajayi, Agrahau John Chagwa, Obafemi Elvis and Garba Aminu Sule Usman.

Although the report found Abdul Shehu, the command’s second-in-command, as having exhibited management incompetence by failing to advise the commandant it recommended no sanction against him.

The report recorded Mr Shehu, a deputy commandant of corps, as informing the committee that he was relegated to the background in the operation.

He testified that upon discovering the fatalities on 17 September, he issued N10,000 cash to Obafemi Elvis, also a deputy commandant of corps, to purchase white burial shrouds from Kasuwan Gwari market to cover and evacuate the corpses to the morgue.

The report also accused Garba Aminu Sule Usman, a deputy suprintendent of corps, of “gross comptence” without giving details. It named him among those recommended for administrative disciplinary sanctions.

It also recommends lifting the suspensions of several officers found not culpable in the deaths and commending personnel who raised warnings or assisted the investigation.

Committee recommends criminal proceedings

The committee asked the Civil Defence, Correctional, Fire and Immigration Services Board to convene an extraordinary session within 30 days to consider the dismissal of the six officers. It also recommended that the case file be transmitted to the Attorney-General of the Federation for criminal prosecution.

The proposed offences include murder, torture, inhuman and degrading treatment, and criminal negligence.

The committee further recommended reforms to NSCDC supervision, detention procedures, documentation and emergency response arrangements.

The Federal Ministry of Interior confirmed receiving the report on 27 October, with the minister indicating that it would be forwarded to the Attorney-General of the Federation.

The materials reviewed by PREMIUM TIMES do not establish whether the recommended dismissals or criminal proceedings have commenced.

World.title: Tinubu welcomes Airtel’s open network launch
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has welcomed the launch of Airtel Nigeria’s Open Network initiative, describing it as a positive step towards greater transparency, consumer protection and improved telecommunications services in Nigeria.

The initiative, unveiled in Lagos on Friday, 30 October 2026, at an event attended by the Executive Vice Chairman of the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), Aminu Maida, allows subscribers to access information about network developments in their areas and report service difficulties directly to the operator.

President Tinubu said the initiative aligns with his administration’s commitment to encouraging private-sector investment, expanding digital infrastructure, and ensuring Nigerians benefit from more reliable and accessible telecommunications services.

He welcomed the growing emphasis on transparency in the sector, including the NCC’s public network coverage maps, performance information and consumer satisfaction surveys, which help Nigerians better understand the services available to them and hold operators accountable.

The president also highlighted the federal government’s recent Zero-Rated Access to Educational Platforms and Content Initiative, implemented through the NCC in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Education and telecommunications operators.

The programme, designed to provide eligible students with up to 100MB of free daily data to access approved educational websites and learning resources, reflects his administration’s determination to make digital opportunities more accessible, particularly to young Nigerians.

President Tinubu recalled his meeting with the Founder and Chairman of Bharti Airtel, Sunil Mittal, at the State House, Abuja, in February 2025, during which he reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to creating a favourable environment for telecommunications investment, strengthening the regulatory framework and protecting critical digital infrastructure.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He welcomed Airtel Nigeria’s continued investment in network expansion, which has seen its infrastructure grow from approximately 15,000 sites two years ago to more than 17,000 nationwide.

The expansion includes more than 1,050 network sites added during the company’s 2025/26 financial year, including 657 5G sites.

President Tinubu said sustained investment in telecommunications infrastructure is essential to expanding broadband access, improving network capacity, and supporting businesses, education, and economic opportunities across Nigeria.

He commended the NCC, under the leadership of Dr Maida, for its continued efforts to strengthen regulatory oversight, promote transparency and protect telecommunications consumers.

The president urged operators to sustain investment in network expansion, particularly in underserved communities, and ensure that customer complaints receive timely attention.

He emphasised that the success of telecommunications investment and innovation must ultimately be measured by the experience of Nigerians who depend on these services for their livelihoods, businesses and everyday communication.

President Tinubu reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to maintaining a business environment that encourages responsible investment and innovation while ensuring that consumer interests remain central to telecommunications development.

He called on operators to translate their investments into better network coverage, fewer service disruptions and more responsive customer service for Nigerians.

Bayo Onanuga

Special Adviser to the President

(Information & Strategy)

October 30, 2026

World.title: 2027 Politics Watch: From Atiku’s register demands to Tinubu’s borrowing defence, Friday’s roundup
World.content:
Opposition demands for scrutiny of Nigeria’s voters’ register intensified on Friday after an official of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) said registration officers had introduced irregular entries, including AI-generated photographs, into the database.

Atiku Abubakar sought the identities of implicated officials and election-material contractors, while the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) demanded answers about reports of deceased people remaining on the register. INEC said it was correcting irregularities ahead of certification on 15 December.

The exchanges unfolded alongside a dispute over President Bola Tinubu’s borrowing plans, questions about the Peoples Democratic Party’s (PDP) support for his re-election and conflicting accounts of campaign incidents in several states.

Atiku demands names and preservation of evidence

In a statement issued on Friday by his campaign’s strategic communication director, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku demanded the identification and prosecution of officials found responsible for irregular registration records.

The African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate also called for an independent forensic audit and the preservation of voter records, image files, access logs and audit trails for independeAtiku Abubakar and the NDC pressed INEC over questionable voter records as the commission promised corrections before certification. Friday’s exchanges also covered borrowing, nomination disputes, the PDP’s support for Tinubu and conflicting accounts of campaign incidents.nt examination.

He sought disclosure of the companies contracted to produce sensitive election materials and the safeguards governing their work. He threatened court action to compel disclosure if INEC refused to provide the information.

“INEC must not quietly ‘clean up’ the register and bury the evidence,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The statement referred to an allegation that more than 20 million AI-generated images might be involved but provided no evidence to substantiate the figure.

In a separate statement, ADC National Publicity Secretary Bolaji Abdullahi called for an independent forensic audit and an investigation of electoral officials linked to registration irregularities.

Atiku’s media adviser, Paul Ibe, separately asked INEC to disclose the number and geographical distribution of flagged records. Mr Ibe called for an independent forensic audit involving political parties and credible civil society observers. He also sought publication of INEC’s investigation findings and corrective measures, with voters’ personal data protected.

“Every eligible voter must also be protected against wrongful deletion during the cleanup,” he wrote.

He also described INEC’s clearance and rejection of candidates as a distraction from questions about the register.

The NDC raised a different concern. In a statement reported on Friday, campaign spokesperson Chiogo Constance Ikokwu questioned reports that deceased Nigerians remained on the register.

The party sought an audit of INEC’s processes and clear procedures for objections, including an opportunity for people wrongly reported dead to respond.

INEC says officers introduced irregular records

INEC’s Director of ICT, Lawrence Bayode, told ARISE News on Friday that some registration officers across the states had introduced irregular records because they had access to the registration system.

He said the commission knew how some irregularities occurred but could not explain the officers’ motives. He said identified irregularities had been removed and promised that further corrections would precede the final register’s release on 15 December.

Mr Bayode distinguished the suspicious photographs from INEC’s own use of AI for chatbots and logistics, saying the commission had not deployed AI for voter registration.

In its earlier clarification, dated 27 October, INEC said the register published online on 26 October was the preliminary version displayed physically from 9 to 15 October. It said that version did not reflect all ongoing corrections.

Separately, Chairman Joash Amupitan told a mission from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) on Friday that the national register had surpassed 103 million voters and nine of the election timetable’s 14 major statutory milestones had been completed.

The statements reviewed do not establish a verified nationwide total of irregular records. The opposition’s demands extend beyond removing entries to identifying responsibility and allowing independent examination of the evidence.

INEC upholds 66 nomination petitions

INEC also published the outcome of its review of governorship and state assembly nomination complaints.

In the statement, dated Thursday and posted on Friday, it said 41 of 69 governorship petitions succeeded, alongside 25 of 61 state assembly petitions. Together, 66 petitions succeeded and 64 failed.

The commission approved some inclusions and removed names found inconsistent with party membership registers or other nomination requirements. It said the affected parties, candidates and states would appear in updated lists.

Okorocha and Uzodimma contest Imo West ticket

Another nomination dispute featured in Friday’s reporting on Rochas Okorocha’s challenge to Governor Hope Uzodimma.

The Federal High Court had ordered the All Progressives Congress (APC) to submit Mr Okorocha’s name for Imo West. In a Thursday interview, the former governor alleged irregularities in documents supporting Mr Uzodimma’s claim to the ticket.

The governor’s camp rejected the judgement and announced plans to challenge it. The Imo APC also maintained that Mr Uzodimma won the primary.

Tinubu defends borrowing as ADC demands completed projects

The borrowing debate shifted towards what the government could show for its loans.

In an essay reported by Arise News on Friday, Mr Tinubu argued that infrastructure investment would expand production, create jobs and improve living standards. He identified major highways, electricity upgrades and port modernisation among the intended investments.

In an essay reported by Arise News on Friday, Mr Tinubu argued that infrastructure investment would expand production, create jobs and improve living standards. He identified major highways, electricity upgrades and port modernisation among the intended investments.

PREMIUM TIMES previously reported the president’s request for approximately $20.52 billion and €1.045 billion under a supplementary external borrowing plan. The request was referred to Senate committees for scrutiny.

Senator Adams Oshiomhole defended infrastructure borrowing on Friday but said the Senate committee must examine the request and project details before plenary deliberations.

PDP official says Onor remains in race despite Tinubu support

The PDP’s Bayelsa chairman, George Turner, maintained that Sandy Onor remained its presidential candidate, even as he defended the party’s support for Mr Tinubu through the Rainbow Coalition.

Mr Turner said participating parties could retain their candidates while backing agreed candidates at different levels. At the presidential level, he said, the coalition had chosen Mr Tinubu, with participating candidates expected to mobilise support for him.

APC campaign council member Francis Okoye welcomed the support but cautioned against complacency, identifying the ADC and NDC as significant challengers.

Sowore and police dispute Ekiti incident

In Ekiti, Omoyele Sowore and the police gave conflicting accounts of Friday’s incident at a restaurant in Ado-Ekiti.

The African Action Congress (AAC) presidential candidate alleged that government-sponsored armed men attacked him and his team. The police rejected reports that he had been kidnapped, describing an altercation with some individuals and saying officers intervened.

The command said Mr Sowore sustained a minor injury and received medical attention. He disputed its description of the incident. Police ordered an investigation; the allegation of government sponsorship remains unproven.

Enugu venue explains booking dispute

In a response reported on Friday, Amadeo Event Centre said its dispute with organisers of an NDC event involving Peter Obi concerned a booking made for an association’s conference.

The company said the subsequent use of political decorations breached that agreement. It said it eventually allowed Thursday’s event to proceed as a youth town hall meeting.

The centre denied receiving government instructions to stop the event. Governor Peter Mbah had also denied the NDC’s allegation that he intervened.

Katsina arrests follow attack on rally travellers

In Katsina, police announced the arrest of 14 suspects over Wednesday’s attack on APC supporters travelling to the Tinubu–Dikko campaign flag-off in Funtua.

Police said a female passenger was injured and vehicles damaged along the Yashi–Funtua road in Malumfashi. They did not establish the suspects’ political affiliation or motive.

The incident occurred on the approach route. The state APC’s earlier description of a peaceful rally concerned the event at Funtua Township Stadium; it did not specifically address the road attack.

World.title: Hamzat unveils 100-point manifesto, pledges child protection agency, state wealth fund
World.content:
The Lagos State All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate, Obafemi Hamzat, has unveiled a 100-point manifesto, promising to establish a child protection and nutrition agency, create a state wealth fund and introduce a public service delivery office within his first 100 days in office if elected governor.

Mr Hamzat announced the proposals on Friday at the launch of his manifesto and campaign theme, Lagos, Forward Together, organised by the Lagos State APC PBAT-KOH Campaign Council 2027 at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts, Iganmu, Lagos.

The manifesto, which he described as ‘The Lagos Promise’ and called the Hamzat Compact, contains seven pillars covering people, infrastructure, economic opportunities, government operations, inclusion, security and citizenship.

Mr Hamzat said 87 of the 100 pledges were firm commitments within the powers of the state government, while the remaining 13 were aspirations dependent on consultations with the federal government and other institutions, including the courts.

He promised to publish a scorecard against which residents could assess his administration’s performance.

“If one of them is not delivered, it will be noted, and I must own it,” he said.

For his first 100 days in office, Mr Hamzat said he would send a bill to the Lagos State House of Assembly to establish a Child Protection and Nutrition Agency. The proposed agency, he said, would ensure that every child below 18 was either in school or learning a trade and had adequate food.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He also promised to establish a Lagos State Service Delivery Office through an executive order. The office, to be chaired by the governor, would publish baseline figures for assessing the administration’s commitments.

The third proposal is a state wealth fund, which, he said, would have an independent board and publish its accounts to preserve resources for future generations.

Mr Hamzat said his administration would introduce service charters in government offices, setting out the services residents should expect and the standards to be met. He promised that complaints would be acknowledged within 48 hours, answered within seven days and resolved within 30 days.

“Accountability will not wait for the end of my term. It begins in my first 100 days. My manifesto is a promise to Lagosians. The promise, as we all know, has seven letters, seven pillars, and 100 pledges. Inside there are 100 pledges. So as we know, P stands for People First. R stands for Renewal. O stands for Opportunity. M stands for Machinery of Government. I for inclusion. S for security and resilience. And E for every citizen. So seven letters, seven pillars, one word,” he said.

Healthcare, education and jobs

On healthcare, Mr Hamzat promised to increase the number of maternal and child centres from six to 15, complete ongoing hospital projects and build two new general hospitals in Ogombo and Ibeju-Lekki.

He also pledged to upgrade 100 primary healthcare centres to flagship status and recruit more doctors, nurses and midwives.

Among the projects he cited were the new Massey Children’s Hospital, which he said would have 150 beds, and another general hospital project with 280 beds. He also mentioned the Shomolu General Hospital project, expected to provide 150 beds.

“Our promise is that we will deliver two new general hospitals at Ogombo and Ibeju Lekki, expand the capacity of existing general hospitals, and upgrade 100 primary healthcare centres to flagship status. We will strengthen the health workforce. We will hire more doctors, more nurses and more midwives,” he said.

In education, the candidate promised to strengthen the EkoEXCEL programme in public primary schools, improve teaching and learning outcomes and expand opportunities for technical and vocational training.

He said his administration would pursue plans for a University of Medicine and Health Sciences in Lagos and ensure that children remained in school. Mr Hamzat also promised to review teachers’ compensation packages.

“We will review your compensation package, so that your pay matches the work we demand from you,” he said.

On employment, he argued that businesses would create most of the jobs needed in Lagos and that government should focus on removing obstacles to their growth.

He proposed a single schedule of local government charges, easier business permits, improved access to credit and a defined share of state procurement for qualifying small businesses.

He also promised to introduce a vocational placement scheme under which students in technical schools would spend between six and 12 months with employers, with the state paying 40 per cent of their stipends.

For artisans, he proposed free skills certification at their workplaces and in languages they understand.

Mr Hamzat said the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund had provided more than N15 billion to over 21,000 businesses, while businesses supported through the scheme had created more than 300,000 jobs. These figures were presented as part of his account of the administration’s achievements.

Transport, housing and environment

On transportation, Mr Hamzat said his proposed administration would extend the Blue Line rail service to Okokomaiko and work with the federal government to advance the Green Line from Marina to the Lekki Free Trade Zone.

He also promised to connect the Blue and Red rail lines at the National Theatre station, expand ferry services and introduce integrated ticketing across road, rail and water transport.

“Lagos, we must know, is a water state. The lagoon must therefore be our third highway,” he said.

He pledged to dredge an additional 140-kilometre water corridor, optimise ferry routes and procure 75 riverine vessels.

On roads, he promised to prioritise inner roads in collaboration with local governments and local council development areas, while accelerating work on major road projects, including the coastal road along the Lekki-Epe axis.

The candidate also promised to complete ongoing housing projects and develop additional homes through partnerships with the private sector. He proposed mortgages requiring a 10 per cent deposit, single-digit interest rates and longer repayment periods.

On security, he said he would strengthen the Lagos State Neighbourhood Safety Agency and extend its presence to wards across the state’s 20 local government areas and 37 local council development areas. He also promised to expand street lighting and CCTV coverage.

For the environment, Mr Hamzat set a target of 95 per cent waste collection coverage through improved operations by private sector participants. He promised to complete waste transfer facilities, develop a waste recovery facility and complete a waste-to-energy project at Agbowa.
