“On waste, we will strengthen community collections, reach 95% coverage by optimizing the PSP, that is the private sector participant deliveries, and make Lagos cleaner. We will complete the transfer loading stations at Olusosun and Solous III in Alimosho.

“We will deliver a recovery facility and complete the waste-to-energy facility at Agbowa. 30,000 Lagosians already collect and sort this state’s waste, and we will bring them into the system, and we train them, equip them, and pay them properly. Essential work deserves recognition,” he said.

The pledge comes amid persistent challenges with waste collection and disposal in Lagos, where gaps in the state’s waste management system have left some communities struggling with irregular collection and inadequate disposal services.

A Premium Times investigation found that waste collection services remain uneven across the state, with some households receiving regular services while others have limited or no access to formal collection. The investigation also highlighted the pressure on existing disposal infrastructure and the difficulties residents face in managing refuse.

Sanwo-Olu backs Hamzat, cites years of working relationship

Earlier, Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu urged Lagos residents to support Mr Hamzat, describing him as an experienced public servant who had been involved in major decisions and projects during their seven years working together.

The governor recalled that Mr Hamzat had sought the governorship in 2018 but stepped aside after party leaders asked him to allow Governor Sanwo-Olu to emerge as the candidate.

He said Mr Hamzat accepted to serve as his running mate and had remained loyal throughout their time in office.

“In seven years, there has not been one day, not one, when I had to wonder whose side my deputy was on,” Governor Sanwo-Olu said.

He cited the COVID-19 response, the development of the Blue and Red rail lines and the arrival of the first ship at the Lekki Deep Sea Port among the major events in which Mr Hamzat had been involved.

The governor described the candidate as a key participant in the administration’s planning and project implementation, particularly in technical matters.

He framed Mr Hamzat’s candidacy as a continuation of the APC’s successive administrations in Lagos, from Bola Tinubu to Babatunde Fashola, Akinwunmi Ambode and himself.

“There has been one government. There has been one direction. There has been one voice. This is not the time to experiment with Lagos. This is the time to consolidate,” he said.

APC chairman, former deputy governor endorse candidate

The Lagos APC chairman, Cornelius Ojelabi, described the manifesto as a covenant between the party, its candidate and the electorate.

Mr Ojelabi said the APC administrations in Lagos had recorded achievements in infrastructure, transportation, education, healthcare, housing and economic development.

He called for continuity but said it should not prevent the government from addressing shortcomings.

“Continuity must not mean complacency. It must mean building on proven achievements, correcting identified shortcomings, and pursuing greater progress with renewed determination,” he said.

He described Mr Hamzat as a candidate with experience in public service and the private sector, adding that his time as deputy governor had prepared him for the state’s top office.

Former Lagos Deputy Governor Sarah Sosan, speaking on behalf of the state’s Governors’ Advisory Council, also endorsed Mr Hamzat, describing him as a committed public servant with experience as a commissioner and deputy governor.

Mrs Sosan said Lagos should build on its existing development record rather than abandon policies and projects that had worked.

“Lagos is not for experiment,” she said.

She said the manifesto should address the needs of residents in areas including roads, transportation, education, healthcare, security, housing and the environment.

The APC leaders called on party members to mobilise support for Mr Hamzat ahead of the governorship election.

World.title: Obasanjo criticises Tinubu’s borrowings, says debt could destroy generations of Nigerians
World.content:
Former President Olusegun Obasanjo has criticised the Bola Tinubu administration’s continued pursuit of domestic and external loans to finance the national budget and execute projects across various sectors, warning that excessive borrowing could destroy future generations.

Mr Obasanjo, who democratically governed Nigeria between 1999 and 2007, argued that the country’s continued borrowing and reliance on foreign institutions, particularly the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), might not address its economic challenges, insisting that the institutions were not established to solve Nigeria’s problems.

The former president spoke on Friday in Abeokuta, the Ogun State capital, at the Ajibosin Platform, a public forum themed “Leveraging Artificial Intelligence to Solve Grassroots Problems and Accelerate National Development.”

Tinubu’s borrowing plans

The Tinubu administration, like its predecessor, has continued to rely on domestic and external loans to finance government projects, with several borrowing requests submitted to and approved by the National Assembly.

On Tuesday, President Tinubu sought the National Assembly’s approval to proceed with the processing of external loans worth $20,517,755,901 and €1,045,083,643 under the 2026–2027 Supplementary External Borrowing Plan.

The request came about five months after the National Assembly approved a $516.3 million loan from Deutsche Bank AG to finance the construction of the Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway, a flagship infrastructure project under the administration’s Renewed Hope Agenda.

The loan has a tenure of nine years, including a grace period of up to three years, with an interest rate capped at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange’s Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) plus 5.3 per cent annually.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The facility is backed by insurance from the Islamic Corporation for the Insurance of Investment and Export Credit, the insurance arm of the Islamic Development Bank.

In March, the National Assembly also approved a $6 billion external borrowing plan for the federal government.

Of the amount, $5 billion was to be sourced from First Abu Dhabi Bank to support the national budget, while a $1 billion export finance facility from the United Kingdom, arranged by Citibank, was earmarked for the rehabilitation of Tin Can Island Port and the Lagos Port Complex.

President Tinubu has repeatedly defended his administration’s borrowing decisions, stating that loans are necessary to finance critical infrastructure and other development projects.

On Thursday, the president defended his administration’s borrowing plans, saying, “The real question is not how much we borrow, but what we build, what value we create and what future we leave behind.”

In April, he said his administration would continue to borrow whenever necessary, insisting that borrowing should not be viewed negatively.

Mr Tinubu spoke at the State House during a meeting with Plateau State leaders led by Governor Caleb Mutfwang and the APC National Chairman, Nentawe Yilwatda.

“If we have to borrow, we borrow. Borrowing is not leprosy, we just have to work hard to be able to pay for it,” the president had said.

Debt destroys generations

Reacting to the president’s remarks, Mr Obasanjo described the comparison of debt with leprosy as “absolute nonsense”, stating that excessive borrowing could burden generations yet unborn.

“And for anybody to say debt is no leprosy, is absolute nonsense. Debt is worse than leprosy. Because leprosy destroys only one person. Debt destroys generations,” he said.

The former president also faulted Nigeria’s economic management, recalling that when he started his farm 47 years ago, the naira exchanged at N1 to $1.85.

“When I started my farm, 47 years ago, naira to the dollar was one naira to $1.85. Forty-seven years ago. What has Nigeria done in 47 years that we now have 1,500 naira to the dollar? What have we done?” he asked.

He also questioned the capacity of the country’s political leadership to make decisions capable of improving the living conditions of Nigerians.

“What do our leaders know? And what do they not know? And from what they know, what can they do for us?

“World Bank and IMF were not designed for us. They were not built by us. They were built before we became independent. And that’s the people who would determine what we do,” he added.

Mr Obasanjo further cautioned against blindly adopting economic prescriptions from foreign-trained experts without considering Nigeria’s peculiar economic circumstances.

Nigeria’s debt profile

Nigeria’s debt burden has increased in recent years as the federal government has relied on domestic and external borrowing to finance budget deficits and infrastructure projects.

Although the country’s debt-to-GDP ratio has generally been considered moderate compared with that of some peer economies, analysts have raised concerns about the government’s limited revenue base and its capacity to meet debt obligations.

A substantial share of government revenue goes towards debt servicing, limiting the funds available for infrastructure, public services and other development priorities.

The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have repeatedly urged Nigeria to strengthen revenue mobilisation, improve tax collection and ensure that borrowed funds support productive investments capable of generating economic returns.

The federal government has maintained that external borrowing is necessary to address the country’s infrastructure deficit, finance development projects and meet its budgetary obligations. Officials have also argued that borrowing on favourable terms can help manage financing costs and support economic growth.

World.title: Five key lessons from Nigeria Health Watch’s 2026 Health Conference
World.content:
Nigeria has seen advances in medical research, technology, and healthcare innovation, yet many communities still struggle to access essential health services.

From infectious disease outbreaks and maternal deaths to inadequate financing and shortages of health workers, the country’s healthcare challenges extend beyond the availability of new technologies.

These challenges dominated discussions at the 2026 Future of Health Conference, organised by Nigeria Health Watch, where experts examined how promising innovations could be translated into practical improvements in healthcare delivery.

The 11th edition of the annual conference brought together policymakers, researchers, health professionals, innovators, development partners and private-sector representatives to discuss ways to strengthen Nigeria’s health system.

The discussions focused on moving beyond pilot projects and isolated successes to interventions that can reach more people, improve health outcomes and remain effective over time.

Across presentations, panel discussions and partner sessions, five key lessons emerged.

1. Innovation must deliver measurable results

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

One of the conference’s central messages was that developing a new technology or healthcare intervention does not automatically translate into better health outcomes.

Experts emphasised that an innovation’s success should be measured by its ability to solve real problems, improve access to care, and produce lasting results.

This means looking beyond introducing new technologies to whether they are affordable, accessible and sustainable.

For example, a medical device may improve diagnosis in a health facility. Still, its impact will remain limited if no trained workers can operate it or systems ensure patients receive appropriate treatment.

The discussions also highlighted the importance of addressing financing, infrastructure and workforce challenges that often prevent promising innovations from reaching communities.

The lesson was that innovation should be judged not only by what has been developed, but by the difference it makes in people’s lives.

2. Reliable data can change health decisions

Another major lesson was the importance of accurate data in understanding health challenges, measuring progress and guiding government decisions.

A presentation on Nigeria’s HIV response illustrated how inaccurate estimates can affect the interpretation of health programme performance.

According to the presentation, a national survey revised the estimated number of people living with HIV in Nigeria from 3.2 million to 1.8 million.

The revision substantially changed the reported treatment coverage figure, demonstrating how improved data can alter assessments of progress without an equivalent immediate increase in the number of people receiving treatment.

The example showed why reliable population estimates are important when evaluating the effectiveness of public health interventions.

Research on malaria drug resistance provided another illustration.

Researchers are using molecular analysis of malaria parasites to identify patterns of drug resistance across different locations, generating evidence that could help inform treatment policies and public health responses.

However, experts stressed that collecting data and conducting research were not enough.

The findings must also be communicated clearly to policymakers and incorporated into health programmes to influence decisions and improve outcomes.

3. Communities must be involved in health solutions

Discussions on Lassa fever research highlighted the importance of involving communities in disease surveillance, research and healthcare delivery.

Researchers involved in the ENABLE study explained how community engagement helped identify infections that might otherwise have gone undetected.

In some cases, symptoms such as tiredness were not initially considered serious enough to raise concerns about possible infection.

The experience demonstrated how working closely with communities can improve understanding of diseases and help researchers identify cases that may be missed through routine surveillance.

The research also examined how Lassa fever affects different population groups, including children, and the need to better understand the long-term health effects survivors experience.

Beyond infectious diseases, the discussions showed that community participation can help health workers identify barriers to care, understand local concerns and develop more appropriate interventions.

The broader lesson was that communities should not simply receive healthcare interventions. They should also help shape how those interventions are designed and delivered.

4. Primary healthcare requires trained workers, not just equipment

Maternal healthcare discussions drew attention to the challenges pregnant women face in accessing essential services, particularly in underserved communities.

A presentation on a Project HOPE-supported initiative in Bwari Area Council of the Federal Capital Territory described efforts to improve maternal healthcare across 10 primary healthcare facilities.

The initiative combines health worker training, point-of-care testing equipment and ultrasound services to strengthen antenatal care.

Under the arrangement, five facilities serve as hubs equipped with point-of-care ultrasound machines, while the remaining facilities refer pregnant women to the hubs when scans are needed.

The intervention aims to improve access to ultrasound examinations during pregnancy and support the early identification of complications requiring further medical attention.

However, the presentation also highlighted that providing equipment is only one part of improving healthcare.

Health workers need appropriate training, mentorship, and ongoing supervision to use diagnostic tools effectively and interpret findings.

ALSO READ: Nigeria Health Watch to host conference on scaling health innovations

Facilities also need functional referral systems to ensure that patients requiring additional care can access it.

The lesson was that strengthening primary healthcare requires coordinated investment in equipment, skilled personnel and service delivery systems.

Without these supporting structures, even useful technologies may fail to deliver their intended benefits.

5. Epidemic preparedness must begin before an outbreak

The final major lesson centred on preparing for disease outbreaks before they occur.

Experts highlighted the importance of sustained investment in vaccine research, diagnostic tools, manufacturing capacity and partnerships among governments, researchers and the private sector.

Discussions on the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations’ (CEPI) 100 Days Mission illustrated the importance of early preparation.

The initiative aims to develop safe and effective vaccines against a new pandemic threat within 100 days of identifying the threat, with a focus on achieving initial authorisation and readiness for manufacturing at scale.

The target does not mean that entire populations would be vaccinated within 100 days.

Rather, it requires scientific research, vaccine platforms, regulatory processes and manufacturing arrangements to be sufficiently developed before a new outbreak emerges.

Experts also identified sustained financing as a major challenge, particularly because the benefits of preparedness are often less visible when there is no active public health emergency.

The discussions emphasised the need for long-term partnerships among governments, philanthropic organisations, researchers and industry to support equitable access to vaccines and other essential health technologies.

The lesson was that effective outbreak response depends largely on the investments, systems and partnerships established before a public health emergency begins.

World.title: Süper Lig: Osimhen scores again as Galatasaray thrash Konyaspor
World.content:
Victor Osimhen continued his impressive goalscoring form as Galatasaray strengthened their grip on top spot in the Turkish Süper Lig with a commanding 4-0 victory over Konyaspor on Friday.

The Super Eagles striker opened the scoring in the 12th minute, taking his league tally to nine goals in eight appearances this season as Okan Buruk’s side moved to 22 points after 10 matches.

Galatasaray made an early statement when Osimhen rose to meet Gabriel Sara’s free kick with a powerful header, giving the hosts the lead.

The Nigerian came close to doubling his tally before the break, but his effort from the left side of the penalty area in stoppage time was tipped over the crossbar.

Yunus Akgün had earlier made it 2-0 in the 28th minute, finishing from outside the box after a well-worked corner involving Sara and Batrakov.

Galatasaray maintained their dominance after the restart, with Aleksey Batrakov extending the lead in the 49th minute. The Russian midfielder collected Sara’s pass inside the area and finished past the goalkeeper to register his first league goal for the club.

The hosts added a fourth from the penalty spot in the 55th minute after VAR overturned referee Cihan Aydın’s initial decision to award a corner following an incident involving Rafael Leão. The Portuguese forward converted the spot kick to register his first goal for Galatasaray and complete the rout.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Osimhen was substituted in the 61st minute after recording five shots, three on target, and contributing another goal to Galatasaray’s winning performance.

The result also ended a difficult run for the Istanbul giants, who had lost four of their previous six visits to Konyaspor, including a 2-0 defeat on their last trip.

Awaziem plays full match in Konyaspor Defeat

Fellow Nigerian Chidozie Awaziem featured for the full 90 minutes but could not prevent Konyaspor from suffering a heavy home defeat.

The defender arrived on the back of a match-winning performance against Gençlerbirliği, where he scored twice in a 2-0 victory, but faced a difficult evening against the league leaders.

Awaziem recorded two interceptions, three clearances and three recoveries, won three of his four ground duels and completed 97 per cent of his passes.

The appearance was his eighth league outing of the season, taking his playing time in the Turkish top flight to 607 minutes.

Galatasaray, who have now won eight of their 10 league matches, will turn their attention to the UEFA Champions League, where they are scheduled to host VfB Stuttgart on Tuesday, 3rd November.

World.title: Abiodun’s Road Revolution: From forgotten communities to connected economic corridors, By Kayode Akinmade
World.content:
Infrastructure development is one of the most visible measures of governance because its impact is felt in the everyday lives of citizens. A good road connects communities, shortens travel time, facilitates commerce, improves access to healthcare and education, enhances security and creates opportunities for economic growth. Beyond the convenience of transportation, roads are critical instruments of social integration and economic transformation.

For Ogun State, whose strategic location places it at the intersection of major commercial and industrial activities in Nigeria, road infrastructure is particularly important. Sharing boundaries with Lagos, the country’s commercial nerve centre, and serving as a major gateway to the Southwest and other parts of the country, Ogun requires an extensive and efficient road network to sustain its expanding population, growing industrial base and increasing commercial activities.

It was against this background that Governor Dapo Abiodun placed infrastructure development at the centre of his administration’s development agenda upon assuming office in May 2019.

The task before the administration was enormous. Years of inadequate maintenance, increasing population pressure, rapid urbanisation and the expansion of commercial activities had left several roads across the state in deplorable conditions. Many communities, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas, had endured prolonged difficulties accessing neighbouring towns, markets, schools, healthcare facilities and other essential services.

For some communities, travelling a few kilometres could become an exhausting experience, especially during the rainy season. Farmers struggled to move their produce to markets, traders incurred additional transportation costs, while residents of emerging urban settlements faced the daily frustration of deteriorating roads.

The Abiodun administration therefore adopted a statewide approach to road development, recognising that infrastructure should not be concentrated in a few urban centres but distributed across the state’s 20 local government areas.

More than seven years into the administration, the scale of the intervention is reflected in the approximately 1,700 kilometres of roads constructed or rehabilitated across the state since 2019. The government has set a target of delivering 2,000 kilometres before the end of its tenure.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The figures represent an extensive infrastructure programme involving the construction of new roads, reconstruction of failed roads, rehabilitation of existing routes and the provision of supporting infrastructure.

But beyond the kilometres, the more important story is what these interventions mean for communities and the state’s economy.

CONNECTING COMMUNITIES, OPENING UP OPPORTUNITIES

One of the defining features of the administration’s road programme is its attention to communities that have historically struggled with poor road access.

In Ogun West, the reconstruction of the Ilaro–Owode Road has strengthened connectivity across the Yewa axis, while the completion of the Odo-Afa and Afon bridges along the Imeko-Afon corridor has addressed critical transportation challenges in rural communities.

Other interventions, including the General Hospital–Aferiku Road and Oke Erinja–Erinja Road Phase 2, have improved access to communities in Yewa South.

These projects demonstrate the importance of infrastructure beyond major urban centres. For farming communities, an accessible road can determine how quickly agricultural produce reaches markets, how much farmers spend on transportation and how much value they ultimately derive from their investments.

In a state with considerable agricultural potential, connecting farming communities to markets is central to food security, rural development and poverty reduction.

The same development philosophy is evident in other parts of the state.

In Obafemi-Owode Local Government, the Mowe–Ofada and Siun–Owode roads have improved access within rapidly developing communities. The Siun–Owode–Ofada corridor is particularly significant because of its connection to economic activities and settlements along the Lagos–Ibadan Expressway.

In Ifo Local Government, the rehabilitation of roads such as Akute–Gbero–Isase, Alhaji Kosoko, Ajuwon–Akute and other adjoining routes has addressed long-standing transportation difficulties in communities experiencing increasing population growth and urban expansion.

For residents of these communities, road infrastructure is not an abstract government achievement. It is about spending less time in traffic, reducing vehicle maintenance costs, improving access to workplaces and making daily commercial activities less stressful.

REBUILDING THE INDUSTRIAL CORRIDORS

Perhaps nowhere is the economic significance of road infrastructure more evident than in Ogun’s industrial belt.

Ogun is home to several manufacturing clusters, industrial estates and commercial centres, many of which depend on efficient road networks for the movement of raw materials, finished products, workers and other logistics.

The reconstruction of the Ota–Abeokuta Road, a major 70-kilometre corridor, is one of the significant interventions in this regard. The road serves communities and commercial establishments across the Ado-Odo/Ota and Abeokuta axes.

Similarly, road projects around Lusada, Alapoti, Igbesa and other industrial communities are important to the continued expansion of manufacturing activities in Ogun West.

The Lusada–Alapoti Road and other adjoining routes are particularly relevant to industrial development in the Agbara–Ota axis, where manufacturing companies depend on reliable transportation infrastructure.

The administration’s road programme also complements its broader efforts to attract investments and position Ogun as a preferred destination for industrial and commercial enterprises.

The relationship between roads and investment is straightforward. Investors require access to industrial locations, efficient movement of goods, dependable logistics and connectivity to major markets. Without these, the cost of doing business increases and the attractiveness of an investment destination diminishes.

This explains why road infrastructure remains an essential component of the administration’s economic development strategy.

The emerging industrial developments around the Gateway International Airport, the proposed Gateway Deep Sea Port and the Blue Marine Economic Zone further underscore the importance of expanding and improving road connectivity across the state.

These projects require an integrated transportation network capable of supporting industrial production, maritime activities, warehousing, distribution and international trade.

URBAN RENEWAL AND THE GROWING POPULATION

Ogun’s proximity to Lagos has created enormous demographic and economic opportunities, but it has also placed considerable pressure on existing infrastructure.

Communities such as Mowe, Ibafo, Magboro, Arepo, Akute, Ajuwon, Alagbole, Ijoko and Ota have experienced rapid population growth as more people seek residential accommodation outside Lagos.

This expansion has increased demand for roads, drainage, public transportation and other essential infrastructure.

The administration’s interventions in these areas are therefore significant to the management of urban growth.

The reconstruction of Magboro Road, Alagbole–Ajuwon Road, Akute–Ajuwon Road and other connecting routes reflects the government’s response to the transportation challenges associated with expanding settlements.

These projects are expected to improve connectivity within the communities and strengthen their links with Lagos and other parts of Ogun State.

In Abeokuta, the state capital, several road projects have also been undertaken to improve mobility and enhance the urban environment.

Similar interventions across Sagamu, Ijebu-Ode, Ikenne and other major towns form part of the wider effort to improve road infrastructure throughout the state.

FROM ROAD CONSTRUCTION TO ECONOMIC TRANSFORMATION

The significance of the road revolution should ultimately be measured by its contribution to economic and social development.

A road connecting a rural community to a major market is an economic asset. A road providing access to a hospital can make a difference in emergency situations. A road linking an industrial estate to a major highway can improve productivity and reduce logistics costs.

These are the practical outcomes that give meaning to infrastructure investment.

The Abiodun administration has consistently argued that its infrastructure policy is designed to democratise development by ensuring that communities across the three senatorial districts benefit from government interventions.

With approximately 1,700 kilometres of roads constructed or rehabilitated since 2019, the administration continues to pursue its 2,000-kilometre target.

The government has also incorporated inherited road projects into its programme, demonstrating that infrastructure development requires continuity and sustained investment beyond political and administrative transitions.

Nevertheless, the scale of the remaining infrastructure needs must not be overlooked. Several communities continue to demand improved roads, while increasing traffic, population growth and heavy-duty industrial vehicles place additional pressure on existing infrastructure.

The challenge, therefore, is to sustain the pace of construction, ensure quality delivery, maintain completed roads and prioritise projects according to their economic and social importance.

Road construction must also be accompanied by adequate drainage systems, proper engineering standards and effective maintenance arrangements to ensure that public investments deliver lasting value.

THE ROAD AHEAD

As Ogun State moves towards the final phase of the Abiodun administration, the ambition of delivering at least 2,000 kilometres of roads provides a measurable benchmark for assessing the government’s infrastructure programme.

But the broader significance of the initiative extends beyond the numbers.

From the rural communities of Yewa to the industrial clusters of Agbara and Ota, from the expanding settlements along the Lagos–Ibadan Expressway to the commercial centres of Ijebu-Ode and Sagamu, road infrastructure is an important part of the state’s evolving development story.

The objective is to create a connected Ogun where communities are not isolated by poor roads, farmers can move their produce more efficiently, businesses can operate with reduced logistical constraints and residents can enjoy improved access to opportunities.

The journey is far from complete. The demands of a rapidly expanding state will continue to require investment, planning and sustained attention to infrastructure.

Yet the approximately 1,700 kilometres of roads already constructed or rehabilitated provide a substantial basis for examining the administration’s road development record.

Ultimately, the true measure of a road revolution is not simply the number of kilometres delivered. It is the number of communities connected, the economic activities stimulated, the transportation difficulties reduced and the opportunities created for the people.

That is the larger development story behind Abiodun’s road infrastructure programme: moving Ogun from isolated communities towards an increasingly connected network of economic corridors.

World.title: US, S/Korea, Japan vow ‘complete’ N/Korea denuclearization
World.content:
The United States, South Korea and Japan reaffirmed their commitment to the “complete denuclearization” of North Korea on Saturday, as Pyongyang continues to reject disarmament ahead of possible talks with Washington.

Speculation is mounting over a potential meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at next month’s APEC summit in China, with Trump making repeated overtures to Pyongyang for nuclear talks.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and his Japanese counterpart Toshimitsu Motegi “reaffirmed their resolute commitment to the complete denuclearization” of North Korea during talks on Friday on the sidelines of a Group of 20 (G20) meeting in Atlanta in the US state of Georgia, the US State Department said.

They also pledged “full implementation” of UN Security Council resolutions, including a ban on supporting revenue for North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.

Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea, which is backed by Russia and China, has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law, with its regime repeatedly declaring its atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible.

– Open to meeting –

Trump has made repeated overtures to Pyongyang for nuclear talks, while scaling back joint military drills with ally South Korea.

The mercurial US leader even bucked long-held US policy last year by conceding that North Korea was already “sort of a nuclear power”, while reaching out to Pyongyang for talks, saying he was “100 percent” open to a meeting — a suggestion that went unanswered.

Analysts and South Korea’s spy agency say Kim may have conveyed Pyongyang’s position on potential talks with Trump to Beijing during a recent visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong.

South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung — who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions — suggested in September that Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North’s nuclear programme in return for sanctions relief.

Critics have said such an approach risks tacitly accepting North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to win sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal.

Analysts say China may also be moving towards tacit acceptance, pointing to the omission of North Korean denuclearisation from statements after Kim and Chinese President Xi Jinping met in June.

Pyongyang denounced a joint statement on Saturday by a group of nations monitoring sanctions implementations against it, vowing that “the stereotyped sanctions racket of the US and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK (North Korea) as a nuclear weapons state”.

World.title: NYSC Members Kidnap: ‘I didn’t know passengers in my bus had AK-47 rifles – Driver tells court
World.content:
The suspects.

By Chidi Nkwopara

One of the drivers from whose bus prospective members of the National Youths Service Corps, NYSC, were kidnapped on October 1, has told the court he was unaware that two of his passengers had AK-47 rifles in a bag.

Read Also: NYSC kidnap: DSS witness exposes how suspects were identified

The Department of State Services, DSS, on Friday, called two witnesses in the ongoing suit, HOU/22C/2026, filed against Usman Aliyu, Mohamed Aliyu and Babangida Ali, over the kidnap of 20 prospective NYSC members. The graduates were travelling to their orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states.

Led in evidence by the Principal State Counsel, Mr. Ekezie Nwauzor, the second prosecution witness, PW2, a commercial motorcyclist, Mr. Light Timothy, gave a graphic account of how the first and second accused persons hired him to take them to where their colleagues were staying.

According to PW2, his two passengers were carrying a bag, which he never knew the content until they reached their lonely destination, where AK-47 rifles were brought out from it.

He recalled that when his passenger put a call to someone, his intonation sounded Hausa or Fulani and the fellow urged him to ply the Umuguma-Okuku Road in Owerri West Local Government Area of Imo State.

PW2 also told the court that at a point, fear gripped him and he wanted to go back but not long after, four men jumped out of the bush, collected the bag, opened it and brought out the AK-47 rifles.

Timothy also told the court that he would have been killed for wasting time on the road, if not that one of them pleaded on his behalf and he sped off from that point.

In his own evidence, the third prosecution witness, PW3, and Akwa Ibom Transport Company driver, Mr. Sunday Udoh, confirmed that he and another driver, Jeremiah, were carrying NYSC members from Ibadan, to their orientation camps.

They had a stopover at Onitsha and left 5.30am on October 1, 2026, adding that heading towards Owerri and not long after passing a checkpoint, he noticed two stationary mini buses.

He told the court that on sensing looming danger and he quickly tried to reverse but his vehicle hit something behind and they were stuck.

According to Udoh, he switched off his vehicle, ran to the other side of the highway, hid in the nearby bush and watched events from there.

Udoh, after identifying Usman Aliyu as one of the attackers, also said that the kidnappers took away five of his passengers and 15 from Jeremiah’s bus, into the bush.

After thorough cross-examination of the two witnesses by the defence counsel, Paschal Ofoma, Justice Emeka Orafu adjourned the matter for further hearing to November 3, 2026.

Vanguard News

World.title: Enugu APC releases updated campaign council list
World.content:
The Enugu State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) has released an updated list of its Campaign Council.

In a press release on Friday, the State Chairman of the party, Dr. Martin Chukwunweike, and the State Secretary, Hon. Chukwudi Nnadozie, said the update had become imperative as more critical stakeholders across the state expressed their readiness to be part of the team to deliver President Bola Tinubu, Governor Peter Mbah and all APC candidates in the 2027 general elections.
