World.title: U.S. set to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, despite risk they’ll be returned to Taliban
World.content:
The Trump administration is preparing to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum seekers to Pakistan on the first such flight of its kind, a senior administration official told NBC News — a move critics say could put their lives at risk.

The proposed deportation flight, which has not been publicly announced, could take place as early as Monday, according to rights advocates and families of detainees.

Among those facing deportation are relatives of Afghans who worked with the U.S. military in its 20-year war against the Taliban, which is now back in power. The deportees could face severe repercussions should Pakistan return them to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan as is widely expected.

Afghans driven from their country by war and political instability have been welcomed by the U.S. for decades, including tens of thousands who fled the country following the chaotic withdrawal of U.S.-led forces in 2021. President Donald Trump halted admissions for Afghans and other refugees when he returned to office last year as part of a broader immigration crackdown.

His administration has deported thousands of people to countries that are not their own, many of them in Africa, in what immigration lawyers say is an effort to skirt international laws against returning asylum seekers to the countries they fled from. The legality of these so-called third-country deportation agreements is set to be debated by the Supreme Court in December.

It is not clear what kind of formal agreement the U.S. may have with Pakistan, but the senior administration official said the U.S. charter flight would not be able to land there without the Pakistan government’s knowledge and approval. The deportation plan was earlier reported by Bloomberg and The New York Times.

Bloomberg cited a federal government official familiar with the plans as a source for its report, while The New York Times cited three U.S. officials.

Shawn VanDiver, president of the San Diego-based advocacy group AfghanEvac, said it had confirmed that in recent days at least 80 Afghans have been moved to Louisiana from 34 other ICE facilities around the country, 19 of them without legal representation.

He said it was possible that there were hundreds of Afghans at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center, which has served as a hub for ICE detainees before their deportation from the U.S.

If the U.S. sends Afghan detainees to Pakistan, they are not likely to be there long. Pakistan, which has hosted millions of Afghan refugees for decades, launched a sweeping crackdown in 2023, pressuring hundreds of thousands of Afghans to leave the country and forcibly deporting others.

They are arriving to an Afghanistan battered by multiple humanitarian crises, including widespread malnutrition, as well as an ongoing military conflict with neighboring Pakistan and a dramatic rollback of women’s rights under the Taliban’s hard-line Islamic policies.

VanDiver said the Trump administration would most likely be aware that Afghans sent to Pakistan would be at high risk of being returned to Afghanistan.

“You don’t have to be that smart to figure out that they’re sending them to Pakistan so that Pakistan will finish the job,” he said.

Regardless of whether they worked with the U.S. military, VanDiver said, any Afghans flown from the U.S. would be viewed with suspicion by the Taliban and at risk of persecution, imprisonment or worse.

That does not appear to be a major concern for the White House, said the senior administration official, who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

“The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’” the official said.

VanDiver and others say the Trump administration’s treatment of Afghan allies could also have long-term consequences for U.S. national security by discouraging people in other countries from working with U.S. forces in future conflicts.

Asked whether the Trump administration was concerned about that, the official said, “I don’t think they care.”

The White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.” ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

A State Department spokesperson said the agency had “no plans to announce.”

“We reaffirm our position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security and prosperity of their citizens,” the spokesperson said.

Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.

The senior administration official said the Afghans on the flight could include people with deportation orders, people who were turned down for asylum and people whose temporary protected status was terminated by the Trump administration. Many of the Afghans facing deportation requested asylum after crossing into the U.S. from Mexico, VanDiver said, and some of their cases are still pending.

‘We just sat there and cried’

Charlotte, a U.S. citizen whose Afghan husband has been in ICE detention since early 2025, said he had been moved to the Louisiana facility from Pennsylvania this month and told he would be deported in early November. She declined to be identified by her full name out of concern that her husband could be targeted by the Taliban.

Charlotte said she and her husband, whose asylum case has been pending for nine years, were visiting family in Maryland last year when he accidentally crossed into West Virginia and was pulled over. Though he was carrying his valid Illinois driver’s license, he did not have his work permit with him.

“When he was pulled over,” she said, “the sheriff actually said, ‘I’m an ICE agent. You’re going to immigration custody. I don’t care if the charges are dismissed, or I don’t care if you have a five-year work permit or Social Security card. I don’t care if you’re legal. Trump’s administration just took over — you’re going directly to immigration custody.’”

Charlotte sold their home in Illinois and moved to Maryland with their son, now 6, in order to be able to visit her husband at the ICE facility where he was held in Pennsylvania, about 100 miles away.

“I lost my nice house, our car, we left everything behind,” she said.

Over the next 20 months, when she took her son to see his father at the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, they were always separated by plexiglass.

“They never let him hug him one time,” Charlotte said. “We just sat there and cried every time.”

But at least they knew where he was and that he was OK, she said. Now that he’s in Louisiana, she said, “we can’t even visit or even say goodbye, he’s over 1,200 miles away.”

With her husband potentially being sent to Pakistan or Afghanistan — a country he hasn’t been to since 2016 — the uncertainty is even greater; Charlotte said he is growing his beard to comply with the Taliban’s strict rules for men’s facial hair.

“I’m just terrified that he’s not going to be safe,” she said, “or he’s going to be held in the jail and there’s nothing I can do.”

Charlotte said she believed her husband had been targeted for deportation because of a past conviction for a nonviolent crime that has since been resolved.

“I still don’t think this should end our entire life, for a child not to see his dad,” she said.

“He’s completely devastated and traumatized,” she said of their son. “He wants to fight. He wants to go protest. He wants to speak to Donald Trump. He basically knows so much more than he should.”

The preparations for the deportation flight come nearly a year after a shooting in Washington that killed one National Guard member and seriously injured another. The suspect, an Afghan national who served alongside U.S. troops in Afghanistan and was evacuated to the U.S. in 2021, had been granted asylum by the Trump administration. Immigration restrictions were tightened after the shooting.

VanDiver said the Trump administration may also be using the Pakistan flight as a test case for Camp As Sayliyah, a U.S.-run camp in Qatar where more than 1,000 Afghans who had been slated for resettlement in the U.S. have been stranded since Trump returned to office last year.

Asked about VanDiver’s claim, the White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson again said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.”

According to AfghanEvac, the camp was housing 287 men as of July, 319 women and 433 children. Most of them have been approved for U.S. resettlement after extensive vetting, and many of the adults worked alongside U.S. forces in Afghanistan.

The group at Camp As Sayliyah also includes 150 relatives of U.S. military service members, AfghanEvac said.

00:39 Afghan refugees in Qatar protest over travel suspension 00:00 00:00

The State Department said earlier this year that everyone would be removed from the camp by March 31, a deadline that was later extended to Sept. 30. In September, the Trump administration delayed its closure by another nine months, The Associated Press reported.

Earlier this year, the administration considered sending the Afghans at Camp As Sayliyah to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which is experiencing the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

In a statement on Friday, AfghanEvac accused the Trump administration of planning the Afghan deportation flight as the country is distracted by next week’s midterm election, “hoping no one is watching.”

“The government won’t say where these flights land, because it knows what happens to the people on them when they do,” the group said. “A government confident in what it is doing does not hide it.”

World.title: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
World.content:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.

The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protesters and groups of police charging to disperse protesters in Rome on Friday night.

After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe, more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.

The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France, where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.

Demonstrators gather at the Piazza della Repubblica in Rome on Friday. Sara Monetta / NBC News

Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.

In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.

00:40 Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome 00:00 00:00

Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”

The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”

Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”

“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” added Luca, who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.

Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.

They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.

Student protesters in Rome on Friday. Sara Monetta / NBC News

Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.

Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.

But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.

A man draped in the Palestinian flag joins a protest at the Piazza della Repubblica in Rome on Friday. Sara Monetta / NBC News

“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.

The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.

World.title: Daylight saving time ends Sunday. Here’s what to know as clocks ‘fall back’
World.content:
Clocks across much of the United States will fall back once again Sunday as daylight saving time comes to an end.

Congress and some states have tried multiple times this decade to get rid of the twice-yearly exercise but to no avail.

President Donald Trump has expressed support for ending the time changes, arguing that permanent daylight saving time would allow for more daylight to parallel daytime habits while shrinking after-hours activity, including crime. But many health and sleep experts argue against it, citing risks to health and safety.

Here is what to know as we prepare to spin our clocks back Sunday — or let our cellphones do it instantly.

When does daylight saving time end?

Daylight saving time started at 2 a.m. March 8 and ends at 2 a.m. Sunday.

Unlike in the spring, when we lose an hour and the clocks skip the 2 o’clock hour entirely, we will gain an extra hour Sunday, with clocks jumping from 1:59 a.m. back to 1 a.m.

The sun will also start setting earlier across the United States as we head into the late fall and winter.

The extra hour doesn’t necessarily mean more revelry on Halloween night: While some jurisdictions allow bars to serve last call according to Sunday’s updated time, California rules say bars must stop serving alcohol two hours past midnight, regardless of 1 a.m.’s repeat.

How long will standard time last?

Standard time across the United States will remain, as will earlier sunsets and darker evenings, until spring rolls around and daylight saving time starts once again on March 14.

Daylight saving time will end next year on Nov. 7.

The standardized start and end dates have been changed throughout the years, but since 2007, daylight saving time has started the second Sunday in March and ended the first Sunday in November, according to the Astronomical Applications Department of the U.S. Naval Observatory.

Why do we observe daylight saving time?

The practice, established by the Standard Time Act in 1918, according to the Astronomical Applications Department, is an effort to extend the daylight hours we have in the summertime by pushing off sunset an extra hour.

Daylight saving time, a contested idea after it was passed, was quickly repealed in 1919, becoming a local matter. It was re-enacted during the early days of World War II and observed from 1942 to 1945, according to the department.

After the war, the implementation of daylight saving time varied from state to state until the Uniform Time Act was passed in 1966, standardizing the dates of daylight saving time but allowing local exemptions if states or localities didn’t want to participate.

President Richard Nixon briefly moved the nation to year-round daylight saving time in 1974, but the extended morning darkness was widely panned and blamed for incidents of students being struck by vehicles. Congress subsequently reversed his time changes after Nixon resigned later that year.

Which states don’t observe?

Hawaii and most of Arizona don’t observe daylight saving time and therefore don’t change their clocks twice a year, according to the Astronomical Applications Department.

The U.S. territories of American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and the Northern Mariana Islands also observe permanent standard time, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Do other countries do this?

Most countries observe some version of “summer time,” according to the department, not all of them on the same schedule as the United States.

Most of the countries in the Northern Hemisphere that observe daylight saving time are in Europe and North America.

Some Southern Hemisphere countries also observe some version of daylight saving time, but below the equator, the seasons are swapped, so the start and end dates of their “summer time” are reversed from ours.

According to the Pew Research Center, only about a third of all countries observe daylight saving time. About half of all countries observed it at one point but no longer do.

What recent efforts have been made to end the practice?

Almost all states have considered legislation to stay on standard or daylight saving time, and 19 states have passed bills or resolutions to implement it year-round in the last seven years, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. But because federal law doesn’t allow for year-round daylight saving time, the states would have to wait for Congress to pass a bill to make the change.

The Senate passed the Sunshine Protection Act in 2022, which would make daylight saving time permanent year-round, but the bill didn’t advance in the House.

A version of the bill introduced in the House in January 2025 stalled in the Senate in summer.

In early October, Trump in a post on Truth Social urged Senate Republicans to “get moving” on the bill, saying the clock changing process “costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine.”

What do health experts say?

Some studies suggest that observing daylight saving time year-round could reduce the number of traffic accidents and the amount of crime.

But many health and sleep researchers aren’t in favor of permanent daylight saving time, namely because of the potential hazards of dark mornings, which would mean more children walking or driving to school in the dark.

Sleep experts prefer the back-and-forth of the clocks to permanent daylight saving time, and point to the increased risks of health problems when clocks aren’t closely aligned with the sun.

World.title: Daylight saving time is almost over. Here's what to know.
World.content:
Millions of Americans will gain an hour of sleep this weekend when the twice-a-year time change commonly known as daylight savings ends for 2026. Most of the U.S. will "fall back" an hour when the clocks change at 2 a.m. on Sunday.

Here's what to know about what's formally known as daylight saving time as it ends for the year:

What is daylight saving time, and why do we have it?

Daylight saving time is the period during the year, from March to early November, when the majority of the U.S. operates one hour ahead of standard time.

The move effectively "saves" an hour of daylight from the morning and adds it to the evening during the spring and summer months when the days are the longest. In the fall and winter months, when the days are shorter, the U.S. returns to standard time, with daylight coming earlier in the morning.

For example, in Boston on Saturday, before the time change, the sun will rise at 7:16 a.m. and set at 5:39 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. On Sunday, back on standard time, sunrise will be at 6:17 a.m. and sunset will be at 4:37 p.m.

The U.S. first adopted daylight saving time in 1918 during World War I as an effort to conserve fuel after Europe implemented its own time change, according to the Congressional Research Service. After the war, Congress repealed the clock switch but gave states the option to continue observing it.

During World War II and the 1970s energy crisis, Congress brought year-round daylight saving time to the U.S., again with the goal of reducing energy consumption. These experiments didn't last long.

After the war, the U.S. let states and municipalities decide for themselves if they wanted to keep daylight saving time and when to observe it. (Congress didn't establish a uniform start and end for the time change until 1966.) In the '70s, continuous daylight saving time was stopped before reaching the 10-month mark.

Will the U.S. move to year-round daylight saving time?

Earlier this year, legislation to once again make daylight saving time last all year long cleared a major hurdle in Congress. The bill, called the Sunshine Protection Act, passed the House in July and went to the Senate. The legislation would also let states opt out of daylight saving time altogether before the law takes effect.

President Trump, who supports the bill, accused a fellow Republican, Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, of holding up the legislation. Mr. Trump even posted to social media what he said was Cotton's cellphone number and urged people to call the senator to express their support for the measure.

In response, Cotton noted Congress has tried permanent daylight saving time before, only to go back to the twice-yearly time change "once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter."

There is a ticking clock for the Senate to take action on the bill. The legislation and any other bills awaiting approval in Congress are set to expire in early January when the new class of lawmakers elected in Tuesday's midterm elections takes office.

If the bill does die, the effort to change daylight saving time will have to start over and be approved by the House and the Senate before it can go to the president.

Did the time change today?

The time won't change until Sunday.

For 2026, the end of daylight saving time comes during the overnight hours after Halloween, giving revelers an extra hour of enjoying late-night costume parties — or an extra hour of sleep to recover from their fun.

But for parents of young children, the time change can be more of a trick and less of a treat, potentially disrupting their kids' sleep schedules until they adjust.

What day and time does daylight saving time end in November 2026?

Daylight saving time officially ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1.

Americans have been "falling back" on the first Sunday of November since 2007, when the most recent changes to daylight saving time took effect. A 2005 law moved the end date from the last Sunday of October.

Do we lose or gain an hour when daylight saving time ends?

Most Americans will gain an hour when daylight saving time ends, making up for the hour they lost when the clocks "sprang forward" in March.

When will daylight saving time start again in 2027?

Daylight saving time is set to begin in 2027 on Sunday, March 14, at 2 a.m. local time. The time change starts on the second Sunday of March, which falls on such a late date next year because the month starts on a Monday. In 2026, daylight saving time started on March 8.

The start date was also changed in 2007 to extend the length of daylight saving time, which previously began on the first Sunday of April.

Which states don't do daylight saving time?

Daylight saving time is observed in every state except for Hawaii and most of Arizona. The Navajo Nation, which is located in part of Arizona, observes the time change to stay on the same time as their communities in the neighboring states of New Mexico and Utah, according to the tribe.

The U.S. territories of American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands also don't observe daylight saving time.

Will my phone change for daylight saving time automatically?

Phones should change overnight to display the correct time if they're set to update automatically.

Apple, Google and Samsung have support pages with instructions for changing the clocks on their devices. Carriers like Simple Mobile and Straight Talk have also posted steps online for checking the settings on other phones.

World.title: U.S. approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
World.content:
The State Department approved on Friday the sale of 500 Patriot missile defense systems to Ukraine at a cost $2.1 billion.

In a statement released Friday, the State Department said the purchase will be paid for by Ukraine with donations from Canada and European allies such as Germany and Norway, and that no U.S. funds are involved in the sale.

"This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe," the department said. It also added the principal contractor in this agreement is Lockheed Martin and that there would be "no adverse impact" on U.S. defense readiness.

Assembling Patriot missiles at Lockheed Martin's production facility in Camden, Arkansas. CBS News

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauded the decision, and thanked President Trump, but warned that it may take years for the munitions to be delivered to Ukraine.

"We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger," Zelenskyy appealed on Friday evening.

In a post on X, the Ukrainian president said there had been more than 30 Russian strikes on his country's energy infrastructure in the past two weeks, targeting "the systems that sustain life in our cities and communities."

He appealed to the United States and European allies to provide Ukraine with the Patriot systems currently in their own stockpiles and replenish their arsenals with these 500 missiles, purchased by Ukraine, in the coming years.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stands in front of a Patriot air defense missile system at a military training area in Germany on June 11, 2024. Jens Büttner/picture alliance via Getty Images

"We are asking for decisions that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but at the very moment the threat is there," Zelenskyy added.

Ukraine has long warned of dwindling supplies of Patriots, which it uses to intercept strikes from Russia, and has previously accused the U.S. of slowing down deliveries of the critical missiles.

The development comes amid ongoing tensions between Ukraine's president and Mr. Trump, who faced criticism for waiving new sanctions on Russia just days before they were expected to take effect.

World.title: Judge orders DOJ to stop trying to "intimidate" California election officials
World.content:
A California judge late Friday ordered the federal government to stop demanding that state and local election officials separate out ballots or not count certain votes from alleged noncitizens, and to stop threatening officials with criminal prosecution if they do not comply.

The ruling from U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson came in response to a lawsuit filed a day earlier by labor unions and other groups, accusing the Trump administration of intimidating California election workers and interfering in the administration of the midterms.

The Justice Department has pressed officials in California this month to separate out mail ballots for roughly 20,000 people it alleges are not U.S. citizens, and has issued grand jury subpoenas for officials in Los Angeles County — part of a sweeping campaign by the Trump administration. Federal officials have also suggested for months that election workers could be prosecuted if they fail to stop noncitizens from voting.

The lawsuit cited the head of the Justice Department Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, sending letters to all 50 states and Washington, D.C., threatening to criminally prosecute local election officials in July, and the department's latest demand for lists of names of voters they believe are possibly noncitizens, as examples of unlawful conduct.

The judge on Friday found federal officials have likely violated the Voting Rights Act of 1965's prohibition on "attempting to intimidate, threaten or coerce" people who help others vote. She also said the government was acting outside its legal or constitutional authority.

"One of the hallmarks of a fair election is the freedom to exercise the right to vote free from threat, fear, or intimidation," she wrote. "Free exercise of the right to vote is a core tenet of our democracy. It requires safeguarding to ensure full participation and public trust in our elections."

Thompson also wrote: "Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters."

The judge issued a temporary restraining order that expires on Nov. 16, and scheduled the next hearing for Nov. 13.

In addition to blocking the Justice Department from threatening criminal prosecutions or demanding that officials separate out ballots, Thompson ordered the Justice Department to inform the court of any pending search warrant applications or subpoenas.

CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

The ruling was issued after another California federal judge on Wednesday denied the Justice Department's request to compel California to set aside more than 20,000 ballots for alleged noncitizens. He found that it violates "longstanding constitutional principles" giving states the authority to administer their own elections. The Trump administration appealed the matter to an appellate court, which also rejected a request to segregate the ballots on Friday.

World.title: Family of real estate CEO wounded in Toronto home invasion, officials say
World.content:
A search is underway for three armed men who broke into a mansion in Toronto, Canada, belonging to a real estate CEO in the early morning hours Thursday and attacked and injured the family inside, authorities said.

The suspects, who were masked, forced their way through a back entrance of the five-bedroom home in the Bridle Path neighborhood at around 3:40 a.m. local time, wielding guns and a hammer, Toronto police said.

Once inside, police said they went to the second floor of the home and confronted 75-year-old David Morton, his wife, 64-year-old Doriana Morton, and their two adult daughters, Maggie and Cristina.

"There was a demand made for valuables from within the home," Toronto Police Service Inspector Kristy Smith told reporters. "Whether or not they escaped with anything is uncertain at this point."



Police said David Morton, CEO of the MAC Group, and his daughters, ages 28 and 26, tried to fight off the intruders when shots were fired.

All three sustained gunshot wounds, Smith disclosed. And in a separate statement Friday, David Morton said that all four family members were also attacked by the suspects with the hammer.

David Morton said that he and his two daughters were still hospitalized Friday with gunshot wounds, but he did not provide details on their conditions.

"What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience," David Morton said in his statement. "... It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home."

The three male suspects, all believed to be in their 20s and wearing dark clothing, fled the scene in an SUV, police said.

"All these houses have good security," Cecil Hawkins, a former resident of Bridle Path, said. "So I'm kind of surprised. Shooting people in the house, it just seems mind-boggling."

According to Toronto police, there have been 119 home invasions so far in 2026, up 32.2% over this time last year.

Thursday's home invasion happened in the same neighborhood where a mansion belonging to rapper Drake was targeted in multiple break-in attempts in May 2024. A security guard for Drake was also wounded in a shooting outside the home at that time.

World.title: DOJ calls Alaska Senate allegations "troubling," asks to segregate ballots
World.content:
Anchorage, Alaska — The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska said new reporting on the origins of an independent candidate's Senate campaign "has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets" to the state, as federal officials in a separate civil case seek to segregate some of Alaska's Senate ballots.

Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for the District of Alaska, called the allegations about how Daniel J. Sullivan — a man with the same first and last name as incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan — ended up on the ballot "troubling."

"We are aware of the recent New York Times reporting regarding the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, that they orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J. Sullivan as a sham candidate, and we are taking that extremely seriously," he said in a press conference in Anchorage.

But Heyman declined to detail what specific crimes are being investigated, saying he's "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not."

"That's what we do, is we investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories, so I'm not going to comment on what those theories are, and I'm also not going to put the cart before the horse," he said.

Asked by CBS News why the Justice Department is choosing to escalate the case ahead of the election, Heyman said, "We're not escalating anything except to the extent that a new article came out."

"This has been going on sort of quietly for several months, with the intent not to escalate anything," he said, adding that investigators are going to take allegations involving election integrity seriously, even if a few days before the election.

Republicans have claimed that Daniel J. Sullivan is a plant by Democrats to confuse voters and boost the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, in one of the most competitive Senate races in the country.

Peltola and national Democrats have strongly denied any involvement in his campaign. Peltola said Thursday she is "not interested in tricking voters" and "knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent."

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has argued Republicans have been linked to their own efforts to stack the Alaska ballot in order to help their preferred candidates, including in this year's Senate primary and in other elections.

State election officials initially determined Daniel J. Sullivan was not eligible to appear on the ballot, accusing him of a "deliberate attempt" to confuse Alaska voters. But the decision was overturned by state courts, which ruled that state officials didn't have the authority to exclude a candidate based on their interpretation of "good faith."

The controversy drew renewed scrutiny after the New York Times reported that operatives linked to Peltola's campaign helped recruit the second Sullivan to run. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into the matter and the Justice Department has issued subpoenas targeting several Democratic officials.

In a separate civil case, the Trump administration has sued to block Alaska from certifying the results of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses because of "voter confusion."

On Friday, the Justice Department asked for a preliminary injunction, saying it wants to "ensure the preservation and segregation of ballots that may be impacted by voter confusion." The government also asked for expedited discovery for the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, and requested that a judge rule on the matter by Monday. The filings heavily rely on The New York Times' reporting.

"Daniel J. Sullivan does not seek to serve in the U.S. Senate but rather seeks to confuse voters," the filing says. "Accordingly, there will indeed be voter confusion caused by this frivolous candidacy."

Federal government lawyers said they want to "preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."

The state of Alaska opposed the request, arguing the Justice Department's lawsuit "lacks any merit." They also said votes are "comingled in the ballot box on Election Day" and therefore can't be segregated without violating ballot secrecy requirements, and noted that "the ballots (whether segregated or not) will not reveal any voter's reasons for voting for Daniel J."

And they said an order to preserve ballots is unnecessary since the state already saves ballots for 22 months.

"The United States' delay further undermines its request for expedited consideration. It waited until two weeks before Election Day to file a lawsuit about issues that arose months ago," the state said.

During the news conference, Heyman also said that he had been recused from the matter some time ago, but that the recusal "has officially been rescinded." Heyman said he had been recused because he was being considered for a judicial nomination, which is no longer the case.

World.title: El-Sayed and Stevens feud ahead of key Michigan Senate race
World.content:
Washington — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his Democratic primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, clashed Friday ahead of a Sunday campaign event where both were expected to make a rare appearance together.

The public rift between the two Democrats comes just days before one of the country's most hotly contested Senate races, as Republican nominee Mike Rogers seeks to peel off centrist Democratic voters. El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens offered starkly differing visions for the future of the party during the primary, and although Stevens endorsed El-Sayed after he won the nomination, the two largely haven't campaigned alongside each other.

In a statement Friday evening, El-Sayed said Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago."

The dig came hours after Stevens demanded that El-Sayed — a vehement critic of U.S. aid to Israel — apologize for suggesting during the campaign that "Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, health care, and child care."

"Abdul promises to get money out of politics," Stevens said in the statement. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."

She also urged El-Sayed to condemn an ad from an outside PAC that she said was antisemitic. The video ad features a couple in a grocery store talking about needing to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf because "we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians." The man and woman in the ad then complain about the billions in military support that the U.S. has provided Israel.

El-Sayed's campaign said earlier this week it was not affiliated "in any way" with the ad, which was created by the political action committee Rebellion PAC.

"No one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign," his campaign said in a statement.

In her Friday statement, Stevens also called on El-Sayed to take down his own ad featuring the far-right podcaster and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson.

It's unclear what the dustup means for their Sunday appearance.

Stevens said she planned to appear with El-Sayed at a Detroit church, alongside South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. An announcement from El-Sayed's campaign about his appearance with Clyburn did not mention Stevens.

Earlier this week, Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Later that day, Stevens said in a CNN interview that she would vote for El-Sayed, saying "we're a household divided," but she called on his campaign "to shut out the hate and to call it out."

World.title: Do you have seasonal affective disorder? How to tell — and what to do about it
World.content:
Do you have seasonal affective disorder? How to tell — and what to do about it

Annelise Capossela for NPR

This story was originally published on Oct. 23, 2020, and has been updated.

When psychiatrist Dr. Norman Rosenthal moved to the United States from South Africa in 1976, he felt less energetic during the harsh winters.

Life Kit Seasonal Affective Disorder is real. Here's how to get through it Seasonal Affective Disorder is real. Here's how to get through it Listen · 17:15 17:15

He noticed other people felt the same way. "Just like the autumn leaves, they became depressed on schedule," says Rosenthal. "In spring, the condition reverses itself." He studied the problem, and published the first research on the syndrome and coined the term seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, in 1984.

About 1 in 20 people in the U.S. have SAD, and it typically lasts about 40% of the year, according to the American Psychiatric Association. If you have it, you may feel sluggish or depressed, oversleep, overeat, gain weight and be uninterested in doing things you previously enjoyed. Many more people have the winter blues, a milder version of SAD, where you feel like a sadder, sleepier or slower version of yourself.

Sponsor Message

With winter just around the corner, here's why you may feel this way — what you can do to feel better.

1. Recognize the symptoms

For many people, SAD makes things feel difficult every fall when it gets darker earlier, but better in the bright days of spring and summer, Rosenthal says.

One of Rosenthal's patients described themselves as feeling like a bear in the winter and wanting to hibernate. "So if you feel any identification with a hibernating bear, you might well have SAD," he says.

Women are about four times more vulnerable than men , and the condition is more common in the Northern Hemisphere.

While some people don't feel different at all when the seasons change, Rosenthal says others are quite disabled by it. People diagnosed with SAD, he says, are "people who would go to a doctor because the problem was bad enough."

Rosenthal says it can be hard to recognize a pattern, because the symptoms creep up on you. "For example, it might be a little bit serious in September and a little worse in October and a little worse in November. It's a bit like the story of the frog in the bowl that keeps getting warmed up, and he doesn't realize he's going to die because it happens so incrementally."

Sponsor Message

But, he says, recognizing your symptoms and taking them seriously are critical, because SAD can be debilitating or worse.

2. Let there be light

A fundamental part of the physiology of this condition is that some people just need more light . One often recommended fix for this is a SAD lamp. Rosenthal says these lamps generate light that's far more intense than indoor lighting — about 10,000 lux, a measurement of light.

This light is absorbed through the eyes, not the skin — but, he says, don't stare at it. Rosenthal says he places it so that the light is shining down on him, just like it would if it were a sunny day. "That's how we evolved to see light — with the heavens above and the sun shining down, so that it comes and hits the bottom part of our retina." The morning is often the best time, and the earlier the better.

He says if you use the lamp for about 20 to 30 minutes a day, you should feel a difference within two weeks. If you don't, return it.

Studies suggest that the value of preventive light therapy is inconclusive and that it's really a patient's preference whether to use it or not. But as a treatment for those who have seasonal affective disorder, SAD lamps have made a big difference.

Remember, even if you use a SAD lamp, make sure you are still trying to get as much natural light as possible. Go outside, even if you don't feel like it, because even when it appears overcast, you are getting light from the sun. Remember that small things can make a difference, so trim any overgrowth around your windows and clean the panes.

3. Be thoughtful and consistent about what (and when) you eat

Rosenthal says people with SAD have a tremendous appetite for carbohydrates. "They crave sweets and starches. And needless to say, that puts on weight, and they can't always take it off in the summer, so every year they're ratcheting up a little more, a little more, and it's a real problem."

Sponsor Message

Emily Manoogian, a clinical researcher at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies, says people with SAD usually have a delay in their circadian rhythm, "these 24-hour rhythms we have within our body."Just like light, food is an important cue to your body. "If you are eating, your body thinks it should be awake."

Make sure to stop eating three hours before you go to sleep, so your body knows to rest. By just controlling the time you eat and keeping it within a consistent 10- to 12-hour window, you're giving your body a strong cue to tell it the time of day, regardless of anything else that's going on.

deimagine/Getty Images

4. Make time for movement

Exercise is another environmental cue that helps signal to your internal clocks what time it is. It's a cue that says "wake up," Manoogian says.

"Exercising during the active time of your day can help your body know what time of day it is and stimulate the brain to be awake at the right time of day, then allow your body to rest in the evening," she says.

Rosenthal says when it's cold and dark and you don't feel energetic and aren't active, it can turn into a vicious cycle. "You don't feel like getting up in the morning, so you pull the covers over your head, so you get less light. So you feel more depressed, so you feel even less like getting up. Whereas if you force yourself to get up, then push yourself to do all these things, then you can feel much better," he says. So try to push through and get some physical activity.

5. Reduce stress

Rosenthal says seasonal affective disorder has three main causes: a genetic component, a lack-of-light component and stress.

Stress may come from a lack of motivation. "When you've got things to do and you're feeling down and not thinking straight and not feeling effective, that's when you can really feel most depressed," Rosenthal says.

Sponsor Message

So try to reduce stress as much as you can. You may want to decorate a room with bright colors and photographs that make you smile. You may want to see a therapist and talk through how you feel. You may want to try meditation. Rosenthal says the effects of practicing meditation and SAD haven't been fully studied yet, but he believes it can help. Be proactive about making pleasurable plans.

Rosenthal says a lot of people do really well following these simple tips. But if you don't find yourself feeling better or if SAD is interfering with your personal relationships or work, he says, medication can also be very effective.

And keep in mind that none of this will make the disorder go away, but as Rosenthal puts it: "It's not a cure, but ... sometimes the SAD dies of neglect."

This story was edited by Malaka Gharib and Sylvie Douglis. The visual editor is Beck Harlan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.

World.title: Oyster stocks have plunged in the Chesapeake. This resident wants to bring them back
World.content:
Oyster stocks have plunged in the Chesapeake. This resident wants to bring them back

toggle caption i Ari Daniel/NPR

John Consoli stands on the edge of his pier, which juts out from the southern tip of Maryland's Kent Island and into the Chesapeake Bay. He leans over and hoists a mesh the size and shape of a pillowcase out of the water.

It's packed with oysters. He manages to get it onto the pier. "These are brand new oysters from this year," he says. "When I got them, they weighed nothing. And this is just three months of growth. The net is chock full, I can hardly pull it up."

Once he gets his breath back, Consoli marvels at these molluscs. "I think I'm more enthusiastic about something that's like a rock than anybody else could possibly be," he says with a big grin. "I really can't think of many more creatures that do the good that oysters do."

Sponsor Message

Oysters underpin the Chesapeake's coastal and estuarine ecosystem. Each adult filters up to 50 gallons of water a day. Cleaner water leads to a healthier bay and more sea grass. "That helps crabs and other organisms," says Consoli.

Plus, oyster shells are a habitat unto themselves. "Because of all the nooks and crannies," he explains, "a lot of small fish and crabs live and eat amongst them and hide, so it creates a biodiverse environment. I even found a seahorse, which was incredible. I've never seen a seahorse in my life!"

Robots scanning for oysters

Oyster reefs used to abound in the Chesapeake, but overharvesting decimated their ranks — by over 99% by 2011, according to one estimate. This monumental shift in the bay contributed to poorer water quality and less habitat for other species.

Oyster farming in the Chesapeake has expanded in recent years, despite environmental and disease challenges, says Ryan Carnegie, a biologist at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. He adds that wild oysters have also made a partial comeback, helped by better management and investments in restoration. But, says Elizabeth North, a fisheries oceanographer at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science, "current oyster populations are likely still a fraction of these historic populations."

Consoli's goal, therefore, is to be a caretaker of sorts, stocking the bay with ever more oysters and looking after their wellbeing. He floats them just below the surface where he says the nutrients are concentrated to help them grow quickly. And although his oysters aren't intended for eating, a cleaner bay does mean better habitat for those that are harvested commercially.

Sponsor Message

Consoli came to oyster conservation in a roundabout way: He's a professional photographer at the University of Maryland and he was doing a shoot involving the campus's oyster research — namely, efforts to understand and support oyster reefs.

"Seeing great minds coming together to solve problems showed to me that there's a real need here," he says.

Miao Yu is one of the great minds who inspired Consoli that day. She's a mechanical engineer at the University of Maryland who has observed that despite the recent, modest gains in oyster abundance, farmers continue to face two daunting tasks — both of which are stymied by the bay's murky waters.

The first is knowing where to plant the babies. A young oyster needs to settle upon a hard substrate. But finding that ideal spot is much easier said than done. "Sometimes it's dropped into [the] mud," she explains — where the young oyster suffocates and dies.

The second task involves figuring out where and when to harvest the adult oysters. "It's the biggest challenge," she says. "We cannot see like a couple feet down there."

This means that the recovery of oysters, often via dredging, tends to be inefficient, and even damaging: It can harm the seabed or pull up oysters that aren't yet ready for harvest.

The fishermen, she says, "don't have a whole picture of what's going on. So our goal is to transform that guesswork into precision."

Yu is trying to do that with the help of robots. She and her team frequently work inside the Neutral Buoyancy Research Facility on campus, which houses a giant cylindrical tank.

toggle caption i Ari Daniel/NPR

On a recent fall morning, one of Yu's PhD students, Michael Xu, uses a joystick to steer a raft-like robot called Oysterbot. Oysterbot, which the team built in-house, consists of a collection of electronics and cables atop a couple of pontoons. A sonar is mounted below.

Sponsor Message

"We're able to do a large-range scan to get a general view of what's going on down there," says Xu.

The team can also deploy a smaller off-the-shelf robot known as the BlueROV to examine something underwater more closely through a live video feed. Together, the two robots paint a portrait of the seabed.

The lab then uses AI to stitch the visuals together and analyze them "to determine if the oysters are present, how many of them are alive or dead, and how big they are," says Xu.

They're still refining the algorithms, but Yu says the eventual goal is "to turn that sonar image map into an oyster information map." In other words, she wants to provide farmers with actionable intelligence to know when and where to plant and harvest their oysters.

Beyond the Chesapeake, her team has conducted field work along the shoreline of Washington state and the Gulf coast. Yu is hoping that within a decade, the technology could be modified and scaled to coastlines nationwide, "so that we can help the oysters for the entire United States."

Peer to Pier

This interest in aiding oysters elsewhere appeals to Consoli as well. Ever since he got hooked, he can't help but spread the good word to a growing number of neighbors with access to the bay.

"Every time I meet a new person, I ask them, 'Hey, do you like oysters?" he says. "And even if they say no, I say, 'Well, somebody in your family likes oysters. Have to be! You have a brother, uncle, a brother-in-law.'" Once he establishes such a connection, he says to them, "Hey, can you grow them? It's not that hard."

And most of the time, Consoli finds that people are quite receptive. That includes a couple of octogenarian neighbors of his on Kent Island.

Sponsor Message

"I really am impressed that the oysters clean the bay," says Earl Collins.

On one occasion, Ann Ziegler, who lives a couple doors down from Consoli, says she pulled her oysters out of the water with her family to eat them raw. "And then, at Thanksgiving, since no one had died, we ate them again," she says.

Consoli has also met new neighbors through this work, like John Patrick. "It's just amazing the amount of marine life that I've seen around the pier since I've had these oysters in the water," he says. "I had croaker, crabs and eels in here this morning."

Even Consoli's dental hygienist has gotten involved.

Perhaps most ambitiously, Consoli worked with a local restaurant called Libbey's Coastal Kitchen a couple months ago to place a million baby oysters around their dock pilings.

"We had eight people in wetsuits and life jackets," he says. "There were jellyfish everywhere. It was probably the most difficult installation we could ever do."

Restaurant operator Andrew Westlin says he was instantly attracted to the idea.

"This was a no-brainer for us, honestly," he says. "We felt that this was a cool way for us to give back and just be part of the community." Soon, there will be a sign next to the pier explaining the oyster project to any restaurant customers and passersby.

Consoli's wife, Kathy, says all this oyster work is "the most hardworking hobby there is. I call him now the Pied Piper of oysters because I think he's up to 80 people possibly."

She's right. He calls it his Peer to Pier Network.

"We're really just trying to make sure that we can restore as much as we can to the bay," says Consoli, "whether that's with robots or other techniques… It teaches me just how something that seems so insignificant can make a difference."

World.title: Plans for a data center threaten scenic wilderness and dark skies in West Virginia
World.content:
Plans for a data center threaten scenic wilderness and dark skies in West Virginia

toggle caption i Chris Jackson for NPR

DAVIS, W.Va. — Stretching nearly a million acres through the rugged mountains of eastern West Virginia, the Monongahela National Forest links some of the state's best known natural attractions. The vast area ranges from the ski slopes of Canaan Valley to the dark skies of Blackwater Falls and Spruce Knob and includes the small towns of Davis and Thomas that serve as gateways for visitors to the region.

For the past seven months, Kaleb Skelton, his wife, Ella, their 2-year-old son, Ryder, and dog Mabel have lived in a camper in this corner of West Virginia's "almost heaven." Kaleb is finishing a seasonal stint as a campground manager on a lake near Spruce Knob, the state's highest point.

On clear nights atop the isolated peak, they get to experience a river of stars in one of the very few pockets of darkness remaining in the Eastern United States. The area has become a draw for amateur astronomers.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Chris Jackson for NPR

During summer's new moons, Kaleb says, one in four campsites he oversees is occupied by someone with a telescope. He thought his family's cabin in eastern Texas offered "the craziest" dark skies he'd ever seen, "but coming out here definitely rivals it."

A dark history for 'Stump Town'

Those inky-black nights — and the natural beauty they shelter — are now under threat from what many residents see as a modern-day version of extractive industries like logging and mining that once defined the region. In a place where tourism, outdoor recreation and community are deeply intertwined, a gigantic power plant and data center campus in nearby Tucker County would bring large-scale development into the heart of it all.

A stark image of the town of Davis from 1885, during the heyday of logging, is a reminder of that transformation. The photo shows a handful of squat buildings amid a broad clearing littered with forest remains.

They used to call it "Stump Town," says Kim Williams, president of the Snow Sports Museum of West Virginia in Canaan Valley. At the turn of the century, massive first-growth trees dominated the landscape.

Then, logging companies "came in and clear-cut the whole valley and everything around it," he says.

By the early 20th century, entire mountainsides of red spruce and eastern hemlock had been stripped bare. Then came the coal companies, which left the nearby Blackwater River acidic and dangerous to drink.

Today, the scars still show. The big trees won't return for generations, but a century of natural regrowth, conservation and deliberate restoration means the land is on its way to healing.

While few expect that the latest tech boom presages anything like the environmental destruction of the past, many see the proposed new Ridgeline data center as a big step backward, undoing the progress the local community has made to recover.

A roughly 785-megawatt generating plant is slated to be the first part of "a large-scale data and energy infrastructure project designed to support artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and enterprise systems," according to Purcellville, Va.-based Fundamental Data LLC, the company behind Ridgeline.

toggle caption i

The complex would rely primarily on natural gas, with diesel as a backup fuel source. Power generated on-site, rather than purchased from the regional grid, could ease some concerns about the project's effects on electricity rates. It does not, however, resolve concerns over air and water pollution.

Sponsor Message

Located on a reclaimed coal-mining site, plans are for an initial 291 acres that could eventually expand to 10,000 acres — 15 square miles — and include parts of neighboring Grant County, according to local news reports.

Speaking to NPR, Casey Chapman, listed in court documents as Fundamental Data's "responsible individual," declined to speculate on the facility's ultimate size, saying only that "if fully developed … it would be thousands of acres."

Light pollution is a common complaint from residents living near data centers. Chapman says the company will use "well-designed" lighting to help minimize the effects of sky glow, in an effort not to jeopardize nearby Blackwater Falls State Park's pursuit of an official dark-sky certification.

An analysis by the Northern Virginia Astronomy Club, which hosts an annual star party in the region, found that Ridgeline's initial footprint could increase sky glow near Blackwater by 528%, transforming its nighttime rural sky to one comparable to a suburban area. (The same analysis found only a minimal impact on Spruce Knob.)

But safety and security — not light pollution — take precedence, Chapman says. The facility will be "an industrial plant that runs around the clock," he notes. "Crews need proper lighting to operate and maintain equipment safely."

Opponents face an uphill battle

Chip Chase is among the skeptics. He runs White Grass Ski Touring Center, a popular cross-country ski area that he helped found 45 years ago. He is a fixture in the local community that he describes as "Vermont, with Southern hospitality."

"If you're an outdoor person, this place is paradise," he says. "People come here to get away from data centers. People want dark skies here. People want to have a peaceful, quiet recreational area."

toggle caption i Chris Jackson for NPR

Economic development, however, is a top priority for the state of West Virginia. It ranks among the poorest in the country and has the unique distinction of having lost population since 1950.

Sponsor Message

John Deskins, director of the West Virginia University Bureau of Business and Economic Research, says data centers could be a boon. "As long as we're making sure that we follow all the proper procedures around noise pollution, water pollution, [and] other elements of environmental pollution ... I think they're a good opportunity," he says.

It is those proper procedures that worry people in Tucker United, a grassroots group opposing the data center plans. As in so many other places across the country, they are battling what they see as a lack of transparency.

The first anyone in the community heard about the Ridgeline project was March 2025, when an obscure notice appeared in a local newspaper announcing the request for an air-quality permit for a proposed power plant, says Davis Mayor Alan Tomson. A resident called him to ask if he knew anything about it. "I told her that I did not," Tomson says. He then called the mayor of neighboring Thomas. "He also had not heard anything about it."

toggle caption i Chris Jackson for NPR

From there, Tomson says, things moved quickly. A month later, the Republican super-majority in both houses of the state legislature passed a highly unusual bill exempting certified microgrid districts and high-impact data centers from county or municipal zoning or any local restrictions related to horticultural, noise, viewshed, lighting, development or land use.

A lack of guardrails

Opponents quickly gathered 1,000 signatures on a petition urging Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey to veto the bill. They were unsuccessful. Signing the legislation, the governor noted the state's need to "continue to focus on economic development and utilizing our many natural resources," adding that "companies will now be able to quickly build, expand, and increase job creation right here in West Virginia."

"They completely got rid of any … sort of regulation or guardrails for these data center developments," says Tucker United spokesperson Nikki Forrester. "They want to sell us out, … extract our resources and leave us with the mess."

toggle caption i Chris Jackson for NPR

The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection approved Fundamental Data's air-quality permit without, according to Tucker United and other activist groups, conducting a comprehensive assessment of the facility's potential public-health impacts on the surrounding valley. When asked by NPR about Tucker United's concerns, the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection responded that it "does not comment on active litigation" and declined an interview request.

Sponsor Message

Opponents of the project subsequently commissioned their own analysis finding that the Ridgeline plant could cause between $19 million and $35 million a year in health-related damages and premature deaths.

Tucker United, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy and the Sierra Club challenged the air-permit decision in court. Their appeal was dismissed in August on jurisdictional grounds. The groups say they will go to the state's Supreme Court.

Chapman says Tucker United's air-quality study assumes Ridgeline will emit the maximum amount of pollution allowed by its air permit for an entire year, when in fact the permit sets an upper limit and "we're going to operate within those limits," he says.

There are other environmental concerns. Forrester notes that Canaan Valley's bowl shape and temperature inversions can trap air pollutants near the ground. As for water, she says, "storing 30 million gallons of diesel right on a creek that feeds into our water supplies is really dangerous and puts not just our community, but every community downstream at risk."

toggle caption i Chris Jackson for NPR

Fundamental Data's Chapman says the storage would be safe and that all of the tanks would not need to be filled at any given time.

In addition to the potential environmental and health hazards, many residents find it particularly galling that West Virginia House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, a Charleston-based attorney with the law firm Bowles Rice, is listed as lead attorney for Fundamental Data in the permit dispute.

"Here's a guy who's writing laws [and] sponsoring legislation while under contract for one of the people that he's working for," complains Gary Berti, a retired homeowner in Davis. "To me, that's a conflict of interest."

In an email to NPR, Hanshaw stated: "I am not now, nor have I ever been, employed by Fundamental Data. I am a partner in a law firm. It is public record that the law firm of Bowles Rice is currently counsel for Fundamental Data in a litigation matter pending in West Virginia."

Sponsor Message

Jobs are needed, but at what cost?

Fundamental Data believes building the Ridgeline facility would bring thousands of temporary jobs and about 500 permanent ones in IT, electrical and cooling systems, engineering and security.

While no two data center campuses are alike, a Brookings Institution study found that on average, data centers produce around 100 to 200 permanent jobs.

Berti agrees that West Virginia needs jobs, but "there are places that need it more than others," he says, and is skeptical that data centers would bring many permanent workers to the area.

And if artificial intelligence ends up being more hype than substance, he says, it could be a repeat of history.

"A lot of times they leave us behind," he says, referring to the coal and logging industries. "When I moved here 40 years ago, it was two rundown towns," he says, referring to Davis and Thomas. "Look at them now. They're doing well."

toggle caption i Chris Jackson for NPR

Given that history of exploitation, Tomson, the mayor of Davis, says he thinks the data center developer thought it could run roughshod over residents. But they got more than they bargained for, he says.

"This is a very educated community," Tomson says. "Many of the people here that have retired had very high-level scientific and technological careers elsewhere, and they bring that knowledge and expertise to bear on this situation."

Despite the organized opposition, some residents have voiced support. Tucker County Sheriff Jake Kopec thinks much of the criticism amounts to fear-mongering. The landfill for Davis and Thomas blocks the view of the Ridgeline facility from those towns, he says. "I really believe that you would drive past it and not even know it's there."

Kopec acknowledges that the dark skies will be less dark. But he says the county has more immediate needs that the Ridgeline facility would help remedy, including better-paying jobs and tax revenue to fund essential public services. "We have no cops on after midnight in this county, but we serve a million-plus visitors a year," he notes.

Sponsor Message

A vibrant arts scene

Davis and Thomas — both with populations of roughly 600 people — are not only a base of operations for skiing, hiking, mountain biking and white water rafting, but they've also developed a lively arts and music scene.

"This area was just about written off," according to Tomson. "And what ended up happening was music and artists discovered the city of Thomas, and there was a beginning of a resurrection of the area."

On a Sunday night in October well before the start of the ski season, there's a poetry reading at Creature in Thomas and a few doors down at the Purple Fiddle, a standing-room only performance by Driftwood, an Americana/folk rock band from Binghamton, N.Y.

Most of the hundred or so people in the bar are tourists like Adam Brooke, from Charlottesville, Va. He has been visiting the area for the past decade, taking in the mountains and the color of the fall leaves.

"We're mostly hikers," he says. "We just like getting out there on some of the lesser known trails and just enjoying nature for a bit."

Drawing hope from past environmental wins

Despite the obstacles, opponents of the Ridgeline facility remain optimistic. They're buoyed by the growing national opposition to data centers.

In their own state, Gov. Morrisey — a strong advocate for data centers in the past — appears to be pumping the brakes somewhat, with a recently proposed 20-year plan for "responsible" data center development. It's not much, Tucker United's Forrester says, but it's something.

She also points to the region's past grassroots successes. "Tucker County does have a long history of fighting bad development proposals … but we've been successful in every single one of them."

toggle caption i Chris Jackson for NPR

Forrester and others point to two major environmental fights in the 1970s: a proposed hydroelectric project that would have flooded Canaan Valley and part of Dolly Sods — a protected wilderness area now popular with hikers and skiers. A second, at Otter Creek, saw the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy successfully challenge plans for coal exploration and road construction in the Monongahela National Forest. Both were halted.

Sponsor Message

Those victories are tempered by the region's darker past, too, she acknowledges.

"They're playing by the same playbook they've always played here," Forrester says. "People don't want to relive that history again, and they will fight every step of the way to make sure that doesn't happen."

World.title: Can I trust the polls? And other questions from listeners about the 2026 midterms
World.content:
Can I trust the polls? And other questions from listeners about the 2026 midterms

toggle caption i Stephen Maturen/Getty Images

📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App

Ahead of Election Day, there are a lot of questions about what might happen, what the implications of different outcomes might be and even what it's like to cover elections. In collaboration with the NPR Politics Podcast, listeners sent in their questions about the election and politics for our political correspondents to answer.

Many political polls have been wrong recently. How can you as a reporter provide an accurate news piece utilizing poll results?

This is a common question every election cycle, but it's a little like saying, "I don't like the media because the media is biased." There are good polls and bad polls just like there are good reporters and bad reporters.

Sponsor Message

There have no doubt been some high-profile misses, particularly at the state level. National polls have actually been pretty good when it comes to the horse race, with a slight underestimation of Republican turnout. But remember, these polls have margins of error. That means a poll with +/- 3 or 4 percentage points is actually a range of 6 to 8 points. That's important because in a country with very close elections, the kind of precision that Americans expect sets up the polls for failure because they're not intended to be that specific. They set more of a fuzzy range.

State surveys have seen a lot of junk polls, even a couple fake ones this time around. So it's really important to pay attention to the quality of the pollster. The reason for this is because of the decline of local journalism. Local newspapers and TV stations just don't have the kind of money that national outlets do to pay for good, rigorous and frequent polling.

Horse-race polling isn't even the best use of polling. I talk a lot about polls, but you rarely hear me talking about specific margins between candidates, unless there's been a trend moving the needle in a certain direction. The races are close, within margin of error in many places, and that's all that really needs to be conveyed. Unfortunately, some outlets emphasize the horse race, but the best stuff is underneath. Are there trends over time with statistically significant movement on important questions and issues? For example, we wouldn't know how quickly public opinion moved on important issues, approval ratings, attitudes and how strongly people feel about those things without this data.

Sponsor Message

Also, for those who don't think reporters should use polls at all, understand that campaigns and corporations spend millions of dollars on polling to inform where they spend money, where they travel and what messages to use. They use the same pollsters you hear about externally. All that said, polling is one tool. It's not everything, and it should be mixed with historical context, reporting with campaigns, and being on the ground, which are all priorities of NPR's as well. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

Do you prefer reporting on midterms or presidential election years? Are there unique opportunities that midterms have?

Presidential elections are certainly easier to cover in the sense that there are two sides who are looking to be in one job. Plus, regular people are very interested in presidential elections, as is evident by the decline in turnout from presidentials to midterms. But midterm elections are also consequential — and can be a lot of fun.

You get a lot of quirky candidates in down-ballot races sometimes with interesting storylines that might not see a lot of daylight in a presidential election, which is like a solar eclipse. Plus, I got my start covering midterm elections, researching the 2006 elections and learning about every single congressional race, and it was fascinating — the characters, the different types of places and economies and people in this very large country. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

Reporting during the midterms is so much more fun! Rallies for presidential candidates have tons of security and stadium-size venues. A lot of sitting and waiting, using your camera zoom and being stuck in a press pen.

Tagging along with a candidate for House or Senate, especially early in the cycle, can be so much more intimate. This year, I've covered candidates at an antique shop, a farmer's market, a UAW picnic, a family farm and a smokejumper-themed brewery. There is more opportunity to see candidates up close, watch them interact with voters and even ask them questions. - Sam Gringlas, NPR congressional reporter

I personally like all elections, which is what makes a presidential year so great, you get a whole smorgasbord of contests. The top of the ticket certainly consumes a lot of oxygen but I've found you can often learn more about how the election is going by spending time with congressional candidates or even candidates for the state legislature. And, unlike midterm years, more voters are engaged, which makes for better voter interviews. But, please check back in a week and a half to see how my sleep debt is doing and whether I still say I "like all elections," because this may just be the light at the end of the tunnel pre-election euphoria speaking. - Tamara Keith, NPR senior political correspondent

Sponsor Message

Is there a race you're watching out of your own curiosity that may not "matter" at the national level?

Every race counts when it comes to the balance of power in the House and the Senate. But I have been joking that following the twists and turns in Nevada's 2nd Congressional District is now my hobby. I did a story about this race about a month ago and it has only gotten more wild since. It is a district that President Trump won by 14 points that hasn't been represented by a Democrat in its more than 40 years in existence. But Republicans ended up nominating a Trump-backed candidate with a ton of baggage who only moved to the district to run for congress. In an interview with me, he blamed his grandkids for one of his missteps.

Democrats nominated a former Miss Nevada turned state legislator, who has been running a very solid campaign. The retiring Republican congressman is using colorful language to trash the GOP nominee every chance he gets and announced that he voted for a Libertarian instead. So, it's just totally messy. The Republican is still favored to win but I am watching closely because I just want to know how this drama ends. - Tamara Keith, NPR senior political correspondent

There are a lot of redistricting ballot measures before voters. In Maryland, voters are going to consider whether to [amend the state constitution which would ultimately] allow Democrats to add one more seat there. That one actually looks like it might not pass, which is surprising because this is a Democratic state. You'd think Democrats want to give their Democratic lawmakers an edge to create a new seat.

Coloradans are considering a ballot measure that would basically make it harder for their legislature to mid-decade redistrict, which a lot of other states did. And then in Missouri, they're going to be weighing another question about whether to allow congressional redistricting that would help Republicans flip a seat there.

Sponsor Message

Then there's Alaska. Every cycle they go back and forth about this primary system that they have and ranked choice voting. It is going before them again. It's always a squeaker. It's always really close. But voters have stood by their top four primary nonpartisan primary system and their ranked choice voting. - Ashley Lopez, NPR political correspondent
