I'm paying very close attention to places like Michigan and Texas and what they tell us about the Senate. There's a couple of really interesting House races that I think are going to tell us something, especially in South Florida and South Texas with Latinos and how they move in this election, because they're quite the swing group at this point. There are a couple of governors' races and ballot initiatives across the country.

In California, I'm really interested to see how this wealth tax ballot initiative does. There's been a ton of money, tens of millions of dollars spent on that, and it's going to be interesting to see if in a place like California that do tend to be the ones out front on a lot of these kinds of experiments, if it winds up passing or not.

I'm also curious about something like the Nevada governor's race. And Nevada is always a really interesting place because people have a real independent streak. You've got two candidates here in Gov. Joe Lombardo, the Republican who was elected in 2022, and he's going against the state's attorney general, Aaron Ford. There's been all this talk about crime and about Trump and the high unemployment rate. But then you dig into some of their backgrounds. Ford has had to talk about how, as a college kid, he made some bad decisions, including running into trouble with the law. I think the outcome there is going to be really interesting to see, asking voters whether they're going to take the dirt of what happened with somebody a decade or so ago versus the national political climate. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

Sponsor Message

How is the executive branch going to be affected if Democrats take one or both houses of Congress in the midterms?

Midterms tend to be a check on the party that holds the White House. The way that happens, first and foremost, is when there's split power in Washington, legislation comes to a standstill unless there's compromise and with only about 10% of congressional districts being competitive, there isn't much incentive to meet in the middle.

Some issues that have bipartisan support, like guardrails for artificial intelligence, could see progress. But the president is not in favor of restrictions on AI. The biggest effect of a Democratic House or Senate will be investigations and oversight of the current administration. One thing that could be politically tricky for Democrats is how far they go with impeachments, if they go there. Republicans paid the political price for their impeachment investigations of former President Clinton in the late 90s.

Loading...

Only twice since World War II has the president's party picked up seats in a midterm — once in 2002 after 9/11 and the preceding midterm in 1998. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

Are political debates dead? And if not, when they are held, are they doomed to be ever more divisive at the expense of platforming policies as they have been in recent years?

In midterms, you have incumbents who are reluctant to get on a debate stage because they don't want to give a challenger oxygen and raise their profiles. The thing about debates is that sometimes people don't feel like they get a lot out of them, because politicians are talking-point machines. The job of journalists and interviewers is to try and get them off of those and to press on vulnerabilities so voters get a clearer understanding of what those candidates want to do and why they want to do it.

That's a real service to voters when done well, considering the only things voters see or hear from politicians otherwise is pre-packaged campaign ads, speeches or curated social media clips. Pressing them on their policies in a debate is an important part of the Democratic process, and a big platform for people who need to increase their name identification, so, no, I don't think debates are dead. In fact, I think with what could be a record number of candidates in this upcoming presidential election, you're gonna see a lot of debates. Just wait. – Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent.

Sponsor Message

What from this year's midterms are you watching as potential indicators for the presidential election in 2028?

Jon Ossoff's margin in Georgia. LOL. Ossoff has emerged as a dark-horse potential presidential candidate, despite his denials. They always deny they're running until they do. There are a handful of potential 2028 Democratic candidates who are governors running states where they are heavily favored to win reelection, people like J.B. Pritzker in Illinois, Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, Wes Moore in Maryland. What do they say on Election Night to give any clues about what they do next. Or will they simply say how proud they are of their records running their states, which, by the way, can be hints of messages for… 2028.

There will be lots to learn from how Democrats affiliated with democratic socialism or the very progressive wing of the party perform on election night compared to moderates in various places. That could set the stage for the issue debates in the 2028 Democratic primary. Also, how do Republicans run post-Trump? Do any start to distance themselves in the days and weeks following the midterms, trying to lay out a different direction, while walking the line to keep MAGA on board?

You can't really read into how states go in midterms to say whether they're going to be competitive in 2028. These are just very different electorates than much-higher turnout presidential elections. The margin for the Senate will be interesting for 2028 and what it means for the potential of a governing majority for the next president. - Domenico Montanaro, NPR senior political editor and correspondent

Thank you to Courtney, Nathaneal, Chad, Erin, Renata and Tyson for the questions.

World.title: After last year's storm, this remote Alaska town is still picking up the pieces
World.content:
After last year's storm, this remote Alaska town is still picking up the pieces

toggle caption i Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK

Last fall , the remnants of Typhoon Halong tore through numerous small Alaska Native villages off the road system in Western Alaska. The storm destroyed infrastructure, floated homes off their foundations, and displaced over a thousand people. A year later, hundreds remain displaced as the slow work of repair in a remote part of the state continues. And in one of the hardest hit communities – the small town of Kipnuk – people still aren't sure when they'll be moving back.

Sponsor Message

'Working as fast as we can'

The village of under 200 homes is situated on the wide open tundra and only consistently accessible by plane.

A year ago, 90% of the residences here were damaged by the remnants of Typhoon Halong, according to the State of Alaska's Emergency Operations Center. Dozens were swept off their foundations, some with families still inside . The community is now largely scattered across Alaska – some outside the region their ancestors have lived in for thousands of years.

toggle caption i Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK

Throughout the past year, crews have been working on repairs.

On a clear day in August, Eddie Chuckwuk's construction crew attempted what sounded like magic: raising a building back onto its foundations using air compressors.

Chuckwuk is one of several dozen people who have been working long days to rebuild the place where he grew up.

"We're working as fast as possible as we can to get the people back in town," Chuckwuk says. "That's what I just want to see – for everybody to come back and enjoy where they grew up instead of being placed in a different place … where they're not used to. It's pretty hard."

toggle caption i Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK

Challenges remain in moving back

This work is critical to getting Kipnuk's homes in shape to live in again, but the town is far from being fully restored.

Sponsor Message

According to the state, most people in Kipnuk didn't have home or flood insurance. They estimate that funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency will make most of the homes livable by Thanksgiving – meaning replacing wet insulation and repairing windows, doors and roofs. But the funds won't be enough to return some severely damaged homes to how they were before the storm. The state is currently appealing for additional funding to build replacement housing.

There's also no estimate on when the school will reopen.

Leona Paul, who has been working as a cook to feed the construction teams, says even if the houses are habitable, some people were too traumatized by the storm to return.

"I think it's too overwhelming for them," she says, "especially the older people."

And climate change is making towns like Kipnuk more vulnerable to future storms . Most people in town want to rebuild the village somewhere safer but the funding they have received so far from FEMA can only go towards restoring what was damaged . Kipnuk hasn't yet found the money to move.

toggle caption i Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK

Living away from home takes a toll

Right now residents may not have a better option other than moving back. Many say living in bigger towns, or cities like Anchorage, has been tough. People aren't speaking as much Yugtun – the native language. They're farther from loved ones. Their kids, who are used to playing all over town, have to watch out for cars.

Leona Paul, who spent part of the summer in Kipnuk, says she likes being there. "You're free to do anything you want," she says. "In a city you just can't do whatever you want."

Being displaced from the village has also meant separation from the Alaska Native cultural practices of hunting and gathering traditional food on the land.

Some residents, like Burt Paul's family, traveled home for the summer to practice subsistence and be together.

Upriver from Kipnuk on a lush tundra bluff, his family filled buckets with sweet, orange salmonberries, or naunraqs as they are called in coastal Yugtun. He says after last fall's destruction – he didn't know when he'd see these native plants growing again.

"It beats my mind that I see food growing, grass growing, fish coming in," he says.

toggle caption i Samantha Watson/KYUK

Paul's family evacuated after the storm, but he stayed behind in Kipnuk, acting as a community leader through the aftermath. Usually, his family goes camping and berry picking for days. This summer, their trips were shorter – confined to when everyone was in town.

Sponsor Message

Short as those trips may have been, he says they were important: "We have to keep things going some way, somehow, no matter what situation we go through," he says.

He's not sure when his family – or his village – will all be back together again.

World.title: Oil company earnings skyrocket — again
World.content:
Oil company earnings skyrocket — again

toggle caption i Susan Montoya Bryan/AP



Oil companies made billions this quarter, they told investors on calls this week. ExxonMobil earned $15.4 billion, more than doubling its earnings compared to this time last year.

Shell nearly doubled its own earnings, at $10.8 billion.

Chevron's were up 180%, at $9.9 billion.

Together, the three companies pulled in just over $36 billion this quarter.

As with the soaring profits oil companies recorded last quarter , it's largely due to the war in Iran disrupting the global oil supply. Less oil is moving through the Middle East, so the oil in other parts of the world has become much more valuable.

Brent crude is now trading around $113 a barrel . For context, before the war began, it was about $70 a barrel.

Sponsor Message

Meanwhile, demand for oil and refined products like gasoline, diesel and heating oil hasn't changed much. People still need them to heat homes , drive cars, run tractors and truck everything we buy around the country.

Dan Pickering, founder of the financial services firm Pickering Energy Partners, says that big oil companies are profiting as they meet that demand. " The majors are able to sell their barrels that they produce in the U.S. or Latin America or Europe for much higher prices," he said. "So the Middle East's loss is generally the gain of oil and gas companies in the U.S. and Europe."

On their earnings calls, oil company executives said a good chunk of their profits were going to their shareholders through dividends and stock buybacks. Shell's buyback was one of their biggest ever. Exxon announced its highest-ever quarterly dividend.

But for the most part, Pickering says, these companies are in a wait-and-see stance — they're not really spending that money on things like new drilling projects, because they know they're in an unusual moment.

"This is a period where the high prices are driven more by geopolitical events than anything else," he said. Since it's hard to predict how long those will last, he continued, "You put the money in the bank and watch to see what happens as we move into 2027."

Sponsor Message

Pickering says this makes sense because oil is a cyclical industry — prices move up and down. Companies want to hold onto their cash when times are good so they can insulate themselves when they're not so good.

A supply shock, amid two ongoing wars

The rising cost of oil has pushed up what drivers pay at the pump. Gasoline now costs about $1.20 more per gallon than it did a year ago, according to AAA . Diesel hit a record high in September , and is still close to that high.

Exxon CEO Darren Woods was one of the few to directly address the issue on an earnings call, saying, "We recognize the impact high prices have on people's lives and economic growth."

Exxon's solution, he said, is to boost production. " With products in short supply, our teams have done everything they can to keep prices down by maximizing production," he said.

Chevron CEO Mike Wirth made a similar point, telling investors, " What we can do is what we can control, and that's help consumers get as much as they possibly can out of our systems."

On these calls, executives from all the companies pointed out that they're dealing with a massive supply shock. The war in Iran, as well as Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries , have taken a lot of global refining capacity offline.

The executives indicated that they don't see the situation changing anytime soon.

"If you'd asked me six months ago, would I have thought that oil prices were going to be where they are today — no," Shell CEO Wael Sawan said on his company's call. "Personally, I thought we were at a high there, and we were essentially looking at what was going to be a temporal spike."

But because the war has gone on this long, global oil reserves are at much lower levels. The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at low levels; Europe released some of its crude oil and diesel.

"We're now seeing more and more structural stability in that higher oil price simply because we are seeing that inventory levels are being drawn down very quickly, and it's going to take quite some time to be able to refill that inventory," Sawan continued.

Sponsor Message

Calls for a windfall tax

Democrats in both chambers of Congress have called for a tax on windfall profits — excess profits that come about because of geopolitical forces outside of their control, not because of innovation. Bills introduced this spring would return some of those profits to Americans through tax rebates.

Earlier this year, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), who sponsored a windfall tax bill in the Senate, said he hopes it will also spotlight how climate-friendly renewable energy is increasingly more cost-competitive than fossil fuels . " Wind, solar, and battery power, they're not raising their prices," Whitehouse told NPR at the time.

Isabella Weber, an economist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, has studied how windfall taxes worked in other countries. She says windfall taxes are a way to bridge the gap between what the oil companies make and what most people pay for that oil.

"The companies that are running this essential sector have been reaping record profits amidst the worst energy supply crisis that we have had in several decades," she said. "This is a contradiction that, I think, raises fundamental questions about how we organize our economy, how we organize our society, who benefits, who loses."

"When emergencies generate massive windfall profits," she continued, it creates "this crazy situation where the worst of times ends up being the best of times, which is problematic on a deeper level."

While the oil executives didn't mention windfall taxes on this week's calls, last quarter, Exxon's Woods called them a " misguided policy ." He said they penalize companies that are trying to be successful in a volatile industry.

As the midterms approach, the Trump administration has taken measures to bring down the price of fuel, particularly diesel, including temporarily loosening federal rules for dyed diesel, which is used in farming, and lifting sanctions against Russia to allow more diesel to enter the world market.

But these efforts are unlikely to bring down U.S. prices — the amount of fuel Russia can release would make up only a small portion of U.S. daily demand, and dyed diesel is still not accessible to most drivers.

Sponsor Message

In any case, significantly lower prices are unlikely to materialize by Tuesday.

World.title: 100 years later, Harry Houdini's death still haunts Detroit
World.content:
100 years later, Harry Houdini's death still haunts Detroit

toggle caption i AP Photo

This Halloween marks the 100th anniversary of the death of the legendary magician Harry Houdini.

He earned his reputation by freeing himself from traps that seemed impossible for a mere mortal to survive.But Houdini couldn't escape the ultimate fate waiting for him in Detroit on Oct. 31, 1926, and his spirit still haunts the Motor City.

A life defying death

Houdini performed in Detroit 19 times between the early days of his career in 1894 and the final show of his life in 1926.

The trajectory took him from being a bottom-of-the-bill act to one of the most famous entertainers in the world.

Sponsor Message

He escaped obscurity by declaring no set of handcuffs or jail cell could hold him. He dangled upside down from office buildings wearing a straitjacket, dramatically removing them in full view of those raptly watching below. Sometimes the buildings housed a local newspaper, ensuring free publicity for Houdini's upcoming stage shows.

In 1906, Houdini jumped two dozen feet from Detroit's Belle Isle Bridge into the frigid river below, bound with two sets of police handcuffs. He emerged unscathed, but the legend around it grew. The escape artist had leaped into a hole in ice covering the river, the story went, finding air pockets to breathe in before finally surfacing.

Reports from the time show the river was not actually frozen. But that didn't stop movies decades later from portraying it that way.

He even scared his assistants

As his fame grew, and a series of other magicians began copying his escapes, Houdini ramped up the stakes, stacking one increasingly death-defying feat on top of another.

By 1914 he had unveiled his signature stunt, the Water Torture Cell, a coffin-sized box, filled with water.

Houdini was lowered into it head first, both his ankles and the top of the box locked. A curtain was raised to hide the magician's method of escape from the audience.

Sponsor Message

Even Dorothy Young, who toured with Houdini as a stage assistant when she was 17-years-old and had seen the act many times, had goosebumps.

"Mrs. [Houdini] always stood in the wings because they had a secret code in case he couldn't get out," Young said in a 2004 interview with NPR. "I always watched because it was very exciting!"

Houdini's final show

Young was the last surviving person to have worked with Houdini before she, too, died in 2011.

A few years before her death, Young recalled how many movies exaggerated the circumstances of Houdini's demise. He did not, as at least one movie depicts, dramatically struggle to escape the torture cell.

Houdini's death likely stemmed from an incident just before his arrival in Detroit.

Houdini routinely boasted that he could withstand any blow to his stomach. In his dressing room at a show in Montreal, a college wrestler accepted that challenge and punched him several times before Houdini could tighten his muscular midsection.

"One time he showed me that he had a way of doing it," Young said. "And to think those boys didn't give him a chance to get himself protected."

Houdini was in severe pain, and doctors advised him to rest. But he refused to cancel a series of shows already scheduled in Detroit.

Houdini was under financial pressure to fulfill his contract, according to Jeremy Dimick, a curator at the Detroit Historical Museum.

Dimick said Houdini only made it through one performance.

"He doesn't have the strength to put his makeup on before the show, and he's kind of collapsing during the intermissions of the show," Dimick said. "And then he has to be literally carried from the Garrick Theater back to his hotel."

Houdini was taken to Grace Hospital, where doctors found he had ruptured his appendix.

Sponsor Message

Several days and two surgeries later, on Halloween, Houdini breathed his last.

Houdini's Detroit haunts have vanished

Now the theater, the hotel, even the hospital are gone.

The Detroit funeral home that embalmed him became a girls' art school, which also eventually shut its doors.

But two decades ago, the then-head of the school, Juanita Hammond would take visitors up a creaky set of stairs to a locked storage area with an indented floor once used to drain bodily fluids from corpses.

"Houdini was laid out here by the Hamilton Funeral Home, in this room here," Hammond said on a tour in 2004.

Hammond said some students worried the magician's presence never left the school.

"Some say, 'I'm not going back to the kitchen because I might see Houdini,'" she said.

Searching for his spirit

The escape artist's wife, Bess Houdini, spent years trying to see or talk with her husband again after his death. She held séance after séance searching for his ghost, though the magician himself spent his final years exposing psychics he said preyed on the bereaved.

But at a séance on Halloween a decade after her husband's death, Bess Houdini finally said good night to Harry.

She reenacted the scene in a movie a few years later, appearing in a cameo as herself.

"And you remember what he always said about these things? That it was impossible for the dead to return," she said. "This proves he was right. For if it would have been possible, I would have had some sign from him in the past 10 years."

Still trying to make contact

That has not stopped others from trying to reach the Great Houdini in the great beyond, sometimes incorporating old pieces of his stage act.

At the American Museum of Magic in Marshall, Mich., about 100 miles west of Detroit, John Sherwood banged on an empty, aged metal can from Houdini's workshop that has been the centerpiece of several séances.

Sponsor Message

"That is the Houdini milk can," Sherwood said. "Houdini would jump into this while it was filled with warm water, and he would be locked inside with six Mastodon locks."

Like the torture cell, a screen surrounded the milk can to prevent the audience from seeing how Houdini escaped.

He would invite the audience to try to hold their breath while he was doing it.

After several minutes with no sign of Houdini, the crowd would scream for his assistants to let him out.

In reality, Houdini would have escaped long before and would be backstage reading a newspaper while the tension built.

Finally, with the crowd's anxiety at a fever pitch, Houdini's assistants would splash him with water — since he had dried off by then — and the Master of Suspense would emerge from behind the screen, theatrically panting.

The audience would erupt in cheers.

Will Houdini return for a bite to eat?

Decades later, Sherwood said séance participants would surround the milk can and other Houdini artifacts as they tried to contact him.

Sherwood said some séances have tried to coax the magician back to the land of the living "by essentially appealing to Houdini's Jewish heritage by placing a lox and bagel sandwich into the milk can and invited Houdini's spirit to take a bite out of it."

Sherwood is orchestrating another séance this Halloween. Though previous attempts were not successful, Sherwood said the centennial of Houdini's death might be the perfect time for the magician to appear, if for no other reason than Houdini's sense of showmanship.

"I've always said that the greatest publicity stunt that Harry Houdini ever pulled off was dying on Halloween because after that the mythology about him grew by leaps and bounds," he said.

It has also conjured conspiracy theories. Was Houdini's death certificate altered to purposely make it appear he died on Halloween? Was the wrestler who punched him a hitman sent by angry psychics to assassinate the escape artist?

Sponsor Message

In some ways Houdini's death mirrors the stunts he performed in life — shrouded in mystery.

World.title: Your writing was flagged as AI. What does that actually mean?
World.content:
Your writing was flagged as AI. What does that actually mean?

toggle caption i karetoria/Getty Images

Ghostwriter Sally McGraw was hoping to land a job developing a book proposal for a prospective client. But after submitting a writing sample, she got an unexpected response: an email telling her that multiple artificial intelligence detection tools had flagged her work as machine-generated.

"I was floored because I had not used AI to generate the text," McGraw said. "I'd written it all myself."

Having spent more than 20 years as a professional nonfiction writer, McGraw said she was angry that her work had been dismissed as AI-written.

"You know where you see a cartoon character going red from their chin all the way up to the crown of their head? I felt my ears starting to burn," she said. "I thought, what is going on?"

Sponsor Message

McGraw said she assured the client she had written the proposal herself, but decided not to press the issue because she considered the job "minor."

toggle caption i Sally McGraw

In an email to NPR, the client confirmed that she had screened McGraw's work for AI. But she said the results were not the determining factor in choosing to hire a different writer, instead citing experience and fit. McGraw says she was paid for her writing samples, but believes the detector results cost her the opportunity to write the full book proposal.

As editors struggle to keep up with a growing influx of AI-generated content, some are turning to detection tools to help sift through the mounting number of submissions. But these tools aren't perfect: They've been known to falsely flag human-written work as AI, which can leave writers with little idea of what triggered the result and how to prove otherwise.

"Everyone knows that these screeners are not 100% accurate," said McGraw.

Editors are overwhelmed by AI-written submissions

Neil Clarke, publisher and editor of Clarkesworld, says a flood of AI submissions at the science-fiction magazine has put pressure on the editing staff.

In 2021, the publication received roughly 1,100 submissions a month. By February 2023, after AI agents like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini started to become widely available, that number had doubled, forcing Clarke to temporarily close its submission portal. He estimates his own workload has increased by about 30%.

Sponsor Message

"It's introduced an element of mistrust into the process," he said.

When AI writing detectors disagree

While AI detectors have gotten more sophisticated in recent years, the companies behind the detectors acknowledge that the tools aren't foolproof. Researchers have found that different AI detection tools can reach dramatically different conclusions about the same piece of writing.

In a study published in June, in the International Journal for Educational Integrity, researchers compared the accuracy of four widely used detectors. They tested 160 academic papers comprising four different categories: entirely human-written, entirely AI-written, a combination of the two, and AI material rewritten by a human.

Among the four detectors, Pangram was the most consistently accurate, correctly identifying the use of AI in 37 of the 40 papers with the combined text and in 37 of the 40 papers where a human rewrote AI-generated text.

Pangram CEO Max Spero, in an emailed statement, said his company's detector can make mistakes, particularly when there is not much writing to evaluate.

Previously published writing can pose an additional problem, says Chris Callison-Burch, a professor of computer and information science at the University of Pennsylvania.

"Many AI detectors work by asking a large language model how predictable a passage is," Callison-Burch said. "The catch is that the language models also tend to find text from their training data unusually predictable."

That could explain what science blogger Janelle Shane encountered in late 2022 when she tested excerpts from her 2019 book about how AI works, You Look Like a Thing and I Love You. One detector reported a 98.7% confidence that a passage was machine-generated.

"This is a clear, glaring, blinking-light false positive," Shane said. "I had written this text myself."

An unpublished draft like McGraw's writing sample wouldn't face that particular problem, Callison-Burch said, but could still be falsely flagged based on patterns in the writing style.

Sponsor Message

Detectors look for clues in word choice, punctuation and the way sentences are put together. The word "delve," frequent em dashes, and ideas grouped in lists of threes can trigger an AI-positive result, he said. So can opening sentences with adverbs such as "notably" or "crucially," or posing a question immediately followed by answering it.

At the same time, those are familiar habits for human writers. Callison-Burch says detectors weigh patterns across a whole piece, so an em dash or a particular word alone doesn't necessarily mean that a bot was used.

What's at stake for writers

The Authors Guild, an organization that advocates for writers' rights, said in May that the use of AI detectors "creates an environment reminiscent of witch hunts," with writers worried about false accusations and how to defend themselves.

"A false positive can cost an author their publishing contract and reputation, and a false negative, when AI-generated work slips through reputable publishing undetected, can cause readers to lose their trust in authors and the industry," the Guild wrote.

Clarke, the sci-fi magazine publisher, sits somewhere in the middle. He says that while he doesn't personally use AI detectors to screen incoming manuscripts, he thinks certain detection tools could help overwhelmed editors manage the volume, provided they check the detector's findings. But he cautions against turning suspicions into accusations that could damage a writer's reputation.

"Submissions should end in rejection, not an accusation," he said.

McGraw says the fear of another accusation has changed how she writes. She says she now avoids using certain words and sentence constructions, and occasionally leaves out commas she used to include, hoping the inconsistency will help prove that a human wrote the text.

"I miss my em dash. It was something that I learned in journalism school and I've used it for decades," she said.

Sponsor Message

The ghostwriter also sees the irony. Large language models learn from human prose, yet she says feels the pressure to make hers look less like AI.

"It's like trying to fool a machine into thinking I'm not a machine," McGraw said.

And she worries about facing another accusation when a bigger opportunity is on the line.

"I'm bracing for the time when it's an assignment that I'm really gunning for and the outcome makes or breaks me," she said.

World.title: This Texas midterm race has huge stakes, both for Donald Trump and the country
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, no race has more at stake than the battle to become the next senator for Texas.

The contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico matters for Americans across the U.S., as the outcome could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate for the remainder of Donald Trump’s presidency.

"If we lose Texas, we're going to lose the country," Paxton has told the Republican faithful at numerous campaign rallies.

The stakes are particularly significant for Trump, since all the reasons the Republicans risk losing in Texas trace directly back to him.

Trump pointedly inserted himself into the Texas race from the start by endorsing the scandal-ridden Paxton to become the Republican candidate over long-serving incumbent Sen. John Cornyn.

Paxton's sketchy ethical record, sky-high prices for gas and diesel triggered by Trump's war on Iran and heavy-handed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) tactics are all driving what appears to be a dramatic shift in voter sentiment.

WATCH | Trump hits rally circuit in last big push before U.S. midterms : Trump hits rally circuit in last big push before U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:34 U.S. President Donald Trump held a rally in Florida, and recommitted to events in Kansas and Iowa as Republicans try to fend off surging Democrats in the last weekend before the U.S. midterms.

No Texas Democrat has been elected to the U.S. Senate since 1988, the year before Talarico was born. Despite that history, and despite Trump carrying Texas by 13 percentage points just two years ago, polling averages suggest a Democrat win this time is a distinct possibility.

Paxton's campaign is based on low taxes, cracking down on illegal immigration and supporting Trump's agenda. Talarico's key themes include stopping cuts to health-care funding, imposing term limits on members of Congress and shifting the tax burden from the middle class to corporations and the wealthy.

'Most corrupt politician in Texas'

Both candidates have described the consequences of the election in monumental terms, frequently depicting their opponent as extreme.

The race "isn't just red versus blue," Paxton told a recent rally in the Dallas suburb of Allen. "It's the America our founders gave us versus something they would never recognize.”

"Ken Paxton is everything that's wrong with our politics," countered Talarico later that same day at a rally in Fort Worth. "We are running against the most corrupt politician in Texas."

The corruption cloud hanging over Paxton, the state's attorney general since 2015, includes a grand jury indictment for securities fraud and impeachment in the Texas House for abusing his office to help a political donor. (The fraud charge was eventually dropped after he struck a plea deal, and the Texas Senate declined to convict following his impeachment.)

Voters attend a joint midterm election rally in Weslaco, Tex. on Oct. 25 for three Democratic Party candidates: James Talarico for the U.S. Senate, Bobby Pulido for the U.S. House and Gina Hinojosa for state governor. (Michael Gonzalez/The Associated Press)

Paxton casts Talarico — a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who has served in the state legislature since 2019 — as a dangerous, leftist radical.

"A vote for James Talarico is not just a vote for his radical agenda," Paxton told the Allen rally. "It's a vote for every dangerous idea that Democrats across the country are putting forward right now.”

Paxton's backers go even further in their rhetoric.

'We cannot let evil win'

Lydia Elizondo, the Republican running for district attorney in the South Texas county of Hidalgo County, introduced Paxton at a rally last week.

"We cannot let evil win," Elizondo told the crowd. "That evil has a name, and its name is James Talarico."

One tangible sign of the high stakes: The Senate race in Texas is poised to become the single-most expensive non-presidential campaign in U.S. history.

Spending on advertising by the candidates, parties and corporate-funded political action committees since the Texas primaries began has surpassed $500 million US, according to data compiled by the firm AdImpact.

WATCH | Will Trump accept the results of the midterms? 'I will if they're honest': Trump accused of mounting fear-based intimidation campaign ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:47 Critics accuse U.S. President Donald Trump of mounting a fear-based campaign designed to intimidate voters ahead of next week's midterm elections. Trump has offered a $1-million US reward for election fraud tips, while administration officials have repeatedly refused to rule out sending federal officers to the polls.

Much of that spending has been bankrolled by one rich Texas resident who also happens to be the wealthiest man on Earth.

Two of Elon Musk's political action committees have funneled more than $210 million US to help the Paxton campaign, according to election finance filings.

The Musk-funded ads are primarily aimed at motivating Republicans to vote by invoking culture-war fears about the consequences of a Talarico win.

One ad claims Talarico wants "taxpayer-funded sex-change surgeries on kids." Another claims he backs "putting parents in jail if they do not support surgically transitioning their children." Talarico has rejected the accusations as lies.

The Democrat has in turn made Musk's investments in the Paxton campaign part of his argument to voters.

"Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat," Talarico said as the Fort Worth crowd booed the name of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO.

James Talarico, the Democrat candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, speaks at a campaign rally in Fort Worth on Oct. 19. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

"But on November 3rd, we will deliver a crystal-clear message to the world's first trillionaire. We will let Elon Musk know that Texas is not for sale."

Early turnout in Texas leans Democrat

Advance turnout figures provide some evidence the Democrats' messaging may be working more effectively than the Republicans'.

During the first week of early voting in Texas, people who'd previously voted in a Democratic Party primary slightly outnumbered those who'd voted in a Republican primary, a scenario that a Republican political consultant described as unprecedented.

At a polling station in the South Texas city of Edinburg, first-time voter Laysha Chavez said the key factor driving her decision was the way ICE deportations have separated families who've lived in the U.S. for many years.

"Seeing that happen really breaks my heart because you never know who it could be next. It could be your friend; it could someone close to you," Chavez, a biology student, told CBC News.

There's a range of polling evidence suggesting that Hispanic voters in Texas, who swung toward Trump in record numbers in 2024, have soured on Republicans in 2026.

Also in Edinburg last week, Paxton drew around 100 people to an evening rally, including Ruben Martinez, who said he supports the Republican Party in part for how it deals with illegal immigration.

"It's like, right now here, we're waiting in line to get in," Martinez told CBC News outside the venue. "So it's not fair that somebody just comes out of nowhere and goes straight to the door and maybe fills up the last seat."

'I'm a Talafreako'

While polling suggests pocketbook issues such as the price of gas and diesel are top of mind for midterm voters, those who back either Paxton or Talarico often bring up values as the chief motivator of their support.

Daniel Mitchell attended the Talarico rally in Fort Worth wearing a black T-shirt with the words "I'm a Talafreako," co-opting the derisive nickname that Trump and others have used for the Democrat.

"I think what [Talarico] is doing for Texas is great, how he presents an idea that we can have a change that uplifts everyone," Mitchell told CBC News.

Mitchell's view of the Republican candidate? "Paxton's a fraud," he said. "Just down to his personal life and the policies he's supporting, you can tell that he sells out for whatever makes him happiest in the moment."

After Paxton's rally in the Dallas suburb of Allen, supporters wrote messages on his campaign bus. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Paxton's personal life came under public scrutiny last year when his wife, a Texas state senator, filed for divorce, citing "biblical grounds" and accusing him of adultery.

Neither that nor the corruption allegations sway the Christians who are among Paxton's most ardent backers.

At Paxton's rally in Allen, attendees wrote messages of support on the campaign bus, many on Christian themes.

Mardi Day, a resident of nearby Plano, chose "Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord" as her message.

"I believe that's how the United States is going to stay a strong nation, by following Jesus Christ and our Constitution," Day told CBC News.

Another rally attendee, Gloria Jones, said her top political priority is undoing what she called a "massive immigration problem" from Arab countries.

"How are we going to get rid of all these radical Muslims?" Jones said. "They want to practise Sharia, they need to go back to their country and practise there."

Steve Ceh is a pastor at Solomon's Porch Ministries in New Braunfels, Tex., and a member of Pastors for Paxton, a group of 27 Christian leaders who endorsed the Republican candidate. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Steve Ceh, pastor of Solomon's Porch Ministries in New Braunfels, a city of 120,000 near San Antonio, is one of 27 Pastors for Paxton, a statewide group of Christian leaders praying for the Republican candidate.

"Every man that runs and every woman that runs is a flawed person," Ceh said when asked by CBC News to describe Paxton's positive traits. "So we look beyond the personality of that person and we vote policy, and he is directly in line with Christian values."

Ceh criticizes Talarico for what he calls a "severe leftist ideology" that can't co-exist with biblical principles.

"In Texas, when you start to threaten people's beliefs, values, they're going to go out and vote," he said. "[Talarico] will not win in Texas. I'm not even worried about it."

Trump, however, is worried enough about it that he has travelled to four cities in Texas since Oct. 1 to urge the MAGA faithful to get behind Paxton and raising the spectre that Democrat control of Congress would mean "communists" in power.

"You have to vote for Ken," Trump told a rally in Corpus Christi on Tuesday. "Otherwise, all of the great things we've done are going to change very quickly."

World.title: How to tell whether your lithium batteries are a fire risk — and what to do if they are
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

We've heard a lot about how dangerous hot, fast-moving lithium battery fires are and their rising number — more than 1,500 in communities across Canada last year.

But most of us also keep and charge smartphones, power banks, e-bikes, vacuum cleaners, drills and lots of other lithium battery devices at home without any issues.

So are all the fire warnings overblown? Are some kinds safer than others? Can batteries really go from safe to risky? What are the warning signs? And what should you be doing about this?

How safe are lithium batteries really?

Experts generally agree that overall, lithium batteries are very safe.

Vinny Gupta, assistant professor of fire safety engineering at the University of Waterloo, notes that more than 10 billion battery cells are now manufactured every year . "And we typically only hear about safety issues in just a few of them."

The problem is when the systems fail and they do catch fire, it's "quite dramatic," acknowledged Gupta, who does research that involves intentionally making them fail and catch fire to study their fire risk.

Safety measures typically built into consumer lithium batteries include temperature sensors, pressure relief valves to vent potentially flammable gases and systems to prevent overcharging.

So do you really need to take measures like watching them as they charge and unplugging them as soon as they're done charging, as firefighters advise ?

WATCH | Regina fire chief offers tips on avoiding battery fires: Regina fire chief gives reminder to check charging devices | Duration closed caption 2:11 Lithium-ion batteries are found in everything from phones and tablets to e-bikes and e-scooters. Regina Fire Chief Layne Jackson says you should keep an eye on your charging devices. It's one of many fire prevention precautions Regina Fire & Protective Services is highlighting this week.

It's true that the battery should automatically stop charging.

But experts note that a battery that has been safe all along can become a fire risk at some point.

How can a lithium battery that was safe become a fire risk?

David Giles, CEO of TempAlert, a Halifax company that sells heat-sensing battery-monitoring stickers, said even if people are using batteries as intended, they can become damaged and therefore hazardous.

That could be due to a defect. Or it could be due to an event, such as an e-bike or e-scooter collision.

He says that when you drop your phone, you may notice if you crack the screen. "But you also may have done other internal damage that might not show up right away" — including damaging the battery.

TempAlert makes heat-sensitive stickers that change from black to yellow at 60 C, indicating a problem with your battery. (TempAlert)

Heat, such as from charging your battery in the sun, can also cause damage.

Gupta said one of the most common ways to cause a battery to fail is by overcharging it. Typically, batteries are designed to prevent that, but some are more poorly designed than others, and the risk increases if they're tampered with or paired with the wrong charger.

Giles says that's easy to do, since most have connectors that fit into many devices. But he warns they may be designed for different voltages. The wrong charger "could be ramming, you know, 80, 90 volts into a battery only designed for 40. That's when you start having a major problem."

Repeatedly charging and recharging a battery over time can also eventually cause it to wear out and fail.

When that happens, does the battery catch on fire right away?

Here's the good news — usually no.

"Batteries don't just go into thermal runaway instantly," Giles said. Thermal runaway is a term for when a battery starts to rapidly self-heat, generating more heat and creating a feedback loop that can lead to a fire. "It progressively gets worse and worse."

Lithium batteries are found in many devices, including e-bikes, and most are safe. (Grant Linton/CBC)

When a battery first starts failing, it may feel hot to touch while charging — Gupta says that's "the earliest indication" that something is wrong. At that point, it will usually cool when you unplug it.

Giles said that may happen repeatedly before it stays hot even after being unplugged.

So how much time do you really have before you have a dangerous fire?

"To be honest, we don't really know," Gupta said, as it depends on what is going on inside the battery and the self-heating process is exponential once underway.

Giles said it could take days or weeks of charging and use, or it could take just 20 minutes.

WATCH | How do you put out a lithium battery fire?: What to do when a lithium battery is on fire | Duration 1:36 Firefighters say lithium battery fires are hotter, faster and harder to put out than other kinds of fires. So what does it take? Copious amounts of water — or maybe not.

Are some kinds of lithium batteries less dangerous from a fire safety perspective?

The short answer is no.

The two most popular lithium battery chemistries are NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) and LFP (lithium iron phosphate), which have different materials in their cathodes.

Several readers wrote in to suggest that LFP is less combustible and prone to overheating.

But in Gupta's opinion, "It's hard to really say if one chemistry is safer than [the] other … there are trade-offs."

It's true that LFP is less energy dense and goes into thermal runaway at a higher temperature (about 235 C, compared with 200 C for NMC). It also ejects fewer solid fragments of battery when overheated — but more gas, Gupta said: "And that gas is often laden with both toxic and flammable products."

So, how do you stay safe?

Buy batteries with Canadian safety certifications such as CSA, cUL, cETL on the charger. Make sure you use the correct charger with your battery, even if another one fits in the charging port.

These are the kinds of certification marks you should look for on your battery charger, according to the Government of Canada lithium-ion battery safety website. (Health Canada)

Keep an eye on your charging battery and its environment. Charge your device or battery on a hard, non-flammable surface (not on a couch or bed), where you can see it. Gupta recommends not putting the device in the path that you would need to use to escape in case of a fire incident.

Know the danger signs of a damaged battery. They include feeling too hot, swelling, bad smells, gas or smoke.

There are some devices that can help identify these signs, such as:

TempAlert or other temperature-sensitive stickers that you can apply to the battery.

that you can apply to the battery. Heat detectors or alarms. Reader Adrian Hill of Crystal Beach, Ont., said he purchased one of these that he installed above the spot where he charges his e-bike.

A carbon monoxide detector. Gupta said many lithium batteries release carbon monoxide when overheated.

Know what to do if your battery overheats. Unplug it and get it to a safe, non-flammable place (such as outdoors, a sink or a bucket of sand) if possible. Don't try to charge it again, even if it cools, Giles says.

This is Call2Recycle's kit for dealing with damaged, defective or recalled lithium batteries at hazardous waste facilities. (Call2Recycle)

If it cools down, you can take it to a technician or hazardous waste disposal site. Do not put it in the trash. Call2Recycle has more detailed information on dealing with damaged, defective and recalled batteries .

If the battery continues getting hotter or releases gas or smoke, you're really in the danger zone.

"If you smell anything, that's bad," Gupta said. "You should leave and call the fire department."

Lithium batteries are around us everywhere and that's not going to change any time soon, he added. For the most part they're safe, but "it's important for people to be aware of the fact that they can fail and there are very simple things we can do that go a long way towards improving our personal safety."

World.title: 'No one is safe' as Ebola outbreak surges to more than 10,000 cases, Africa's top doctor warns Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the world's fastest-growing outbreak of Ebola hit more than 10,000 confirmed cases this week, Africa's top doctor warned there could be "massive" spread into additional countries — and even other continents — unless countries such as Canada offer more support.

"No one is safe today," said Dr. Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), in an interview with CBC News from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Friday.

"We are calling on all African countries to increase the level of preparedness. But we're also calling our Western countries, especially Canada, because Canada is where my heart is."

Kaseya is from Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and has led Africa CDC for the past three years. But he has called Canada home since 2013. He told CBC News he has been living apart from his family — his three children attend university in Toronto, and his wife remains in Laval, Que. — as he works to end an unprecedented crisis that began in his home country.

He singled out Canada as an ally to African health officials, though he said more can still be done.

"This is my message to Canadians: No fear, no panic, but take it seriously, and even talk to your parliamentarians, talk to other people you know, if they can provide more support for this outbreak," he told CBC News.

"I really want to be back home to celebrate with my family, but we need to stop this outbreak before doing that."

Death toll surpasses 5,000

Kaseya's comments follow a grim new milestone in this year's Ebola outbreak. Confirmed cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo have surpassed 10,000, while the latest report from the country's public health institute shows the death toll has surpassed 5,000.

The outbreak was first declared in mid-May, but scientists suspect the Bundibugyo strain of the virus had been spreading undetected for months in some of Congo's most remote regions.

Ongoing conflict, public distrust and the lack of an approved treatment or vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain have further complicated efforts to contain the outbreak.

It is now the country's largest-ever outbreak and the fastest-growing and second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded — behind only the West Africa Ebola crisis, which infected more than 28,000 people, mainly across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, from 2014 to 2016.

"If this outbreak [continues] like that, with the same magnitude, in one year we'll have more than what West Africa had in two years and a half," Kaseya said.

"But it won't be just a few countries. It will be more countries. It can also affect some other continents."

A much smaller number of infections have already appeared in neighbouring countries, including Uganda, Kenya, and most recently in Nigeria, which reported its first Ebola infection in a decade.

That patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat, was flown to Switzerland for treatment on Monday , the latest in a series of patients evacuated to European countries since the outbreak began.

Kaseya said imported infections could continue as teams on the ground struggle to slow community transmission in new areas of Congo.

The risk to Canada remains low, he added, though he implored Canadian officials to "move from low to zero by supporting [Africa] to stop the outbreak where it is currently."

WATCH | Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo's history: Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo’s history | Duration closed caption 2:05 The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is officially the deadliest in the country’s history, and health officials worry the crisis will only get worse when children return to school.

Canada offered $8M to Ebola fight

Canada committed $8 million to the Ebola response in May, including $2 million for Africa CDC to accelerate surveillance and strengthen biosecurity measures. In late July, Health Canada also authorized Moderna to launch a clinical trial of its vaccine targeting the Bundibugyo virus.

The federal government also introduced temporary border measures aimed at reducing the risk of Ebola entering and spreading in Canada, including outbreak alerts issued for Kenya and Nigeria in October.

"The Government of Canada will continue to monitor the situation closely and may adjust these measures, as appropriate, based on evolving evidence and the epidemiological situation both in Canada and internationally," the Public Health Agency of Canada told CBC News in a statement this week.

Alongside those official efforts, Canadian research teams are also working behind the scenes to study this once-rare form of Ebola.

University of Winnipeg microbiologist Jason Kindrachuk said Canadian and Congolese scientists have sequenced more than 1,000 genomes to date, offering insights into how the virus is behaving and whether existing vaccines may offer cross-protection for the Bundibugyo strain.

But he stressed there are "finite resources" for that collaborative, cross-border work.

WATCH | Congolese students separated from loved ones due to travel restrictions: Congolese students in Montreal separated from loved ones due to Canada travel restrictions | Duration closed caption 1:45 In May, Canada implemented temporary measures restricting entry into the country for foreign nationals arriving from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda or South Sudan due to Ebola risks. As a result, many Congolese students in Montreal face a difficult dilemma: they want to visit their families, but fear the restrictions will prevent them from re-entering Canada for their studies.

Canadian scientists 'scramble' for research funding

"We're trying to scramble with funds from whatever sources we have to be able to keep things like genome sequencing alive, to keep testing alive … so I think at some point we need to see bigger investment, and certainly sustained investment, from the high-income areas of the world," Kindrachuk said.

"I think there's a real need for Canada and other countries to step up."

Kaseya praised Canada's efforts to date, including the close collaboration between African and Canadian health officials, but agreed that the threat of Ebola could persist for months without broader support to end the crisis.

"We'll continue to work hard to keep Canada safe — we'll do our best to keep all other countries in the world safe — but … if we do not provide support, we cannot guarantee that all of us will be safe," he said.

World.title: Here’s why only half of Ontario is turning its clocks back this weekend
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some Ontarians will turn their clocks back one hour this weekend, while others will not. CBC's Dale Manucdoc breaks down what you need to know.

Some provinces are ending time changes. What about Ontario?

Clocks in most of Ontario are turning back one hour on Sunday, marking the end of daylight saving time, but they’ll stay put in a large chunk of the province — splitting it into two time zones.

Northwestern Ontario is following suit with a number of western provinces and territories that have permanently switched to daylight time as a part of a major shake-up to Canadian time zones. Alberta, Manitoba, Northwest Territories and most of British Columbia are no longer changing their clocks twice a year.

The Ontario government wants all of Ontario’s clocks to do the same. In 2020, the province passed the Time Amendment Act , which would strike down all the divisive clock changing.

But the law won’t come into effect unless Quebec and New York do the same thing. A news release from Ontario's attorney general says it’s important the three jurisdictions stay aligned to ensure synchronicity when it comes to trade, the stock market and broadcasting.

Those trading partners are also considering the change, but so far, it’s been a stalemate and no one wants to make the first move.

No advantage to changing first: professor

Patrick Baylis, an associate professor of economics at the University of British Columbia, says it is a wise choice for governments to hold off on making any time zone changes until their trading partners do.

"There's no first-mover advantage to changing time before everybody else does," Baylis said. "It just means you, sort of, sow a bit more confusion in your own area."

WATCH | Canada's new time zones, explained: Confused about Canada's new time zones? It's about to get complicated | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 8:15 Manitoba is the latest province to stop switching between daylight and standard time, following the same decision made by B.C., Alberta and the Northwest Territories over the last year or so.

Quebec is among the provinces who will be turning back clocks this weekend. But the newly elected Parti Québécois government plans to change that soon.

In a recent Facebook post, Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said about the time change: "This is probably the last year we'll be imposing such unnecessary constraints on ourselves."

In New York, Republican Sen. Joe Griffo sponsored senate bill S3380 that would establish daylight saving time as the standard time in the state throughout the year.

The U.S. House of Representatives has passed the bill, Griffo said, but he still needs action from the senate to push it forward.

"The Congress, under the Uniform Time Act, has, ultimately, determination to tell us what time we can be on," Griffo told CBC Toronto. "You can't have 50 states doing 50 different things, which I understand and appreciate."

For now, unless the two chambers of the U.S. Congress can get on the same page and Quebec also implements the change, Ontario will be stuck with two time zones.

According to the province, Ontario’s northwestern time zone will switch from eastern to central time zone west of the 90th meridian, a north-south line of longitude that crosses northwestern Ontario.

World.title: Facing a potential $40M US tariff bill, this American importer is suing Trump to end some tariffs on Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Inside a sprawling refrigerated warehouse, tucked into an industrial neighbourhood not far from New Jersey's Newark Airport, you'll find a new front in the U.S.-Canada trade war.

It's the headquarters of Gellert Global Group, a third-generation, family-owned food distribution company that is suing the Trump administration over its 50 per cent tariffs on certain Canadian goods and seeking refunds.

In one of his first broadcast interviews since launching the lawsuit, Thomas Gellert, the company's CEO, says he felt he had to do something.

"We can't sustain a tariff like this on these products for much longer," he said during an interview with CBC News on the floor of the warehouse in Elizabeth, N.J.

Gellert Global Group imports roughly $80 million US worth of Canadian cheeses every year, including Celebrity goat cheese produced by Mariposa Dairy in Lindsay, Ont. It also imports a range of Canadian-produced brie and camembert products. That means the business could be paying $40 million US in tariffs for the year.

"Customers are not going to take price increases. Everyone is sort of beat down and tired from inflationary pressures," Gellert said, confirming that his company is eating the cost of the tariffs for now.

Under Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, U.S. President Donald Trump, seen speaking to reporters in Maryland Thursday, has the right to impose tariffs on countries that have discriminated against the U.S. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

Gellert tried to get exemptions for these products in meetings with American lawmakers and diplomats, including U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra. In those conversations, he says he highlighted the fact that American-produced milk is being used for some of the cheese products hit by tariffs, arguing that, in the end, the policy is hurting U.S. farmers too.

Those lobbying efforts were not successful. And with no Canada-U.S. trade deal appearing to be on the horizon, Gellert decided he had to take legal action.

"Frankly we don't have time to wait for things to settle on their own," he said.

"We have a business here to run."

The lawsuit was filed by the Liberty Justice Center, a non-profit, non-partisan legal advocacy organization. It is the same organization that successfully challenged Trump's IEEPA tariffs, which were struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court earlier this year.

"We felt like our job wasn't done if the President keeps putting illegal tariffs on different countries," said Sarah Albrecht, the chair and CEO of the Liberty Justice Center.

Tariff technicalities

The Trump administration imposed this round of tariffs after trade talks with Canada broke down in August.

The duties are applied through Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, also known as the Smoot-Hawley Act, a Depression-era law that had never been used before for tariff purposes.

The law gives the president the power to impose tariffs of up to 50 per cent on imported goods from a country that has discriminated against the U.S.

The Trump administration has argued that Canada's decision to retaliate against previous rounds of U.S. tariffs amounts to discrimination. It specifically cited the banning of American alcohol products by certain provinces, protections for the Canadian dairy industry and measures related to the auto sector.

In a statement released the day the lawsuit was filed, the Liberty Justice Center said Section 338 cannot be used as an "all-purpose authorization for the executive branch to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises."

Among the arguments the group is making, it says there's a disconnect between allegations of discrimination by Canada and the products Trump is targeting with the tariffs. It also says the Trump administration illegally rushed the implementation of some of the tariffs. And it claims Trump does not have the authority to impose tariffs in this way.

"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," Albrecht said.

Initially, the tariffs applied to roughly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, with targets including cement, road salt, hockey sticks and other items. However, the list has been adjusted twice to remove some products and add others.

Some of the changes were made at the request of Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, as she finds herself in a tough re-election race. She has sought exemptions for products important to businesses in her home state, as the trade war with Canada is proving unpopular there.

WATCH | Trump shifts tariffs on Canadian goods as he hints at trade deal; Carney remains cautious: Trump to lift some tariffs on Canada before U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:41 Ahead of the U.S. midterms, the Trump Administration is lifting 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian products but adding them to others. The President also suggested a trade deal may be close, but Prime Minister Mark Carney was more cautious.

Experts mixed on strength of Trump's tariff justification

Since the tariffs were first announced, legal experts have offered varying opinions on whether the measures would survive a legal challenge.

"There's a good chance it could get reversed," said Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer and partner at King & Spalding International Trade Group.

"I think the administration may have a tough time identifying the reasons why these particular products or these particular actions by Canada are discriminatory."

Lawyers for the Trump administration will have to make the connection, Majerus says, between the alleged discrimination and why the U.S. tariffs offset that discrimination.

"The fact that there have been adjustments [to the product list] since they've been put in place ... I think it may undermine their claim as well," he said.

However, the Trump administration is expected to put up an intense defence.

"I think they can make some creative arguments on how they're able to kind of invoke the authority broadly," Majerus said.

"It's a bit of a blank canvas in terms of how the courts are going to look at this."

A display of Celebrity goat cheese and other Canadian cheese products. Gellert Global Group says U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods are threatening its business and the Canadian producers it works with. (Katie Simpson/CBC)

Fears of losing shelf space

If there isn't a resolution by next year, Gellert says his company will have to reassess how it handles the tariffs and whether it is sustainable to keep importing these Canadian goods.

"If we stop selling a product — to get back on the shelf would be very difficult," he said.

"We don't want to lose shelf space."

He also says that if these Canadian products are not available to U.S. consumers, there aren't readily available American alternatives to replace them.

"There is not enough goat milk in the United States to support demand," he said.

"And the existing goat cheese factories that are here, even if they're importing frozen curd, they don't have the capacity. So that's the reason why we work with our Canadian partners."

The goat cheese issue specifically weighs heavily on Gellert. He says he worked closely with the family that owns Mariposa Dairy and encouraged them to invest in production to grow their business.

"I do feel some sort of sense of personal responsibility to that community, that we've encouraged them to build up infrastructure to help support the business — and now that's at risk," he said.

"If we stop buying, they start culling goats. It's not something that can be brought back again."

World.title: Alberta separatist Jeff Rath kicked out of governing United Conservative Party
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Separatist leader Jeff Rath, who rose to prominence in the lead-up to the Alberta referendum in his white cowboy hat, has had his membership revoked by the governing United Conservative Party.

In an email sent to Rath on Thursday and viewed by CBC News, Dustin Van Vugt, the party's executive director, said that Rath's "words and actions have made clear" that he does not support the party or its objectives.

"Your public conduct in relation to our party and leader has not met the basic standard of decency we expect of our members when they disagree or otherwise."

His membership was revoked immediately, Van Vugt wrote.

After Albertans voted decisively to remain within Canada on Oct. 19, Premier Danielle Smith made it clear the UCP would be a federalist party going forward. But with pre-referendum polling suggesting that independence was popular among UCP members, there's been much speculation about how she would address the separatist faction within her base.

Ahead of next month's party AGM, any aspiring board members are now required to sign a declaration that they'll abide by the results of the referendum.

Rath is the first separatist leader to be asked to leave.

In a phone call, Rath said his ouster had less to do with his separatist beliefs than with how he's expressed his criticisms more broadly.

"I'm a very loud and effective critic of Danielle Smith," he said.

"She obviously does not want free speech in the party."

In an email, a party spokesperson said the decision was made because of Rath's "public conduct toward the party and its leader."

Rath said he also received an email from the UCP notifying him the party had refunded the $239 he paid in order to attend next month's AGM.

Rath and Smith have publicly sparred over their differing views on Alberta’s place in Confederation. Rath has dismissed the premier as an "avowed federalist" and mused about trying to push her out of the party leadership.

Smith, meanwhile, has maintained that she was always on team Canada and, after the referendum, warned anyone not on board that they would need to join a different party.

But their debates have occasionally veered into more personal territory.

Earlier this week, Rath accused Smith of colluding with federalist leader Thomas Lukaszuk in a personal text exchange he posted online. When pressed by NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi during question period Thursday, Smith appeared to try to distance herself from Rath by noting his past financial contributions to the Opposition party.

"He's actually an NDP supporter," she said.

Rath told CBC News he once attended a leadership event for then-NDP leader Rachel Notley, largely because, he said, she was once his classmate in an honours political science class.

Speaking to reporters Friday, Smith confirmed the party's executive director had pulled Rath's membership.

"He’s never supported me ... He never supported me during the leadership, he never supported me in my time in office, and he certainly doesn’t support me now," she said.

"That’s irrelevant," she added. "What is relevant is that he has said publicly things like he wants to come to the AGM to turn the UCP into an independence party. And we are not an independence party."

Rath says he will be consulting with legal counsel and will "likely" file an appeal of the decision.

Either way, he says his work trying to speak to members and have Smith replaced as party leader isn't over.

World.title: U.S. charges 5 more Canadians with voter fraud offences amid Trump administration crackdown
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. Department of Justice says charges have been laid against five more Canadians for voting fraud-related offences, the latest in a flurry of similar prosecutions ahead of next week's midterm elections.

According to a tally compiled by CBC News, at least 20 Canadians have now been either charged or sentenced in the U.S. this year in federal election integrity investigations. Most charges have been filed since last month, with allegations typically dating back several years.

The five latest cases were announced in a series of news releases Thursday and Friday from U.S. attorney's offices in Missouri, Tennessee, North Carolina and Wisconsin. They all involve Canadians living in the U.S. — most of them listed as lawful permanent residents — accused of falsely claiming citizenship to cast a ballot, or illegally voting in a past election.

The defendants in the latest cases are between 58 and 68 years old, according to the Department of Justice.

"The right to vote is fundamental to American citizenship and a cornerstone of our republic," Dan Bishop, the U.S. attorney for the Middle District of North Carolina, said in a statement.

Bishop said the recent charges "serve notice that those who violate our election laws, including non-citizens who register and vote, will be investigated and prosecuted."

U.S. federal prosecutors and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) — a branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement — have in recent weeks repeatedly highlighted their efforts to crack down on voter fraud.

"Anyone who unlawfully votes will be found and brought to justice!" HSI said Friday in a post on X.

This photo released by U.S. authorities claims to show a 69-year-old Canadian woman charged with 'illegal voting by an alien' during her arrest after dark. (U.S. Department of Homeland Security)

In one instance last week, a 69-year-old Canadian, a lawful permanent resident living in Florida, was indicted on charges of making a false statement claiming U.S. citizenship to vote and "illegal voting by an alien," prosecutors said.

The woman allegedly registered to vote in 2021 and then cast a ballot in the 2022 U.S. general election.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security released a photo of the woman during her arrest with her face blurred. The image appeared to show her dressed in a housecoat and slippers, surrounded by federal agents outside a home after dark.

Several of the charges were brought by federal prosecutors named by the Trump administration, such as Ellis Boyle in Raleigh, N.C.

"This is the worst type of constitutional assault on our independence and liberty," Boyle told reporters earlier this month.

U.S. attorney Ellis Boyle at a news conference in Washington, D.C., on April 28. (Cliff Owen/The Associated Press)

U.S. authorities have announced similar charges against citizens of several other countries including Australia, Colombia, Cuba, Jamaica and the United Kingdom.

The efforts align with U.S. President Donald Trump's long-running false claims of widespread voter fraud in federal elections.

"The timing tells us why it's likely they're doing this," said David Becker, executive director of the non-partisan Center for Election Innovation and Research, in a recent interview.

He insisted what little non-citizen voting occurs in the U.S. has not affected the outcomes of elections.

WATCH | Canadians warned to stay out of U.S. elections as arrests ramp up: Canadians sternly warned to stay out of U.S. elections as arrests ramp up | Duration closed caption 2:08 The U.S. embassy in Ottawa sternly warned Canadians against 'attempting to participate or influence U.S. elections in any way' ahead of the midterms. U.S. agents have ramped up arrests against non-citizen voters, including Canadians.

"This is likely an attempt to try to sow doubts about the election, in advance of an election in which the president and his administration might fear the voters might reject them," Becker said.

Last week, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa said in a statement Canadians account for the "second highest total of prosecutions for fraudulent or illegal voting of any country."

The embassy pointedly warned "all Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way. Americans decide America's elections."

Bill Essayli, the most senior federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said last week that 156 individuals had been charged with “voting fraud-related offences” across the country since the start of the current Trump administration.

It’s a relatively small figure, given the number of people who cast a ballot in the U.S.

According to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, more than 211 million citizens were active registered voters for the country’s 2024 general election.

World.title: Carney says, unequivocally, Canada seeking to become the EU's 1st associate member
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is working to become the European Union's first associate member, his most definitive statement on the issue to date after hosting the bloc's leaders in Montreal this week.

It still remains unclear what that would look like and cost.

This year's Canada-EU summit saw Canada and European officials finalize a number of negotiations and launch a long list of new commitments as part of a deeper alliance, but the issue of what to call the allies' deeper partnership has somewhat overshadowed the work between Ottawa and the 27-member bloc given some members are against the proposal.

"We are working toward the deepest possible partnership, short of accession because of our geography, with Canada becoming the European Union's first associate member," said Carney in his closing remarks.

"Over the coming months, we will determine the substance, scale and scope of this form of membership."
