MONTERREY — This guide is for expats, digital nomads and long-stay visitors who want to plan November around the events that actually matter. Here are the confirmed things to do in Monterrey November 2026, with dates, venues, prices where published and practical advice for getting tickets.

November in Monterrey is a month of big stadium shows, trade fairs at CINTERMEX and a long holiday weekend around Revolution Day on Monday 16 November. The weather is mild to warm, with cooler evenings, so pack a light jacket for nights at Parque Fundidora.

Ticket platforms vary by event, so check the official venue or organiser page before you buy.

6 to 8 November: Karol G at Estadio BBVA

Friday 6 to Sunday 8 November Karol G — Viajando por el mundo Tropitour Estadio BBVA, Guadalupe metropolitan area The Colombian superstar brings her stadium tour to Monterrey for three nights, the headline concert run of the month. Expect a full production with a huge crowd, so arrive early and use the metro or a ride-share to avoid parking chaos at Estadio BBVA. Check Ticketmaster México or the venue page for the exact on-sale link.

11 to 15 November: Trade Fairs and La Conve 66

Wednesday 11 to Thursday 12 November Expo Eléctrica y Solar Norte 26 CINTERMEX, Parque Fundidora / Obrera · Price not stated

Wednesday 11 to Thursday 12 November Expo Franquicias Monterrey CINTERMEX, Parque Fundidora / Obrera · Price not stated A business and investment fair focused on franchise opportunities in northern Mexico. It is aimed at entrepreneurs and investors, but curious expats can learn a lot about the local business landscape. Bring identification if you plan to enter business-to-business areas.

Saturday 14 to Sunday 15 November La Conve 66 CINTERMEX, Parque Fundidora / Obrera · Price not stated A multi-fandom pop-culture convention, with international guests, cosplay, gaming and exhibitor halls. It is the month’s standout event for anyone into comics, anime, sci-fi or gaming culture. Buy tickets in advance if possible, as popular days can sell out.

16 to 21 November: Revolution Day, Mon Laferte and Banda MS

Monday 16 to Tuesday 17 November Mon Laferte Auditorio Citibanamex, Parque Fundidora / Obrera The Chilean-Mexican singer-songwriter plays two nights at Auditorio Citibanamex, bringing her emotionally charged blend of bolero, rock and Latin pop. Monday 16 November is the Revolution Day public holiday, so the first show is a good option for a long weekend night out. Check the official ticket platform for seat availability.

Friday 20 November Banda MS Arena Monterrey, Parque Fundidora / Obrera One of Mexico’s most popular banda groups plays Arena Monterrey, with a setlist full of romantic and party anthems. The arena is inside Parque Fundidora, so you can eat nearby before the show. Tickets are in high demand, so secure them through the official seller early.

Saturday 21 November David Bisbal — Tour Eternos 2026 Auditorio Citibanamex, Parque Fundidora / Obrera The Spanish pop star brings his Eternos tour to Monterrey the night after Banda MS plays at Arena Monterrey. Bisbal’s powerful voice and romantic repertoire draw a devoted Spanish-language pop audience. Confirm the exact stage and entry time on the official ticket page.

26 to 30 November: Trueno, María José, Carlos Rivera and Yandel

Thursday 26 November Trueno Auditorio Citibanamex, Parque Fundidora / Obrera The Argentine rapper brings his sharp lyricism and high-energy hip-hop to Auditorio Banamex. It is a strong pick for a younger crowd or anyone following the Latin American urban scene. Check the venue’s official ticket partner before buying.

Friday 27 November María José Auditorio Citibanamex, Parque Fundidora / Obrera

Saturday 28 November Carlos Rivera Arena Monterrey, Parque Fundidora / Obrera

Monday 30 November Yandel Sinfónico Arena Monterrey, Parque Fundidora / Obrera

Planning Your Monterrey in November

November is one of the best months to be outdoors in Monterrey, with mild to warm days and cooler nights. Pack light layers and a jacket for evening concerts, especially at open-air venues like Escenario GNP Seguros.

Cold fronts can arrive suddenly, so check the forecast before heading to Parque Fundidora.Mexico’s Revolution Day public holiday is observed on the third Monday of November; in 2026, it falls on Monday 16 November.

Banks and many offices close, but shopping centres and entertainment venues generally stay open. The long weekend is a good time for the Mon Laferte show.

For getting around at night, ride-share apps are widely used in Monterrey, and the metro is practical for reaching Parque Fundidora and the Auditorio Citibanamex area. Traffic around Estadio BBVA can be heavy on concert nights, so leave early or use public transport.

Parking at CINTERMEX is available but fills up during large expos.Ticket platforms vary by event, so always confirm the official seller before paying.

Ticketmaster México is a common option for major concerts, while CINTERMEX handles its own expo registrations. Foreign cards often work online, but some platforms may require a Mexican billing address, so have a backup payment method ready.

For weekly listings, check the culture pages of El Norte and Milenio Monterrey, which publish updated event calendars. The Municipio de Monterrey website is useful for public events and holiday notices.

If you are settling in rather than visiting, start with our Monterrey expat city guide and the Moving to Mexico guide. More culture picks are in our Mexico City November guide and on the Mexico news hub.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the biggest events in Monterrey in November 2026?

Karol G plays three nights at Estadio BBVA from 6 to 8 November, and La Conve 66 runs at CINTERMEX on 14 and 15 November 2026. Mon Laferte, Banda MS and Carlos Rivera also play major shows later in the month.

Is there a public holiday in Monterrey in November 2026?

Yes, Mexico’s Revolution Day public holiday is observed on the third Monday of November; in 2026, it falls on Monday 16 November. Banks and many offices close, but entertainment venues generally remain open.

Where do most big concerts take place in Monterrey?

Arena Monterrey and Auditorio Citibanamex are both inside Parque Fundidora, while Estadio BBVA is in the Guadalupe metropolitan area. Escenario GNP Seguros is another major outdoor concert venue in the city.

How do I buy tickets for events in Monterrey?

Ticketmaster México is a common platform for major concerts, while CINTERMEX handles registration for its expos. Always confirm the official seller on the venue or organiser page before paying.

NIGERIA · COMPANY RESULTS

Key Facts — The country Nigeria is Africa’s most populous nation, and Zenith Bank is one of its largest banks.

— What happened Zenith Bank reported pre-tax profit of US$690 million for the nine months to 30 September 2026.

— The swing Loan impairment charges fell 70.5%, offsetting a trading loss and lower income.

— After tax Profit after tax fell 11.6% to US$502 million as the tax charge rose 65%.

— Still open The results data shows no nine-month dividend and no full-year profit forecast.

Zenith Bank profit before tax reached N928.8 billion (about US$690 million) in the nine months to 30 September 2026, the Nigerian lender reported. That is 1.2% above the N917.4 billion (about US$682 million) of a year earlier, in results published on Friday 30 October 2026.

The result matters to US readers because Nigeria is a major emerging market and its banks hold much of the country’s savings and dollar trade. Zenith Bank profit held up only because the bank set aside 70.5% less money for bad loans than last year.

The Headline Numbers

Zenith Bank profit before tax for the nine months was N928.8 billion (about US$690 million), up from N917.4 billion (about US$682 million) a year earlier. Profit after tax fell 11.6% to N675.8 billion (about US$502 million) from N764.2 billion (about US$568 million).

Gross earnings, meaning total income before costs, dropped 15.0% to N2.87 trillion (about US$2.13 billion). Earnings per share fell 11.8% to N16.41 (about US$0.012).

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Bad-Loan Charges Matter

Impairment charges are money a bank sets aside for loans that may not be repaid. Zenith’s charge fell 70.5% to N230.8 billion (about US$171 million) from N782.8 billion (about US$582 million).

That drop of N552.0 billion (about US$410 million) was the main support for Zenith Bank profit. Last year’s charge was very high, so the comparison is unusually favourable.

Trading Gains Turn to Losses

Zenith booked a trading loss of N229.2 billion (about US$170 million), against a gain of N277.7 billion (about US$206 million) a year earlier. The swing in trading results was the biggest drag on earnings after lower interest income.

Interest income fell 4.5% to N2.62 trillion (about US$1.95 billion), and income from treasury bills fell to N573.0 billion (about US$426 million). Interest paid out fell faster, down 15.4% to N688.7 billion (about US$512 million), which kept net interest income near N1.93 trillion (about US$1.43 billion).

Fees Up, Costs Up, Tax Up

Net fee and commission income rose 26.6% to N256.9 billion (about US$191 million), helped by electronic banking fees. Operating expenses rose 17.6% to N625.6 billion (about US$465 million).

The tax charge jumped 65.1% to N253.0 billion (about US$188 million). That explains why profit after tax fell although pre-tax profit rose.

A Larger Balance Sheet

Total assets grew 10.3% to N34.39 trillion (about US$25.6 billion). Customer deposits rose 14.5% to N27.11 trillion (about US$20.1 billion), and loans rose 24.2% to N11.64 trillion (about US$8.65 billion).

Third-quarter pre-tax profit was N290.9 billion (about US$216 million), up from N276.6 billion (about US$206 million) in the second quarter. The bank’s shares closed at N119 (about US$0.09) on Friday 30 October 2026, down 11.2% over the month.

What It Means for US Readers

Zenith Bank is listed on the Nigerian Exchange in Lagos, so most US investors reach it through Africa-focused funds or foreign brokers. The Zenith Bank profit result shows a large Nigerian lender protecting earnings through lower loan provisions rather than stronger lending income.

American firms that sell goods or services in Nigeria depend on banks like this one for payments and dollar trade. For related coverage, see our report on the Access Holdings results delay.

What Is Not Known

The results data does not state whether the board will pay an interim dividend beyond the N1.50 (about US$0.001) per share proposed with half-year results. It also gives no full-year profit forecast.

It is unclear whether Zenith Bank profit will keep this support from low bad-loan charges in the fourth quarter. Naira conversions here use about 1,345 naira to the US dollar on 31 October 2026.

More: Nigeria news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much profit did Zenith Bank make?

Pre-tax profit was N928.8 billion (about US$690 million) for the nine months to 30 September 2026. Profit after tax was N675.8 billion (about US$502 million).

Why did profit after tax fall?

The tax charge rose 65.1% to N253.0 billion (about US$188 million). That outweighed the small rise in pre-tax profit.

What are impairment charges?

They are funds a bank sets aside for loans that may go unpaid. Zenith’s fell 70.5% to N230.8 billion (about US$171 million).

Did Zenith Bank’s income grow?

No, gross earnings fell 15.0% to N2.87 trillion (about US$2.13 billion). Fee income rose, but interest income and trading results fell.

When were the results published?

The bank published its nine-month results on Friday 30 October 2026. They cover the period to 30 September 2026.

World.title: Costa Rica Cuts Growth Forecast to 3.2%
World.content:
File photo, 2005. Downtown San José, Costa Rica’s capital, seen from the Jade Museum. (Photo: Wikipedro, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COSTA RICA · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Costa Rica is a stable Central American democracy that relies on exports from free trade zones, where multinational companies make chips, medical devices and business services.

Why it matters Growth in a close US trading partner is slowing, with free-zone exports hit by closures of electronics-component plants and by global trade tensions.

Why now The central bank presented its monetary policy report on Friday, 30 October 2026, with lower growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027.

What happened The central bank cut its 2026 growth forecast to 3.2% from 3.4% in July and its 2027 forecast to 3.3% from 3.5%, and gave a first 2028 forecast of 3.6%.

The numbers Exports are projected to grow 1.4% in 2026 after 8.6% in 2025, free-zone output 3% after 12.7%, and free-zone jobs fell by 1,691 to 195,410 in the year to August 2026.

What it means for you US companies with plants in Costa Rican free zones face slower export growth, and analysts say a stronger colón against the dollar weighs on competitiveness.

Still open How many more free-zone jobs are lost, whether more multinationals shrink their plants, and whether zone output rebounds to the projected 4.6% in 2027.

Power Index Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 in Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 36.5 points (October 2026 edition).

In Plain English The Banco Central de Costa Rica, known as the BCCR, is the central bank, and its monetary policy report, called the IPM in Spanish, sets out its forecasts for growth, prices and trade. Free trade zones are areas where companies, mostly multinationals, produce for export under special tax rules. The colón is Costa Rica’s currency, and the reference rate is the central bank’s daily buy and sell price for the US dollar. The CCSS is the Costa Rican Social Security Fund, whose counts of formal workers come from payroll contributions.

Costa Rica’s central bank cut its 2026 growth forecast to 3.2% on Friday, 30 October 2026, down from 3.4% in July and well below the preliminary 4.6% recorded in 2025. The Banco Central de Costa Rica, known as the BCCR, also lowered its 2027 forecast to 3.3% from 3.5% and gave a first forecast of 3.6% for 2028.

The slowdown matters in the United States because the free trade zones of Costa Rica generate an important share of its goods exports, and La Nación names US chipmakers Intel and Qorvo among the companies that ended manufacturing there. The bank’s report says the cut for 2027 mostly reflects a smaller contribution from net external demand, because exports are expected to expand less.

What the Forecast Says

The bank’s report says output grew 2.7% in the third quarter after 3.5% in the second, as manufacturing fell in both trade regimes, and that the oil import bill rose by almost US$700 million in the first nine months of 2026. The bank presented the figures through its president, Róger Madrigal, at a news conference on 30 October.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 with 36.5 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (75); weakest: military means (0). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB). See the full index, the business lens and the data →

La Nación reports that growth rests mainly on domestic demand, and El Financiero reports that household consumption is projected to grow 2.5% in 2026 after 3.8% in 2025. La Nación adds that two international bodies see faster 2026 growth, with the UN regional commission ECLAC at 3.7% and the International Monetary Fund at 3.3%.

File photo, 2023. The Banco Central de Costa Rica building in San José, with the bank’s name on the facade. (Photo: MyCatIsAChonk, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Download the PDF checklist

Exports and Free Trade Zones

The bank projects export growth of 1.4% in 2026 after 8.6% in 2025, and La Nación reports that Madrigal tied the slowdown to the exit of two companies and to medical-device exports growing more slowly than in 2025. The bank had foreseen the effect of the Intel and Qorvo manufacturing exit on 2026 exports since July 2025, La Nación adds.

Output in the free trade zone regime is projected to grow 3% in 2026 after a preliminary 12.7% in 2025, before rising 4.6% in 2027 and 5.3% in 2028. The regime of companies that pay income tax is projected to grow 3.3% in 2026, then 3.1% and 3.3% in the next two years.

Jobs, Wages and the Colon

Madrigal said the number of free-zone workers, measured as a three-month moving average, fell from 197,101 to 195,410 between August 2025 and August 2026 (1,691 fewer, or 0.9%), while real wages there rose 2.8% on average. The BCCR report says the fall was concentrated in administrative and support services (4,052 fewer), professional and technical services (2,674 fewer) and information and communications (2,286 fewer), partly offset by 4,761 more manufacturing workers.

Madrigal attributed the job decline to adjustments by global companies, and La Nación quotes him saying “Costa Rica no se exime de eso”, meaning the country is not exempt. La Nación notes that he did not mention the colón’s appreciation against the US dollar, which analysts cite along with US tariffs, the war in Iran and higher oil prices as pressures on competitiveness.

The BCCR reference rates for 30 October were ¢450.80 buy and ¢455.44 sell per US$, a midpoint of ¢453.12, as shown by La Nación and El Financiero with the central bank as the source. The social security fund CCSS counted 200,602 formal workers in the special regime through September, almost 2,000 fewer than a year earlier, and La Nación says business services show the largest drop.

Inflation Outlook

Inflation was 0.3% year on year in September, the bank’s presentation shows, and the report projects a gradual rise toward its 3% target, to about 2.7% in the second half of 2027. El Financiero puts the September reading at 0.34% after 16 months of negative readings, and CRHoy says the bank expects prices to rise on fuel costs, farm inputs and the El Niño weather pattern.

El Financiero reports that the bank sees downside inflation risks from weaker global growth and upside risks from supply shocks and El Niño. Readers tracking Costa Rica’s public finances can also follow the report on the bond plan before the Assembly.

What It Means for You

For US companies with plants in Costa Rica’s free trade zones, the BCCR projects slower export growth in 2026 and a rebound in zone output to 4.6% only in 2027. For US travelers and importers, analysts consulted by La Nación say the colón’s appreciation against the dollar, at ¢453.12 per US$ on 30 October, weighs on Costa Rican competitiveness.

For US investors, the report separates a cooling free-zone sector from a steadier domestic regime that the BCCR projects to grow 3.3% in 2026. Household consumption is projected to grow 2.5% in 2026, which supports the bank’s view that growth rests mainly on domestic demand.

What Is Not Known

La Nación names Intel and Qorvo as the exiting companies, while the BCCR report refers only to closures of firms making electronic components and boards. The BCCR report also does not say how many free-zone jobs the closures cost, since the job losses it lists were concentrated in services.

The BCCR report bases the 2026 estimate on activity so far this year and the expected last quarter, and it does not split the 0.2-point cut by cause. It is also unclear how many more free-zone jobs will be lost, since the BCCR figures run only to August 2026 and the social security count to September.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much will Costa Rica’s economy grow in 2026?

The central bank projects 3.2% growth for 2026, down from 3.4% in its July report and below the preliminary 4.6% of 2025. It projects 3.3% for 2027 and 3.6% for 2028.

Why did Costa Rica’s central bank cut its forecast?

The bank says its 2027 cut mostly reflects a smaller contribution from net external demand, as exports are expected to expand less. La Nación reports that its president tied slower 2026 exports to the exit of two companies and slower medical-device growth.

Are jobs in Costa Rica’s free trade zones falling?

Slightly, since free-zone employment fell from 197,101 to 195,410 workers between August 2025 and August 2026, a 0.9% drop. Real wages in the zones rose 2.8% on average, according to the central bank president.

What is the dollar exchange rate in Costa Rica?

The central bank’s reference rates on 30 October 2026 were ¢450.80 buy and ¢455.44 sell per US$, a midpoint of ¢453.12. Analysts told La Nación that the colón’s appreciation hurts competitiveness.

What is inflation in Costa Rica?

Inflation was 0.3% year on year in September, according to the central bank’s presentation. The bank projects it will reach about 2.7% in the second half of 2027, against a 3% target.

Sources: Banco Central de Costa Rica, Informe de Política Monetaria, 30 October 2026; Banco Central de Costa Rica, IPM presentation, 30 October 2026; La Nación, 30 October 2026, growth forecast; La Nación, 31 October 2026, free-zone jobs; CRHoy, 30 October 2026; El Financiero, 30 October 2026.

World.title: Colombia’s Central Bank to Buy US$2B
World.content:
File photo, 2026. The Barranquilla branch of Colombia’s central bank, the Banco de la República. (Photo: Jdvillalobos, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · CENTRAL BANK

Key Facts The country Colombia is South America’s second most populous country and a major oil and coal exporter, and its peso floats freely against the US dollar.

Why it matters Investors in Colombian peso bonds, including those who hold them through US funds, watch the central bank’s dollar reserves as protection against outside shocks. A bigger cushion can steady the peso when global interest rates and risk move.

Why now The central bank’s board approved the purchase on Friday 30 October 2026, one day after the new government filed its fiscal rescue bill in Congress.

What happened The central bank will buy US$2 billion directly from the Treasury before the end of 2026, at the market exchange rate on the day of the deal. It adds to a reserve-building plan of up to US$4 billion that began in August.

The numbers US$2 billion is about 6.3 trillion pesos at the 30 October rate of 3,166.91 pesos per US$. The policy rate stays at 12.25% after a 4-3 board vote.

What it means for you No rule changes for US travellers, importers or exporters today. US holders of Colombian peso assets get a larger dollar cushion if the purchase and the August plan go ahead.

Still open The date and number of tranches, how the bank will offset the extra pesos, and how much of the US$4 billion plan is already bought.

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

In Plain English BanRep is the Banco de la República, Colombia’s central bank, which sets interest rates and manages the country’s international reserves. International reserves are the foreign currency and other assets a central bank holds to back its currency and to pay for imports in a crisis. The TRM, or Tasa Representativa del Mercado, is the official daily exchange rate of the peso against the US dollar. In BanRep’s put-option auctions, the winning bidders gain the right to sell dollars to the central bank, which they can use only when the TRM is below its moving average. The Treasury and public credit directorate is the Finance Ministry office that manages the government’s cash and debt. The Rescue Law is the government’s fiscal bill, filed on 29 October, that cuts spending and changes taxes.

Colombia’s central bank, the Banco de la República (BanRep), authorised on Friday 30 October 2026 the direct purchase of US$2 billion from the national government, to be carried out through the Finance Ministry’s Treasury before the end of the year. The deal will be priced at the market exchange rate on the day it is carried out, and the dollars will join the international reserves that back the peso.

The decision came on the same day the board held its policy rate at 12.25% in a 4-3 vote, and one day after President Abelardo De La Espriella’s government filed its Rescue Law in Congress. The purchase adds to a reserve-building plan of up to US$4 billion that BanRep announced on 31 July 2026, so the bank is now collecting dollars through two channels.

What BanRep Approved

BanRep’s release, published at 13:27 Bogotá time on 30 October, says the purchase will go through the Treasury and public credit directorate of the Finance Ministry and will be carried out during what remains of 2026. It gives no date and does not say whether the deal will be one transaction or several, Portafolio noted.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The bank said the government has dollars available to sell and that the purchase comes at a time of high international uncertainty, with high global interest rates and tight financial conditions. In that setting, it said, more reserves, meaning more dollars of backing, help the country face possible episodes of external instability.

At the official TRM of 3,166.91 pesos per US$ for Friday 30 October, published on Colombia’s open-data portal, US$2 billion equals about 6.3 trillion pesos. The final peso sum depends on the rate on the day of the deal, and the Treasury will receive it in pesos while BanRep takes the dollars.

The Reserve Plan Behind It

BanRep announced on 31 July 2026 a programme to build up to US$4 billion in international reserves gradually, using monthly auctions of put options. The first auction was scheduled for 3 August for up to US$400 million, and the options can be exercised only when the TRM is below its moving average.

The bank used the same mechanism in 2024 and accumulated about US$1.5 billion, according to its announcement. Its new release says the plan continues on the same terms and calendar, so the Treasury purchase comes on top of it and the two channels could together add up to US$6 billion.

File photo, 2008. Office towers in the business district of Bogotá, Colombia, seen from the Torre Colpatria. (Photo: Jose David Parra, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Why the Peso Market Cares

BanRep said the size of the purchase takes into account its effect on peso liquidity, and that it will adopt compensating measures so that short-term rates stay in line with the policy rate. Because the bank pays the Treasury in pesos, the operation puts more pesos into the banking system.

The policy rate stands at 12.25%, with annual inflation at 6.3% in September and analysts expecting 6.9% in December, according to the board’s policy-rate communique of the same day, and the rate decision split the board 4-3. That communique also stresses the importance of a rigorous study of the rescue bill filed a day earlier, and BanRep manager Leonardo Villar said a fiscal adjustment helps monetary policy meet its goals, Portafolio reported.

The Rescue Bill in Congress

The government filed the Rescue Law bill in the House of Representatives on 29 October, Portafolio reported, aiming to cut public spending by 2.2% and to change several taxes. The five main points are set out in an earlier explainer, and Congress has not yet voted on the bill.

Vice President José Manuel Restrepo said at the filing that the bill aims to avoid an economic crisis, the loss of 360,000 jobs and a possible recession, Portafolio reported. The purchase is a separate decision, but the bank’s own communique calls public finances a first-order factor in its effort to bring inflation to target.

What It Means for You

US investors in Colombian peso bonds, or in funds that hold them, get a larger dollar cushion if the purchase and the August plan go ahead, which helps when global rates and risk appetite swing. The purchase changes no rule for US travellers, importers or exporters.

Travellers and exporters should keep watching the TRM, because the deal is priced at the rate of the day it is carried out. More background on the country is on the Colombia news hub.

What Is Not Known

BanRep gave no date for the purchase and did not say whether it will be one transaction or several, and the peso value is not fixed because it depends on the rate on the day. The release does not say where the Treasury’s dollars come from or how the Treasury will use the pesos.

It is also not known how much of the US$4 billion plan has been bought since August, or which compensating measures BanRep will use to keep short-term rates at the policy rate. Congress has not voted on the rescue bill, so the fiscal path behind the deal is open.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Colombia’s central bank approve on 30 October?

The central bank’s board approved the direct purchase of US$2 billion from the national government through the Finance Ministry’s Treasury. The purchase must happen before the end of 2026 at the market exchange rate on the day.

Why is the central bank buying dollars from the government?

The bank said the government has dollars available to sell and that more reserves help against external shocks. It cited high global interest rates and tight financial conditions.

How big is Colombia’s reserve-building plan?

A programme launched on 31 July allows up to US$4 billion in purchases through monthly put-option auctions. The new US$2 billion Treasury purchase comes on top of it.

What is the TRM?

The TRM is Colombia’s official representative market exchange rate, published each day in pesos per US$. On 30 October it was 3,166.91 pesos per US$.

Did the central bank change interest rates on 30 October?

The central bank held its policy rate at 12.25% in a 4-3 vote, so the rate did not change. Three board members favoured a 25-basis-point increase.

Sources: Banco de la República, board release on the USD 2,000 million purchase, 30 October 2026; Banco de la República, policy-rate communique, 30 October 2026; Banco de la República, reserve accumulation programme, 31 July 2026; Colombia open-data portal, TRM series, 30 October 2026; Portafolio on the purchase, 30 October 2026; Portafolio on Villar and the rescue bill, 30 October 2026.

World.content:

GHANA · COMPANY RESULTS

Key Facts — The country Ghana is a West African nation where MTN Ghana counts 34.3 million mobile subscribers.

— What happened Nine-month profit after tax was GH¢7.75 billion (about US$664 million).

— Growth Profit rose 43% from GH¢5.42 billion (about US$464 million) a year earlier.

— Payout Both companies pay GH¢0.03 per share on Thursday 10 December 2026.

— Still open No full-year profit forecast, only revenue growth and margin ranges.

MTN Ghana profit rose 43% to a combined GH¢7.75 billion (about US$664 million) after tax in the nine months to 30 September 2026. The figure covers MTN Ghana’s phone business and its separate mobile money arm, and the company published it on Thursday 29 October 2026.

The result matters to US readers because MTN Ghana belongs to MTN Group, the South African mobile company listed in Johannesburg. All cedi amounts here use about 11.67 cedis to the US dollar, the rate on 31 October 2026.

Who Is MTN Ghana

MTN Ghana is the local business of MTN Group, a South African company that runs mobile networks across Africa. Its legal name is Scancom PLC, and it trades in Accra as MTNGH on the Ghana Stock Exchange, as in our MTN Group company profile.

Since 31 March 2026 its mobile money business has been a separate company, MobileMoney Fintech Limited, or MMFL. Shareholders hold both companies together, so the firm reports a combined view that it calls illustrative rather than formal consolidated accounts.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Ghana markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Numbers in Plain English

Service revenue, the money earned from customers, rose 33.5% to GH¢23.15 billion (about US$1.98 billion). Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, called EBITDA, rose 40.6% to GH¢14.28 billion (about US$1.22 billion).

The EBITDA margin reached 61.5%, up 3.1 percentage points, even though costs grew 23.2% to GH¢8.93 billion (about US$765 million). Pre-tax MTN Ghana profit climbed 47.0% to GH¢11.38 billion (about US$975 million), and tax took GH¢3.63 billion (about US$311 million) of it.

Data and Mobile Money Lead Growth

Data was the biggest earner behind the MTN Ghana profit, with revenue up 44.5% to GH¢13.45 billion (about US$1.15 billion). Mobile money revenue grew 24.4% to GH¢5.37 billion (about US$460 million), and voice calls added GH¢3.08 billion (about US$264 million).

Digital services such as gaming and video nearly doubled to GH¢642 million (about US$55 million). The company counts 22.0 million active data users, up 16.1%, and 18.9 million active mobile money users, up 6.9%.

A Strong Third Quarter

The July to September quarter of MTN Ghana profit extended the run of strong growth at MTN Ghana. Service revenue rose 35.7% to GH¢8.19 billion (about US$702 million), and profit after tax rose 42.6% to GH¢2.62 billion (about US$225 million).

The company added about 1.5 million mobile subscribers in the quarter, bringing the total to 34.3 million. Its chief executive, Stephen Blewett, called the growth broad-based across the connectivity and fintech businesses.

Dividends, Cash and 5G Spectrum

The boards of both companies declared a third-quarter dividend of GH¢0.03 per share (about US$0.003), payable on Thursday 10 December 2026. Shareholders on the register at the close of business on Thursday 26 November 2026 qualify.

Free cash flow nearly doubled to GH¢7.40 billion (about US$634 million), while capital spending fell 27.2% to GH¢3.16 billion (about US$271 million). The telecoms regulator notified MTN of a 5G airwaves award costing US$202 million, as covered in our report on the 5G spectrum award.

The Economy Behind the Profit

The company said Ghana’s average inflation fell to 4.2% in the first nine months of 2026, from 17.3% a year earlier. It also noted that the cedi lost 12.1% against the dollar over the period, ending September at 11.71 per dollar.

The company called the operating environment supportive despite the currency swings. The Bank of Ghana, the central bank, expects inflation to stay within a range of 8% to 10%, according to the report.

What It Means for US Readers

US investors can follow MTN through the parent MTN Group in Johannesburg, while the Ghana shares trade on the Ghana Stock Exchange in Accra. The results show that MTN Ghana profit can grow sharply while the cedi weakens.

The company expects margins to ease to the mid-to-high-50% range with 5G spending. The US$202 million spectrum cost shows how much capital a 5G rollout needs.

What Is Not Known

The company gave no MTN Ghana profit forecast for the full year, only ranges for revenue growth and margins. It will review its three-to-five-year targets at the end of the year.

The combined figures are not formal consolidated accounts, so the separate profit of each company differs from the headline. The company has not said how much revenue the new spectrum will add once 5G is switched on.

More: Ghana news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much profit did MTN Ghana make in nine months?

MTN Ghana and its mobile money arm made a combined profit after tax of GH¢7.75 billion (about US$664 million). That is 43% more than a year earlier.

What is MMFL?

MobileMoney Fintech Limited holds MTN Ghana’s mobile money business since 31 March 2026. Shareholders own both companies together.

Which period do the results cover?

They cover the nine months from 1 January to 30 September 2026. The company published them on Thursday 29 October 2026.

When is the next dividend paid?

The third-quarter dividend of GH¢0.03 per share (about US$0.003) is paid on Thursday 10 December 2026. Holders on the register on Thursday 26 November 2026 qualify.

What does the company expect for the full year?

It expects service revenue growth in the low-to-mid-30s percent. It also expects an EBITDA margin from the high-50s to the low-60s percent.

Sources: Scancom PLC (MTN Ghana), performance report for the nine-month period ended September 2026 (combined with MMFL), 29 October 2026; Scancom PLC (MTN Ghana), investor relations, financial results, 31 October 2026.

World.title: Peru Growth May Fall to 2% If El Nino Lasts
World.content:
File photo, 29 March 2017. A road partly under floodwater during the 2017 coastal El Niño emergency, photographed during a Defence Ministry visit to Piura. (Photo: Galería del Ministerio de Defensa del Perú, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

PERU · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Peru is a Pacific-coast economy built on copper, gold and fruit exports, and its north is the region most exposed to coastal El Niño rains.

Why it matters US investors and fruit importers face a longer weather shock, because a university worst case puts Peru’s 2027 growth at 2%, against 3% in its milder scenario, if El Niño lingers.

Why now A University of Lima report, described by La República on Friday 30 October 2026, weighs a long El Niño just as the national forecast for the event was extended.

What happened The national El Niño commission now sees extraordinary-strength sea warming until February 2027 and the event lasting to June 2027, while the university’s worst case has growth at 2%.

The numbers The economy grew 3.2% in August 2026 and 3.1% from January to August, against a worst-case 2% for 2027 and private investment slowing from above 14% to about 6.5%.

What it means for you Watch northern Peru, where forecast rain and floods threaten export farming, fishing and transport, because supply and prices of some goods could tighten in early 2027.

Still open How long the event really lasts, and how much of the government’s El Niño spending reaches projects in time.

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

In Plain English ENFEN: the multisectoral commission that issues Peru’s official El Niño alerts and forecasts. Its communiqués have kept the coastal El Niño alert active for months. Coastal El Niño: a warming of the sea off Peru’s coast that brings heavy rain to the north and centre of the country and normal or lower rain to parts of the south. It also pushes anchovy and other fish away from their usual areas. University of Lima observatory: the Observatorio Económico, Financiero y Social is the university’s economic research unit, and its report is titled 100 días: perspectivas y retos económicos. Its 2027 numbers are scenarios, meaning what-if projections with stated assumptions, and not government forecasts.

Peru’s economy could grow only 2% in 2027, against 3% in a milder scenario, if the coastal El Niño lasts into the third or fourth quarter, according to the worst case in a University of Lima report that La República described on Friday 30 October 2026. The same day Infobae reported that ENFEN, Peru’s national El Niño commission, now expects the event to last until June 2027, with extraordinary-strength sea warming until February 2027.

For US investors and importers the numbers matter because Peru is a large exporter of copper, gold and fruit, and the regions at greatest risk include Piura, Lambayeque and La Libertad, home to export farming. The Economy Ministry’s own latest data show growth of 3.2% in August 2026 despite El Niño, so the 2% case is a university warning and not a government forecast.

Earlier reports on this site cover the US$5.2 billion El Niño plan and the US$2.4 billion extra spending bill. This article adds the new forecast and the growth scenarios.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What ENFEN Now Expects

ENFEN says sea warming off Peru will keep an extraordinary magnitude until February 2027 and then ease gradually, with the event lasting until June 2027, Infobae reported on Friday 30 October. Its previous forecast, communiqué 18-2026 as reported by Gestión on 17 October, saw the extraordinary magnitude lasting until January 2027 and strong conditions until early autumn.

Between November 2026 and January 2027 ENFEN expects above-normal rain on the north and central coast and in parts of the western highlands, with moderate to strong episodes, and north-coast rivers including the Tumbes, Chira, Piura, La Leche and Jequetepeque could run above usual. From December the higher flows would spread to the central coast, including the Chillón, Rímac and Lurín basins around Lima.

Air temperatures could set new records along the coast, and sea level is expected to stay above normal, which together with abnormal swells raises the risk of flooding and coastal erosion. At sea, anchovy would stay deeper and closer to shore, which limits its availability to seabirds and sea lions, ENFEN warned.

File photo, 2017. A farmer with crates of avocados at a harvest in Aguar-Caujul, Peru. (Photo: Areyes108, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the University Scenarios Say

The university’s economic observatory set out two 2027 scenarios in its report, La República reported on Friday 30 October. In the first, with an extraordinary El Niño until the second quarter of 2027 and 50% execution of fiscal measures for maintenance and infrastructure, GDP would grow 3%.

In the second, with the event lasting into the third or fourth quarter, weaker world growth and only 30% execution of those fiscal measures, growth would slow to 2%. Economist Julio del Castillo of the university said private investment should close 2026 with growth above 14% but advance only about 6.5% in 2027, as firms postpone projects until the emergency ends.

Del Castillo said the main channels would be higher prices and interrupted transport routes, and that price increases have already begun and could intensify in the first quarter of 2027. The report names Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque and La Libertad as most exposed to heavy rain and flooding, with consequences for export agriculture, fishing and transport, and Lima, Callao, Áncash and Ica as exposed to landslides that could disrupt supply chains and food prices.

Business expectations stay optimistic in the report, with the three-month index at 57 points and the twelve-month index at 68 points in September, above the 50-point line that separates optimism from pessimism. The scenarios are the university’s own assumptions, and the report is not an official forecast.

Where the Economy Stood Before the Shock

Peru’s Economy Ministry said on Thursday 15 October that GDP grew 3.2% in August 2026, the 29th consecutive month of expansion, and 3.1% from January to August. Fishing fell 17.3% in August on lower catches of squid, scallops and jack mackerel, and mining and hydrocarbons fell 5.5% on lower zinc, gold and copper output, in a context the ministry described as marked by the coastal El Niño.

Economy Minister Elmer Cuba said on 7 October that the government is weighing expansive fiscal measures, because non-primary sectors face oil and diesel price shocks and higher global interest rates on top of El Niño. “Fiscal policy cannot be neutral: it will have to be expansionary,” he told a Peru-Japan business council.

The Instituto Peruano de Economía (IPE), a Lima research institute, cut its 2027 growth projection to 3.2% from 3.4% on 13 October and kept 3.3% for 2026, La República reported. Without an extraordinary coastal El Niño, the institute estimates that growth would reach 4.2% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027.

Fruit and Export Farms at Risk

Peru’s agricultural exports reached US$8.334 billion from January to August, up 2.3%, with avocados at US$1.343 billion, blueberries at US$1.050 billion (up 47.9%) and grapes at US$816 million (up 17.6%), La República reported from Agriculture Ministry figures. August shipments grew only 0.9%, to US$1.493 billion, and the ministry projects about US$15 billion for 2026, close to the US$15.013 billion of 2025.

The university report lists export agriculture among the activities at risk in Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque and La Libertad, the regions with the heaviest forecast rain. La República’s account of the report gives no figure for lost fruit exports.

What to Watch Next

The sol closed at S/3.470 per US$ in the interbank market on Friday 30 October, a weekly depreciation of 0.4%, El Comercio reported. Trader Jorge Luis Huayta of Kambista told El Comercio that attention next week would center on October consumer prices, due Monday 2 November, because of their weight in the central bank’s coming policy decisions.

What It Means for You

US importers of Peruvian fruit and US investors in Peruvian assets should treat the 2% case as a stress scenario and watch rainfall and road reports from the north after November, when ENFEN expects rain to intensify. The ministry’s own recent data still show growth above 3%, and the minister says the government is weighing expansive fiscal measures to cushion the shock.

Travellers heading to northern Peru and the coast between November and March should expect a higher risk of heavy rain and road disruption, while ENFEN forecasts normal or lower rain for the southeastern highlands, where Cusco lies. The Peru country page tracks the follow-up.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how long the event will last, because the university’s worst case assumes the third or fourth quarter of 2027 while ENFEN’s latest forecast ends in June 2027, the end of autumn. It is also not known how much of the government’s El Niño money will be spent in time, since the university’s scenarios simply assume 50% or 30% execution.

No official government growth forecast for 2027 that reflects the new ENFEN outlook appears in the reports cited, and none puts a number on damage to fruit exports. The University of Lima’s full report was not accessible, so its figures here come from La República’s account.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much could Peru’s economy grow in 2027?

A University of Lima worst-case scenario sees 2% growth if El Niño lasts into the third or fourth quarter of 2027. Its milder scenario sees 3%, and both are university scenarios, not government forecasts.

How long will El Niño last in Peru?

ENFEN’s latest forecast, reported by Infobae on 30 October, has the event lasting until June 2027. Extraordinary-strength sea warming is expected until February 2027 before easing gradually.

Which parts of Peru face the most rain?

ENFEN expects above-normal rain on the north and central coast from November 2026 to January 2027. The University of Lima names Tumbes, Piura, Lambayeque and La Libertad as most exposed to flooding.

How did Peru’s economy perform before the shock?

The Economy Ministry reported 3.2% growth in August 2026 and 3.1% from January to August. Fishing fell 17.3% in August, and mining and hydrocarbons fell 5.5%.

What does it mean for US fruit buyers?

Peru’s agricultural exports reached US$8.334 billion from January to August, led by avocados, blueberries and grapes. Northern farming regions are among those the university report sees as exposed to heavy rain.

World.title: ICE Reportedly Arrests Cuban Aged 70
World.content:
File photo, 2009. The headquarters of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Washington. (Photo: Ser Amantio di Nicolao, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

CUBA · IMMIGRATION

Key Facts The country Cuba is a one-party communist state about 90 miles (145 km) from Key West, and Florida is home to a large Cuban exile community.

Why it matters ICE field office chiefs can revoke the release of people living free on orders of supervision, a status that can apply to Cubans with old removal orders.

Why now An ICE order dated 10 June 2026 was posted online on 29 October 2026, and a Cuban news site now carries news of the arrest of a 70-year-old Cuban with a 2009 deportation order.

What happened A 70-year-old Cuban man with a deportation order from 2009 is described as arrested by ICE, and his name, place of arrest and record are not available.

What it means for you Cuban families with relatives on supervision should know that a local ICE chief can decide to revoke a release, and an immigration lawyer can explain the grounds.

Still open Who the man is, where and why he was arrested, and how many people on supervision face revocation.

Power Index Cuba ranks 14th of 14 in Cuba ranks 14th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 22.5 points (October 2026 edition).

Periódico Cubano, a Cuban news site, published a report that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested a 70-year-old Cuban man who has had a deportation order since 2009. The full text of that report, the man’s name, the place of arrest and any ICE statement were not available for review, so the case is treated here as an unconfirmed report.

Separately, ICE order DO99-004, dated 10 June 2026 and posted by the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) on 29 October 2026, lets local ICE field chiefs revoke the release of immigrants who live free on orders of supervision. Orders of supervision are one way people with old final removal orders stay out of detention, which is why the order matters to Cuban families in cases like the one reported.

What the ICE Order Says

The order was issued and took effect on 10 June 2026, and it hands the authority of the executive associate director of ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations to field office directors, deputy field office directors and assistant field office directors. The authority cannot be passed down further, and it stays in effect until it is rescinded.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Cuba ranks 14th of 14 with 22.5 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (53); weakest: economic weight (0). Alignment group: Closer to Beijing. Some pillar data are incomplete for Cuba; see the index notes. WatchNo sovereign rating; economy contracting (-3.8%); incomplete data (‡). See the full index, the business lens and the data →

For people released on an order of supervision after less than 180 days of detention following a removal order, the officials may revoke the release if the purposes of release have been served, a condition was broken, enforcing the removal order is appropriate, or other circumstances show release is no longer appropriate. For people released because there was no significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future, the order allows revocation only after a violation of a release condition or when changed circumstances make removal likely.

The text names no nationality, announces no operation and revokes no release by itself, and it cites two federal rules, 8 CFR 241.4 and 8 CFR 241.13. The Cuban outlet CiberCuba wrote on 30 October that it may matter for Cubans with final orders who live under supervision, including holders of Form I-220B, and noted that it does not order mass revocations.

What a Final Removal Order Means

Under 8 USC 1231, when a person is ordered removed the government must remove that person within 90 days, a span the law calls the removal period. A person who is inadmissible, removable on certain listed grounds, or judged a risk to the community or unlikely to comply may be detained beyond that period and, if released, is subject to supervision terms.

The federal rule 8 CFR 241.13 sets review procedures for people detained after the removal period who give good reason to believe there is no significant likelihood of removal, to the country named in the order or to a third country, in the reasonably foreseeable future. That is one legal route by which people with final orders can end up free on supervision, and the June 2026 order now lets local chiefs pull that release back in defined cases.

File photo. ICE officers lead a handcuffed man during a targeted enforcement operation in Dallas, Texas. It does not show the arrest in this report. (Photo: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Third Countries and the Supreme Court

On 29 September 2026 the US Supreme Court stayed a 25 February 2026 federal district court judgment in Massachusetts and took up the case known as D.V.D. (No. 26-426), which will be argued in its December 2026 session.

One of the questions is whether the government’s guidance on removals to third countries is unlawful under 8 USC 1231(b), the Due Process Clause or the Convention Against Torture rules, and Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson would have denied the stay.The stay is covered in Rio Times reporting on the third-country ruling, and Telemundo 51 in Miami published a report on 30 October 2026 about a Cuban man who says he was sent to Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic.

He told the station he shares space with about 32 people, mostly Cubans, and the station said the Department of Homeland Security had not answered its questions by publication.Telemundo 51 also cited data from the Migration Policy Institute that the third-country policy involves cooperation agreements with about 35 nations.

The same report quotes an immigration lawyer who says a pending family petition does not protect a person from deportation when an order exists.

What Is Known About the 70-Year-Old

The Periódico Cubano headline says the man is 70 years old and has had a deportation order since 2009, and it promises to explain what he did. Nothing else from that report could be confirmed, and the ICE news page could not be searched, so no agency release on the case was reviewed.

A 2009 order would be more than 16 years old, and the headline does not say what happened to the man in the years since. Whether the man was on an order of supervision, and whether the June 2026 delegation played any role in his arrest, is not stated in anything opened.

What It Means for You

For Cuban families in Florida and elsewhere, the practical point is that a release on an order of supervision is not permanent, and local ICE chiefs now hold the authority to decide on revocation in defined cases. People who report to ICE on supervision should keep every condition of their release and carry the paperwork, and CiberCuba advises consulting a specialized immigration lawyer.

For other readers, the report points to how a decision made in 2009 can still shape enforcement in 2026, and the Supreme Court’s December hearing on third-country removals could change where people with final orders can be sent. Rio Times Cuba coverage follows the policy and the people it touches.

What Is Not Known

The man’s name, the city of his arrest, the date, his criminal record and the ICE office that held him are not available. No ICE or Department of Homeland Security statement on the case was reviewed.

It is not known how many people on orders of supervision are affected by the June 2026 order, or whether any release has been revoked under it. The order does not say how Cuban nationals specifically are treated.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was a 70-year-old Cuban arrested by ICE?

Periódico Cubano reports that ICE arrested a 70-year-old Cuban who has had a deportation order since 2009. The reason, the place and any ICE statement are not available.

What does ICE order DO99-004 do?

It lets ICE field office directors and their deputies revoke releases of immigrants on orders of supervision in defined cases. It was issued on 10 June 2026 and posted publicly by AILA on 29 October 2026.

Can ICE deport Cubans to a third country?

The Supreme Court paused a lower-court judgment on 29 September 2026 and will hear the case in December. Telemundo 51 reported on 30 October that a Cuban man was sent to the Central African Republic.

What should a Cuban on ICE supervision do?

Keep every release condition, carry the paperwork and ask a specialized immigration lawyer about the grounds for revocation. CiberCuba gave the same advice on 30 October 2026.

World.title: Costa Rica Hotel Wins Two World Travel Awards, Putting Tárcoles in the Spotlight
World.content:
A hotel on Costa Rica’s Central Pacific coast has won two international tourism awards, bringing attention to Tárcoles, a area known for its crocodile-filled river, fishing traditions and surrounding tropical forests. Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda, part of Marriott International’s Autograph Collection, was named Costa Rica’s Leading Boutique Hotel 2026 and Mexico & Central America’s Leading New Hotel 2026 at the World Travel Awards.

The recognition comes less than a year after the hotel opened in January 2026 and marks an early achievement for a property competing in Costa Rica’s established tourism industry. The awards were announced at the World Travel Awards Caribbean and Americas ceremony, held in Jamaica on October 11.

Established in 1993, the World Travel Awards recognize hotels, airlines, destinations and other tourism businesses through online voting by travel industry professionals and the public. Verified industry professionals receive double voting weight, and awards are presented in national, regional and worldwide categories.

Santa Lucía’s two victories were in the national boutique hotel category and the regional new hotel category, placing it ahead of other nominated properties in Costa Rica, Mexico and Central America. José Eduardo Arteaga, general manager of Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda, welcomed the recognition, saying it provides an opportunity to introduce more international travelers to Tárcoles and Costa Rica’s Central Pacific region.

Arteaga said the awards also help showcase the variety of tourism experiences available in Costa Rica, particularly in communities outside the best-known tourist destinations. Near Carara National Park and the Tárcoles River in Puntarenas province, the hotel has 84 guest rooms on a 150-hectare (371-acre) property surrounded by tropical forest.

The property combines traditional Costa Rican hacienda-style architecture with modern rooms and activities focused on nature and local culture. Guests can participate in birdwatching, guided nature experiences, traditional Costa Rican cooking and cultural activities. The hotel also offers restaurants, a spa and other amenities.

Its location provides access to Carara National Park, known for its scarlet macaws and diverse birdlife, as well as the Tárcoles River, where visitors frequently see large American crocodiles along the riverbanks. The surrounding region offers beaches, wildlife tours and outdoor activities, making Tárcoles an accessible destination for travelers exploring the Central Pacific coast.

Beyond attracting visitors, the hotel says its operations support the surrounding economy through employment in hospitality, food service, maintenance and other services. The company also reports purchasing goods and services from businesses in the area. Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda promotes what it calls regenerative tourism, an approach intended to support forest conservation and strengthen connections with nearby communities. The extent of those environmental and economic benefits has not been independently quantified.

The awards come as Costa Rica’s tourism industry continues to report growth in international arrivals and visitor spending. According to the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT), Costa Rica welcomed 1,733,596 international visitors during the first six months of 2026, an increase of 7% compared with the same period in 2025.

Of those visitors, 1,605,360 arrived by air, representing year-over-year growth of 7.8%. Meanwhile, figures from the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) show that foreign visitors spent approximately $3.356 billion during the first half of 2026, an increase of 8.5% compared with the previous year.

Tourism also remains an important source of employment, accounting for 167,661 direct jobs during the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC). For Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda, the two awards offer international recognition during its first year of operation. For Tárcoles, they provide another opportunity to draw attention to a part of Costa Rica where wildlife, local traditions and tourism remain closely connected.

World.title: For First Time, Costa Rica Votes Against UN Call to End US Embargo on Cuba
World.content:
Costa Rica voted against the annual United Nations resolution calling on the United States to lift its economic embargo on Cuba, the first time the country has opposed the measure since the General Assembly began voting on it in 1992.The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 votes in favor, 17 against and 25 abstentions. General Assembly resolutions are not binding, and the embargo remains in place.

Costa Rica was the only Central American country to vote no. Nicaragua and Panama voted in favor, Honduras abstained, and Guatemala and El Salvador did not take part.The vote completes a gradual shift. Costa Rica abstained in 1992 and then backed the resolution for more than three decades. In October 2025 it abstained for the first time in that span, and in July 2026 it was one of nine countries to vote against a procedural motion to reopen debate on the embargo.

The change follows a sharp break with Havana. In March, under then-President Rodrigo Chaves, Costa Rica closed its embassy in Cuba and asked Cuban diplomats to leave, citing growing restrictions on freedoms and worsening living conditions on the island. The government later reaffirmed the split.

In September, then-Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar said a review of Costa Rica’s position would mean changing how the country votes on the resolution. He said the government views the hardship facing Cubans as imposed by their own government, argued that Latin American governments had been too lukewarm toward Havana, and ruled out restoring diplomatic ties until Cuba is free. Tovar made the remarks shortly after meeting US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington.

Wednesday’s vote was the first on the resolution under President Laura Fernández, who took office in May. It came two weeks after Ana Elena Pinto became foreign minister on Oct. 15, during a month of turnover in the country’s diplomatic and trade leadership that included the dismissal of the trade minister. The Foreign Ministry has not published an explanation of the vote.

Costa Rica joined a bloc of opponents that grew from seven countries in 2025 to 17 this year. Alongside the United States and Israel, it included Argentina, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Hungary and Ukraine. Support for the resolution fell from 165 votes in 2025 and 187 in 2024. Germany and Italy, which had previously voted in favor, abstained.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz rejected the idea that the embargo is the only cause of Cuba’s economic problems, arguing that there is no blockade and pointing to Cuba’s trade with other countries and some US exports to the island. He said the number of countries changing their position had tripled and that he expected it to keep growing.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla said the sanctions directly harm the Cuban people, mainly by restricting access to food, medicine and fuel, and said US pressure would not prevail over the facts. Cuban officials accused Washington of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions and other penalties if they supported the resolution.

The General Assembly has passed versions of the resolution regularly since 1992. The votes carry political weight but have no power to lift the embargo.

World.title: Four Detained in Costa Rica Over Sedative-Spiked Rides From Bars
World.content:
Costa Rican authorities detained four men yesterday who are suspected of offering rides to people leaving bars in San José, drugging them with a sedative and then using their phones and bank cards to empty their accounts. Agents from the theft section of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) and prosecutors from the specialized cybercrime unit raided homes in Grecia, in Alajuela province, and in Aserrí, south of the capital.

The suspects are two brothers plus two other men and authorities have identified eight victims so far. Losses are put at about 10 million colones, or roughly $22,000. According to investigators, the suspects approached people who had been drinking outside bars in San Jose during the early morning hours and offered them a private transport service. During the ride, the victims were allegedly given water mixed with drops of clonazepam, a prescription sedative.

Once the drug took effect, the group allegedly took the victims’ cell phones and bank cards. Investigators say the cards were then used for purchases and cash withdrawals, and the victims were left next to the road. The four men are under investigation for alleged computer fraud and aggravated robbery however they have not been charged and the case remains open.

Authorities have not disclosed which bars or neighborhoods were involved, the ages of the suspects, or whether any of the victims were foreign visitors. The case is the latest in a series of thefts in Costa Rica that rely on speed and surprise rather than force, including one this week in which thieves emptied a rental car in eight minutes.

Anyone who believes they were targeted in a similar way can report it to the OIJ through its confidential line at 800-8000-645.

World.title: Costa Rica Celebrates National Masquerade Day With Traditional Parades and Music
World.content:
Costa Rica is celebrating one of its most colorful traditions this weekend as giant masks, lively marching bands and characters from local folklore take over streets and public spaces across Costa Rica. National Traditional Masquerade Day, observed every October 31, brings communities together for a celebration that has been part of Costa Rican culture for generations.

The Ministry of Culture and Youth has organized a series of free activities for today and tomorrow including street parades, musical performances, workshops and cultural exhibitions. The main celebration is scheduled for Friday in downtown San José, where three groups of traditional masked performers and musicians began marching at 11 a.m. from Plaza de la Democracia, Parque Morazán and the Simón Bolívar Urban Nature Park.

The groups then make their way through the capital before gathering around noon at the National Center for Culture (CENAC), across from Parque España. The event is open to the public and will feature the oversized masks and traditional music that have made these celebrations a familiar part of life in Costa Rica.

Unlike Halloween, which shares the same date, Costa Rica’s masquerade tradition has its own history and characters. The masks represent figures from local legends, including La Segua, La Llorona, the Devil, Death and La Giganta, along with a collection of other characters that have entertained and occasionally frightened generations of children.

Some of the figures tower over spectators, with enormous heads and exaggerated facial features made from papier-mâché, fiberglass or other materials. Beneath the masks are performers who dance, chase spectators and interact with the crowds as traditional marching bands, known locally as cimarronas, provide the music.

The bands typically include trumpets, trombones, drums and other instruments, producing the loud, energetic rhythms associated with Costa Rican town festivals. For many Costa Ricans, the sound of a cimarrona approaching is enough to bring back childhood memories of neighborhood celebrations, school festivals and the excitement of watching the masked characters move through the streets.

The tradition has roots in colonial-era celebrations, particularly in Cartago, where Spanish festivities gradually mixed with Indigenous customs and local folklore. Over time, communities such as Barva, Aserrí, Escazú and Cartago became important centers for the creation and performance of traditional masquerades.

The modern national celebration began in Aserrí on October 31, 1996, when local cultural organizers and artisans held a parade to promote Costa Rican traditions at a time when Halloween was becoming increasingly popular. The following year, the government officially declared October 31 National Traditional Masquerade Day through an Executive Decree.

The celebration received further recognition in 2022 when Costa Rica’s Legislative Assembly declared traditional masquerades a national symbol under Law 10239, acknowledging their importance to o cultural identity. Today, the tradition remains an important source of work for artisans who design, sculpt and paint the masks, often teaching their techniques to younger generations.

Acting Culture Minister Sally Molina Villalobos has emphasized that the celebrations are not simply about entertainment. They also recognize the craftsmanship and dedication required to keep the tradition alive. This weekend’s activities extend well beyond San José. In Cartago, a free masquerade and cimarrona festival is scheduled for Friday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Plaza Mayor, with traditional performances and workshops.

In Limón, the Civic Center for Peace will offer mask painting, traditional Costa Rican games, storytelling and a parade accompanied by a cimarrona on Friday afternoon, from 4 p.m. to approximately 6:20 p.m. The Public Library in Liberia, Guanacaste, will host a free afternoon of Costa Rican legends on Friday from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m., inviting community members to share traditional stories.

On Saturday, the celebration continues in Escazú, where Escazú Village will host free activities from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. The program includes traditional masked characters, a cimarrona performance, children’s mask-making workshops and costume competitions. Families attending the Escazú event will also find activities designed to introduce younger children to the history and artistic traditions behind the masks.

In the San Carlos area, the community of Marsella will hold traditional games, mask-making activities and a neighborhood parade on Saturday morning. Other cultural institutions are participating with exhibitions and special events, including an artisan mask display at the José Figueres Ferrer Cultural and Historical Center in San Ramón, which continues through November 6.

Not every event is free. The National Band of Guanacaste will perform a special concert at the National Theater in San José on Saturday at 7 p.m., with general admission tickets priced at ₡4,000 and discounted tickets at ₡2,500 for students and older adults. The weekend’s celebrations come at a time when Costa Rica continues working to preserve its traditional arts and customs while welcoming cultural influences from abroad.

For residents and visitors unfamiliar with masquerades, the events offer a chance to experience a side of Costa Rica that goes beyond beaches, rainforests and national parks. The colorful masks, lively music and interaction between performers and spectators are a reminder that our cultural heritage remains an important part of everyday life, particularly in smaller towns where these t

World.title: Lufthansa to Drop Costa Rica Route in 2027 as Sister Airline Adds More Flights
World.content:
German airline Lufthansa will stop operating its flights to Costa Rica in December 2027, but travelers will not lose the connection to Europe. Instead, sister airline Discover Airlines will take over the Frankfurt–San José route and increase service from five to six flights per week. The change, announced on October 29, will take effect on December 14, 2027, with Discover Airlines operating flights to Juan Santamaría International Airport using Airbus A350-900 aircraft.

The Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) confirmed that Lufthansa will continue operating the route through December 13, 2027, before handing it over to Discover, which belongs to the same airline group. For anyone flying here, the important point is that the route is not disappearing. Lufthansa Group will continue to fly to Costa Rica from Germany, although the airline operating the flights will change.

However, there is one important difference in the new schedule. Of the six weekly flights, four will operate nonstop between Frankfurt and San José. The other two will follow a route that takes passengers from Frankfurt to San José, continues to Belize City and then returns to Germany. That means passengers leaving Costa Rica for Frankfurt will need to pay attention when booking. Although the total number of weekly flights will increase, two of the return services will include a stop in Belize.

The change follows negotiations between the ICT and Lufthansa Group that began more than a year ago. Tourism officials said the goal was to move the route to an airline more focused on vacation travelers, which better matches Costa Rica’s tourism market. Discover Airlines specializes in leisure travel and operates from Frankfurt and Munich, serving destinations popular with tourists. It is part of Lufthansa Group, allowing passengers to continue using Frankfurt as a connection point for other destinations in Europe and beyond.

Another significant change will be the aircraft itself. Discover plans to introduce the Airbus A350-900 on the Costa Rica route, replacing the aircraft currently used by Lufthansa. The A350 is a modern long-distance aircraft designed to carry passengers across continents with improved fuel efficiency. Discover expects to receive its first A350 in June 2027 and a second aircraft in December, when the Costa Rica service is scheduled to begin.

The airline is gradually expanding its long-distance fleet, with additional A350 aircraft expected in 2028. The announcement comes as Lufthansa is already increasing its presence in Costa Rica. For the current European winter season, which began October 25, the airline expanded its Frankfurt service from three to five weekly flights and introduced Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner aircraft with its newer Allegris cabin design.

Germany remains Costa Rica’s largest source of European tourists. According to ICT figures, 54,794 German visitors arrived in Costa Rica between January and September 2026, an increase of 8.1% compared with the same period in 2025. The Frankfurt connection is particularly important because it serves both German vacationers and travelers connecting through one of Europe’s busiest international airports.

For Costa Rica’s tourism industry, the planned increase in weekly service provides another opportunity to attract European visitors, especially during the busy winter travel season. Passengers planning trips for late 2027 should keep an eye on the new schedules as Discover Airlines updates its booking system. The airline has confirmed the planned route changes, but final operating details and aircraft assignments may still be adjusted before the service begins.

World.title: High Tides Flood Homes in Costa Rica’s Puntarenas
World.content:
High tides flooded homes in Puntarenas on Thursday, October 29, with authorities warning that elevated tides could continue along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast through Saturday, October 31. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) reported flooding in Barrio El Carmen and the community of 20 de Noviembre in Chacarita.

Seawater entered homes, and photographs from the affected areas showed flooded patios and corridors, with furniture and household belongings standing in water. Members of the Puntarenas Municipal Emergency Committee visited the communities to assess damage, identify families’ needs and coordinate assistance. Initial reports did not specify the number of homes affected or provide an estimate of financial losses.

Thursday’s flooding followed repeated high tides earlier in the week. Residents of El Carmen described moving appliances and other belongings off the floor and staying awake to monitor water entering their homes. Flooding was also reported earlier in the week at Playa Zancudo in Golfito and Playa Preciosa in Puerto Jiménez, extending the effects beyond the city of Puntarenas.

The University of Costa Rica’s Oceanographic Information Module, known as MIO-Cimar, warned that the period of unusually high tides could last through Saturday. The CNE urged residents of coastal communities with a history of tidal flooding to watch local conditions and take steps to protect their belongings.

The conditions are associated with spring tides, the higher tides that occur around the new and full moon when the gravitational effects of the Sun and Moon reinforce one another. These events occur regularly and are unrelated to the spring season. MIO-Cimar coordinator Rodney Mora said warmer Pacific waters associated with El Niño were also contributing to higher sea levels, worsening the effects in vulnerable coastal communities. Water expands as it warms, allowing high tides to reach farther into low-lying areas.

El Niño does not cause spring tides, but the combination can increase the risk of flooding along the coast. Mora also warned that similar conditions could recur in November and December, urging coastal residents to prepare for further episodes.

World.title: Costa Rica Gas Prices Jump Sharply as Regular Fuel Becomes More Expensive Than Premium
World.content:
Drivers in Costa Rica will soon be paying considerably more at the pump after the public services regulator approved yet another round of fuel price increases, including a 12.38% jump in regular gasoline that will make it more expensive than premium fuel. The Public Services Regulatory Authority (ARESEP) approved the adjustment a couple of days ago, with the new prices announced yesterday. Regular gasoline will increase by ₡89 per liter, climbing from ₡719 to ₡808, while premium gasoline will rise by ₡42, from ₡764 to ₡806.

That creates an unusual situation at Costa Rica’s gas stations. Regular gasoline, traditionally the cheaper option, will cost ₡2 more per liter than premium, while diesel will also reach ₡808 following an increase of ₡23. The higher prices have been approved but will not take effect until the regulatory resolution is published in the official government newspaper, La Gaceta. Under the resolution, the new rates begin the following day. An exact implementation date had not been confirmed as of Friday morning.

At the new price, filling a 40-liter (10.6-gallon) tank with regular gasoline will cost ₡32,320 (about $71), up from ₡28,760 (about $64) today, an increase of ₡3,560 (about $8) per fill-up and with regular. Drivers filling a larger 60-liter (15.9-gallon) tank will pay ₡5,340 more than before.

For those who commute daily, operate delivery vehicles or regularly travel between Costa Rica’s major cities, the additional expense could quickly add up.
