World.title: Special episode: An exclusive interview with Canadian PM Mark Carney
World.content:
In this special edition, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney sits down with POLITICO’s chief EU correspondent Zoya and Ottawa bureau chief Nick Taylor-Vaisey for an exclusive interview.

With Canada and the European Union exploring a much closer partnership, Carney discusses his vision for Canada’s place in a changing world, the future of transatlantic relations and what it would take to build a lasting alliance with Europe. And with Donald Trump reshaping relations between traditional allies, how far is Canada prepared to go in charting a new course?

If you have a question or comment, don’t hesitate! Message us on our WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

World.title: 8 things we learned at the EU-Canada summit
World.content:
Those challenges have pushed the EU and Canada into a rapidly developing partnership that eclipses anything attempted by Brussels with a non-member country since the bloc was formed.

Here are all the key things POLITICO learned during the EU-Canada meetings.

Carney finally embraced ‘associate membership’

Initially reluctant, the Canadian prime minister came around by the end of the summit to endorse von der Leyen’s controversial label for the global alliance the EU and Canada are building.

Carney set a six-month deadline to firm up the ground rules of what “associate membership” is, trialing an induction process that could be a model for other non-European countries.

“With Canada becoming the European Union's first associate member, in the coming months we will determine the full substance, scale and scope of this new form of membership,” he said Friday.

Carney added he will meet periodically with von der Leyen to track progress, including a return trip for the College of European Commissioners to meet with their Canadian counterparts in March.

World.title: Tusk-Nawrocki battle escalates as chief judge is ousted from Poland’s top court
World.content:
Outside the tribunal, protesters clashed with police, who said objects had been thrown at officers and three people detained after climbing over the court’s fence. Police said they had deployed to maintain security following warnings of threats to judges and staff, but had not entered the building.

PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński took part in the protest and tried to force his way into the court building. He accused Tusk of staging a “coup” against the court and turning Poland into a “police state,” and demanded presidential intervention.

President Karol Nawrocki, a PiS ally and rival of Tusk, interrupted his official trip to Senegal, declaring, “At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland.”

Tusk was defiant. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote on X. “After years of PiS lawlessness, it’s a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way.”

The tribunal, which can strike down legislation, helped impose a near-total abortion ban under PiS and challenged the supremacy of EU law. Last December, the EU’s top court ruled that it failed to meet European standards of judicial independence.

But efforts to change the court’s makeup have met resistance. Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority. They took their oaths in parliament instead, but Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.

World.title: Mark Carney puts deadline on EU ‘associate membership’ push
World.content:
“Today, we move towards associate membership for Canada,” Carney said, describing it as “the deepest possible partnership short of accession.”

The two sides have set a June 2027 deadline to determine the terms and boundaries of their intensifying relationship — an alliance that comes with a payment schedule. Carney danced around a question pressing him on how much associate membership will cost the Canadian public.

“We don’t view this as paying, personally,” Carney said, stressing the alliance as a “positive” project.

Von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa, standing either side of Carney, presented the experiment as a necessary survival strategy to thrive in an increasingly dangerous world.

“The concept of an associate member is uncharted territory but we have the ambition, trust and creativity to shape it together,” Von der Leyen told reporters. “To be crystal clear, this is not a partnership against anybody, but for our common strength.”

Canadian government officials who spoke to reporters after the press conference confirmed legislation won’t be necessary to legitimize Canada’s EU associate membership status.

World.title: The Rutte way or the Carney method? Scaramucci says Europe’s Trump strategy is off the Mark
World.content:
“There’s two models of behavior: one is [NATO Secretary-General] Mark Rutte and one is [Canadian Prime Minister] Mark Carney. I think Mark Carney is handling him better. The Canadian people are with him, even if it causes some level of economic hardship,” Scaramucci said.

“Rutte, on the other hand, is making a big mistake. Because when you equivocate or flatter him, when you act in the manner that Mark Rutte has acted, all you’re doing is losing his respect. You’re not gaining anything,” he added.

Rutte has often lauded the U.S. president: “I just like the man. I think what he is doing for NATO is great news,” the military alliance chief said in an interview with POLITICO this summer.

Europe has seemingly yielded to Trump’s wishes on numerous occasions. The EU-U.S. trade deal was criticized as playing in Washington’s favor, while European allies agreed to a 5% of GDP spending target by 2035 at last year’s NATO summit in The Hague, matching Trump’s headline demand.

Carney, by contrast, has been more unwilling to bow to Trump’s pressure. He walked away from U.S. trade talks, saying Ottawa could not accept the offer or the demands — and promised to match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.

In the interview, Scaramucci also lambasted members of Trump’s own Republican Party. “That is the other side of this story: the cowardice of the political servants that are supposed to check Donald Trump, the members of the Republican Senate caucus and the House caucus,” he said.

World.title: Russian citizen faces spying charges in Poland after photographing railways
World.content:
Police found a large amount of evidence suggesting that the man took pictures of strategic infrastructure systematically. “There were photographs of various places and important communication facilities, not only in Poland,” Łukasz Dutkowiak, a spokesperson for the Lower Silesian police, told Radio Wrocław.

Prosecutors are now investigating “activities for foreign intelligence against the Republic of Poland,” the regional authority added.

Poland has faced multiple sabotage attacks against its military and railway infrastructure over the past year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Ukrainian nationals of “cooperating with Russian services” after a November 2025 attack damaged a rail line close to the Polish-Ukrainian border.

Fires broke out at a drone-components plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna and an aircraft-parts facility in Lublin in late August. In September, a Starlink communications station was set on fire near Warsaw.

“Russia does not even have to cross our border,” Tusk said after the September attacks. “It is already waging a hybrid war against us using drones, acts of sabotage and disinformation on the internet.”

European officials have pointed to an escalation of sabotage attacks from Russia over the past few months, as President Vladimir Putin seeks to disrupt military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv.

World.title: Unrest in France is nightmare fuel for Macron’s heirs
World.content:
They are facing a divided field of mainstream candidates on the center and center-right, including two former prime ministers under Macron in Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, and Bruno Retailleau, a former interior minister. These candidates have struggled to settle on a common message in response to the crisis — let alone agree on who the best candidate would be to avoid their nightmare scenario of a runoff between Mélenchon and Le Pen.

‘Out of ideas’

Three officials supporting centrist and conservative candidates told POLITICO that they were concerned the events of the past few weeks would cause lasting damage to their campaigns.

“It’s definitely going to kill us,” said one campaign official who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “We cannot be the solution anymore, only the problem.”

A Philippe supporter went as far as suggesting his champion was ill-equipped for the moment. “It’s exactly what he doesn’t need,” the supporter said last week, drawing parallels between the protests and the 2018–2019 Yellow Vest movement under Philippe’s premiership. “He doesn’t know how to do this. He’s not empathetic, and he’s not pretending to be.”

“Honestly, I don’t know how we’re going to get through this. Things are tough, and we’re out of ideas,” a centrist MP said.

The protests have taken place two Saturdays in a row and are expected to continue in the weeks to come. High school students are demanding better learning conditions while the wider public are protesting the cost-of-living crisis. The movement has been marred by scenes of vandalism and looting, especially on Oct. 17, when Macron’s government appeared to have underestimated both the scale of the protests and the potential for violent unrest.

World.title: Kärcher boss: Less regulation, more action to get Europe and Germany fit again
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

For some time now, we in Europe are facing a perfect storm. Geopolitical crises are casting a shadow over the European economy. The unpredictable trade policy of the U.S. keeps threatening, without warning, to raise tariffs and erect trade barriers – a toxic scenario for free global trade and export-oriented companies.

 

Meanwhile, China is no longer merely a low-cost manufacturer but has become a highly aggressive technological competitor that, with its tremendous speed, threatens to outpace key European industries in future-oriented fields.

Meanwhile, China is no longer merely a low-cost manufacturer but has become a highly aggressive technological competitor Hartmut Jenner Chief Executive Officer (CEO) & Chairman of the Board of Management Alfred Kärcher SE & Co. KG

What is often perceived as pure technological supremacy or even innovative strength is, however, largely the result of a well-targeted governmental industrial policy. Massive subsidies in key strategic industries, along with a currency policy artificially focused on competitiveness, are leading to noticeable market distortions and overcapacity.

For private companies operating on a market-based basis, this creates an imbalance that makes fair global competition almost impossible.

Europe risks deindustrialisation

The consequences for the industrial heart of Europe are alarming. The loss of tens of thousands of industrial jobs and the decline in production volume show that deindustrialization is not an abstract threat – it is happening right now.

Kärcher’s head office in Winnenden, Germany (c) Kärcher

When plant closures and production relocations are being negotiated in key German industries such as the automotive and manufacturing sectors, it must be clear even to the most optimistic observer: We are at a critical turning point.

As a family-owned company with 170 subsidiaries in 87 countries, Kärcher has weathered these turbulent times robustly thanks to its balanced business model – combining B2B (editor's note: Business to Business, i.e. corporate customers) and B2C (editor's note: Business to Consumer, i.e. private customers) – and its unconditional focus on customers. We are investing significantly in research and development, setting new standards in autonomous cleaning robots and battery technologies, and driving digitalization across all areas of the company.

In 1950, Alfred Kärcher developed Europe’s first hot-water high-pressure cleaner (the ‘DS 350’ steam cleaner) (c) Kärcher

However, even innovation leaders cannot withstand increasingly challenging operating conditions and unfair competition in the long term. Hartmut Jenner Chief Executive Officer (CEO) & Chairman of the Board of Management Alfred Kärcher SE & Co. KG

However, even innovation leaders cannot withstand increasingly challenging operating conditions and unfair competition in the long term. Considering the massive rise in structural and employee costs, expanding capacity or increasing headcount in domestic production is no longer economically feasible.

Reform fatigue and regulatory zeal are holding back investment

While the latest economic forecasts – which expect Germany’s growth to return to 1.3 percent this year – seem cautiously optimistic at first glance, we must not be misled by this modest increase. What we are seeing here is largely “borrowed growth,” artificially driven by special government funds, defense contracts, and subsidies.

A short-term boost fueled by debt is no substitute for a real, self-sustaining recovery in private investments. And the causes of the ongoing weakness are largely homegrown: a creeping reform fatigue and a regulatory frenzy on the part of government institutions that hinders rather than facilitates investment. Instead of promoting entrepreneurship, regulations from Brussels to Berlin are suffocating the courage to embrace change.

Instead of promoting entrepreneurship, regulations from Brussels to Berlin are suffocating the courage to embrace change. Hartmut Jenner Chief Executive Officer (CEO) & Chairman of the Board of Management Alfred Kärcher SE & Co. KG

The ongoing uncertainty among people in Germany is also having an impact on society. The rise of political extremism is a clear sign that many people are calling for greater reliability and noticeable reforms. To regain confidence in our country’s economic strength and future viability, we now need clear direction and bold action.

In 1984, Kärcher launched the world’s first portable high-pressure cleaner for domestic use. Its slogan was ‘Clean with high pressure – just like the professionals’. (c) Kärcher

For me personally, the attitude towards “working hard” has been ingrained in me since childhood on my parents’ family farm. Success doesn’t just fall from the sky; for me, it consists of 97 percent hard work and dedication, 2 percent talent, and 1 percent luck.

Success doesn’t just fall from the sky; for me, it consists of 97 percent hard work and dedication, 2 percent talent, and 1 percent luck. Hartmut Jenner Chief Executive Officer (CEO) & Chairman of the Board of Management Alfred Kärcher SE & Co. KG

If we want to secure our prosperity and our social standards, we must once again recognize that value creation is the precondition for prosperity – and not the other way around. If you rest, you rust – that applies to people just as much as it does to economies.

In 1975, the first production plant outside Germany opened. Today, Kärcher operates in 87 countries. (c) Kärcher

Germany needs a fitness programme

That is why we need a real fitness program for Germany. Rigid rules, excessive bureaucracy, high energy costs, and steadily rising non-wage labor costs are poison for our business environment. If the total amount of social security contributions consistently far exceeds the historically critical threshold of 40 percent, then tax breaks, selective government subsidies, and special funds will amount to nothing more than ineffective paper measures as long as the business environment itself remains entrenched in its current state.

Instead of tackling the root of the problem, authorities are allowing a flood of regulations to continue Hartmut Jenner Chief Executive Officer (CEO) & Chairman of the Board of Management Alfred Kärcher SE & Co. KG

While the federal government’s political reform efforts are heading in the right direction, they fall far short of what is needed. Instead of tackling the root of the problem, authorities are allowing a flood of regulations to continue – regulations that tie up valuable employee time and cost our companies millions. Money and personnel that are needed for core business operations and innovation are being wasted on documentation requirements alone. This cannot be solved with cosmetic fixes.

We need the courage to provide real relief. A key lever for this would be, for example, a cultural shift within the administrative system: In the future, government departments must see themselves as digital enablers and service-oriented partners to the economy – pragmatic, fast, and AI-supported. If other countries are already moving toward eliminating reporting obligations overall, this must send a clear signal to Germany and all Europe.

More work, less bureaucracy, and a resolute trade policy

Furthermore, we should not avoid necessary debates on the labor market. Demographic trends require an increase in the overall volume of work in the economy. Incentives for overtime, flexible working hours, practical rules regarding continued pay during medical leave, and a noticeable reduction in bureaucracy when employing skilled workers are essential.

The lastest “Kärcher Intelligent Robotic Application”, or “KIRA” for short – the first fully autonomous cleaning robots were launched by Kärcher in 2003. (c) Kärcher

Those who reflexively condemn such debates as an attack on workers’ rights are turning a blind eye to reality and putting precisely those jobs at risk that they claim to be protecting. Hartmut Jenner Chief Executive Officer (CEO) & Chairman of the Board of Management Alfred Kärcher SE & Co. KG

Those who reflexively condemn such debates as an attack on workers’ rights are turning a blind eye to reality and putting precisely those jobs at risk that they claim to be protecting. At the same time, we need a resolute trade policy at the European level that guarantees fair competition and consistently punishes rule-breakers – because free trade only works when everyone follows the same rules.

If we truly want to secure our competitiveness in the long term, we don’t need a bureaucratic approach – we need a return to a can-do mentality: less regulation, more personal responsibility, ambitious investment incentives, reliable framework conditions, and, above all, the courage to tackle issues properly and comprehensively once again. Real change begins in the mind – it’s time to act.

Alfred Kärcher SE & Co. KG was founded in 1935 and generated almost 3.5 billion euros in revenue in 2025. The family-owned company based in Winnenden, Germany, earns 86 percent of this abroad. The Kärcher Group operates 170 companies in 87 countries and employs 17,000 people worldwide. Kärcher's portfolio comprises more than 3,000 products for cleaning and care, with Kärcher high-pressure cleaners being particularly well known.

World.title: The seven days I thought I might have breast cancer
World.content:
Nine o'clock on an ordinary Monday morning. The designated day of an appointment I'd put off for a year, maybe two — too long.

 

I get undressed and enter the room. It's all just routine — isn't it?

"Madame, don’t move. I have to move you into the right position. Turn slightly. Not like that. Let me do it. Stay still. You're too stiff; relax.” The woman is touching me, moving, flattening and squeezing one of my breasts into the machine. It ends up looking as flat as a slice of the Italian sliced cheese 'Sottilette'.

And then the other one. “Turn around. Let me move it.” The process starts again with my breasts being squeezed sideways, which is unpleasantly painful, something many women are familiar with.

When it's over, I'm left alone in a tiny room — half naked, waiting. In that small barren space, my mind races, hitting highs and lows, thinking of the glimpse I got of the X-ray images of my breasts, of the shapes and shadows, looking like the branches in a stylised painting of a giant oak tree.

Is there cancer hidden in those pictures that I can’t interpret? Don't we all think that after looking at those black-and-white encrypted images?

I’m not even sure how long I've been surrounded by those four claustrophobic walls when the door finally opens and I'm moved to another dark room to wait for a doctor and the next examination. But first the smiling doctor says: “Your mammogram is absolutely fine.” And the frown you didn’t even realise was carved into your forehead disappears. You breathe in deeply and then exhale for a long time.

It's time for the echography. You start talking as the lubricating gel is smeared on one breast and then on the other. The scanner's moving probe sends sound waves bouncing off the tissues in your breast, revealing shadows, white and black stains, waves, darker patches.

Suspicious area detected during breast ultrasound. Lyon, October 2026. Monica Pinna

There's a whole world in our breasts we totally ignore and that is just impossible for us to read. I'm explaining to the radiologist how much I hate all this, how almost every woman in my family has had breast cancer and how anxious this all makes me, when she starts focusing the probe on the one particular area and stops talking. She pushes the probe down, then moves it and presses down again. There is silence.

“I think you need a little biopsy." All my fears materialise in that one moment and a single sentence. “There is a darker patch there that doesn’t disappear as I move the probe. It’s best to check it.”

Two days later I returned, wanting the follow-up to happen fast and to quickly know the outcome. In other countries, beyond France, my adopted home, I could have had to wait days between a mammography and an echography and for weeks before the biopsy was done.

First a local anaesthetic, then a small cut which I don’t feel; the doctor smiles reassuringly, but I remain tense and at the same time already off somewhere else in my mind. A long cannula goes deeply into my flesh five times. Some bloody flecks of whitish flesh emerge and are placed in tiny glass containers.

Insertion of a biopsy cannula into a suspicious area of the breast. Lyon, October 2026. Monica Pinna

That was the beginning of a week I will never forget.

I would wait seven days before finally learning if I had cancer. I entered a sort of parallel world, where everything came through a filter and seemed far away. My body and my life were on hold. Plans suspended. A work trip and meetings with friends were postponed. I had started the process of acceptance, with that taboo word – cancer – becoming a possible option. It was possible that I would enter that same room days later to be told that I had to be operated on and then would need chemo.

Everything every cancer patient goes through. Fear, waiting, uncertainty. A time when friends you wouldn’t have thought of show up and when some of those you would have expected to stick with you might disappear. Deep fears resurface and people around you react differently. I was definitely floating, preparing myself. Bracing. The same feeling you'd have about a flight you're due to take when a storm is hitting.

"I have it, I don’t have it. I don’t know. I must wait."

Spiralling thoughts take you into the depths of your mind and your fears, sometimes a long way down. You recall your mother’s experience, as she went through the same fears, was operated on, had radiotherapy and made it through. You recall your auntie who didn’t. Your cousin who is now a beautiful and bright survivor. You think of her sister, who had to have her stomach removed, but who is always smiling and serene despite the medical checks she will have to endure for the rest of her life.

While you recall the faces and the stories of those who made it and those who didn’t, you float, detached from the world. The student protests, the riots and looting in French cities that I would have run to cover as a journalist are just a faraway noise.

The morning of the results, it's like I'm in a different dimension.

I'm trying to prepare myself for the worst, like bracing for an emergency landing. My appointment is at midday and I start wandering the streets of Lyon at 9.00 am. I walk like a lost soul for kilometre after kilometre. The hilarious part is that all this is happening to me during Pink October, the annual breast cancer awareness month. Launched in the United States in 1985, it's become one of the world’s most recognisable public-health campaigns. So, during my “week off”, I would regularly be seeing pink ribbons and breast symbols all over the place.

Worldwide, millions of euros are raised every year, yet organised breast screening participation in France remains below 50%. And look at me: I’m a journalist. I know the statistics; I’ve seen serious illness in my family. And yet I delayed making an appointment. Pure fear. How could I, or anyone, be ready to be told you have cancer? Still, it happens. And early detection can save your life.

Early detection: not only a question of fear, but of access to care

When breast cancer is detected before it spreads, five-year survival approaches 100%, compared with 38% for women diagnosed at an advanced stage. Despite its importance and the European Commission pouring around €80 million to strengthen screening across the bloc under its ‘Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan’ access to screening remains uneven across Europe, meaning that the chances of an early diagnosis can still depend on where a woman lives, not only on her fears. That’s due to screening organisation, access to appointments, out-of-pocket costs and awareness of the benefits of screening, as well as social inequalities, reveal latest research by the EU and the OECD..

As Luis Seijo, Co-chair of the European Cancer Organisation’s Prevention, Early Detection and Screening Network, has said, “Inequalities in cancer screening are costing lives.”

But disparities in Europe exist not only regarding early screening but how long it takes from screening to getting the diagnosis, ranging from a median of eight days in Denmark to 32 days in Romania.

While in my case it took just over a week, for Maria Assunta who lives in the Italian region of Sardinia, it took seven times longer.

She has been having annual breast checks since the age of 40, around ten years before the age generally recommended for routine screening in the European Union. Four years ago, when she was 46, a routine ultrasound revealed a 4-centimeter lump in one breast. She underwent a biopsy one month later and received her breast cancer diagnosis three weeks after that.

Maria Assunta is now in the follow up phase, with checks every 6 months. She describes the care she received “excellent both from a human and medical point of view” and calls her doctors her “angels”. Since going through this experience, she has become a passionate advocate for prevention and early detection.

Maria Assunta taking part in the walk in support of research into women’s cancers. Cagliari, Italy, 18 October 2026. Monica Pinna

Timeline from diagnosis to start of the treatment also differs across countries. In Maria Assunta’s case, there was almost no interval between the diagnosis and the start of the treatment. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) identifies long waits for specialist consultations, imaging and diagnostic tests as a concern in several countries, including Ireland, Greece, Romania and Spain.

Walk in support of research into women’s cancers. Cagliari, Italy, 18 October 2026. Monica Pinna

Stalled process of screening participation

While early detection has improved over the long term and mortality has declined, according to the OECD and European Commission’s “Health at a Glance: Europe 2020”, progress has stalled in many countries and screening participation continues to vary sharply across Europe.

Compared with 2019, breast cancer screening rates rose in nine EU countries with available data, with the largest increases observed in Slovakia by over 12%, followed by Croatia and Estonia.

Preventive breast cancer screenings 2019-2024 Eurostat

Breast cancer on the rise in the EU

As for my own story, the time finally came. I went in and waited for another half an hour till my name was called.

“I can reassure you, there is nothing, but it was best to check,” the doctor said with a smile. All my tension eased; I thanked her and shook her hand like a perfectly polite Italian. But even so, I remain disoriented by everything that has happened.

I was lucky, but every year around 360,000 women in the European Union receive a breast cancer diagnosis, 61,000 in France. Breast cancer is on the rise in Europe due to demographic changes, reproductive patterns — with later and fewer pregnancies — lifestyle habits and metabolic and hormonal factors, with research ongoing on environmental chemicals, pollution and diet impacts too. Statistics show that one in eleven women will develop breast cancer at some point in their life. It doesn’t mean they will die from it, but it doesn’t mean they will have an easy path through it either.

What happens for those who receive a breast cancer diagnosis?

I was lucky enough to walk out of that room with the same life I had before. But for many who receive a different diagnosis, the fear, uncertainty and sense of suspension I experienced for just seven days can become a lasting part of their lives.

So, is the mind cared for as much as the body, whether the journey leads to recovery or, ultimately, the end of life?

OECD’s 2026 European Cancer Inequalities Report found that only sixteen EU countries out of 27, plus Norway and Iceland, include psychological support in the cancer care pathway, and provision remains uneven.

In France, psychological care is part of the official package of supportive cancer care, alongside pain management, nutritional support and social assistance. In Italy access remains limited despite legal requirements and guidelines. A 2024 study of around 3,000 people with cancer found that only 20% reported receiving psychological support, while just 16% said a therapist had helped them throughout their cancer treatment. Much of this support still depends on private initiatives.

Eleonora is now 52 and lives in the Italian city of Genoa: She underwent a mastectomy at the age of 39, after a four-centimetre lump was discovered in her breast during the first ultrasound she had ever had.

In the thirteen years since her diagnosis, she has become a volunteer with the non-profit association Braccialetti Bianchi and a Qigong instructor. Rooted in traditional Chinese medicine, Qigong is one of the complementary practices the association offers to hospitalised patients and those undergoing rehabilitation. Other activities include circle dancing, yoga, empathic support, biodanza* and shiatsu. Eleonora says these therapies “can make the entire cancer journey just more bearable”.

Eleonora participating to a circle dance session in Genova. Braccialetti Bianchi association, 2026

This free support programme was launched around thirty years ago by a group of doctors working at the San Martino Hospital of Genoa. Maria Giuseppina Vidili is one of the oncologists who helped establish the initiative. She specialises in cancer rehabilitation, and she explains doctors and associations do what they can facing limited national budgets and healthcare cuts. She said she has worked tirelessly for years to build friendly spaces for patients at any stage of their cancer pathway.

She retired four years ago and never stopped offering complementary activities, saying that doctors and associations are on the frontline to fill in the gaps of the national healthcare system, at least in terms of psychological support.

According to the Italian Federation of Voluntary Associations in Oncology (FAVO), only around 20% of hospitals provide specialised psycho-oncology support. Such support becomes even less available once cancer treatment has ended. Doctor Vidili says a standardised psycho-oncology service should be available throughout the country. Initiatives like the one she launched are still limited to a reduced number of people. Some Italian hospitals, she says, don’t even have rehabilitation units.

Oncologist Maria Giuseppina Vidili during a Qigong session with cancer patients. Genoa, September 2026. Maria Giuseppina Vidili

Pink October, every month

The day after I received my all-clear, and I’m supposed to go back to work, answer emails, make calls to set up interviews, plan my next reporting trip. To pick up where I left off, as if nothing had happened.

But something did happen and has left a mark.

I wrote most of this article that morning, between 5 am and 9 am. I just had to get it off my chest – literally – hoping that sharing my experience would help even one single woman face her fears and go for regular screenings. But writing this was also a way to delve into a subject that people still prefer to look away from, including myself. I struggled to research and discuss cancer as if it were any other journalistic topic. It comes with a burden.

Today, my thoughts are with those fighting to live and those working to find new cures. Awareness campaigns matter, but awareness alone is not enough. Women need access to screening, prompt diagnosis and appropriate care. They also need to be encouraged to put their health first, even when fear makes it tempting to look away.

Psychological support and complementary therapies should be accessible to everyone, everywhere, not just to the limited number of people who can currently benefit from them across the EU.

And one thing is for sure: my next screening appointment will be on time.

World.title: Zelenskyy thanks US over deal for 500 Patriot missiles but warns delivery could take years
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has praised the US for its "strong decision" to approve the sale of 500 much-coveted Patriot missiles to Ukraine - but he has warned that delivery could take years.

 

The US State Department announced on Friday that Washington had green-lit a package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion as Kyiv continues to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks.

"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media in response.

"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he continued. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."

Earlier this week, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on a batch of missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.

Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian attacks, and the rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need. Russia has repeatedly sought to target Ukraine's power grid over wartime winter periods as Moscow has looked to break the country's resolve.

Dwindling stocks of interceptors have already encouraged Russia to ramp up missile attacks in recent months, and there are fears this trend could lead to an especially brutal winter for Ukrainians.

"The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses," Zelenskyy said overnight. "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach."

A Patriot missile mobile launcher is displayed outside the Fort Sill Army Post near Lawton, Okla., on March 21, 2023. Copyright 2023 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including incoming aircraft and ballistic missiles.

Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriots through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.

As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.

World.title: Syrian curriculum changes spark debate over removal of images and historical figures
World.content:
A set of changes made to a number of school textbooks in Syria has sparked a wave of criticism and reactions on social media, after they included alterations to pictures and artworks, among them adding the hijab to drawn female figures, removing images of women and children, covering statues and replacing paintings and works of art. The revisions have also affected teaching content dealing with political life, citizenship, democratic participation, local administration and the media.

 

These changes have reopened the debate over the standards used by the Ministry of Education when it reviews curricula, and how far they take into account Syria's social and cultural diversity, amid questions about the nature and aims of the amendments, and whether they fall simply within a review of content linked to the former regime or go further towards reshaping how society is represented in school books.

Changes to images, illustrations and educational content

Comparisons posted on social media between different editions of school textbooks show amendments to material for several grades, including the early years and seventh grade, as well as the sixth-grade primary textbook "Social Studies".

It emerges that this last book, reissued for the current academic year, originally dates back to the 2012–2013 school year, with changes added that include the removal of material linked to the former regime, alongside lessons on local administration, political life, citizenship, the media and democratic participation.

The changes were not limited to texts; they also extended to images and illustrations using Photoshop. Hijabs were added – and in some cases long robes – to drawn female characters, entire pictures of women were deleted, statues were covered, and sculptures and artworks were removed or replaced with others.

The visual alterations to paintings and expressive illustrations became a main focus of controversy, after committees removed the world-famous painting "Mona Lisa" and deleted a drawing showing a girl skipping rope beside two children in textbooks for early age groups.

The revisions also extended to historical figures and symbols. The Phoenician princess Elissar, founder of Carthage, was affected when a painting depicting her on a hunting trip was dropped and replaced with another portrait that had been digitally modified to cover the chin and neck – a step critics saw as imposing contemporary ideological standards on an ancient historical era.

One of the examples that provoked ridicule and debate was dressing a pharaonic statue in a striped shirt, which many users likened to prison uniforms.

Accusations of "falsifying history" and erasing national symbols

A new batch of visual comparisons circulated on social media documented far-reaching changes introduced to the new Syrian school curricula in particular history books, with the new editions showing the removal of prominent national and pan-Arab figures and the alteration of the content of historical passages, amid sharp questions and concerns about systematic ideological and sectarian exclusion.

Activists highlighted information that caused widespread anger and was described as "a blatant falsification of history". The updated curriculum contains passages portraying the "martyrs" executed on 6 May by the Ottoman governor Jamal Pasha, known as the Butcher, as "agents of Britain and France", instead of their historical description as symbols of the national movement resisting Ottoman colonial rule.

The changes also include deleting the picture of Sultan Pasha al-Atrash and replacing it with that of Sheikh Saleh al-Ali, a move that raised fears of exclusion on sectarian grounds. The alterations further removed a photograph of the late Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser.

The revisions reached school maps too, with the district of Iskenderun and the occupied Syrian Golan omitted from one of the maps, as well as the deletion of a paragraph on the role of Syrian women in resisting the French Mandate. This has raised questions about the motives behind these changes and their impact on the historical narrative presented to pupils.

Artistic inconsistencies and satire on social media

The nature of these changes and how they were carried out unleashed a wave of sarcastic comments on social platforms, where many users felt some of the alterations were random and lacked unified artistic standards to ensure visual coherence within a single textbook.

The most widely shared example in this context is a female doctor character in first-grade books who appears wearing a hijab on one page and without a hijab on another.

The comments did not stop at the artistic side, but also questioned the rationale for removing artworks and illustrated characters from school textbooks, and the criteria used to decide which images should be kept, modified or removed.

Parents criticise the changes and warn of their consequences

Among parents, objections went beyond the quality of the illustrations or the inconsistencies in modifying them, to the implications of these changes and their possible impact on how children view society and diversity.

Speaking to Euronews, Alia, the mother of a lower-secondary pupil, said she had not at first noticed the amendments because of the poor print quality and lack of detail in the drawings, pointing out that the heavy academic content and padding make it difficult for both parents and pupils to focus on visual details.

She argued that editing images of historical figures by adding a hijab raises questions about the purpose of such a step, and felt that replacing the pictures with new drawings would have been a more logical option than tampering with the original works. She warned that imposing a single pattern in the way women are depicted could shape how social diversity is presented to children, instead of promoting values of harmony and coexistence.

She added that priority should be given to developing the curricula and keeping pace with global shifts in education, rather than becoming preoccupied with cosmetic changes that add no clear educational value. In her view, such practices risk deepening divisions and fuelling intolerance instead of reducing it.

Alia went on: "The highest priority in this critical phase should be to fundamentally develop the educational curricula and keep up with the latest global changes in the education sector", considering that focusing on superficial visual adjustments does not serve the learning process or offer pupils any clear educational benefit.

Concluding her remarks to Euronews, she warned that the persistence of such practices within educational institutions could produce the opposite effect, as they help to deepen ideological divisions in society and feed exclusionary and fanatical thinking rather than mitigating it and strengthening shared citizenship values.

In the same vein, Jaber, the father of a primary-school girl, expressed even stronger concerns in his interview with Euronews, arguing that these visual changes cannot be separated from ideological orientations that risk being entrenched in society's consciousness through the education system. Jaber called on international organisations concerned with children's rights to take urgent action to safeguard children's right to receive balanced and neutral education.

He summed up his objection with a stark contrast between global technological progress and the regression of local curricula, saying: "While the world has reached leaps forward in developing artificial intelligence, we in Syria are still drowning in sterile arguments over covering women's images and deleting artworks from school textbooks".

From satire to accusations of trying to impose an ideology

On the other hand, reactions went beyond mockery of how the changes were implemented and raised deeper questions about their cultural and social dimensions. Critics and observers accused the ministry of seeking to impose a specific ideology through the education system, arguing that changing the visual appearance of female characters and removing elements of global artistic heritage reflects a deliberate effort to reshape children's perceptions and build a new social identity.

Some believe these concerns are particularly sensitive in a country such as Syria, marked by religious, cultural and social diversity. Their fear is that, if adopted as a lasting approach, such changes could entrench a one-sided view of Syrian society and sideline its historical pluralism and the natural differences in ways of life that distinguish it.

Part of the controversy centres on the distinction between two separate steps: the first involves removing content linked to the former regime, and the second relates to altering artistic illustrations or deleting educational topics on citizenship, political life and democratic participation.

While some see purging the curricula of the previous era's legacy as part of a normal modernisation process, the other changes raise questions about the educational and cultural foundations that govern how content is selected and directed.

Others argue that the published amendments alone are not enough to conclusively prove the existence of a coherent policy to impose a specific ideology. To reach an objective assessment of this accusation, they say, it is essential to see the official standards adopted, define the real scope of the changes and their causes, and compare them with the broader orientations the new curricula will adopt in the coming phases.

Ministry of Education: curricula respect diversity and do not adopt a single line

For its part, Syria's Ministry of Education on Monday rejected, in an official statement, the reports circulating on social media about new changes to images and content in the school curricula, describing this information as "inaccurate" and asserting that no new changes have been approved to the curricula in force for the current academic year.

The ministry clarified in its statement that the changes carried out since the fall of the former regime were limited to a single amendment that was announced and fully detailed in January 2025. According to the statement, that change focused mainly on removing the symbols and ideological content of the ousted regime and correcting the images and material linked to it, especially in the social studies and Islamic education curricula after they were merged and unified, in order to safeguard the diversity of Syrian society and strengthen the presence of all its components and cultures.

The ministry stressed that its plans to develop the curricula aim first and foremost to meet Syrians' aspirations and to entrench the values of citizenship and belonging, a culture of law and respect for others. In this context, it announced the completion of the "national framework for curricula" and the adoption of modern scientific standards that place the learner at the centre of the educational process, with the aim of fostering critical thinking, analysis and creative problem-solving, as well as enhancing life and digital skills, with the new curricula to be introduced gradually in line with the approved procedures.

The ministry attached to its release original samples and images from school textbooks to demonstrate the visual and social diversity they contain and to counter the circulating claims, calling on the media and the public to verify information carefully, rely on official sources and avoid being drawn into rumours.

The ministry's official statement, however, failed to defuse the crisis. It was met with a broad and fierce wave of criticism from activists and education watchers, some of whom went as far as accusing the ministry of "lying and concealing the truth".

Critics argued that the ministry's denial of any new amendments is completely at odds with the evidence and live visual comparisons taken from the textbooks distributed in schools.

On 17 August 2026, the Syrian Ministry of Education announced the adoption of unified curricula in all provinces for the 2026–2027 academic year, based on the previous year's curricula known as the "Damascus curriculum". It stated that it had completed the preparation of national standards for the new curricula in preparation for moving to the drafting phase.

On 14 September 2026, Syrian Education Minister Mohammad Abdulrahman Turko told a parliamentary hearing that the ministry had removed images and symbols linked to the former regime from the last two editions of schoolbooks.

He indicated that a single curriculum had been adopted across the different provinces, with a two-year transition period granted to pupils who had studied under the previous curricula.

Turko added that the ministry had referred the national standards for building the new curricula to the Higher Council for Education in preparation for starting to write the textbooks once those standards are approved.

World.title: Travelling beyond the borders of Baku through fiction
World.content:
From the poetry of medieval Azerbaijan to contemporary novels reaching readers from across different continents, Baku's relationship with the written word is rooted in centuries of cultural exchange.

 

Today, that literary heritage is finding new expression as authors, publishers and readers from Europe, Asia and beyond came together in the Azerbaijani capital for the twelfth year running.

The 12th Baku International Book Fair saw 32 countries taking part in an event which was not simply about discovering the latest books.

It was an opportunity to explore how literature connects hearts and minds across languages, generations, and geographical barriers by blending and sharing ideas and stories.

At a time when technology is transforming how tales are told, published, and consumed, the fair also questioned how books will remain an intrinsic and vital part of our futures.

12th Baku International Book Fair Euronews Baku Bureau, October 2026

Where history meets the modern word

Azerbaijan's literary traditions stretch back centuries and have been shaped by its position at the crossroads of Europe and Asia.

The 12th-century poet Nizami Ganjavi features heavily.

He was born in what is now Azerbaijan and became one of the most influential literary figures of the Persian-speaking world, with his works travelling the globe. He continues to be celebrated today.

Centuries later, writers and poets include Muhammad Fuzuli, who contributed to a rich literary tradition that developed across different languages and cultural influences.

This heritage provides a historical and rich backdrop to the country's modern relationship with international literature, where translation, publishing partnerships and literary festivals help stories reach audiences far beyond local borders and countries of origin.

For Iranian novelist Parinoush Saniee, literature offers a way of exploring the relationships between individuals and the societies in which they live.

Parinoush Saniee signing her book during 12th Baku International Book Fair Euronews Baku Bureau, October 2026

Her internationally recognised novel The Book of Fate follows the life of an Iranian woman through decades of personal and political change, examining themes of identity, family, education and the expectations placed upon women.

Saniee explained that she initially assumed her work would only resonate regionally, but she was quickly surprised by the global reaction.

"The first translation of my book was into Italian," Saniee recalled.

"When I saw all that reception and various journalists came from different places, I asked them what was interesting about the book for you. They said it was close to us. We also had such experiences. It was very relatable."

Although rooted in Iranian society, the questions raised in her writing resonate far beyond its borders. The works have been translated into numerous languages and demonstrate how literature can offer readers an understanding of lives and experiences different from their own.

She observed this same phenomenon when the novel became a bestseller in Norway, proving that universal themes of suffering and endurance translate seamlessly.

"Human suffering, lifestyles, issues, and problems are overall very impactful for humanity, and we all understand it," Saniee stated. "Therefore, it doesn't matter where it is from."

Darren Simpson during 12th Baku International Book Fair Euronews Baku Bureau, October 2026

Reaching younger minds

British author Darren Simpson, meanwhile, approaches storytelling through the imagination of younger readers.

He is known for novels such as Scavengers and The Memory Thieves, where he creates unusual worlds and characters exploring friendships, belonging, identity and the challenges of growing up.

Simpson echoed the sentiment that human emotion makes storytelling cross borders effortlessly, noting that children across the globe seek the exact same things from a narrative.

"When I see children from all around different countries connect to my stories in the same way, it speaks to me about the universal nature of a lot of feelings about people's needs and their desire to connect," Simpson explained.

His works reflect the importance of children's literature at a time when arguably young people have an unprecedented choice of digital entertainment and books are not necessarily the most popular choice. Yet, he highlighted that the local reception at the fair had been incredibly inspiring.

"I have been struck in Azerbaijan by how much passion there is here in the young readers," he added.

12th Baku International Book Fair Euronews Baku Bureau, October 2026

Championing local voices

Alongside its international offerings, the fair is also celebrating the locals who have helped to shape Azerbaijan's contemporary literary identity.

One of those is Reyhan Yusifgizi, a prominent voice in Azerbaijani children's science fiction who brings a unique academic background in computer science to her writing.

When discussing how to cultivate reading habits in a digital age, Yusifgizi explained that increasing a child's interest requires a two-step approach.

"First, this depends on the author," Yusifgizi noted. "They must write well, write in a modern way. With simple language, they must interest the child."

However, she stressed that the second factor is often the most fundamental.

"The parent directly influences the child. The parent stands between the author, the book, and the child," she said.

"First of all, the parent must demonstrate it through their own experience, their own example. They need to read."

Azerbaijani writer and publicist Elmira Akhundova reflected on the profound emotional weight that physical books carry compared to fleeting digital news. For her, literature's ultimate purpose is to promote peace and multiculturalism.

"What is at the end of the most difficult, the saddest book? It is light," Akhundova said.

"It is a call towards tolerance. We must hear these humanistic calls and instill them in our young generation," she told Euronews.

She challenged the next generation to seek out complex, philosophical narratives rather than settling for easy entertainment, noting that every story should ultimately lead the reader towards hope.

"A book must absolutely be geared toward humanism," she added, asserting that no matter what, a book "must be on the sunny side of the street."

The future of the written word

It is recognised that the relationship between books and their readers is changing.

Digital publishing, audiobooks and new forms of storytelling are reshaping the literary landscape, but rather than replacing traditional physical books entirely, there is an advantage to the technological advancements.

Books can now travel at lightning speed. A touch of a button can transport us to another universe, and perhaps that is what makes an international literary gathering even more relevant today.

Beyond the book stands, authors are choosing to move from the desktop to have those important physical discussions, drawn together by that love of narrative.

And what better place to have those conversations than the gateway between East and West?

World.title: Curfews, 70,000 police and Halloween fears: France braces for fresh protests
World.content:
Authorities in France are bracing for another potentially tense day of protests, with a source close to the country's Interior Ministry warning of a "very high risk of public disorder" on Saturday.

 

Around 70,000 police officers are to be deployed across the country as people take to the streets once again on Halloween.

For the third consecutive weekend, trade unions, students and members of the yellow vest movement are set to hold demonstrations, protesting over school conditions and the cost-of-living crisis. This comes days after the French government outlined several policies addressing student grievances on Monday, which unions have branded as insufficient.

Authorities are rolling out a ramped-up security operation this weekend, as they did on 24 October, in response to the widespread violence and looting that overshadowed otherwise peaceful demonstrations on 17 October.

The source close to the Interior Ministry warned on Friday that "calls for undeclared gatherings in public squares across France have proliferated," along with "plans for unauthorised marches towards places of power and state institutions."

On Thursday, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez declared that protests in city centres had been banned and that only those "on the outskirts of cities" would be permitted. He added that organisers had been asked to "provide guarantees" that demonstrations would occur in "good conditions."

For their part, trade unions and the yellow vest movement have criticised these measures. In a joint statement issued on Wednesday, major unions said they would explore "all possible avenues of appeal against this general and disproportionate ban on the exercise of a public freedom that is essential in a democracy."

Nuñez also said on Thursday that the fact that protests coincided with Halloween could encourage unrest, which may run into the night. He warned that gatherings seeking to pass off as Halloween celebrations would be banned, while also calling out social media posts from groups including "ultra-left circles" that have urged individuals to back a "revolution" and "insurrection."

The heightened security measures come amid as human rights groups continue to accuse French law enforcement of using excessive force against protesters.

A number of law enforcement officers who were on leave had been called back to duty across France, while others have had their rest days cancelled.

Meanwhile, Paris police imposed a curfew on Saturday and Sunday night in districts that experienced significant unrest on 17 October.

The final route for the march in Paris on Saturday has been set for the eastern outskirts of the capital, from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton, after the Council of State (Conseil d'État)overturned an administrative court's decision that had authorised a demonstration between Bastille and Nation.

France's student protest movement began in mid-September, after pupils staged demonstrations against school conditions in the Parisian suburbs. The movement rapidly spread nationwide, leading unions and political forces to join.

The demonstrations - which come around six months before France's presidential elections - have since expanded into a broader social movement against the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices.

World.title: France aims for 'responsible' 2027 budget as Fitch downgrades outlook
World.content:
Equipping France with a "responsible" budget for 2027 is the goal announced by the French government as bad economic news continues to mount.

 

Ratings agency Fitch has kept France's sovereign debt rating at A+, but has cut its outlook from "stable" to "negative", citing weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a bigger deficit than at its previous review last August.

This verdict comes after figures published by Insee on Friday morning showed that French gross domestic product fell by 0.1% in the third quarter, after stagnating in the second quarter and shrinking by 0.2% in the first.

To justify its decision (source in French), Fitch notably highlighted that "the persistence of political fragmentation" and "a difficult social climate", with the mass protests shaking the country, "further complicate the implementation of a lasting fiscal consolidation".

France's rating is nevertheless supported by "the size, wealth and diversification of its economy, the strength of its institutions, its membership of the euro area and the resilience of its banking sector".

"The absolute need to adopt a budget"

In a statement sent to the media on Friday evening, Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said he "takes note" of the US agency's decision to lower France's outlook.

"This assessment confirms the absolute need to adopt by the end of the year a responsible budget that aims to restore the public finances by reducing our deficit to 5%", he continued, adding that the government was "determined to stay on a path of fiscal consolidation".

"In an uncertain international environment, it is imperative to give economic players visibility", the finance minister concluded.

Earlier in the day, reacting to the fall in GDP on Franceinfo, Roland Lescure had described the French economy as "at a standstill". He had also warned that the country would be heading "into the wall" if the "recovery" budget were not adopted.

"I am saying it, I repeat it and I will repeat it to the end: we need a budget, we need a budget deficit of 5% or less", he hammered home.

But the chances of the text being adopted by a parliamentary vote look more than uncertain, given the lack of a majority in the National Assembly and the approaching presidential election.

49.3, ordinances: Fitch expects a push-through

The political debates taking shape six months before the vote "have not significantly increased Fitch's confidence in the possibility of a lasting reduction in the deficit that could stabilise the debt", the agency notes.

"We believe that the budget should be adopted, thanks to the constitutional mechanisms available to the government despite the lack of a parliamentary majority", the Fitch analysts say.

In the event of deadlock in Parliament, Roland Lescure has indicated that the government does not rule out resorting to article 49.3 of the Constitution, which allows a bill to be passed without a vote unless a motion of no confidence is adopted. Another option would be to use ordinances, a procedure that has never been used to pass a budget since the creation of the Fifth Republic in 1958.

Speaking to Euronews, Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University, believes that a budget adopted by ordinance could reduce uncertainty in the short term, but would not restore long-term fiscal credibility.

"Markets generally prefer a contested decision to a prolonged absence of decision. But if a budget adopted by ordinance is seen as fragile, liable to be called into question after the presidential election or as revealing a lasting inability of the political system to build majorities, the positive effect on [investor] confidence could be limited", the researcher explains.

World.title: How many bats are killed by wind turbines? Study warns of ‘shocking’ increase amid clean energy boom
World.content:
Wind energy has been described as a “foundational pillar” in the transition away from fossil fuels – but new research warns that spinning turbines kill a “shocking number" of bats every year.

 

According to the most comprehensive study into the problem to date, 18.7 million bats from 28 different species have died at wind energy facilities across the United States between 1981 and 2024.

The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that 100,000 bats died per year around two decades ago. But by 2021, attributed to the boom in wind energy, the death toll increased to 1.5 million bats annually.

Why bat deaths may have been underestimated for years

Many bats killed at wind farms collide with turbines, but scientists still aren’t sure why this happens. One theory is that they’re attracted by the whirring noise, or that they mistake the structures for trees.

Researchers say bats could also struggle to detect the blades or may be “drawn to them for other reasons”.

Most studies into bat fatalities are based on searches from wind farm operators themselves. But scientists worry that this doesn’t reveal the full picture – as methods used may vary between wind farms and leave room open for underestimations.

For example, scavenging animals might quickly remove the dead bats, or tall grasses could hide the carcasses.

This is why the study authors developed a statistical approach that accounted for missing data and estimated how many bats of each species may have been killed across the country, including at wind farms that had not been monitored.

“Despite using modern statistical methods, the state of data remained a limiting factor in our analysis,” the study states.

How can bat deaths be reduced?

The study argues that changes to the location of wind facilities could lower the risk of bats being killed. For example, wind farms near rivers tended to have higher fatalities – due to many bat species relying on rivers for food, water and navigation.

The characteristics of the wind turbine also had an effect. The team warned that turbines that have less ground clearance were particularly deadly.

A separate study, published in the journal of Applied Ecology this month, looked into 141 wind farms in Europe – where bat species are protected under the EU Habitats Directive.

The study found that avoiding turbine operation when local conditions are “particularly favourable” for bat flight can lessen mortalities by more than 80 per cent.

Some countries, such as Germany, have mandated mitigation measures since around 2010. These typically include risk assessments at site-selection stage and operating restrictions, for instance preventing the rotor from turning during high-risk periods, such as migration seasons, or in weather conditions in which bats are most active.

However, this strategy didn’t reduce deaths for migratory birds – which also fall victim to spinning turbines.

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

Editor’s note: This story was updated at 13:25 on 30 October 2026 to include a statement from lawyers for Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron, sent to us by Ketan Sengupta, who works with the Macron's legal team. It responds to the court’s ruling on Candace Owens’ motion to dismiss the case against her.

In the statement, lawyers for the Macrons said: “We are pleased that the Court rejected Mrs. Owens’ attempt to remove the case from Delaware, where her companies continue to publish and monetize her defamatory falsehoods. As for Mrs. Owens personally, we are keeping all options open to ensure that, in addition to the liability she still faces through her companies, she is held accountable personally.”

***

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Egypt's mahrganat music: from the streets to five-star hotels
World.content:
Born in Egypt’s working-class neighbourhoods, mahraganat music is loud and raw, and these days it is practically impossible to escape. But for the artists behind it, mahraganat is more than just party music: they see it as the latest chapter in Egypt’s rich musical history.

Advertising

In this third episode of the season, we travel to the Egyptian capital, Cairo, to discover the origins of a genre that has become the soundtrack to urban life, despite receiving no official airtime.

Mahraganat evolved from shaabi: music by the people, for the people. Although it rose to prominence during the revolution of 2011–12, it has since become less overtly political.

It remains the music of happiness, partying, joy, and celebration.

Its fast rhythms and loud beats may be a far cry from the golden age of Egyptian music, but mahraganat has been on the scene since the early 2000s and it isn’t going anywhere, any time soon.

We trace its origins and evolution as we speak to one of the godfathers of the movement, his musical partner and a specialist in the genre.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora. Special thanks to Elisa Schouten for her contribution.
