World.title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
World.content:
A wave of shootings and extortion threats has rattled India's film industry. This time, those claiming responsibility are very different from the Mumbai underworld that had Bollywood in its grip back in the 1990s.

"In the entire film industry, whoever works without aligning with us, or works with Salman Khan, will be killed."

This warning was delivered in an audio message by presumed attackers on Indian actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai earlier this month, as they claimed responsibility for the shooting.

The apparent perpetrators said they were connected to Lawrence Bishnoi, a student-politician-turned-gangster who has been in prison since 2014. Notably, police have not confirmed the gang's involvement.

The shots fired at Shroff, which injured his driver, were only the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent figures from the Mumbai-based film industry, popularly known as "Bollywood".

Since 2022, gunmen fired shots at actor Salman Khan's apartment and at the home of filmmaker Rohit Shetty in Mumbai, as well as actor Disha Patani's family home in northern India. Actor Ranveer Singh also reportedly received an extortion demand of nearly $1.1 million (around €980,000).

The attacks have spread to the other side of the globe, with a cafe owned by comedian Kapil Sharma in Surrey, Canada, also hit three times.

For an industry that once lived in the shadow of organized crime, the attacks have revived old fears, harking back to the crime bosses of the 1990s. But experts say the threat facing Bollywood today looks very different from the one it faced three decades ago.

When the underworld ruled Bollywood

In the 1990s, Mumbai's underworld was deeply entangled with the Hindi film industry.

"The mafia was always fascinated with the movie industry," said S. Hussain Zaidi, crime journalist and author of "Dongri to Dubai: Six Decades of the Mumbai Mafia," who has covered organized crime in the city for over three decades.

Gangsters like Dawood Ibrahim, Abu Salem and Chhota Shakeel "were totally obsessed" with Bollywood, he told DW, much like mafiosi who sought a foothold in Hollywood.

During his era, Dawood Ibrahim has been one of the most wanted men in India Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

To the gangsters, films offered glitz and glamor, but also a way to launder their profits. They invested in films "so that they could control the industry and have a legitimate way of making money," Zaidi added.

When producers didn't cooperate, the consequences could be fatal. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar, founder of the label T-Series, was shot dead. In 2000, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan, father of Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, was shot and wounded.

Mumbai's streets were "made red with blood" in 1998, Zaidi said, describing the year as the pinnacle of gang killings.

D. Sivanandhan, the former Police Commissioner of Mumbai, who led the crackdown, says 101 businessmen were shot dead in 1998 alone, or one "every third day," mostly over unpaid extortion demands.

Police efforts were reinforced by a tough new organized crime law passed in 1999, which Sivanandhan calls the "ultimate weapon." Security forces used electronic surveillance and preventive detention, and seized some 2,500 illegal weapons.

"A few encounters also happened, but that is not a policy nor a strategy,” he told DW, referring to police shootouts.

By the early 2000s, the gangs' hold had been broken, and a new Mumbai seemed to be emerging.

A gang run from a prison cell

The man believed to be behind the latest wave of attacks is not from Mumbai.

Bishnoi, 33, comes from a landowning family in the northern state of Punjab and was studying in Chandigarh when he was drawn into violent student politics. Then, he was arrested, incarcerated and eventually turned to crime, says journalist Jupinderjit Singh, author of "Gangs of Punjab."

"He was introduced to the University of Crime through the jail," Singh told DW.

Lawrence Bishnoi was a student politician in the northern city of Chandigarh before gaining notoriety as a gangster Image: Sameer Sehgal/Hindustan Times/IMAGO

Bishnoi went on to build what Singh describes as one of the first criminal syndicates spanning several northern Indian states. Investigators say he still directs operations from prison using concealed phones and messaging apps.

Currently, Bishnoi is held in a jail in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat.

His network stretches beyond India's borders. In September 2025, Canada designated the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity. Last month, the FBI added Satinderjeet Singh, popularly known as Goldy Brar, to its Ten Most Wanted list, offering up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest. US prosecutors described him as the alleged leader of Bishnoi's group in North America.

While Bishnoi comes from an affluent landowning family, his shooters are mostly poor. The gang usually recruits them online.

"There are so many youngsters who want to do something… they are just pulled by the lore attached to Lawrence Bishnoi," Singh explained. "Recruiting is no big issue… They offer money, protection, weapons."

Why target film stars?

For Bishnoi, it seems personal.

In 1998, Salman Khan was accused of killing a blackbuck, an antelope revered by Bishnoi's community. Bishnoi vowed revenge, and many of the attacks targeted people close to the actor, including the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique, which police have linked to the gang.

Singh sees the feud as a bid for respectability. Criminals "always try to find something that makes them a moral guardian," he says, and this case was Bishnoi's "chance to redeem himself."

Salman Khan was granted bail in 2018 as he appealed a conviction for killing two rare antelopes Image: AFP

But money and intimidation matter too.

"Bollywood has a lot of money," Singh added, pointing that the previous generation of gangsters was no longer in position to take advantage.

"With Dawood Ibrahim and his counterparts away, there was a vacuum, and Lawrence Bishnoi is trying to exploit that."

Sivanandhan explained the old Mumbai gangs ran a whole "basket" of illegal businesses, from smuggling to protection rackets and cricket match-fixing. Their members were "local boys," while the Bishnoi gang has “nothing to do with Mumbai,” he added. It targets Bollywood because the industry is "loaded with money" and a "soft underbelly."

"They are using Bollywood as an ATM," he told DW. "Insert a card and collect your money."

Meanwhile, Zaidi sees the attacks mainly as publicity. "It's a way to grab headlines," he told DW. Within hours of the recent attack on Shroff, someone claimed on social media that he was targeted for being close to Khan, a logic Zaidi called "absolutely illogical and absurd."

But publicity is useful to gangs that live off extortion. "The base material of extortion is: create fear," a security professional responsible for the protection of several Bollywood stars, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue, told DW.

Is Bollywood under siege?

Still, experts say its hard to argue that the ongoing violence is comparable to the 1990s crime wave.

"I won't say resurgence, because that would be a bit of an exaggeration," Zaidi said. In the 1990s, several rival gangs fought for control of Mumbai. Today, other than Bishnoi's faction, other gangs are not considered active in Mumbai.

The film industry is also not paying up the way it once did, because the shift to digital payments has made large cash transactions hard to hide, he added.

Sivanandhan disagrees. The shootings at walls and gates, followed by quick claims on social media, are "all aimed at collecting… extortion money," he said. In his view, "cash-rich Bollywood would be coughing up so much, which is enough to run an army of people."

At any case, the fear remains real.

And even if violence is not as prevalent, hundreds of thousands of people rely on the Mumbai film industry for their livelihoods.

"If the fear of the underworld continues, leading names may be forced to leave Mumbai," the All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) President Suresh Shyamlal Gupta wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah.

"Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, and Bollywood will not be allowed to work in the shadow of fear," Gupta wrote.

With security forces seemingly on the back foot, gangsters are likely to continue their campaign.

Several Bollywood stars have already stepped up their security.

World.title: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
World.content:
What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection, as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

How names influence first impressions

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness.



For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.



What do Nigerians think of bullying? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why some names attract negative judgments

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

How humor helps people cope with embarrassing names

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

How an embarrassing name can also offer a sense of belonging

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

Superpower laughter — how humor makes us strong , To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."



Edited by: Richard Connor

World.title: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara to expire amid US, Russia vetoes
World.content:
The mandate of the UN peacekeeping force in Western Sahara will expire on October 31. The UN Security Council could not agree on a resolution to extend the mission.

The fate of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has been left in a limbo after Russia and the United States vetoed each other's draft resolutions on extending the mission that is over three decades long — just one day before the mandate expires.

The peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to oversee a settlement plan and ceasefire between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front in a territorial dispute spanning half a century.

Morocco considers Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, as its territory,

The Polisario Front, which is supported by Algeria and represents the indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.

US and Russia wield vetoes

On Friday, the US tabled a draft resolution at the UN Security Council (UNSC) that would have extended the mandate for one year, while making a Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara the only basis for negotiations to settle the conflict, and cutting the mission's military component.

Last year, the UNSC backed Morocco's autonomy proposal as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.

Friday's failed US draft resolution would have gone further and rebranded the peacekeeping force from MINURSO to MINUSO, dropping the 'R' which refers to referendum on the territory's self-determination.

The US proposal was vetoed by Russia, which slammed it as a "unilateral approach." A total of 11 of the 15 UNSC members voted in its favor and three abstained.

"We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty," Russia's permanent representative to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, said.

"The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach. Therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of ⁠the draft," ​he added.

The US, with its own veto, then blocked a Russian draft that proposed renewing the mission's mandate for another year while preserving the same terms as before.

"Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades," the US representative to the United Nations, Michael Waltz, said after the vote.

Western Sahara: Caught between sovereignty and struggle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How did Morocco and the Polisario Front react?

Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the peacekeeping mission and said that this "should mark the end of the Security Council's involvement and the removal of this issue from its agenda."

The Polisario Front's UN representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing the US resolution that he said "would have undermined the free exercise by the Sahrawi people of their inalienable right to self-determination and independence."

World.title: European diplomats shun Russia at G20 gathering in the US
World.content:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov declined to comment on Russia's participation in the G20 summit in December, telling DW that Volodymyr Zelenskyy should travel to Russia if he wanted talks with Vladimir Putin.

A Group of 20 foreign ministers' meeting in the US city of Atlanta got off to a rocky start on Friday after top diplomats from European nations refused to take a "family photo" along with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is hosting the gathering, decided to scrap the photo before the meeting got underway because Washington didn't want it to become a spectacle or distraction.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters before the first session on Friday that there wouldn't "be a family photo with European partners and Mr. Lavrov together because ... there is no normalcy with Russia."

The two-day gathering of the G20 grouping, which includes the EU, Russia, Germany, India, China, Brazil and other major countries, is meant to be a precursor to a G20 leaders summit later this December.

That G20 leaders meeting in December is set to be hosted by US President Donald Trump at his golf club in Miami.

Rubio stresses unity despite fractures

Rubio still opened the talks by stressing unity on major issues, telling his counterparts that they were in a "critical moment."

"We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises," he said.

He pointed to disruptions to global energy and trade and said many were posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order."

But several countries, including the United States and Russia, are involved in separate wars. Wars in Iran and Ukraine have resulted in a spike in food prices for people around the world .

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pledged to "call on Russia to finally accept Ukraine's offer of a ceasefire, starting in the Black Sea" Image: Megan Varner/REUTERS

While the message is about unity and finding solutions to problems like freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz during the G20 meeting, the reality is that finding common ground will likely be much tougher.

Given a renewed momentum to revive talks to end the war in Ukraine, there was also interest in getting Lavrov to talk about Russia's stance on future talks with Kyiv.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio appealed for unity between members of the G20, despite the US not inviting all of them to the ministers' meeting Image: Erik S. Lesser/AFP

Russia willing to meet Zelenskyy in Moscow, Lavrov tells DW

The US has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 meeting in Miami, but it's unclear whether Russia has accepted the invitation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has previously said that he would be open to traveling to Miami to hold talks with Putin if he were also there.

The Kremlin has so far declined direct meetings with Zelenskyy, with Russia's Sergey Lavrov telling DW on the sidelines of the meeting that Putin is willing to meet with the Ukrainian leader if he travels to Moscow.

"President Putin said if he [Zelenskyy] is willing to meet, let him come to Moscow," Lavrov said. "We will guarantee his safety."

Lavrov declined to say whether Putin will attend the G20 summit this December.

Putin has not attended a G20 leaders meeting since 2019 and only attended a session virtually in 2023.

Russia has also continued with its attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, stepping up drone strikes on water and energy infrastructure.

A Russian drone strike on a railway station in Dnipro on October 29 killed at least 14 people Image: Telegram channel on president ou Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyj

EU top diplomat calls out Lavrov's 'lies'

The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said ministers at the G20 meeting were able to call out Lavrov for his "lies" at the table.

"We were talking about the big geopolitical crises, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergey Lavrov head-on with this," Kallas said on the sidelines of the meeting.

"Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives that we were also able to then rebuke," she said.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also called out Lavrov, saying, "If we are serious about our values and our interests, we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine."

Lavrov says no easing of ties with US, 'no illusions' about diesel deal

Lavrov, who is under international sanctions for Russia's war in Ukraine, was invited to the US at a time when the two countries have appeared to have fostered warmer ties.

Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia earlier this month and also waived new sanctions on Russia's energy. The US announced the move just weeks away from the midterm elections on November 3.

Lavrov said on Friday that despite those efforts, "in practice, no real progress in relations with the US has so far been seen."

How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

South Africa, a founding member of G20, excluded from US meeting

The Trump administration has been embroiled in disputes with South Africa, having imposed visa restrictions on South Africanswho it said were complicit in discriminating against white people.

Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year because US officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group.

But US officials didn't extend that invite to South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group.

"We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary," said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.

With this many issues on the table, it appeared less likely that there would be a joint consensus at the end of the talks.

Instead of a final declaration, the AFP news agency reported, the meeting is expected to end on Saturday with a chair summary drafted by the US.

World.title: Poland: Protesters clash with police over sacked court chief
World.content:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended the firing of top court President Bogdan Swieczkowski as a move to "restore the rule of law."

Protesters gathered outside Poland's Constitutional Court on Friday night, with authorities sending police to the scene to secure the court's grounds.

It all comes after a statement appeared on the top court's website saying President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy had been suspended for one month. Fellow judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska will lead the institution during this period.

According to Warsaw police, officers responded to one judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staff.

Tusk vows to 'restore rule of law'

Swieczkowski is one of a slew of politically aligned judges who were appointed by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS), which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk backed the move in a post on X.

"Restoring the rule of law is our duty," Tusk said.

"After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way," he added.

Officers responded to a judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staff Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

When Tusk's center-left alliance took over after the 2023 parliamentary election, the group announced it would reverse controversial PiS government reforms in the judiciary.

Riot police deployed to court

Dozens of riot police were deployed to the court as followers of PiS protested against the ousting of Swieczkowski through the evening.

The court's official X social media account said there had been a "coup d'etat," with some chanting "Tusk traitor" as they condemned the step taken by the Tusk government.

Polish president cancels trip abroad

Right-wing Polish President Karol Nawrocki reacted to the situation by canceling a planned trip to Senegal.

"At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland," Nawrocki said.

Upon returning to Poland, he entered the Constitutional Court, making his way through the police barricade, his chief of staff said early on Saturday.

"President Karol Nawrocki, accompanied by the First President of the Supreme Court, Zbigniew Kapinski, entered the Constitutional Tribunal building," Pawel Szefernaker wrote on X.

In recent months, Nawrocki had refused to swear in five top court judges nominated by parliament.

When these judges instead took their oath before parliament, Swieczkowski had denied them access to the building.

World.title: Canadian PM Mark Carney discusses talks with the EU, overdependence on the US and how to deal with Donald Trump in a DW interview.
World.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney tells DW that Canada is seeking closer EU ties to "diversify and deepen" partnerships beyond the Americas. Despite German pushback, he said he favors the all-new term "associate membership."

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to DW on Friday after talks in Montreal with European Union leaders seeking to hammer out details of a new, closer partnership between Canada and the EU.

Amid difficult negotiations with US President Donald Trump, representing Canada's biggest trading partner, Carney said that he and his compatriots had come to realize the country was too dependent on the economic powerhouse to the south.

"The lesson we've taken, Canadians as a whole, is we're overdependent on the United States. Too closely connected to the United States. And we need to build our strength here at home and diversify and deepen our partnerships with like-minded countries internationally," Carney said.

Canada is too reliant on the United States, Carney tells DW To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Carney say about EU talks and closer ties to the bloc?

An EU delegation led by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa held talks with Carney and other Canadian officials in Montreal on Friday.

They're discussing the plans floated by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to forge what she called an "associate membership" — a status that does not yet exist for any other country — even as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government resists creating this label. Carney seemed to speak in its favor.

"Well, I think the advantage of what we're doing is that a few things are absolutely clear, irrespective of the exact terminology that's used. President von der Leyen uses associated membership. We use associated membership," he told DW's Katharina Kroll at Port of Montreal Tower.

"What does that mean? It means the closest possible partnership without being a full member of the European Union, because Canada is not in Europe geographically and therefore cannot have accession." Carney said.

Carney and EU leaders met at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal this week Image: Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

What scope for EU-Canada cooperation does Carney see?

Asked if he was looking to create a "new transatlantic bloc without the US," Carney said it was more about diversifying and deepening Canada's other partnerships than excluding by far its largest trading partner.

"We're both partners of the United States, obviously close partners, alliance partners in NATO. And there are many, many opportunities for cooperation with the United States," he said. "But in many cases, there'll be much deeper cooperation for Canada between Canada and Europe than Canada and the United States."

He mentioned both existing areas of cooperation like the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), calling it "one of the most successful free trade agreements in the world," and also pointed to research cooperation and programs like Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ enabling student exchanges.

But Carney also pointed to areas where the two sides could seek to expand cooperation, naming areas like space technologies, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.

Carney said that, like von der Leyen but possibly unlike Germany's Friedrich Merz, he uses the term associate membership to describe the status Canada seeks Image: Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Is Canada concerned the talks could alienate the US, or Trump?

Despite his well-documented difficulties with Donald Trump — perhaps most crudely exemplified by Trump's attempts to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, or his posting AI videos imagining him as an ice hockey player beating Carney up in a fight — Carney said US-Canadian ties were too deep to be derailed by any governments or prime ministers or presidents.

"The bonds between Canadians and Americans are longstanding. They're very strong. And big elements of that will be maintained regardless of the government in Canada, the government in the United States, the combination of the two," he said.

Asked about the best way to deal with Trump, Carney said it was "to be direct, to be clear, to be absolutely clear about your bottom lines are." He said it was important to show respect but also to continue to bring "the negotiations back to the core issues."

But he said the tensions with Trump had demonstrated the need to diversify and to seek Canada's other most natural partners around the world.

Carney has been in the midst of difficult trade talks with Donald Trump, who has at times shown his dissatisfaction with his neighbor to the north as only he can Image: Dmytro Rusanov/DW

He acknowledged that no matter the nature of the talks with the EU, "the scale of the relationship with the United States" would be "very hard to replace."

Asked if he was concerned that the talks could expose him to further tariffs or other punitive measures from the Trump administration, Carney said, "We've been living with this for some time."

"There have been many justifications for trade action against Canada that the United States has had," he said. "Our view is that all of them are unjustified under our trade agreement."

Carney said the crucial message, also for the Trump White House, was that the talks with Brussels concerned a "positive association" and partnership "to help solve global problems" and address global challenges.

"It's not against somebody. It's for. It's a positive act," he said.

Are the EU and Canada moving closer? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DW's Katharina Kroll conducted the interview in Montreal.

World.title: Ukraine: Oleshky residents evacuate war-ravaged city
World.content:
Under the local ceasefire, an aid convoy of 25 buses arrived with humanitarian aid and as transport for fleeing Oleshky residents. The Ukrainian city has been occupied by Russia since 2022 and faces food shortages.

Residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky, in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, evacuated the war-torn city on Friday.

The evacuations come in the fourth day of a ceasefire in the city, the most significant truce since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine over four years ago.

The local ceasefire was brokered by US first lady Melania Trump. Pope Leo XIV also participated in deliberations with Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.

Under the ceasefire deal, an aid convoy of 25 buses, some ambulances, trucks and other vehicles arrived in the city earlier on Friday to deliver food and medicine to residents.

Demining operations preceeded the aid convoy's arrival, with a Russian sapper and one other person killed in the process.

Officials from both Ukraine and Russia came to gether in the rare joint humanitarian effort, which is expected to continue through Sunday evening.

How did the evacuations take place?

According to the plan, an estimated 2,000 remaining Oleshky residents were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian-held territory, Russian-held territory, or to remain in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

If residents chose to go to Ukraine, they would travel 450 kilometers (280 miles) through Russian-held Crimea to reach the city of Anapa in southern Russia. Then they would fly to Belarus before crossing the border into northern Ukraine.

Russia's lead representative on the mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses would transport residents who want to live in Russia.

It remained unclear how many people chose to leave the city, but Melania Trump posted on social media that the convoy had safely evacuated more than 750 people.

Aid convoy reaches frontline town of Oleshky To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Harrowing conditions

Oleshky residents have spoken of the harrowing conditions they have had to suffer in the city, such as traveling along mine-strewn roads in search for food and water.

"The problem is that a lot of people are staying," one woman told Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets.

"I've been told that it's their own choice," Lubinets replied. "At the very least, we'll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through."

Lubinets was in charge of coordinating the operation with Lantratova.

The pair appeared side by side to address reporters and were cordial to one another, something not seen between Russian and Ukrainian officials since the start of the war.

World.title: Una caída cada dos días: la penuria del sistema de seguridad que dejó de funcionar antes del accidente de Urda
World.content:
El LZB, que evita que dos trenes coincidan en el mismo punto, ha dejado de estar en servicio en al menos 170 ocasiones en lo que va de año

A las 8.31 del miércoles, seis trenes que circulan por la línea de alta velocidad que une Madrid-Sevilla y se reparten por un tramo de 63 kilómetros se ven afectados por el mismo problema: se ha caído el sistema LZB, que sirve para que dos convoyes no coincidan en el mismo cantón o pequeño segmento de la línea. La consecuencia es inmediata. Todos se paran. Saben que van a tener que operar al amparo los sistemas ASFA (que mide la distancia entre trenes por balizas y es capaz de detenerlos si superan ciertas barreras de seguridad) y BSL (que se comunica con los trenes por señales en los laterales de la vía). Los maquinistas se ponen en contacto con el centro de coordinación de Adif en Atocha (Madrid), donde nadie parece sorprendido por la situación, según los audios publicados por EL PAÍS. En lo que va de año, el LZB ha dejado de estar en servicio en 170 ocasiones, según explica luego el ministro Óscar Puente. Eso supone que está desactivado casi una vez cada dos días, con incidencias de diferente duración. En este caso, la reactivación de la marcha, para la que se aplican protocolos incorrectos, lleva al desastre: un AVE lanzado a entre 160 y 200 kilómetros por hora percute contra un Iryo totalmente parado en Urda (Toledo), provocando al menos 69 muertos y centenares de heridos de diversa consideración.

¿Qué es lo que ha ocurrido? El epicentro de la crisis está en la estación LZB de Urda. Allí hay una instalación que guarece un grupo de tres ordenadores de los que depende que el sistema funcione en esa zona, para un total de una treintena distribuidos por los cientos de kilómetros de vía que unen Madrid y Sevilla.

Esos tres equipos lanzan órdenes a los trenes en tramos de unos 60 kilómetros. Si dos de ellos no coinciden en el contenido de la orden emitida, el LZB se apaga y frena a los trenes. En el caso de la estación de Urda, fallan dos ordenadores, lo que provoca la caída del sistema. Al mismo tiempo, eso es lo que ofrece una aparente solución: una de las razones por las que los controladores de Atocha permiten avanzar al AVE que acabará estrellándose con el Iryo es que creen que cuando pase esa estación de Urda todo volverá a la normalidad y podrá reengancharse al LZB.

Ocurre que entre esa baliza de reconexión y el AVE está, totalmente parado, el Iryo, frenado por un semáforo en rojo, primero, y por la imposibilidad de reactivar el sistema, después.

El Centro de Regulación de Circulación (CRC) de Adif en la estación de Madrid-Puerta de Atocha, en Madrid (España), a 14 de enero de 2021. Moncloa (Europa Press)

“Aún no sabemos qué generó el problema de comunicación entre los equipos informáticos en la central de Urda”, explicó este viernes Puente, durante una rueda de prensa. “Lo que sí sabemos es que esta incidencia no es una incidencia infrecuente, y que el sistema está diseñado para lidiar con ella”, añade el ministro, que defiende que el LZB (instalado en la línea de Cercanías C-5 y en la de alta velocidad Madrid-Sevilla) es tan fiable como el ERTMS que debe instalarse en toda la red española para cumplir con la normativa europea, y que ya funciona en las líneas que conectan Madrid con Barcelona, Lleida, Burgos y Valencia; Albacete y Alicante; Valladolid, Palencia y León; y en redes convencionales como en varios puntos de Cercanías Madrid.

“En 2026″, sigue Puente, “se ha producido [la caída del LZB] en 170 ocasiones, un número que está dentro de la normalidad europea, y en números muy estables en los últimos seis o siete años, y por debajo de la media registrada en los dos años inmediatamente anteriores: son entre 150 y 200 incidencias al año”.

Puente sabe de lo que habla. En mayo de 2025, el ministro se desplazó a una zona cercana a Urda, Manzaneque (Toledo), para conocer de primera mano cómo se habían vandalizado varias cajas de seguridad que contenían 150 metros de cable de seguridad. Como consecuencia, la alta velocidad quedó paralizada, y 16.000 viajeros se vieron afectados en el intento de llegar a sus destinos. Puente planteó la posibilidad de un sabotaje. Finalmente, se localizaron cinco cortes de cable en la línea que une Madrid, Sevilla y Málaga en un radio de 12 kilómetros. Para la Guardia Civil, fue el producto de “un robo con fuerza”.

El consejero delegado de Iryo, Fabrizio Favara, comparece ante la comisión de investigación sobre los accidentes ferroviarios, en el Senado, a 5 de octubre de 2026, en Madrid (España). Fernando Sánchez / Europa Press (Europa Press)

¿Qué había pasado? Que se había robado el cobre fundamental para que funcione la red ferroviaria. Esa es una de las razones enumeradas este viernes por Puente para explicar las 170 caídas del LZB en lo que va de año.

“El 75% de las 170 incidencias son completamente ajenas al sistema”, sostiene. Y ejemplifica: “Vandalismo, robos de cable, daños como consecuencias de obras, de tareas de mantenimiento, de incidencias climatológicas”.

De hecho, ha dicho el titular de Transportes, en el tramo afectado por la catástrofe se han producido 13 caídas del sistema LZB en lo que va de 2026, la última el 14 de octubre, “una ratio de incidencias por kilómetro de 0,4, la mitad de otras bandas de la línea Madrid-Sevilla”. El ministro defiende que esas cifras son homologables con las de otros sistemas ferroviarios que siguen usando la misma infraestructura que la línea de alta velocidad que une Madrid con Sevilla, como los de Alemania o Austria. Puente no ha dado datos que permitieran comparar la incidencia del LZB con la incidencia del ERTMS de líneas como la Madrid-Barcelona o la Madrid-Valencia.

29/10/28 Día después del accidente de Ave e Iryo en Toledo, cerca de Urda. Personal de rescate siguen buscando víctimas entre los escombros. © Carlos Rosillo Carlos Rosillo

El LZB es tecnología alemana que data de los setenta. Cuando se cae, frena a los trenes, como ocurrió en Urda. Su problema es que la UE ha apostado por el ERTMS y ha quedado restringido a pocas líneas en España y otras más en Alemania y Austria. En el mercado faltan piezas, circunstancia que Renfe, y posteriormente Adif, evitaron comprando un gran stock. El ERTMS está tendido en la línea Madrid-Sevilla desde abril de este año y el salto de una tecnología a otra se producirá en los próximos meses.

¿Cómo funciona el LZB? El sistema supervisa continuamente la velocidad de los trenes y transmite las indicaciones de circulación a la cabina del maquinista, según la Declaración sobre la red de Adif, el documento que recoge las características de la infraestructura y las condiciones de acceso para las empresas ferroviarias. Sin embargo, cuando el programa de seguridad automatizado falla, el control pasa a ser manual, algo que en Transportes se normaliza por cuanto también pasa en el transporte aéreo o en el naval: “La última ratio de seguridad siempre es humana, pero con asistencias”.

No obstante, los problemas del LZB en España ya habían sido motivo de crítica. Este sistema opera en el corredor Madrid-Sevilla desde su inauguración, allá por los años noventa del siglo XX. Como consecuencia, convive con trenes que no tienen que ver con los primeros que circularon, y que están en la vanguardia tecnológica. Es el caso de los Iryo y los Alstom Eurodúplex que opera Ouigo, y que tuvieron que adaptarse para poder rodar hasta Andalucía.

El consejero delegado de Iryo, Fabrizio Favara, alertó el 5 de octubre en el Senado de las desconexiones del sistema de señalización de la línea Madrid-Sevilla y los problemas para reanudar la marcha que producía en sus convoyes.

“Cada vez que la señal del tren se desconecta de la señal de tierra, el tren se para. No se puede mover y lleva bastante tiempo reconectarse y empezar nuevamente el servicio”, señaló el ejecutivo italiano ante la comisión de investigación sobre los accidentes ferroviarios de Adamuz (Córdoba) y Gelida (Barcelona). Veintitrés días después, una caída de ese mismo sistema precedió al accidente de Urda (Toledo).

Los problemas del Iryo con el LZB

A las 8.41, la maquinista del Iryo transmitió al centro de Atocha que no podía mover su convoy: “He tenido una pérdida de transmisión con velocidad a Meta 40 [con la velocidad limitada], he ido circulando en BSL, estoy detenida en señal de entrada de Urda”. Los supervisores del centro de Atocha advirtieron a la maquinista de que no la autorizaban a rebasar esa señal. La persona al mando le ordenó desconectar y volver a conectar el LZB para reanudar la marcha “con marcha normal”.

Nada cambió cuando, alrededor de las 8.48, la conductora insistió en que el problema del Iryo se mantenía.

—No me está permitiendo el tren reiniciar el sistema LZB y por eso estoy todavía detenida ante la señal de entrada.

—Vale, conforme, pues nada, cuando pueda, y si tiene problemas nos llama.

Cada uno de los trenes que cruza la línea Madrid-Sevilla lleva embarcados sistemas LZB que se comunican con los de tierra. El no poder levantar los del Iryo lo convirtieron en un obstáculo. La maquinista trató de reiniciar el tren en dos ocasiones, tal y como informó este periódico. En cada una de las operaciones invirtió entre tres y cuatro minutos, según fuentes cercanas a Iryo. El protocolo de la compañía obliga a contactar con el equipo de mantenimiento en busca de asistencia al segundo intento fallido. En consecuencia, la maquinista estableció una doble comunicación, con el centro de control de Adif y con su empresa, mientras el AVE se dirigía hacia su posición a “marcha normal”, según se le ordenó desde Atocha. Y así, el AVE embistió al Iryo a las puertas de la localidad de Urda.

World.title: De las tecnológicas del LZB a las operadoras de trenes: cuáles son las empresas presentes en el accidente de Urda
World.content:
Thales e Hitachi Rail están junto a Adif, Renfe e Iryo en el centro de la conversación tras el siniestro

Las primeras hipótesis sobre las causas del accidente ferroviario del miércoles, en el que murieron al menos 69 personas, apuntan a un error humano de operadores de Adif tras una caída de los sistemas de señalización de las vías. A la espera de que las investigaciones determinen la cadena de responsabilidades, el siniestro salpica a la empresa encargada del mantenimiento del LZB, Hitachi Rail GTS.

La línea de alta velocidad entre Madrid y Sevilla cuenta con el sistema de protección LZB, que falló momentáneamente la mañana del accidente por un fallo informático de los servidores de la central de Urda. “Aún no sabemos qué generó la incidencia en el sistema”, dijo este viernes el ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente. “Estos sistemas utilizan soportes físicos para su comunicación, y esos soportes físicos fallan”.

La línea está actualmente renovándose para poder migrar a otro sistema, el ERTMS. Ambas tecnologías son sistemas avanzados de protección; el cambio a ERTMS ha sido impulsado por la Unión Europea por razones de interoperabilidad, para unificar todos los sistemas de señalización y facilitar la circulación entre países.

Estas son las principales empresas involucradas en el transporte ferroviario y las tecnologías de seguridad que están ahora en el centro del debate, incluyendo las que han sido encargadas de implantar y mantener el sistema LZB estos últimos años.

Thales

Thales es una multinacional francesa que cotiza en la Bolsa de París. Diseña y fabrica sistemas y equipos eléctricos para defensa y ciberseguridad. Ha sido durante años uno de los grandes fabricantes mundiales de sistemas de señalización y control del tráfico ferroviario. Llevaba vinculada al mantenimiento del sistema LZB desde prácticamente la inauguración de la línea entre Madrid y Sevilla para la Expo de esta última en 1992.

La tecnología LZB, de origen alemán, es un sistema de protección automatizada de trenes. A través de un cable desplegado a lo largo de las vías de tren, el sistema obtiene información continua sobre el tipo de vagón que circula por arriba —sabe su longitud, su velocidad máxima y su capacidad de frenado—. También recibe datos sobre la posición de otros trenes. Así, puede calcular cuánto pueden avanzar de manera segura. Por ejemplo, si hay un vagón estacionado más adelante, indica al maquinista cuándo debe empezar a reducir la velocidad para no alcanzarlo. Si el conductor no reduce la velocidad, también puede activar los frenos automáticos.

Adif renovó a Thales el contrato de mantenimiento de la señalización de la vía —que incluía expresamente el LZB— en 2011 por poco más de 28 millones de euros. La empresa francesa mantuvo esa responsabilidad durante años, hasta 2024.

Thales también ganó el contrato para transitar de este sistema al ERTMS. Adif AV se lo adjudicó en 2021 por más de 93,8 millones de euros, IVA incluido. Encargaba a Thales implementar la nueva tecnología europea en sustitución del LZB.

La línea Madrid-Sevilla es la única línea de alta velocidad española que todavía usa el LZB. La principal diferencia entre ambos es que el ERTMS-2 utiliza balizas y comunicaciones por radio en lugar de cables. En un principio, estos trabajos tenían un plazo de ejecución de 52 meses. El sistema está instalado y se activará en 2027.

Hitachi Rail

Thales segregó su negocio ferroviario en GTS Transportation Spain. El 31 de mayo de 2024, la japonesa Hitachi Rail, filial de uno de los conglomerados empresariales más importantes de Japón, compró GTS Transportation. La operación se valoró en 1.660 millones de euros y la empresa pasó a llamarse Hitachi Rail GTS Spain.

Desde Thales explican que las actividades ferroviarias de la empresa fueron completamente transferidas a Hitachi Rail desde ese momento, y que ahora es Hitachi Rail GTS Spain la empresa que gestiona las mismas en España, incluido el mantenimiento del sistema LZB y la implementación del ERTMS.

De hecho, ese mismo año, en 2024, Adif adjudicó un nuevo contrato a la UTE de GTS Transportation Spain —aún era propiedad de Thales— y SISTEM, por 87,31 millones con IVA, para la señalización del corredor sur, que incluye los sistemas LZB. “Aún no sabemos qué generó el problema de comunicación entre los equipos informáticos de la central de Urda; hay que esperar a que Hitachi Rail obtenga el permiso correspondiente para extraer sus registros y analizarlos”, indicó Puente este viernes.

De hecho, ese mismo año, en 2024, Adif adjudicó un nuevo contrato a la UTE de GTS Transportation Spain —que entonces aún era propiedad de Thales— y SISTEM, por 87,31 millones con IVA, para la señalización del corredor sur, que incluye los sistemas LZB.

“Aún no sabemos qué generó el problema de comunicación entre los equipos informáticos de la central de Urda; hay que esperar a que la empresa Hitachi Rail obtenga el permiso correspondiente para extraer sus registros y analizarlos”, ha confirmado Puente. El ministro ha informado esta mañana de que el sistema LZB ha fallado este año 170 veces, una cifra que ha situado “dentro de la normalidad europea”.

El acuerdo de SISTEM e Hitachi Rail GTS Spain con Adif tiene una duración de cuatro años, prorrogable por uno más, por lo que continúa vigente. Desde la empresa prefieren no hacer declaraciones.

Por otro lado, Hitachi Rail es uno de los fabricantes del tren Iryo implicado en el accidente, un modelo ETR 1000, que la japonesa construyó junto a la canadiense Bombardier, antes de que esta vendiera su negocio ferroviario a la francesa Alstom en 2021. Lleva circulando poco más de una década por Italia, y llegó a España con la liberalización del mercado y la entrada de Iryo. Es un modelo con tracción distribuida; es decir, que sus motores están repartidos en los bajos de varios coches, y no solo concentrados en la cabeza tractora.

Hitachi Rail España también se encarga del mantenimiento de toda la flota de Iryo en el país.

Siemens

La empresa alemana es uno de los grandes fabricantes mundiales de trenes y sistemas de señalización ferroviaria a través de su división Siemens Mobility. Fabricó el AVE de Renfe siniestrado, de la serie 103, conocida comercialmente como Velaro E. Empezó a circular en 2007 y se produjeron 26 unidades. Al igual que el ETR 1000 de Iryo, tiene tracción distribuida.

Siemens también participó en el consorcio encargado de distribuir el LZB a lo largo de la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Sevilla en sus inicios.

Iryo

Iryo es una empresa de alta velocidad controlada mayoritariamente —con el 51%— por el grupo italiano público Ferrovie dello Stato. También participan en ella Air Nostrum y Globalvia, ambas españolas. Es uno de los principales competidores de Renfe en el mercado español de alta velocidad desde que se liberalizara el servicio y empezara a circular un año después, en 2022.

En el convoy viajaban 147 personas; han fallecido por lo menos 40. Las anomalías en los sistemas de señalización habían detenido el tren. La maquinista intentó arrancar dos veces el tren, sin éxito, por lo que avisó al centro de control de Adif de que seguía parado.

La investigación de la compañía va a tener que aclarar por qué la conductora no pudo retomar la circulación, y si este hecho está conectado de alguna manera con los fallos del sistema LZB. El consejero delegado de Iryo, Fabrizio Favara, advirtió hace unas semanas de los problemas que generaban estas caídas del sistema: “Cada vez que la señal del tren se desconecta de la señal de tierra, el tren se para. No se puede mover y lleva bastante tiempo reconectarse y empezar nuevamente el servicio”.

Renfe

Renfe, a través del AVE, ha sido el único operador de la red de alta velocidad hasta la liberalización de las vías que se hizo efectiva en 2021. Desde entonces ha competido en varias rutas con Ouigo e Iryo, pero sigue siendo la empresa líder del mercado español de la alta velocidad; conserva entre el 50% y el 67% de los viajeros en estas rutas, según los últimos datos de la Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC). Es una empresa pública que depende del Ministerio de Transportes.

El convoy de AVE siniestrado había salido a las 8.00 de la estación de Atocha en Madrid. Su llegada a Sevilla estaba prevista para las 10.39. Llevaba a bordo 378 pasajeros, de los que 24, al menos, han fallecido.

Por ahora se desconoce a qué velocidad exacta iba el AVE en el momento del impacto, pero el primer informe técnico de la Autoridad Independiente para la Investigación Técnica de Accidentes (AITAT) estima que circulaba a una velocidad de entre 160 y 200 kilómetros por hora.

Adif

El Administrador de Infraestructuras Ferroviarias (Adif) es la empresa pública que se encarga de gestionar la red ferroviaria de España. Esto incluye tanto el mantenimiento de las vías como las instalaciones de seguridad y los sistemas de control de la circulación. Lo hace junto a Adif Alta Velocidad, otra entidad pública del mismo grupo. La compañía depende del Ministerio de Transportes.

Adif administra la instalación ferroviaria y su mantenimiento: vías, estaciones, sistemas de seguridad, de señalización. Para llevar a cabo todas esas labores, contrata a otras empresas más especializadas. Para la limpieza de terminales, por ejemplo, a Clece o Serveo. Para la tecnología, a otras como Thales o Hitachi Rail.

A su vez, la compañía deja a las operadoras como Renfe o Iryo utilizar su red de vías a cambio de unas tarifas que se conocen como cánones ferroviarios.

La caída del LZB provocó el parón de seis trenes que circulaban por la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Sevilla, que pasaron a seguir las instrucciones manuales del centro de control de Adif en Atocha. Un operario de la empresa autorizó al AVE de Renfe a reanudar la marcha a velocidad normal, pese a que el convoy de Iryo seguía parado pocos kilómetros más adelante. Puente aseguró que esa decisión contravenía todos los protocolos de seguridad. El operario que dio la orden se ha acogido ante la Guardia Civil a su derecho de no declarar.
