According to her, options for residential solar financing in Mindanao and other provinces outside the Greater Manila Area remain limited, while the currently available options from government financing institutions are subject to extremely tedious processes and requirements.

Confused about how to navigate all the new possibilities — and remaining constraints — in getting a rooftop solar setup? Here’s what you need to know about the current solar financing landscape and where it may be headed.

What are the financing options?

Financing for solar installations most often come in the form of loans. The most common and accessible of these are from government bodies.

Government employees can avail themselves of a solar loan from the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS).

Pag-IBIG has a home improvement loan that can be used to acquire a solar setup.

Private employees will soon be able to get a loan from the Social Security System (SSS). The rollout for the loan is eyed for early 2027.

The GSIS and SSS loans were announced just this year, in the wake of the Middle East oil crisis and the solar boom that ensued in the Philippines.

Some commercial and rural banks have since followed suit with solar loan options of their own.

For households that cannot put up collateral or have other difficulties meeting the requirements of these institutions, Donggay and Dimalanta said that some solar installers also provide an option called in-house financing. Compared to loans from financial institutions, however, this option usually has a shorter time period — therefore, higher monthly payments — and a higher interest rate.

Some installers also offer lease or lease-to-own arrangements. While Donggay said a wide array of financing options is always welcome, she still strongly advises households to be the full owner of their own solar setups.

“To me, the promise of solar goes beyond just getting clean electricity; it’s also being able to be a prosumer — a producer and consumer of clean electricity,” she said.

When is it a good idea to go solar?

For both Donggay and Dimalanta, a rooftop solar setup is worth it regardless of your household’s current income level or electricity consumption. To them, there is no better time than now to start going solar.

According to Donggay, going solar should be a consideration for anyone who feels the burden of rising electricity rates. She said if a household can save for a vacation, they may as well consider using that amount to invest in solar technology. Savings from that investment will add up in the long run, after all.

Dimalanta shares a similar view.

“We need to look at how much of a household’s income goes toward paying for their electricity bill,” she said. “Most of the time, we want to consider these options (rooftop solar) because we want to keep more of our income for our other needs.”

In the end, it’s a question of where you want your household’s monthly income to go. Staying connected to a traditional distribution utility means endlessly paying a monthly electric bill, with no control over whether those services improve, deteriorate, or get more expensive.

With solar financing options, your endless electricity bills may be replaced with finite monthly amortizations. And because rooftop solar setups have an estimated lifespan of 20 to 25 years, you would basically be free from monthly payments after the loan period is over.

Tips and tricks

There are other ways to make your solar setup more affordable.

Dimalanta shared two tips. First, she said installing batteries right away is not really a necessity — especially since these components are usually the most expensive part of a rooftop solar setup.

“If you are, for example, in the Meralco franchise area or in a franchise area where the distribution utility is relatively reliable — and blackouts don’t frequently happen — maybe you don’t need the battery yet,” she said.

Instead, she advises consumers to ask their installer to set up a battery-ready system. Since battery prices are expected to go down as the technology develops, consumers can buy them later to get even more savings out of their solar system.

Her second tip is for households to apply for net-metering, which is a program that allows qualified consumers with renewable energy systems to sell the excess power they generate in exchange for credits on their electricity bills.

This means that if there are months in the year or times in the day when no one is home or electricity consumption is low, electricity generated during that time could be sold. As a result, the cost recovery on a household’s solar system becomes faster.

“So, a project that would have been projected to take 10 years before you got a return on investment may instead take only five years,” she said.

Long way to go

While solar financing options have come a long way since rooftop solar technologies were first pushed in the country a decade ago, Donggay said the reality is that existing options remain limited — especially outside highly urbanized areas.

That’s not the only way rural areas are disadvantaged when it comes to getting value for their solar setups. Net-metering is a big draw for many prospective solar buyers, but the reality is that off-grid and geographically isolated areas simply do not have that option available.

“But even without net-metering, solar installations can still be worthwhile and can be beneficial to households located in off-grid areas for energy security,” she said. “And then you manage your costs, because [almost all of the power] supply to our off-grid areas comes from diesel plants. And that’s why — while diesel costs continue to increase — your bills will also continue to increase,” she said.

But beyond all that, the fact remains that there are communities where individual solar home systems are still considered too expensive even with the current financing options. Dimalanta acknowledged this.

“And my answer to that is: then let’s make it available to ordinary Filipinos,” she said.

For both Dimalanta and Donggay, one of the key solutions lies in our communities — especially in community solar projects where residents only use the power for their own consumption, without needing to sell it.

“For example, if this entire barangay or this sitio cannot afford individual solar home systems, is there idle land there or is there a rooftop in all these multipurpose halls that will be built?” she said. “Can they host solar facilities that can supply the immediate vicinity [with power]?”

Donggay’s own suggestion is similar: rooftop solar being pre-installed in government housing projects for the urban poor.

“We need to be more creative in how we incorporate solar in other projects that are addressing rural and urban development — especially for the people we know would never be approved for a loan by commercial banks,” she added.

Solar may be relatively more affordable now than a decade ago, but there’s still a long way to go to make it truly accessible to the households that need it the most.

“The answer shouldn’t be: let’s set aside or dismiss solar because it’s only for the rich,” Dimalanta said. “No. I think it poses a real challenge for all of us — government of course included — to make solar affordable to all.” – Rappler.com

Quotes were translated to English for brevity.

World.title: Locked up, then fired up: Bo Kyi’s fight for political detainees
World.content:
Before Bo Kyi could fight for the freedom of political prisoners, he first had to endure imprisonment himself.

In August 1988, the Burmese activist was among the student protesters who were swept up in Myanmar's pro-democracy movement.

Massive demonstrations erupted across Myanmar, then known as Burma, amid growing resistance against the military junta. The protests culminated in a violent military crackdown on August 8, 1988, in what would become known as the "8888 Uprising."

NEVER FORGOTTEN. Activists hold candles and raise three-finger salutes during the anniversary of the '8888 Uprising' in Chiang Mai, Thailand. Photo by Pongmanat Tasiri/SOPA Images/Sipa USA

Bo Kyi, now 61, was a graduating student majoring in Burmese literature at Rangoon University when the demonstrations erupted. At 20, he recalled joining the protests after witnessing the deaths of fellow students.

“They sacrificed their bodies because they want democracy and human rights. So, I have to continue. Their faces really remind me to do something and finish what we need to do.” Bo Kyi

In 1990, Bo Kyi was arrested for his participation in the student-led movement — an experience that would change his life. During his three years in detention, he endured harsh prison conditions and learned about the history of repression and the abuses suffered by ethnic communities in Myanmar.

"Such kind of information from real history really reminded me that we need to change the political system. We need to build up [the] rule of law. We want the military to stay away from politics. Such kind of thing really motivated me for this," he said.

Decades later, Bo Kyi is among the three laureates of the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Award, widely regarded as Asia's equivalent of the Nobel Prize.

BO KYI’S FIGHT. Bo Kyi speaks in an interview in front of photographs of monk-led protests in Mae Sot, Thailand, in February 2008. Photo by Ed Cropley/Reuters

In conferring the award, the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation recognized his work with the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP), an organization he co-founded to document political detentions and provide assistance to people imprisoned under Myanmar's military regime.

"His enduring commitment reflects extraordinary moral courage, personal sacrifice, and an unwavering belief that democracy and human dignity are always worth defending — and that even in the face of oppression, the truth must be told, justice must be pursued, and the freedom to believe must be upheld and defended at all costs," the foundation said.

Political imprisonment

During his three-year detention, Bo Kyi endured repeated interrogations, beatings, and torture.

Yet even in prison, he found ways to keep learning. To cope with the loneliness, he began studying English with a professor detained in a neighboring cell.

When guards were away, Bo Kyi would ask the professor to dictate English words and phrases. He memorized them and wrote them on the concrete floor using a shard of brick.

At one point, he even ate pages from a dictionary to keep them from being discovered by prison guards.

"I still continued studying English for two-and-a-half years in prison even though we were not allowed to possess any writing materials and reading materials," said Bo Kyi.

Documenting political prisoners

Prior to his release in 1993, his fellow political prisoners asked him to tell the outside world about the realities of the conditions inside Myanmar's prisons.

World.title: FACT CHECK: No reports of SC order ousting Marcos
World.content:
There is no ruling or order from the Supreme Court ordering the removal of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who, as a sitting president, is immune from suit

Claim: The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled on a case against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., removing him from office.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube video uploaded by the channel “PINAS BALITA TV” on October 26, 2026, made this claim. The video is titled: “NAKARMA NA! KAPAPASOK LANG! BEBE EM TALUNAN sa mga KAS0NG NA1SAMPA sa KANYA sa K0RTE SUPR3MA?” (Karma at last! Just in! BBM loses in cases filed against him at the Supreme Court?).

Its thumbnail and accompanying captions include: “Pinatalsik! Lumayas ka sa Palasyo!” (Ousted! Get out of the Palace!), further claiming that the SC has finally acted.

As of writing, the video has garnered 21,589 views.

The facts: No official announcements, press releases, or SC decisions confirm the removal of Marcos from Malacañang.

The SC has no constitutional authority to oust a sitting president, who enjoys absolute immunity from suit while in office.

Article XI, Section 2 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution says the president may only be removed from office “on impeachment for, and conviction of, culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust.”

No impeachment case: At present, no impeachment complaint can proceed against Marcos because he is also immune from new impeachment proceedings until February 2027, after the House of Representatives junked two impeachment complaints filed against him in February 2026 for lack of substance.

Under Article XI, Section 3 of the Constitution, no impeachment proceeding can be initiated against the same official more than once within a period of one year.

As of writing, only Vice President Sara Duterte is undergoing an impeachment trial in the Senate impeachment court.

Lack of evidence: The video provides no verifiable court documents, authentic footage, or official statements confirming the claim about Marcos made in its title and thumbnail.

Instead, the clip features commentary from an unidentified male reacting to a third-party media report regarding the constitutionality of budget allocations.

Specifically, he discussed the recent SC decision declaring the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Act unconstitutional. While the High Court’s declaration regarding the budget laws is true, it is unrelated to the claims against the President.

Debunked: Rappler had published a fact-check debunking a claim about alleged criminal charges by the SC against Marcos. – Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com

Lyndee Buenagua is a Metro Manila-based journalist who primarily covers Bicol and Baguio. She is also an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Rakhine Civil Society Urges UN No-Fly Zone as Civilian Deaths Soar
World.content:
Rakhine civil society organizations have urged the United Nations and international actors to declare a no-fly zone over the western state as civilian deaths from regime airstrikes surge to unprecedented levels.

The regime has bombed dozens of civilian targets in the month since a Sept. 28 aerial attack on a busy market killed at least 50 people and drew widespread international condemnation.

The Arakan Civil Society Charitable Organizations (ACSO), an umbrella group of 70 local and international Rakhine groups, is urgently calling on the UN Security Council (UNSC), the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), international governments, and global humanitarian organizations to back their statements with immediate action to prevent further loss of civilian life.

Along with a no-fly-zone, the ASCO is demanding international sanctions to cut off the supply of aviation fuel, weapons and other military equipment that sustain the regime’s aerial campaign.

The appeal follows an escalation in deadly strikes on civilian areas since the market massacre.

“Our local humanitarian workers were on hand to witness the slaughter of children and pregnant women in the Kyauktaw bombing,” an ACSO official told the Irrawaddy, explaining the urgency behind the appeal.

Requesting anonymity for safety reasons, he stated the regime had conducted over 600 airstrikes across Rakhine over the past six months, targeting markets, displacement camps, and monasteries in Thandwe, Ponnagyun, Mrauk-U and Sittwe, and in neighboring Chin State’s Paletwa Township.

Data from the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute, a research body founded by military defectors, shows the regime launched 136 aerial attacks across Rakhine in September alone, leaving 144 civilian casualties — 62 dead and 82 injured. Rakhine logged the highest civilian casualty count in the country, followed by Sagaing with 101 and Magwe (61).

Additionally, the ACSO urged the international community to establish cross-border channels to deliver food, medicine, and basic necessities directly to displaced populations facing severe hardship in war-torn Rakhine.

It also called on the UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar to document human rights violations and ensure that perpetrators are held accountable through national and international justice mechanisms.

The regime ramped up airstrikes in Rakhine after the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) seized 14 of its 17 townships along with Paletwa during its 2023-2024 offensive. Intense battles continue around the capital Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, home to a China-backed seaport and economic zone, as AA forces push to capture the regime’s last remaining Rakhine strongholds.

On Tuesday, the regime’s key allies — China, Russia, and Belarus — blocked international condemnation over its human rights record at the UN General Assembly.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic push for legitimacy since installing himself as president in April after a widely derided election, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, and India. Critics have condemned the diplomatic thaw as normalizing a regime that is deploying military force to subdue its own population.

“If the international community continues to turn a blind eye to the suffering public, we can only conclude that it lacks any empathy,” the ACSO official said.

World.title: Regime Threatens Migrant Workers in Thailand Over Document Boycott
World.content:
Myanmar regime Labor Minister Maung Myint on Thursday warned that migrant workers who boycott the Certificate of Identity (CI) process in Thailand would be banned from returning home if they failed to apply for the document.

With its CI-issuing centers in Thailand seeing very few applicants, the junta’s Labor Ministry has intensified its threats. Before the regime began enforcing remittance requirements as part of the CI application process, the facilities were regularly overcrowded with thousands of Myanmar migrants eagerly seeking the documents.

Migrants are boycotting the CI process as the cash-strapped junta attempts to wring more money out of them. Workers applying for the document must now prove that they remit at least 25 percent of their wages to Myanmar through official channels, as well as a 2 percent income tax payment. Official channels offer far less favorable exchange rates than unofficial channels.

Fearing their hard-earned wages will fund the regime’s military campaigns against civilians, workers have launched an online campaign demanding the Thai government grant legal stay and work permits without requiring a CI, which serves as an alternative document to the Myanmar passport.

The Thailand Migration Reform group urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the framework based on the Pink Card, an identity card issued by Thailand for undocumented foreigners residing in the country.

Maung Myint said the CI process was “a project implemented in cooperation with the Thai authorities,” adding that migrant workers without a CI or a passport and an Overseas Worker Identification Card (OWIC) “would be undocumented.” He added that they would not be allowed to travel back to Myanmar during their time off.

The regime started operating five CI centers across Thailand on October 14, but they have seen few applicants. Those who have attended have paid the extra cost for the application, while most are holding off to monitor the situation.

The boycott campaign has derailed Maung Myint’s goal of matching last year’s total of US$5.6 billion in remittance inflows in 2026. Thailand hosts Myanmar’s largest migrant population, estimated at approximately 4 million.

Since he was appointed labor minister earlier this month, Maung Myint has been pushing for enforcement of the remittance and tax rules in order to squeeze foreign currency from overseas workers, who have emerged as a major source of foreign currency for the regime amid shortages and international isolation.

On Tuesday, he said that by trying to cut off foreign currency inflows to the regime, the campaign was only “driving the people of Myanmar and migrant workers into ruin, instead of damaging the government.” He said the funds were to be used for fuel and gas imports, a claim he has often made.

He accused the campaign organizers of being “gaslighters,” claiming they themselves hold CIs or passports while urging workers not to apply for them.

“He is just acting like a psycho,” Khin Soe, a board member of the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT), which is organizing the campaign, told The Irrawaddy in response to the minister’s claim. “He may not even understand what he said. He just seems to follow orders from above.”

He added that there would be no reason to oppose the regime, or campaign against the CI process, if its policy benefited workers. “I don’t take [his accusation] seriously,” he said.

An ultranationalist with a military background, Maung Myint is known for spreading hate speech against the Muslim community and slandering the National League for Democracy.

During his election campaign in 2020, when he represented the Union Solidarity and Development Party, a lawsuit was filed against him over his use of an inflammatory song that urged voters to choose the party “to protect race and religion and to drive out a group that destroys the race.”

Winning seats in elections in 2010, 2015 and 2025-26, he has served as a minister and deputy minister in various ministries—including labor and foreign affairs—under successive regimes since 2004.

In his new role as labor minister, Maung Myint has become the face of the regime’s efforts to extract funds from Myanmar workers and their families amid the country’s political and economic crises.

World.title: Big Brother Defends Myanmar Regime at UN, Chinese Aid Shortfall, and More
World.content:
China defends Myanmar regime at UN

The UN General Assembly’s Third Committee devoted its 29th plenary session Tuesday to Myanmar’s human rights crisis, hearing reports from Special Envoy Julie Bishop, Independent Investigative Mechanism head Nicholas Koumjian, and Special Rapporteur Kelley Currie. All three highlighted the war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by the military regime.

Of the 23 countries whose delegates spoke, only Belarus, Russia and China defended the regime. Finding nothing good to say about it either, Beijing instead urged the international community to say fewer bad things. “The international community should focus on helping bridge differences and resolving problems rather than intensifying tensions and aggravating turbulence,” China’s representative said.

Myanmar, after all, is “an important member of the ASEAN family and an equal member of the international community,” he added, voicing support for the regime’s pursuit of a development path “suited to its national conditions and supported by its people.”

Beijing bristled when Currie noted that during Min Aung Hlaing’s first 100 days after declaring himself president, he deployed new coercive surveillance technologies “gifted” by China and Russia to suppress dissent.

China’s representative rejected the allegation, calling it “false information,” and urged Currie to carry out her mandate “objectively and impartially” and avoid spreading “unverified” claims that could mislead the public.

Currie hit back directly: “Countries that are most loudly complaining about interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs are ones that are most actively interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs. Those that are talking most loudly about peace are the ones selling the weapons to Min Aung Hlaing that he uses against his own people.”

She challenged Beijing’s denial, saying she would welcome any evidence refuting that China was selling arms or providing political and economic support to the regime. Currie reminded delegates that under UN procedures, China, Russia and Belarus had been given five days to respond before her October report was published—and none of them had.

She cited the 2023 report “The Billion Dollar Death Trade” by her predecessor Tom Andrews as the proof of her claim. The report found Myanmar’s military imported over US$1 billion in arms and dual use goods since the 2021 coup, with China and Russia identified as top suppliers. Chinese state-linked firms provided raw materials and equipment for Myanmar’s ordnance factories including aircraft parts and explosives precursors used in attacks on civilians.

A milestone for China’s cross-Myanmar pipeline

The Myanmar–China crude oil pipeline has transported more than 100 million metric tons of crude oil since it began operations in 2017, PipeChina announced earlier this week. Stretching 771 km from embattled Kyaukphyu in Rakhine State through northern Shan State to Yunnan Province, the twin oil and gas pipelines are strategic lifelines that reduce Beijing’s dependence on the congested and vulnerable Malacca Strait.

One of China’s four major energy import corridors, the pipelines traverse 22 townships across Rakhine, Magwe, Mandalay and Shan, and today ethnic armed organizations such as the Arakan Army (AA), Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) control substantial sections there.

Myanmar is projected to receive around $1.5 billion annually from the pipelines, though the exact profit structure is unclear. It certainly receives a fixed, annual right-of-way payment of $13.81 million for both pipelines plus $1 per ton of crude transiting through the country—PipeChina reckons at an average rate of 35,000 tons a day, most of it disgorged at Kyaukphyu from the Middle East. PipeChina and CNPC own 51 percent, while state-owned Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise (MOGE) holds 49 percent.

The gas pipeline, meanwhile, started operation in 2013 and carries output from the offshore Shwe fields, with a a design capacity of 12 billion cubic meters per year. China National Petroleum Corporation holds a controlling 50.9 percent stake and MOGE just 7.365 percent. Sales of natural gas from Shwe to China are estimated to generate around $1 billion annually.

To finance its stakes, MOGE borrowed around $1.5 billion from the China Development Bank at an interest rate of 4.5 percent, according to Sandhi Governance Institute. Nobody knows how much of that has been paid back or ever will be.

Chinese aid bottleneck throttles Myanmar regime’s budget

Myanmar’s military regime faced severe fiscal strain in the 2025–2026 fiscal year when China withheld approval for multiple projects under the Lancang–Mekong Cooperation (LMC) Special Fund. Naypyitaw’s budget deficit shot up amid overspending by ministries and loss‑making state enterprises.

Deputy Planning and Finance Minister Kyaw Htin admitted that the deficit was exacerbated by failure to secure expected grants, project approvals, and technical resources from Beijing. The Ministry of Cooperatives and Rural Development did submit proposals for LMC financing in 2025, but the response was deafening silence. Likewise, the Industry Ministry budgeted for computer hardware and technical equipment for Chinese experts who were to come to Myanmar for a technology transfer, but they never turned up and the equipment was not delivered.

The reasons are shrouded in mystery. In a recent article in regime newspapers, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia claimed China had backed 140 development projects in Myanmar through the LMC Special Fund. In March, Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said the country benefited from 132—worth $38.6 million—since 2017.

Either way it would be the biggest handout to any Mekong country.

Some older Chinese projects are already falling to pieces. Kyaw Htin admitted that power transmission lines from two China‑backed hydropower plants—the 240 MW Dapein Hydropower Station in Bhamo, Kachin State and the 600 MW Shweli 1 Dam in Namhkam Township, northern Shan State—were damaged and could not be repaired due to “security conditions,” depriving the regime of projected electricity revenues.

Russian grant money that had been promised was also not forthcoming, Kyaw Htin said. The rest of the world has suspended official development aid since the 2021 coup.

More trouble in Shan over Kokang ‘Sinicization’

The past two weeks have seen growing tensions between Shan communities and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) that is consolidating its control in territories it has seized over the past three years.

The Shan State Joint Action Committee (SSJAC)—comprising the armed Shan State Progress Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), the civilian Shan Nationalities League for Democracy, and other Shan opposition groups—issued a statement accusing the MNDAA of undermining ethnic rights, erasing Shan cultural heritage, and imposing Chinese language and governance systems there.

The MNDAA rejected the allegations as “baseless” and “politically motivated” and accused the SSJAC in turn of stirring the ethnic pot.

Earlier this month, Shan civil society organizations also released an open letter warning that the MNDAA’s cultural and administrative practices threaten ethnic coexistence and stability on the Chinese border. And in April, Ta’ang civil society groups condemned the MNDAA after it seized Kutkai, where ethnic Ta’ang communities form the majority.

Founded in 1989 from the remnants of the Communist Party of Burma, the MNDAA is rooted in Kokang, an enclave that is 90 percent ethnic Chinese. Once limited to Laukkai and Kongyan townships, the group has expanded its territory west of the Salween River since Operation 1027, and locals report a great deal of painting over of signboards and other attempts to suppress their languages and identities by their brash new masters.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Hosts Russian Mining Billionaire After Approving Gold Ventures
World.content:
Russian mining billionaire Vladislav Sviblov — head of Russia’s Areal Group — met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Wednesday to discuss cooperation in mineral exploration and mining between the two Western-sanctioned actors.

According to regime media, both sides spoke of “mutual trust and friendly relations” between Myanmar and Russia and discussed cooperation in education, science, and technology.

Formerly known as Highland Gold Mining Limited, Areal Group rebranded after expanding beyond precious metals into base, rare, and strategic minerals. Areal and its owner have been under U.S. and EU sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Similarly isolated by international sanctions after the 2021 coup, Min Aung Hlaing and his regime have been courting economic and diplomatic support from Russia.

On the day that Sviblov arrived in Naypyitaw, Myanmar’s Investment Commission approved 16 new investment proposals — including large‑scale gold mining ventures. The green lights came just weeks after Min Aung Hlaing invited investment in Myanmar’s mineral sector at the Russia–Myanmar Economic Forum in August, touting “value‑added mineral products” as a new export base.

Russia’s sanctions‑hit companies have leaned toward Asian markets since 2022, while Myanmar’s regime, starved of foreign currency, is eager to attract Russian capital.

Regime insiders suggest rare earths may have been on the agenda of Wednesday’s meeting, given the presence of natural resources minister Khin Maung Yi, while Sviblov himself spoke on on rare earths at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum in June.

Myanmar boasts rich deposits of the critical minerals, exporting roughly half of the world’s heavy rare earth elements over the border to China.

Meanwhile, the U.S.’s recent reengagement with Naypyitaw has fueled speculation that a global scramble for rare earth resources is driving Washington’s policy recalibration. Regime supporters now boast that the junta has a “rare earth card” to play, pointing to parallel interest from India.

However, almost all of Myanmar’s estimated 600 rare earth mines lie beyond the regime’s control in territory overseen by ethnic armed groups. Despite repeated invitations by the regime and talk of “strategic partnerships,” Russian [mining?] businesses have yet to make any substantial investments in Myanmar.

World.title: ASEAN Envoy Ends Myanmar Trip With No Public Aung San Suu Kyi Meeting
World.content:
YANGON—The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s special Myanmar envoy, Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, wrapped up a two-day visit to the nation Thursday, with no sign of having met detained democratic ex-leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

The Philippines, which currently holds the rotating chair of ASEAN, has repeatedly called this year for access to Aung San Suu Kyi, who has been detained since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

The status of the 81-year-old has long been a sticking point for the 11-nation ASEAN bloc, which has frozen Myanmar’s leaders out of its summits since the putsch.

Lazaro and regime Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe “held substantive discussions on ways to restore Myanmar’s original role and rights within ASEAN,” according to a statement from Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry.

It did not mention any meeting with Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who authorities say is being held at a “designated residence” in the capital Naypyitaw.

The Philippine Foreign Ministry earlier said Lazaro had spent Wednesday in the eastern state of Shan, overseeing humanitarian schemes aiding those displaced in the civil war triggered by the coup.

This year, analysts say authorities have allowed Aung San Suu Kyi increasing—albeit still extremely limited—contact with the outside world in a bid to shake off their pariah status abroad.

Last week, there were two rare updates on Aung San Suu Kyi.

On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.

Her UK-based son Kim Aris was then allowed a 20-minute consular phone call with her last Thursday, their first spoken communication in more than half a decade.

He told AFP his mother sounded “fairly healthy” but he feared she was being used as a pawn to improve the public image of those detaining her.

The Philippines requested “brief access” for Lazaro to meet Aung San Suu Kyi in April, after authorities said she was moved from prison to house arrest.

In August, when she met Myanmar’s senior Red Cross official, they made a renewed call for access.

World.title: Cartoon Campaign Boosts Myanmar Regime’s Hydropower Dreams
World.content:
The military regime has launched a campaign of cheesy cartoons across the propaganda media to push its bid to revive the shelved Myitsone Dam hydropower project.

Regime newspapers started featuring cartoons since Oct. 20, with uplifting messages suggesting the project will deliver 24/7 cheap electricity to households in Kachin State and beyond while boosting domestic industry.

They also lash out at opponents of the harebrained scheme. On Oct. 25, the Kyemon Daily carried a cartoon portraying critics as obstinate and unwilling to assess the project’s pros and cons objectively. The cartoon insisted the dam would cause no suffering, dismissing public concerns as baseless.

Cartoons have long been a propaganda tool for successive juntas, their simplified, condescending messages used to smear civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, ethnic leaders, and Western governments, while glorifying the regimes’ various leaps forward into the past. The habitual public response is to laugh at them.

The project to dam two tributaries to the Irrawaddy River, the N’Mai and Mali, was conceived under dictator Than Shwe. It was suspended in 2011 under President Thein Sein after unprecedented opposition over potential environmental destruction, mass displacement, the sites’ cultural significance for the Kachin people, and lack of transparency.

But now, the regime of Min Aung Hlaing is making relentless efforts to revive the project. Naypyitaw is touting it as a solution to its chronic electricity shortages—even though, under the original contract, most of the power generated by the dams was to have been exported to China.

As part of the new campaign, the regime has been marshalling local populations into a publicity blitz. Regime-appointed Kachin State Chief Minister Khet Htein Nam and the Myitsone Support Committee have staged more than 50 public meetings across the state, often strong-arming locals into attending. Yet executives from the mooted Chinese dam developer have been conspicuously absent.

With the cartoon strips across national newspapers, the campaign is going nationwide.

Officials insist the dam will bring many benefits, particularly to foreign investors setting up factories in Myanmar, and any seismic and environmental risks have been ironed out since the project was first proposed.

Experts warn otherwise. They point out that blocking river flow could allow seawater intrusion into the Irrawaddy delta, damaging agriculture and drinking water supplies. Sudden releases during monsoon season could also cause flash floods downstream.

Amid the revival campaign, resistance remains strong. Civil society groups, ethnic organizations, and ordinary citizens continue to oppose the project.

And a China analyst notes that the supposed Chinese financiers and builders are nowhere to be seen, no feasibility studies are being conducted, and Beijing has anyway long graduated from the need for extra power from the Myitsone project over the last 25 years.

“It’s really just the regime one-sidedly making efforts to revive the project because it sees Myitsone as leverage for political gain,” she said. She also pointed out that Myanmar would likely have to repay heavy costs incurred by the project’s suspension, which the cash-strapped regime can ill afford.

Indeed, during Min Aung Hlaing’s latest Beijing trip, Chinese officials made no mention of the dam, emphasizing instead the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor projects (CMEC) under its sweeping Belt and Road Initiative.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Begins Releasing Rakhine Deportees After Malaysia Pressure
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime has begun releasing hundreds of ethnic Rakhine deported from Malaysia last month after Kuala Lumpur sought clarification on their detention.

The first Rakhine deportees were released on Wednesday, just 48 hours after Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan faced questions about their fate in parliament.

Malaysia deported nearly 1,500 Myanmar refugees and migrants in late September, including over 400 from Rakhine, where the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) has seized 14 of the state’s 17 townships and is now pushing to claim the capital Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, home to a China-backed seaport and economic zone.

While other deportees were allowed to return home on arrival, the ethnic Rakhine were held for interrogation at two military detention centers in Yangon’s Thanlyin and Hlaingthayar. Those with identification cards were allowed to return home starting Wednesday, according to the Khamee Youth Unity Association, citing testimony from a released individual.

The association, which represents an ethnic subgroup of Rakhine, stated that 26 Khamee individuals were among the detainees.

Previous efforts by their families to secure the deportees’ release had fallen on deaf ears, with the regime offering no explanation for their prolonged detention.

“My younger brother was only set free yesterday,” a Khamee man, who requested anonymity due to security concerns, told The Irrawaddy. “I didn’t even know he was among those released.”

He had been seeking his brother’s release since October 21 after being informed of his detention by a regime administrator. He was told the delay was due to incomplete paperwork for a national registration card and smart card.

“Once we sent the complete documentation over, he was released within a week.”

The regime barred ethnic Rakhine from returning to their home state in late 2023 and early 2024 as AA forces made sweeping gains on the western front.

Malaysia sent back 1,479 Myanmar nationals on September 29, in the first phase of a repatriation plan that has drawn heavy criticism from the United Nations refugee agency and international rights groups. Kuala Lumpur claims all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation under the plan to deport 5,000 Myanmar nationals in stages from Malaysia, where over 10,300 others remain in detention.

The United Nations warns that civil war triggered by the 2021 coup makes safe repatriation impossible under international law. Concerns are rising over reports that the regime is forcibly conscripting returnees into the military.

Malaysia has repatriated around 8,000 citizens by air and 1,500 by sea so far this year, according to regime data cited by AFP.

World.title: Myanmar Navy Loses 3 More Ships as Arakan Army Tightens Sittwe Noose
World.content:
The Arakan Army (AA) said it destroyed three military vessels at the mouth of the Kaladan River in Rakhine State on Monday, bringing the total number of Myanmar Navy ships eliminated in the past month to six.

AA spokesman Khaing Thukha said two of the vessels were sunk and the other wrecked. “We commend our officers and technicians for this successful operation,” he posted on Telegram.

A frontline source confirmed that three Navy vessels had been obliterated on Monday, dealing a further blow to the regime’s Rakhine counteroffensive. Dubbed Operation 4926, the counteroffensive has dragged on for nearly two months without progress as the AA tightens its siege on the state capital, Sittwe. Despite repeated assaults, regime troops have failed to secure AA‑held Nga Pyi Island, which guards the river mouth.

Both sides have suffered casualties, but the AA claims regime losses are heavier with around 50 soldiers killed on the first day of fighting at Nga Pyi Island alone.

The island is a key AA stronghold, blocking regime access upriver to AA-controlled Pauktaw and Ponnagyun townships.

The assault on Nga Pyi began on Oct. 7, spearheaded by gunboats and landing craft and backed by air and artillery strikes from encircled Sittwe.

The move aims to break the AA’s blockade of the Kaladan River corridor while shielding the Navy’s Shwe Mingan base in Sittwe, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

Regime troops are waging defensive battles around Sittwe on three fronts: the Shwe Mingan naval base, along the Sittwe–Ponnagyun border, and near Mayu River in Rathedaung Township. Sources say the AA has seized several regime outposts near Shwe Mingan and along the Sittwe–Ponnagyun road.

With its frontline bases collapsing, the military has resorted to air and artillery strikes against villages in Pauktaw and Ponnagyun townships.

Clashes have also intensified down the coast in Kyaukphyu Township, where AA forces are attacking regime positions near Taung Maw Oo naval base. A frontline source said the military has already lost two outposts in the area.

The AA controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships along with Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State, with the regime maintaining a foothold in Sittwe, Kyaukphyu, and the sparsely populated Manaung island.

World.title: Kazakhstan Establishes Diplomatic Relations With All UN Member States
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has completed the establishment of diplomatic relations with all United Nations (UN) member states after signing a joint communiqué with Nauru (Naoero), becoming the 195th country with which Kazakhstan has established diplomatic ties on Oct. 31, the Foreign Ministry’s press service reported.

Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Kairat Umarov and Naoero’s Permanent Representative Lara Erab Daniel signed the document, marking an important milestone in the country’s diplomatic history.

The communiqué lays the foundation for bilateral cooperation based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law, including mutual respect for national sovereignty and territorial integrity, equality of states and non-interference in each other’s internal affairs.

During the meeting, the two sides discussed prospects for political dialogue and expanding trade, economic and humanitarian ties. Potential areas of cooperation include trade, sustainable development, digitalization and human capital development.

They paid particular attention to strengthening cooperation within the UN and other multilateral forums. Both sides emphasized the importance of maintaining regular dialogue on international issues and developing partnerships between Kazakhstan and Pacific countries.

The establishment of diplomatic relations with Nauru reflects Kazakhstan’s policy of expanding international cooperation, strengthening friendly ties and promoting constructive dialogue with countries around the world.

Kazakhstan joined the UN on March 2, 1992, shortly after gaining independence, under General Assembly Resolution 46/224. Since then, the country has expanded its engagement with the organization, including serving as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council in 2017-2018. Kazakhstan has also advanced initiatives on nuclear disarmament, regional security and sustainable development, making the UN an important platform for its multilateral diplomacy.

World.title: One Number Could Save Life: Why Kazakhstan Needs Unified Emergency Hotline
World.content:
Editor’s note: The Astana Times continues a section featuring articles by our readers. As a platform that values diverse perspectives and meaningful conversations, we believe that this section provides space for readers to share their thoughts and insights on various topics that matter to them and the AT audience.

In an emergency, even simple decisions become difficult. Fear takes over. People panic. They may struggle to explain what happened, where they are, or what kind of help they need. Yet this is exactly the moment when we expect them to make the right decision quickly.

For me, this issue is deeply personal. I lost my sibling, and one of the factors was the delayed arrival of an ambulance. Since then, I have understood in the most painful way that emergency response is not simply about phone numbers or procedures. It is about time. And sometimes, minutes can change everything.

Kazakhstan already has a unified emergency number: 112. At the same time, people can call 101 for fire and rescue services, 102 for police, 103 for ambulance, and 104 for emergency gas services. So Kazakhstan does not need another emergency number. The more important question is what happens after someone calls 112.

Imagine a serious road accident. One person is injured and needs an ambulance. Another may be trapped inside a vehicle and require rescue assistance. Police may also be needed to secure the scene. In such a moment, should a frightened caller really have to think about which agency is responsible for what? The system should make that decision. This is the real value of an integrated emergency response system. A single number is only the front door. What matters is what happens behind it: how quickly information moves, how agencies communicate, and whether the right services can be mobilized together when an emergency crosses institutional boundaries.

International experience offers a useful principle. In the United States, 911 provides access to emergency assistance from police, fire, or ambulance services. Across the European Union, 112 provides a common number through which people can reach police, ambulance, or fire services. The systems behind these numbers are not identical, and Kazakhstan should not simply copy either model. But they share an important idea: the citizen should not need to understand the architecture of the government in order to ask for emergency help.

Complexity should sit behind the system, not in front of the citizen. Kazakhstan is already moving in this direction. My professional experience includes close cooperation with the Ministry of Emergency Situations, and through my work I have seen the importance placed on emergency preparedness and interagency coordination.

Recent developments are particularly encouraging. Kazakhstan has updated the rules governing coordination between 112 and other duty and emergency services. The framework covers interaction with police, ambulance and medical aviation, as well as other services that may need to respond to an emergency. Kazakhstan’s civil protection legislation also provides a foundation for 112 to interact with information systems and use relevant information from emergency services and government databases. Telecommunications operators are required to provide 112 with caller-location services. In other words, much of the foundation already exists. The next challenge is to make that integration fully visible where it matters most. That requires more than technology.

First, a call to 112 should be enough to activate the necessary response. If an incident requires an ambulance, police, and rescuers, coordination should happen inside the emergency system rather than becoming the caller’s responsibility.

Second, information should move with the emergency. A person in distress should not have to repeatedly explain the same situation as information passes between services. Dispatchers and responders need a common picture of what is happening, where it is happening, and which resources are already on the way.

Third, citizens need to understand and trust 112. Public communication should make its role simple: when you face an emergency and do not know which service you need or when you need several services at once, there is one door through which you can ask for help.

This is not only a matter of convenience. The World Health Organization treats emergency communication and dispatch centers as a central coordination element of effective prehospital emergency care. The logic is straightforward: receiving information, assessing the situation, and directing the appropriate resources are part of the emergency response itself.

Kazakhstan therefore does not have to build a unified emergency system from the beginning. It has something more promising: an existing 112 service, a legal framework, new coordination rules, and an opportunity to strengthen the connections between them. For someone facing a fire, a road accident, a medical crisis, or several dangers at once, the boundaries between ministries and services should be invisible. A person in crisis should have one responsibility: ask for help. The system should take care of the rest.

I know personally what a delayed response can mean. That is why, for me, strengthening 112 is not primarily about making government more convenient. It is about making help easier to reach at the moment when someone may be having the worst day of their life.

When every second counts, one call should be enough.

The author is Aigul Akhmetova, a graduate student at the Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Public Policy.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Path of Abai: Novel That Preserved World of Kazakh Life
World.content:
ASTANA — Abai is widely regarded as the founder of modern Kazakh written literature and one of the country’s most influential thinkers. His poetry and “Words of Edification,” a collection of philosophical reflections on morality, education, human nature and society, continue to shape how generations of Kazakhs understand their cultural heritage.

Yet to understand Abai, it is also necessary to understand the world that shaped him. This is what Mukhtar Auezov set out to capture in “Abai Zholy” (The Path of Abai), a four-volume epic novel that tells the story of the poet’s life while offering a sweeping portrait of Kazakh society in the 19th century. Through Abai’s experiences, Auezov brought to life the traditions, social structures, cultural practices and everyday struggles of the Kazakh steppe. The novel is not simply a literary biography. It is an account of a society negotiating the relationship between inherited customs and the search for change.

The writer behind the epic

Born in 1897 near Semipalatinsk, in what is now Abai Region, Auezov grew up in a family with close ties to the poet. His grandfather, Auez, was a storyteller who introduced him to literature and helped nurture his interest in Abai’s work. This early exposure would become central to Auezov’s literary and scholarly career. Auezov studied at the Semipalatinsk Teachers’ Seminary before continuing his education at Leningrad State University, where he studied philology.

He became a prolific writer, playwright and literary scholar, researching Kazakh folklore, oral literature and the development of national literature. His interest in Abai began long before the novel appeared. In 1918, Auezov published an essay on the poet’s works and literary significance. He then devoted years to studying Abai’s legacy and the cultural traditions of his era.

The first book of the novel, published under the title “Abai,” appeared in 1942. A second volume followed in 1947, and the larger work developed over the following decade. The completed four-volume epic became Auezov’s defining achievement and brought his writing to readers far beyond Kazakhstan. In 1959, he received the Lenin Prize for the work.

A society brought to life

The historical setting of “The Path of Abai” is as important as its central character. Auezov reconstructs a world in which family ties, clan relationships, customary law and the authority of influential elders shaped much of public and private life.

The steppe is not merely a backdrop. Seasonal migration, access to pastures, livestock and the demands of a harsh climate influence the fortunes of families and the relationships between communities. Environmental hardship could threaten livelihoods, while disputes over land and resources could deepen existing divisions. Through the relationship between Abai and his father, Qunanbai, Auezov explores the tensions between authority and conscience. Qunanbai represents an established order in which power, status and family interests carry considerable weight. Abai increasingly questions injustice and the treatment of vulnerable members of society.

The novel also examines the position of women, marriage arrangements and the expectations imposed by family and community. These themes reveal the restrictions and inequalities embedded in the social order, while the experiences of individual characters show how people negotiated, resisted or suffered under those expectations. The work of Auezov is therefore neither an idealization of the past nor a simple catalog of customs. It presents a society with a rich cultural identity and strong communal bonds, but also with conflicts, hierarchies and human suffering.

The voices of the steppe

One of the novel’s most significant dimensions is its treatment of Kazakh oral culture. Poetry, songs, storytelling and the performances of akyns, poets who traditionally composed and performed verse, occupy an important place in the narrative. These were not simply forms of entertainment. They could preserve collective memory, express grief, criticize those in power and articulate concerns that might otherwise remain unheard.

In his 2018 research article, “Aqyn agha? Abai Zholy as Socialist Realism and as Literary History,” scholar Gabriel McGuire examines how Auezov connected Abai’s literary development with the broader history of Kazakh oral literature. McGuire notes that Auezov had studied earlier poets and their works before incorporating fictionalized versions of historical akyns into the novel. Their encounters with Abai help explain how the poet’s voice emerged from an existing cultural tradition. Abai listens, questions and reflects, drawing on the poetic language and social observations of those who came before him.

This connection is important because it places Abai within a continuing literary history rather than presenting him as an isolated genius. His intellectual contribution becomes more meaningful when viewed against the songs, debates and storytelling traditions of the society around him. Through these voices, Auezov also preserves the concerns of ordinary people: hardship, injustice, loss, love and the search for dignity. The novel becomes a literary record of a culture in which much knowledge and collective experience passed from one generation to another through spoken words.

From Abai’s world to universal questions

Abai’s enduring significance lies partly in the questions he raised about his own society. In his poetry and “Words of Edification,” he reflected on education, moral responsibility, work, ignorance, envy and the need for personal development. Auezov’s novel places these ideas within the circumstances of Abai’s life. Readers see the social relationships and conflicts that informed his thinking, including his growing dissatisfaction with cruelty, arbitrary authority and indifference to the suffering of others.

This historical context does not limit Abai’s ideas to Kazakhstan. Questions about how people should live, what makes a society just and why education matters remain relevant across cultures. The novel offers a way to approach those questions through the particular experiences of the Kazakh steppe.

At the same time, its significance extends beyond Abai himself. Auezov captures a world of family histories, oral traditions, music, customs and social change, giving readers a fuller understanding of the cultural environment from which one of Kazakhstan’s greatest literary figures emerged.

“The Path of Abai” endures because it connects an individual life to the experience of a people. By reconstructing the world around Abai, Auezov created a work that preserves not only the memory of a major thinker but also a richly detailed literary portrait of Kazakh life and its place in the country’s cultural history.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Aviation Industry Gains as FlyArystan Joins IATA
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s low-cost airline FlyArystan has joined the International Air Transport Association (IATA), an industry body representing airlines worldwide.

IATA represents more than 370 airlines across more than 120 countries, accounting for nearly 85% of global air traffic. It develops industry standards covering aviation safety, security, operational efficiency and sustainability.

Membership will allow FlyArystan to collaborate with other airlines and IATA on industry-wide priorities, including safety standards, operational practices and the future development of air transport, the airline’s press service reported.

“Joining IATA is a natural next step for FlyArystan as we continue to expand our network and international presence,” said Johan Eidhagen, the airline’s president and chief executive officer. He added that membership would provide opportunities to exchange expertise with international industry peers and contribute to discussions on the sector’s future.

Rafael Schvartzman, IATA’s regional vice president for Europe, welcomed the airline’s membership, noting the economic contribution of aviation to Kazakhstan.

Air transport directly generates $2.1 billion in economic output in Kazakhstan, Schvartzman said, adding that the participation of growing airlines such as FlyArystan could support further development of the sector.

Earlier, IATA reported that immigration requirements discouraged 43% of surveyed air passengers from visiting a destination, up from 33% in 2025. The findings also showed that travelers are embracing artificial intelligence and biometric technology to simplify their journeys, according to a new IATA survey.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s US Air Links, AI Investment and Infrastructure Plans
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest explores United Airlines’ interest in potential flights to Kazakhstan, Nvidia’s engagement with the country’s artificial intelligence sector, the origins of the apple, plans for large-scale infrastructure investment, and prospects for closer ties between Kazakhstan and the United States.

United Airlines considers Kazakhstan as a potential future destination

United Airlines is considering Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan as possible additions to its international route network, with the airline’s senior network planning executive visiting both countries this year to assess their potential, reported Simple Flying on Oct. 29.

United CEO Scott Kirby discussed the possibility on the Cheeky Pint podcast, naming both countries as potential destinations “down the road.” He said Patrick Quayle, the airline’s senior vice president of global network planning and alliances, had visited Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to evaluate opportunities for future routes.

Nvidia CEO praises Kazakhstan’s AI ambitions and local startup

Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang praised Kazakhstan’s leadership and artificial intelligence ambitions during a public discussion in Astana on Oct. 23, highlighting the country’s decision to make AI development a national priority, reported The Diplomat on Oct. 30.

Speaking during a fireside chat with Zhaslan Madiyev, Huang described President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev as “incredibly visionary” for prioritizing AI development.

Huang also praised Higgsfield, an AI video-generation startup that became Kazakhstan’s first unicorn in September 2025. Madiyev announced during the event that Nvidia had invested an undisclosed amount in the company. The discussion underscored the growing attention Kazakhstan’s technology sector is receiving from major international industry players.

Kazakhstan’s wild apple forests trace the fruit’s origins to Central Asia

The wild Sievers apple, native to the Tian Shan mountains of southeastern Kazakhstan and neighboring Kyrgyzstan, is the ancestor of modern cultivated apples, reported Euronews on Oct. 28 in an episode of its Modern Nomads series exploring the fruit’s origins.

The report highlighted research into the genetic history of apples, including a study of more than 10,000 cultivated varieties. Gulnara Sitbayeva, a doctor of biological sciences, said 46% of the samples contained genetic material from the Sievers apple, providing evidence of its role in the development of modern varieties.

The story also explored the apple’s cultural significance in Almaty, whose name is traditionally associated with a place rich in apples. The region’s heritage includes the Aport variety, known for its large fruit and distinctive aroma, as well as orchards where growers continue to cultivate both traditional and wild apple trees.

Kazakhstan plans $14 billion in infrastructure spending by 2029

Kazakhstan plans to allocate 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) from its National Fund for infrastructure projects by the end of 2029, while aiming to eliminate its electricity shortage over the same period, reported The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 28.

The plans were outlined by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in his annual state-of-the-nation address on Oct. 28. He also proposed declaring 2027 a year of large-scale construction and launching a nationwide program covering roads, airports, railway stations and public facilities.

Tokayev said public funding should help attract private investment rather than cover the entire cost of the program. The report also noted questions over the use of the National Fund’s oil revenues, which were accumulated partly to protect the economy from commodity-price fluctuations and preserve resources for future generations.

Trump reaffirms support for Kazakhstan’s sovereignty ahead of G20 summit

U.S. President Donald Trump reaffirmed Washington’s support for Kazakhstan’s independence and territorial integrity and said he looked forward to meeting Tokayev at the Group of Twenty (G20) summit in December, reported The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 28.

Trump made the remarks in a congratulatory message marking Kazakhstan’s Republic Day, published by the presidential office on Oct. 27.

“Our commitment to your country’s independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity remains unshakeable,” he wrote.

The summit is scheduled to take place in Doral, Florida. Preparations for Tokayev’s participation had been discussed by the two countries’ officials earlier this year.

World.title: Halyk Bank to Tap Global Startup Network to Develop AI Solutions
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Halyk Bank and international innovation platform Plug and Play have announced plans to establish a joint artificial intelligence (AI) competence center in Almaty to develop digital services, strengthen cybersecurity and introduce technologies from the global startup ecosystem.

The center will draw on Plug and Play’s international network of more than 100,000 startups to identify promising technologies, test their applications and integrate selected solutions into Halyk’s existing services, the bank’s press service reported.

The partnership is also expected to create opportunities for Kazakh startups to connect with international technology markets, with Halyk serving as a link between domestic developers and Plug and Play’s global ecosystem.

Focus on practical applications

Halyk is looking to apply AI and other emerging technologies across its retail and business services. The bank serves nearly 11.5 million retail customers, while more than 340,000 business representatives use its Onlinebank application each month.

“The partnership with Plug and Play opens up even more opportunities to introduce new services into our applications, both for retail customers and businesses,” said Murat Koshenov, deputy chairman of Halyk’s management board, adding that the bank would explore solutions in lending, cybersecurity, fraud prevention and risk management.

Roman Mashchyk, deputy chairman of the bank’s management board, said the selection process would prioritize technologies that address specific business and customer needs, can integrate into the bank’s platforms, and offer measurable economic benefits.

“Our approach to selecting startups is very pragmatic. First, we assess the needs of the bank and our customers,” Mashchyk said, adding that the bank would select solutions best suited to those requirements.

From technology development to implementation

Alfredo Gomez Soria, Plug and Play’s regional director for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, said the partnership aims to turn AI opportunities into practical applications. The teams will identify promising startups internationally and test their solutions in real-world conditions.

“We are combining Halyk’s knowledge of the local market and infrastructure with Plug and Play’s international expertise,” Gomez Soria said. “Our task is not simply to talk about artificial intelligence, but to turn technologies into concrete products, more convenient services and more efficient processes.”

Data protection will remain a key consideration. According to Mashchyk, using international technology solutions will not involve transferring customers’ personal data across borders. The bank will integrate new technologies into its infrastructure in compliance with Kazakhstan’s legislation.

The initiative is being implemented in partnership with the United States Consulate and Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, adding a bilateral dimension to the technology collaboration. Halyk and Plug and Play began their cooperation in May 2026, when they signed a memorandum of understanding. Establishing the competence center in Almaty marks the next stage of their partnership.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Begin Electronic Entry Checks Nov. 1, Make QazETA Mandatory in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will begin checking electronic travel authorizations for visa-free foreign at five border crossings on Nov. 1, the first step in a nationwide rollout that will make the permits mandatory in July 2027.

The new QazETA system will initially be voluntary, with travelers allowed to enter Kazakhstan without authorization during an eight-month transition period. Beginning July 1, 2027, eligible foreign nationals who fail to obtain the permit could be denied entry.

The changes are outlined in an Oct. 10 government resolution, which issues a new version of the rules governing the entry and stay of foreign nationals and migration control. The electronic authorization is free and must be requested at least 72 hours before arrival.

Where the checks begin

The first phase will cover the Aktau International Airport in the Mangystau Region and four road border crossings: Urlyutobe in the Pavlodar Region, Aukhatty in the Zhambyl Region, Atameken in the Turkistan Region and Nurly Zhol in the Zhetisu Region.

On Jan. 1, 2027, checks will expand to Astana and Almaty international airports, before reaching all remaining border crossings on March 1. From July 1, 2027, QazETA will become mandatory for all foreign travelers, and the absence of an authorization will become grounds for refusing entry.

During the transition period, which runs through June 30, border officers will inform travelers without QazETA authorization about the new requirements rather than deny them entry solely for lacking the permit.

Who needs QazETA

According to the Kazakh Foreign Ministry, the new requirement will apply to citizens of 85 countries eligible for visa-free travel to Kazakhstan, including citizens of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states.

QazETA will not replace the existing visa-free regime or change how long foreign visitors can stay in Kazakhstan. Most visa-free visitors may stay for up to 30 days per visit, with a maximum of 90 days within any 180-day period.

Citizens of EAEU member states may stay for up to 90 days within a 180-day period. Different limits apply to citizens of Türkiye, who may stay for up to 90 days, and India and Iran, whose visa-free stays are limited to 14 days per visit and 42 days within a 180-day period.

The resolution establishes 29 categories of travelers exempt from obtaining QazETA. They include children under 16, adults aged 65 and older, holders of valid Kazakh visas or residence permits, refugees and asylum seekers, and members of official government delegations.

Exemptions also cover eligible diplomatic passport holders, passengers remaining in international airport transit areas, certain transport crew members and international truck and bus drivers, as well as personnel involved in humanitarian, rescue and emergency medical missions.

How to apply

Travelers can apply for QazETA through the official website, qazeta.kz, or its mobile app at least 72 hours before their planned arrival in Kazakhstan. Applicants must complete an online identity verification process. Once approved, the authorization is valid for 180 days, allows multiple entries and is linked to the passport used in the application. The same passport must be presented at the border.

QazETA is free of charge, but approval does not guarantee entry. Border authorities retain the right to deny admission under Kazakhstan’s migration laws, including in cases involving previous deportations or false information submitted by travelers.

Existing migration control rules stay in place. Individuals and organizations hosting a foreign visitor must notify the authorities of their arrival within three business days.

From pilot to rollout

Amendments to Kazakhstan’s migration legislation, signed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on June 24, established the legal framework for the authorization system. The relevant provisions took effect Aug. 25.

The QazETA platform covers more than a single entry permit. The platform also offers electronic visas, e-residency services and certificates confirming border crossings.

Diplomatic outreach

The Kazakh Foreign Ministry said it had informed all 85 countries of the new requirements through diplomatic channels. Application guidelines will also be published on the websites of Kazakh embassies and consulates, while authorities plan to brief foreign diplomats in Astana, reported Tengrinews.

World.title: Armenia calls for investigation into alleged abuses by Russian company running railway
World.content:
Aram Sargsyan, leader of the Republic Party, has called on Armenia’s prosecutor general to investigate the activities of South Caucasus Railway. If the investigation uncovers any abuses, the politician insists that prosecutors open a criminal case.

Armenia’s railways operate under a concession agreement with South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. Armenia signed a 30-year concession agreement in 2008, handing the management of Armenian Railways CJSC to Russian Railways. However, freight traffic has since halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the company has yet to fulfil its mandatory investment commitments.

Sargsyan says the authorities need to examine:

the efficiency of the company’s operations;

its compliance with its contractual management obligations;

the protection of the state’s property interests.

“I ask you to accept this statement and consider it a report of a suspected criminal offence under the procedure established by the Criminal Procedure Code of the Republic of Armenia,” he said.

The politician’s appeal to the prosecutor general comes amid talks between Armenia and Russia over the railway concession.

Yerevan has long called for changes to the concession arrangement. It argues that a new format would make Armenia’s railway more competitive. In particular, the Armenian authorities have proposed transferring the concession to a third party. Moscow, however, has yet to accept the proposal.

Two weeks ago, Russian Railways CEO Oleg Belozyorov visited Yerevan. Following their meeting, Armenia’s prime minister announced that the two sides had agreed to set up a joint working group. According to Nikol Pashinyan, the group has three months to examine specific questions from the Armenian government and provide answers. The key issue is whether Russia is prepared to invest in the railway. Yerevan will decide on its next steps after receiving the group’s findings.

The Prosecutor General’s Office issued a brief statement, offering no further comment. It said that it had accepted Aram Sargsyan’s application for consideration.

From dismantling infrastructure to declining freight volumes

In his appeal, the leader of the Republic Party recalled an interview that Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan gave to the Russian newspaper Kommersant on 10 September 2018. Discussing South Caucasus Railway, Pashinyan said the company’s alleged abuses amounted to approximately $60 million. He also said law enforcement agencies were investigating the matter and that the public would soon learn the findings.

“I believe it is necessary to clarify how the investigation conducted at the time concluded, what results it produced and whether the state received compensation for any damage it may have suffered,” Sargsyan wrote.

Following Pashinyan’s statement in 2018, the authorities launched criminal proceedings. However, they discontinued the case in March 2021. No further developments have emerged since then. Nor has anyone reported whether the company compensated the state for the alleged damage.

The politician identified five issues in his appeal to the prosecutor general:

1. Dismantling railway infrastructure

“It is necessary to establish the circumstances surrounding the dismantling of railway infrastructure along the Meghri–Kapan section, which stretches for approximately 40km. The investigation should also establish the legal grounds for the work, determine what happened to the dismantled assets, assess whether the company lawfully disposed of the property and examine how it used the proceeds from any sale.”

2. The Ijevan–Aghstafa railway line

“It is necessary to examine the circumstances surrounding the dismantling or deterioration of railway infrastructure along a section of approximately 17km within Armenia. The investigation should assess whether the decisions taken in this regard were lawful and determine whether they caused damage to the state.”

3. Declining freight volumes

“According to published data, railway freight volumes fell significantly during South Caucasus Railway’s management of the network. It is necessary to compare the figures for 2008 with those from subsequent years, identify the reasons for the decline and establish whether poor management, failure to meet contractual obligations or other violations caused it.”

4. Reduction in the workforce

“It is necessary to examine the reasons behind the significant reduction in the number of employees, assess whether the company fulfilled its commitments and identify any possible violations during this process.”

5. Implementation of the concession agreement

“It is necessary to analyse the concession agreement signed in 2008, including its investment and other obligations, assess how the company has fulfilled them in practice, examine the effectiveness of state oversight and determine whether the company has lawfully maintained and used railway assets owned by Armenia.”

Aram Sargsyan stressed that the competent authorities must conduct a comprehensive and impartial investigation.

“The potential damage was inflicted on Armenia and, consequently, its citizens”

The politician believes the issue he has raised with law enforcement agencies is of critical importance. He says the authorities must first and foremost protect state property. He also stresses that the matter concerns Armenia’s economic security, the restoration of railway links and the country’s ability to realise its transit potential.

“The potential damage was inflicted on Armenia and, consequently, its citizens,” Sargsyan argues.

He has therefore asked the authorities to verify the facts that the prime minister presented in 2018 and report the findings of the investigation conducted at the time. He also expects law enforcement agencies to assess the five issues he has raised. If they uncover evidence of a criminal offence, he demands that they open a new criminal case.

Sargsyan says the authorities must establish the scale of the financial damage the state may have suffered and identify those responsible.

“If the authorities establish that a crime took place and caused damage to the state, they must take the measures required by law to secure compensation, recover property that was unlawfully disposed of or reclaim its value,” Sargsyan stressed.

He expects the prosecutor’s office to provide a written response outlining the investigation’s findings and the decisions it has taken.

Investigation into South Caucasus Railway: Aram Sargsyan’s appeal

World.title: Will Turkey open its border with Armenia amid tensions with Baku? Views from Yerevan
World.content:
Turkey-Armenia border: Will it open?

Discussions about the possible opening of the Armenian-Turkish border have intensified in Armenia in recent weeks. Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan has not ruled out the possibility that the border could open before the two sides agree on candidates for new special envoys to oversee the normalisation process.
