World.title: Australia v South Africa LIVE: Aussies on the ropes as Rabada blows away top three
World.content:
It’s do-or-die for Marnus Labuschagne.

He secretly would have been happy that the Proteas batted the day yesterday because it’s given him a chance to save his Test career.

There’s already been calls for Josh Inglis to move to No.3 in the order to start the Australian summer in place for Labuschagne. But he can have his say on that matter today.

After falling for a five-ball duck in the first innings, the pressure will be firmly on the Australian No.3 to deliver, with the Aussies needing 288 runs for victory on the final day.

It means the 32-year-old failed to score a Test century for the 48th time in a row - a record for the number of consecutive innings a batter in Australia’s top four has waited to raise his bat at three figures. He hasn’t scored a Test century since July 2023.

World.title: Pursuit of power may mean compromise
World.content:
Independents option Peter Hartcher paints a miserable picture of the four main political parties competing for attention and votes. Yet he makes no mention of the fifth contemporary force in Australian politics: the community independents in the House of Representatives and the significant independents in the Senate. For the past few weeks, we have had people and politicians across the spectrum rightly lauding the character, leadership, and work ethic of community independent Helen Haines following the shocking incident in Wangaratta. Members of parliament such as Helen Haines have shown just how valuable and valued independents are in our political landscape. At the next election, undoubtedly Labor and the Coalition will lose several seats, but they might not go to One Nation or the Greens; they may instead go to community independents. This would be a good outcome, as would a minority government requiring negotiations with a large crossbench of high integrity, high-quality independents. Graeme Henchel, Yarra Glen

Think compromise Columnist Peter Hartcher identifies significant issues likely to stop any one political party from forming government alone ( Comment , 31/10). Many countries have this problem regularly, including Italy and Israel. They have horse-trading of policies and cabinet positions after elections, with compromises reached. The closest example in recent Australian history involved Julia Gillard’s government. Three pre-teal independents supported Labor on supply and no confidence motions, in return for some policy concessions. On current opinion polling, the Victorian state election might force Ben Carroll or Jess Wilson into similar or wider deals with the Greens or One Nation, whatever the protestations now. In 2028, Anthony Albanese could be forced to promise with the Greens and/or independents more radical carbon emissions cuts, in return for parliamentary support. One Nation might extract concessions from Angus Taylor on migration numbers or a further reduction of climate efforts. Our major parties could avoid the worst of the apocalypse by compromising with close rival parties. John Hughes, Mentone

To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au . Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published.

The forgotten ones

As much as I like Ross Gittins’ explanations of monetary policy, I don’t agree with him about raising the GST (Comment, 28/10). The low wage and welfare benefit recipients are always forgotten when it comes to the GST. Yes, workers would have lower taxes but what if you don’t pay tax or you’re a low-income earner? The price of goods would rise and make life even more difficult for these people. It’d be OK if you earn a decent wage, it’ll all work out but not for people with less money. Even people earning well now have trouble paying their rent. A raised GST would just make it harder to survive every day. Imagine being on the dole and prices rising even more to cover a GST?

Chris Hooper, Castlemaine

The forgotten lesson

Jewish philosopher Hannah Arendt understood something fundamental about political freedom: its greatest enemy is not disagreement, but the abandonment of independent judgment.

Jillian Segal’s latest proposals seem to have forgotten this lesson. In the name of combating antisemitism, she wants greater oversight of public broadcasters, enforceable conditions on arts funding and tighter restrictions on protest. Meanwhile, she identifies progressive social justice advocates as a particularly pervasive source of antisemitism. The irony is extraordinary. People who insist that human rights must apply universally, including to Palestinians, are now being treated as a threat to social cohesion.

Antisemitism is a serious evil. But so is the political habit of turning moral disagreement into grounds for suspicion and institutional punishment. Universities exist to question accepted truths. Journalists exist to scrutinise power. Artists exist, among other things, to disturb our certainties. None should have to demonstrate political conformity to retain public support.

Arendt knew where the suppression of independent judgment could lead.

We should be especially wary when restrictions on freedom arrive dressed in the language of moral responsibility.

Fernanda Trecenti, Fitzroy

An actor’s legacy

The death of Sir Patrick Stewart at 86 is a loss that reaches far beyond the worlds of television and cinema.

While millions will remember him as Captain Jean-Luc Picard of Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier of the X-Men, we should not overlook the distinguished Shakespearean actor whose extraordinary voice, presence and command of language brought such depth to both characters.

Yet perhaps his greatest legacy lies in the message of Star Trek: The Next Generation. Gene Roddenberry’s vision of humanity’s future was one worth aspiring to: a united Earth, free from racism and prejudice, with no nations waging wars against one another, and a humanity that had moved beyond greed and division to embrace knowledge, exploration, and co-operation.

Watching today’s world, with its wars, nationalism, racial hatred, and political division, one wonders how far we have travelled in the wrong direction.

Perhaps the greatest tribute we can pay Stewart, and the fictional captain he brought so magnificently to life, is to remember that this vision was never simply science fiction. It was a challenge to humanity.

Make it so.

Darren Grindrod, Glenroy

Lose-lose situation

With US Defence Secretary (aka Secretary of War) Pete Hegseth busily firing all the expert leaders in US defence and downgrading America’s military strength, why are our leaders continuing to align Australia with America and paying billions of our dollars for submarines we will never get and America can’t actually build? We are aligning ourselves with a “superpower” that can’t even win against Iran and is subservient to Russia. It’s a lose-lose disaster for Australia. Pull out now, PM.

Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights

Childhood’s end

I supervised two VCE exams last week, 50 years after I sat my own finals. It seemed like a blink of an eye since that time, until I read through the General Maths paper and realised I couldn’t answer any of the questions.

Observing these kids, I wondered if their demeanour was a hint of their future: one gazing into nothing; a boy wielding his highlighter like a light-sabre, supremely organised; another, jiggling their leg incessantly as they flipped in a frenzy between exam booklet and calculator.

Many of these students will never again utilise the ″⁣Hungarian algorithm″⁣ (a mystery to me, too), or calculate a seasonal index; but hopefully they’ll retain for a few years some vestige of the sharp analysis required for such a testing time. I feel for these kids. I hope the resilience that got them into this room keeps them strong for what’s outside the door. The world is a scary place, even more so, 50 years on.

Jane Neville, Wattle Flat

Off message

Who in One Nation thinks that cartoons depicting politicians being run over and a colouring book for children, depicting Bluey, obviously scared, being held at knife point, is a legitimate way of getting their message across.

Michael Brinkman, Ventnor

World.title: Mark Latham served with bankruptcy papers while at races
World.content:
PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Mark Latham served with bankruptcy papers while at races Emily Kowal and Max Maddison October 31, 2026 — 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Former NSW One Nation leader Mark Latham’s day at the horse races has ended in a potential loss of almost $180,000 after the MP was served with bankruptcy papers while at the Royal Randwick racecourse. The bankruptcy notice stems from independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich’s successful defamation lawsuit against Latham over a “vile, homophobic” Twitter post from March 2023. Mark Latham departs the Royal Randwick racecourse last year. Sam Mooy Latham was spotted being served with papers by a representative of Greenwich, while attending The Golden Eagle racing event on Saturday. When approached by a News Corp journalist who witnessed the serving, Latham refused to comment, calling the reporter a “nosy dickhead”.



Latham is being pursued for about $180,000 in court-ordered damages and interest. When factoring in unpaid legal costs, his total bill exceeds $500,000. Speaking to the Herald, Latham complained he was targeted by the server and media. “When the left say, ‘Lower the temperature in politics,’ I was followed today for hours at the races (of all places) by some server (to deliver documents my lawyer already had) plus the Tele journalist and photographer,” he said. The Federal Court upheld the original finding that Latham’s post, which was highly graphic and referred to Greenwich’s sexuality, defamed the MP. Greenwich declined to comment on the serving, pointing instead to a statement he made earlier this month after the High Court dismissed Latham’s final appeal.



“Mr Latham defamed me in a sexually aggressive social media post that subjected me to an avalanche of homophobic hate,” Greenwich said. “Mr Latham has repeatedly refused to take responsibility for his actions, instead pursuing appeals through the courts,” he said. Latham has 21 days to pay the outstanding debt. If he cannot, or does not pay, he can then apply for a court to declare himself officially bankrupt. Under the NSW Constitution Act 1902, any member of parliament who “becomes bankrupt or takes the benefit of any law for the relief of bankrupt or insolvent debtors” must have their seat declared vacant. In June, Latham quietly listed his sprawling five-bedroom family home for $2.4 million, but he says it had nothing to do with mounting legal bills and damages owed in his feud with Greenwich. This guide will be updated with comments from Melbourne Cup-winning jockey Michelle Payne assessing each runner’s chances. Ciaron Maher is aiming to become the new Cups King of Australia with seven runners in the race that stops the nation. Point of Law rockets into Melbourne Cup favouritism after winning the Geelong Cup. Getty Images Maher has only won the Melbourne Cup once, with Gold Trip in 2022, but is a strong chance to double that this Tuesday. In our comprehensive runner-by-runner guide, Maher’s strongest opposition will come from Irish trainer Joseph O’Brien, who has five runners.



Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Leading Melbourne Cup chance ruled out, four runners face a nervous wait The horses are named in order of their saddle cloth numbers – from top weight down to bottom weight. 1. Sons And Lovers (GB)

Barrier: 3

6yoG (gelding) 57.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Dylan Browne McMonagle

Career: 23: 6-2-6 Last start: Second of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes Leopardstown Russell says: A dual group 2 winner from Ireland who sounds more like a midday soapie than a racehorse. That being said, in our view he has more chance of winning an Emmy than the Melbourne Cup, considering he has to lug 57.5 kilograms to victory first-up in Australia.



Related Article Cox Plate No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington 2. Trustyourinstinct (IRE) Barrier: 18

7yoG 57kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: James McDonald

Career: 30: 9-7-4 Last start: 4th of 7 G1 Irish St Leger 2816m Russell says: If you believe in the saying, ‘follow the money’, this is the horse for you. He’s owned by Irish billionaire JP McManus, who used to be a bookmaker. That’s a good lead right there. He is also a group 2 winner with a serious chance. Watch to see if McManus bets up big on Cup eve. Top five hope. 3. Knight’s Choice



Barrier: 2

7yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: John Symons and Sheila Laxon. Jockey: Robbie Dolan

Career: 31: 6-3-3 Last start: 14th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Robbie Dolan rides Knight’s Choice to a famous win in the 2024 Melbourne Cup. Getty Russell says: The shock 2024 winner was robbed of the chance to defend his crown in 2025 because of the equine equivalent of a lockdown. Not COVID-19, but strangles – a contagious bacterial disease – that was detected at Macedon Lodge on the eve of last year’s spring. Great run in the Herbert Power two starts back, might have copped interference in Caulfield Cup. Can’t win. 4. Middle Earth (GB)



Barrier: 1

7yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Mark Zahra

Career: 26: 6-2-3 Last start: Eighth of 12 G1 Cox Plate 2040m Russell says: If this galloper’s name has been plucked from J.R.R. Tolkien mythology, then surely his trainer, Ciaron Maher, qualifies as some sort of modern-day wizard. Maher is on fire and has given this fellow the old-fashioned Cup preparation. Bart Cummings’ rule was 10 kilometres – he has racked up 9.94km in five lead-up races. He looked good late in the Cox Plate. A winning chance. 5. Vauban (FRA) Barrier: 22

9yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott. Jockey: Jordan Childs

Career: 33: 10-5-6 Last start: Ninth of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Russell says: The veteran is lining up for his fourth Melbourne Cup – the first two for Irish trainer Willie Mullins before he was sold to Australian connections to be trained by Waterhouse and Bott. He finished sixth last year, but might not be going as well. Although he was first-up in the Geelong Cup, so hard to tell.



6. Enfjaar (IRE) Barrier: 8

7yoG 56kg

Trainer: Roger Varian. Jockey: Ray Dawson

Career: 17: 5-2-3 Last start: Third of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Russell says: Best of internationals in the Caulfield Cup, and in my view, internationals need an impressive lead-up run in Australia if they are to win the Melbourne Cup. He ticks that box. And for those struggling to pronounce his name, Google says Enfjaar means “burst” in Arabic. Top 10. 7. Royal Supremacy (IRE) Barrier: 21

6yoG 56kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Ben Allen

Career: 22: 7-3-4 Last start: 15th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m



Russell says: One of Ciaron Maher’s seven runners, but a lesser chance. Cooked in the Caulfield Cup by a head-scratching ride from visiting hoop Jamie Spencer, he bolted to the front, whacked on the handbrakes and then looked confused when the pressure went back on from the 800m. He was flying before that. Outside the top 10. Trainer Ciaron Maher will have a number of horses running in the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images 8. Wine Dark Sea (GB) Barrier: 23

5yoG 56kg

Trainer: Harry Charlton. Jockey: Damian Lane

Career: 11: 4-2-0

Last start: 11th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Russell says: Purchased abroad by Australian Bloodstock, who have won the Cup with Protectionist and Gold Trip, and was a massive spruik horse leading into the Caulfield Cup. Sadly for punters, he didn’t live up to expectations. Needs a gigantic turnaround.



9. Asterix (NZ) Barrier: 6

8yoG 55kg

Trainer: Chris Waller. Jockey: Jye McNeil

Career: 33: 8-1-2 Last start: 12th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Russell says: Caught up in the backwash of the tragic fall in the Caulfield Cup. A group 1-winning stayer from New Zealand owned by former Kiwi cricket great Mark Greatbatch and now in the Chris Waller barn. An outsider, but any rain will help. 10. Goodie Two Shoes (IRE)



Barrier: 19

8yoM (mare) 55kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Wayne Lordan

Career: 31: 14-2-7 Last start: Tenth of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes 2414m Russell says: A former hurdler who ran a surprise second in the Melbourne Cup last year. Trained by Joseph O’Brien, who has already won the race twice, and owned by Irish billionaire JP McManus. Slightly disappointing last start, but that might have been a pipe opener. Top 10 finish. Goodie Two Shoes (left, with green and yellow silks) finishes second behind Half Yours in the 2025 Melbourne Cup. Joe Armao 11. Juja Kibo (IRE) Barrier: 14

6yoG 55kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Sam Clipperton

Career: 20: 6-3-6 Last start: First of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m



Russell says: In hot form, having won its past two starts, including a big win in the group 2 Metropolitan at Randwick on October 3. Didn’t make the cut for the Caulfield Cup, but many believed he could have won the race. Copped a 1.5kg for the MV Gold Cup win. Still think he brings the B-grade form. Top 10. 12. Hopewell Rock (IRE) Barrier: 15

5yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: George Boughey. Jockey: Zac Lloyd

Career: 10: 3-3-2 Last start: Second of 22 Ebor Handicap 2787m Onesmoothoperator wins the Geelong Cup in 2024. Getty Images



Russell says: Another international with decent credentials, but will have to defy history to win this year’s Cup. No runner has come out of York’s Ebor Handicap and saluted on the first Tuesday in November. But a few have been close – Heartbreak City ran second in 2017, while Purple Moon was a runner-up in 2007. 13. Onesmoothoperator (US) Barrier: 13

9yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: Tim Fitzsimmons. Jockey: Declan Bates

Career: 51: 6-11-6 Last start: 11th of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Russell says: Has gone off the boil. The veteran started second favourite and ran 12th in the 2024 Melbourne Cup after winning the Geelong Cup in the lead-up. Won the MV Gold Cup last year before finishing 16th in the Cup. Not going as well this year. Will be grateful they pay back to last.



14. Soul Of Spain (IRE) Barrier: 5

6yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: Chris Waller. Jockey: Tommy Berry

Career: 26: 5-5-6 Last start: Eight of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Russell says: Ran second in the Sydney Cup over 3200m but has been slightly disappointing at his past two starts, including a seventh in The Metropolitan. World.title: How a ghost story from 200 years ago inspired a Sydney tradition
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life How a ghost story from 200 years ago inspired a Sydney tradition Ellie Busby October 31, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The local legend starts like all good ghost stories do: with a mysterious disappearance, suspicious townspeople and the unnerving appearance of an apparition with a message. However, it’s how the ghost story is remembered and celebrated 200 years later that sets Campbelltown in south-west Sydney apart from any other Halloween tradition in Sydney. The Fisher’s Ghost Festival parade through Campbelltown. James Brickwood The parade was reinstated after demands from residents. James Brickwood The Festival of Fisher’s Ghost, an event that runs for two weeks until November 8 and features a range of ghost-themed community celebrations, is held in honour of Frederick Fisher and the story of his death.



Colourful floats and performers took over the town centre on Saturday in a “ghost parade” – an event residents have been wanting to return for six years. Campbelltown City Council Mayor Darcy Lound said there was still great interest in the ghost of Fred Fisher. “There’s still people who say today [that] you can still hear noises in our historic Campbelltown Theatre because that’s where his house basically used to sit, where the old Town Hall Theatre is now,” he said. “There’s a thing there when they lock up, they say ‘goodnight, Fred’, and it’s a tradition that still goes today.” Campbelltown City Council’s record of Fisher shows he was a farmer who mysteriously disappeared in 1826 after giving his neighbour, George Worrall, power of attorney over his farm while he served a short prison sentence.



Despite Worrall saying Fisher had sailed for England after being released from jail, the townspeople were suspicious, especially after he sold Fisher’s horse and belongings. Fisher’s disappearance remained unsolved for a few months, the case reopening only after new information appeared in an unexpected way: through a ghost sighting. Related Article Prisons Celebrity murderers, disembodied voices and huge expense: A Sydney landmark’s uncertain future “A bloke by the name of John Farley was in the pub having a couple of beers, and ... he was walking home and came across the bridge, and says he’d seen this ghostly figure sitting on the bridge, pointing to an area of the paddock,” Lound said. “So John Farley, in a panic, ran back into the pub and said he’s seen a ghost, it’s pointing to the paddock. It could be where a body is.” As the story goes, Farley was right and Fisher’s body was found in the paddock. Worrall was arrested and found guilty of his murder, and later hanged.



The first annual Halloween Express picnic trains from Central Station left on Saturday with hundreds of passengers in fancy dress. Audrey Richardson Photo: Audrey Richardson Photo: Audrey Richardson It’s a tale Lound says residents are still fascinated by, describing it as Campbelltown “through and through”, and the reason why the tradition of the Fisher’s Ghost Festival has continued for 70 years. For the believers, the ghost of Fisher is set to make an appearance throughout the festival – although this version is depicted as a smiling costumed ghost wearing sneakers.

World.title: Porirua deputy mayor Kylie Wihapi dies
World.content:
Tributes are pouring in, after the death of Porirua deputy mayor Kylie Wihapi, aged 45.

Mayor Anita Baker said she was numb with shock and disbelief at the sudden loss.

"She was such a vibrant, outgoing and generous person, full of life, warmth and a deep love for all of Porirua," she said.

Baker said Wihapi died on Saturday morning, as the result of a fall.

"There will be more to say about Kylie's extraordinary contribution in the days ahead, but right now, my thoughts and deepest sympathies are with her whānau, especially her husband Adam, son Cooper, step-son Arama, her mum and dad Marlene and Rob, her brothers and wider family. My heart breaks for them.

Baker said Wihapi had made history as Porirua's first elected Māori ward councillor.

"She brought wisdom, courage, compassion and an unmistakable energy to everything she did.

"I have lost a trusted adviser and friend, and her fellow councillors have lost a much-loved colleague."

Kylie Wihapi Supplied/Barbara Edmonds Facebook

"Kylie was Porirua through and through. She loved this city, believed in its people and worked tirelessly to make it a better place.

"We will miss her terribly."

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said she was "so very sad to hear of Kylie's passing".

"She was so passionate about Porirua, every conversation with her was of huge pride for the whole community.

"My deep condolences to her whānau... Moe mai rā e te taonga."

Labour MP Barbara Edmonds said she was "heartbroken" at the loss of "one of our most amazing local wahine".

Barbara Edmonds and Kylie Wihapi. Supplied/Barbara Edmonds Facebook

"Kylie was everywhere and anywhere.

"Whether it was on the netball court as a dedicated referee, hosting her annual Pink Breakfast to raise funds for the Breast Cancer Foundation, co-ordinating her annual Christmas pet food drive, filling in for the mayor Anita Baker, coaching netball teams or following her beloved son Cooper on the rugby field side-lines."

Edmonds described her as "selfless" and "always keen for a dress up".

"Her energy for life was just immeasurable. No matter what it was, Kylie always made time for the community of Porirua that she loved so much.

"Thank you e hoa for all that you've done for us and for Porirua. La manuia lau malaga."

Wellington City Council deputy mayor Ben McNulty said he was devastated.

"Kylie was an incredibly warm and welcoming person, and deeply passionate about Porirua.

"To her family, friends and wider community, I am so sorry for your deep loss."

Pāuatahanui general ward councillor Ross Leggett said Wihapi was "true child of Porirua" and "gone far too soon".

"To say the loss of Kylie Wihapi... is a shock would be an understatement.

"I was elected to the council alongside her in 2016, and we were all the better for her openness, humour, warmth and sheer industriousness. She made a fine deputy mayor and gave so much to the city she loved."

The former mayor of Lower Hutt, Campbell Barry, said Wihapi's passing was not fair.

World.title: Nearly 200 schools 'of concern' or worse - Education Review Office
World.content:
The Education Review Office says 199 schools need help for the sake of their students.

Its 2026 annual report says students at those schools are at risk without timely intervention.

The schools included 172 regarded as "of concern" and 27 regarded as having "significant concerns".

"A school may be identified as being 'of concern' where evidence shows significant improvement is required in student achievement, attendance, underperformance across core areas, like learner success and wellbeing, leadership and governance, curriculum, and teaching and learning," ERO told RNZ.

"'Serious concern' is the higher threshold, where problems are more severe or persistent, risks to learners are greater, or previous support and intervention have not produced sustained improvement."

The review office told RNZ the proportion of schools of concern or serious concern was eight percent, which was about the same as previous years.

"The proportion of schools identified as being of concern has been fairly stable over time at around 7-9 percent, although individual schools move into and out of the category, as their circumstances and performance change. ERO has strengthened how it identifies and monitors schools requiring improvement.

"The more significant issue is that too many schools remain of concern for too long and do not achieve sustained improvement, despite receiving support."

ERO's annual report said the schools were concentrated in the upper half of the North Island.

"While these schools remain a small proportion of the overall system, the distribution of concern is not even across the country," the reports aid. "The highest numbers of these schools were located in Tai Tokerau, Waikato, Bay of Plenty/Waiariki, Tāmaki Herenga Waka and Hawke's Bay/Tairāwhiti.

"Schools identified as having significant concerns were more commonly secondary schools, which accounted for approximately two-thirds of all cases in this category. This suggests that, while concerns arise across all parts of the system, challenges in secondary settings are often more complex, and may require more intensive monitoring and intervention."

The annual report said the office reviewed 628 schools and 542 early childhood services this year. It found eight percent of the schools required improvement, half of them in "learner success and wellbeing".

Just one percent were told their teaching needed improvement.

"Around four in five schools reviewed this year are embedding or excelling in leadership (80 percent), teaching and learning (79 percent), and curriculum (81 percent), compared with 67 percent of schools in learner success and wellbeing," the report said.

"This suggests that, while schools are increasingly strengthening the conditions that support improvement, it may take longer for these efforts to be reflected in learner outcomes."

The early childhood education reviews found that one percent of English-medium services required improvement, as did seven percent of Māori-medium services.

The report said four percent of the English-medium schools ERO visited in the past year were already meeting the government's 2030 goal of 80 percent of students attending regularly, but 51 percent were behind or significantly behind the target.

Regular attendance was defined as attending more than 90 percent of the time.

The office found 17 percent of the schools it visited were already meeting the government's 2030 target of ensuring 80 percent of Year 8 students were achieving at or above their expected curriculum level for reading, writing and maths.

A further 69 percent were making progress toward the goal and 14 percent were not making sufficient progress.

World.title: Kiwi Ferns overpower Papua New Guinea for World Cup semifinal spot
World.content:
Papua New Guinea made the Kiwi Ferns work, before they eased clear 40-12 on a soggy Gold Coast and make it three wins from three Rugby League World Cup pool games.

New Zealand will be top qualifiers from Group B for next weekend's semi-finals, where they face Samoa in Newcastle.

While the Ferns romped to a 92-0 win over France in Christchurch last week, their two other matches have been decent contests, including their opening 18-12 defeat of group runners-up Fiji, who will face Australia in the other semi.

PNG were particularly difficult to break down in the first half, with a try to Kaiyah Atai on the stroke of the interval inching New Zealand to a 14-12 advantage.

Play opened up in the second half, with the Kiwis adding five more tries to their overall tally of eight, while keeping their tiring opponents scoreless.

Kiwi Ferns perform their pre-game haka against the Orchids. www.photosport.nz

They started the second spell on the best possible note, when front-rower Otesa Pule scored a runaway 70m solo try almost from the restart.

Backs Mackenzie Wiki and the impressive Abigail Roache both completed doubles after the break, as their team unearthed greater cohesion and reduced the error count.

Duel international Stacey Waaka and Wiki bagged tries early in the match, but both were cancelled out by PNG, who responded with converted tries to Tia Molo and Elsie Albert.

Captain and halfback Raecene McGregor said her team would need to be better in the knockout phase.

"Obviously, I'm proud that we were really resilient and got through it in the end," she told Sky Sport.

"There were a couple of errors in that first half and even in the second half - we need to be better, especially coming into the semis."

World.title: Black Ferns complete series clean sweep of France
World.content:
The Black Ferns have completed a series clean sweep over France with a 36-7 win at Christchurch.

New Zealand's opening try came from an outrageous no-look overhead pass from No.8 Liana Mikaele-Tu'u in the build-up, finished off by wing Shyrah Tuliau-Tua'a.

Scoring and converting the second try, fullback Braxton Sorenson-McGee became the first Black Ferns player to score 100 points in a calendar year. She had another try disallowed moments later for a forward pass in the build-up.

France were rewarded with a try from close range to hooker Maïlys Mailagi on the stroke of halftime, giving them some hope of a second-half comeback.

After the break, Tuliau-Tua'a doubled the lead with a try in the corner, capitalising on some outstanding passing skills from prop Chryss Viliko.

Replacement prop Maddi Robinson powered over for her first test try, but Tuliau-Tua'a left her team shorthanded, when she was yellow-carded for a high tackle.

Unperturbed, New Zealand extended their advantage with a try to replacement Mererangi Paul, before hooker Vici-Rose Green crossed in the final stages to set the seal on victory.

New Zealand won 10 of their 11 tests this year, including four against France. Their only defeat came at the hands of world champions and world No.1 England.

Afterwards, Black Ferns flanker Elinor Plum-King was named World Rugby XVs Breakthrough Player of the Year, while loose forward Kaipo Olsen-Baker was named Player of the Year.

World.title: Ruthless Kiwis bury Fiji to reach Rugby League World Cup semis
World.content:
NZ Kiwis have delivered a statement performance at the Rugby League World Cup, crushing Fiji 78-0 on the Gold Coast to power into the semifinals.

Boom centre Casey McLean crossed for four of their 13 tries, while winger Jamayne Isaako landed every conversion attempt, as New Zealand eclipsed the Bati in every department.

The only blot was a red card to wing Ronaldo Mulitalo for a high tackle, which left both teams to play the rest of the game with 12 players, after Fiji halfback Brandon Wakeham was also sent off for retaliation.

Fiji were expected to provide a stern test, after pushing Australia in a 36-22 defeat in Brisbane last weekend, setting up a virtual quarterfinal against New Zealand, with the losers eliminated.

However, there would be no repeat of the infamous 2017 quarterfinal, when Fiji stunned the hosts 4-2 in Wellington in one of the great tournament upsets.

The scene was set in the opening 13 minutes, as the Kiwis powered across for four tries, with half Jahrome Hughes cantering through a gaping hole to score from their very first set.

That 24-0 lead had doubled to 48-0 by halftime, with Fiji's cause not helped by the loss of experienced captain and hooker Api Korisau to a suspected broken jaw.

The opening exchanges of the second half were overshadowed by Mulitalo's tackle, which resulted in a head injury to opposite Ronald Philitoga, forcing him from the field.

Ronaldo Mulitalo checks on opposite Ronald Philitoga, after his red-carded high tackle. photosport

Both teams came together in a tense exchange, with Wakeham also shown red for throwing a punch.

New Zealand's scoring resumed soon afterwards, with McLean - part of a potent left edge - crossing twice in four minutes to add to his first-half double.

Forwards Briton Nikora and Erin Clark also scored, before fullback Keano Kini bagged his second late in the contest.

Centre Dane Gagai, captain James Fisher-Harris, Mulitalo and forward Xavier Willison also scored tries, as the Kiwis showed why they will be a handful for any side in the knockout stage.

The Bati struggled throughout the game to contain New Zealand's forwards, who produced numerous offloads and rapid play-the-balls.

Their frustration boiled over again late, when prop Jordan Miller was sin-binned for a high shot that sparked another scuffle.

Isaako landed 13 from 14 conversions in 82-16 thrashing of Cook Islands in Christchurch last weekend - a NZ test-record 38-point haul - and his record was even better this time, slotting 13 from 13.

The result means the Kiwis will advance from Group A into the semis, alongside hosts and defending champions Australia.

Their opponents will depend on the result of Sunday night's group match between unbeaten Pacific rivals Samoa and Tonga.

The Kiwis hope star fullback Kalyn Ponga will have recovered for the knockout stage of the tournament, after breaking his forearm in the opening 24-22 loss to Australia just two weeks ago.
